“Wherever the enemy has interests, in the event of aggression, they could fall within the framework of legitimate targets of the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” he said.
Akraminia also urged Qatar to step up efforts to determine the fate of three Iranian pilots missing since an Iranian air operation against a US base in Qatar on March 2.
He said two Iranian Sukhoi aircraft struck the base before being shot down on their return flight. The body of one of the four pilots, Majid Kazemi, was later recovered, while the other three remain missing.
Qatar has denied holding the three pilots, saying its search-and-rescue teams recovered the remains of one pilot but found no evidence that the others were captured.
The remarks come against the backdrop of the conflict between Iran and the US, which began on Feb. 28 with US and Israeli military strikes on Iran and subsequently expanded across the region as Tehran retaliated against US military positions.
The hostilities later drew in several regional fronts and disrupted maritime traffic, while Iran and the US eventually signed a memorandum of understanding on June 18 through Qatari and Pakistani mediation aimed at ending the fighting and setting the stage for negotiations.
Tehran has since accused Washington of failing to fully implement the memorandum, while Qatar and Pakistan have continued diplomatic efforts between the two sides.

====================================================================================================

London rollout of robotaxis delayed amid lack of guidance for firms to follow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
08:48:43 UTC
17:48:43 KST

The rollout of robotaxis on the streets of London is unlikely to happen this year, as regulatory and technical hurdles push back the ambitious schedule set out by the UK government.
Only weeks ago Uber and London-based Wayve were granted the first minicab licences in the capital to allow them to offer self-driving taxi rides to paying customers – but with a human safety driver in place, for now – and said they would start trips “later this summer” before a full public launch.
In 2025, Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, accelerated the proposed timeline for commercial trials of fully driverless taxi services by a year, announcing that they would start in the spring of this year.
However, progress has slowed in recent months and Transport for London (TfL) has still not published the guidance that companies wanting to offer services must follow to win its approval.
Last month, Christina Calderato, TfL’s director of strategy, told the London assembly’s transport committee that the transit authority would not be in a position to start accepting applications “for some time”.
She said: “I do not think we are in a rush to get [the guidelines] out. There is a huge amount of work going on behind the scenes.”
Uber and Wayve have said that more than 100,000 Londoners were on their waiting list for self-driving taxis.
They are racing against Google-owned Waymo and its Chinese equivalent, Baidu’s Apollo Go, to launch self-driving taxi services in London. Robotaxis are now available to hire in more than 20 cities across the US, China and the Middle East.
Earlier this month Zagreb became the first European city to offer autonomous rides to the general public, through Uber, but the service still has a human driver for “onboard monitoring”.
On Tuesday, Waymo announced that it plans to launch commercial operations in Munich, Germany, late next year.
Ben Loewenstein, Waymo’s head of policy and government affairs for the UK and Europe, told the Financial Times that the company was currently “working through the safety approval process” with the transport department and was waiting on TfL’s guidance to gain consent.
He added that Waymo was working towards launching a fully autonomous service “by the end of this year” but would not say whether the company would be able to offer paid rides to the general public in that timeframe.
TfL has granted 15 private hire vehicle licences to Ford Mustang Mach-E vehicles equipped with Wayve’s artificial intelligence driving software, as well as surround cameras and radar.
A TfL-licensed private hire driver will sit in the driver’s seat during trips to intervene if necessary, although the software is expected to control the car.
Uber and Wayve plan to launch small-scale commercial pilots with a driver behind the wheel soon.
For its fully driverless launch Wayve plans to switch to a new Nissan Leaf vehicle that is still in production and is due to launch later this year.
Alex Kendall, Wayve’s chief executive, said the company never claimed it would have a fully driverless operation this year.
“I don’t want to put a timeline on it because we want to make sure we pass through [the regulatory process],” he told the FT. “This work is continuing at pace. London is a significant step up in complexity compared to Phoenix or San Francisco.”
Baidu only began testing vehicles in London at the end of last month and has said it plans to launch public rides next year.
Operating taxis without a driver requires approval via a new process, known as an automated passenger services permit, with the government’s Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency. So far, no vehicles have been approved by the DVSA.
TfL was contacted for comment.

MINSK, 26 August (BelTA) - Approximately 93% of large families have already received one-off government back-to-school financial assistance, the press service of the Labor and Social Protection Ministry told BelTA.
The amount of the one-off payment is Br159.11 per school-age child in the family. Across all regions of the country, over 104,000 large families have already received the assistance, covering 210,000 children. The total amount paid out came to Br33.4 million.
The Labor and Social Protection Ministry also recalled that support for families with school-age children is provided through state-targeted social assistance programs. Nearly 1,000 families have already received such aid, covering 3,000 children, to the total amount of Br2.2 million.
In addition, employees raising schoolchildren may receive assistance at their workplace, in line with collective work agreements and the employee’s local regulations. In July and August charitable campaigns are launched across the country by the territorial social service centers, foundations, and public associations such as School Backpack, Get Your Child Ready for School, To School with a Smile and First-Grader’s Backpack.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has awarded his country’s Order of Freedom to Elon Musk Wednesday, amid efforts to persuade Musk to expand access to his Starlink network.

The Order of Freedom is often awarded to foreign leaders for their support for Ukraine — recent recipients include French President Emmanuel Macron, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda.

Sliman Mansour obituary: The legacy of a Palestinian art pioneer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
08:45:00 UTC
17:45:00 KST

Breadcrumb
Sliman Mansour obituary: Remembering the Palestinian artist behind a nation's visual memory
A major figure in Palestinian art, renowned artist Sliman Mansour has died aged 79, after his family said he had been in critical condition. The cause of death has not been disclosed.
Said to have “lived longer than the entity of Israel itself,” Sliman spent more than half a century building a body of work rooted in Palestine, documenting its landscapes, people and traditions while reflecting the political realities that have shaped Palestinian life.
Over the course of his career, his paintings were reproduced and circulated far beyond galleries, becoming familiar to Palestinians in the homeland and across the diaspora. He became regarded as the "artist of the Intifada" and went on to gain international recognition, establishing himself as one of the leading figures in modern Palestinian art.
For those who knew him personally, however, his death was not only the loss of an important artist, but also the loss of a father.
Following his death, Sliman's family shared a statement on his Instagram account, remembering him not only for the legacy he left behind but for the love and sense of home he gave his family.
"The final chapter has been written.
"With hearts heavy beyond words, we share that our beloved father has passed away.
"To the world, he leaves behind a life filled with beauty, memory, and a legacy that will continue to live through all those he touched. But to us, we lost a father, our source of love, strength and home.
"Though his journey in this world has come to an end, his spirit, his work, and his love will remain with us always.
"May he rest in eternal peace, surrounded by the light and beauty he gave so generously to this world," the statement said.
As tributes continue to emerge following his death, The New Arab looks back at the life, work and evolution of an artist whose paintings became part of the visual record of modern Palestine.
Early days
Sliman's interest in art began when he was still a child, long before he became one of Palestine's most recognised artists.
Born in Birzeit, near Ramallah, in 1947, Sliman was the fourth of six children. His father died when he was four, and his mother later sent him and his siblings to a Lutheran boarding school for orphans in Bethlehem. It was there that a German teacher, Felix Theis, noticed Sliman's ability and encouraged him to pursue drawing and painting.
That early encouragement stayed with Sliman as he grew older and helped set him on the path towards becoming a professional artist.
He studied art at the Bezalel Art Academy in West Jerusalem from 1967 to 1970, before beginning a career that would make him one of the leading figures in Palestinian art.
As his work developed, Sliman drew on a wide range of influences. He looked to the region's ancient civilisations, including the Canaanites, Egyptians and Assyrians, while also taking inspiration from Islamic and Arab artistic traditions.
Calligraphy and geometric forms, in particular, became important elements in his work.
His strongest connection, however, remained with the Palestinian landscape and the life he knew growing up in Birzeit, a focus that became particularly significant in the 1970s as he emerged alongside a generation of Palestinian artists, writers and poets who turned to culture to preserve their connection to their homeland, history, memories and traditions amid continued displacement and political unrest.
Sliman's reputation continued to grow, with his work eventually exhibited across the Arab world and internationally. His paintings entered museums and private collections around the world, and he received numerous awards for his contribution to Palestinian and Arab culture.
His work gradually became more political over the years, and during the First Intifada, he helped set up the New Visions group with fellow Palestinian artists Vera Tamari, Tayseer Barakat and Nabil Anani to reflect the experiences of Palestinians and the injustices faced under Israeli occupation.
After Palestinian artists stopped using Israeli-made art materials, the group began experimenting with mud, straw, wood, leather, henna and natural dyes, with Sliman seeing this shift as part of a wider effort to create art rooted in Palestinian life.
In his own words, Sliman said the experience brought together the work of Palestinian artists who came after the Nakba and a younger generation keeping that tradition alive.
From olive trees to Jerusalem
The land of Palestine was one of the most important subjects Sliman returned to throughout his career.
Olive trees, stone terraces and Palestinian villages appeared again and again, carrying ideas of home, belonging and memory. This can be seen in Olive Harvest (1988), which depicts a Palestinian man and woman in traditional clothing gathering olives, placing everyday rural life at the centre of the painting.
Women were another recurring presence. Sliman often depicted them in traditional embroidered clothing, or tatreez, giving them a strong and grounded presence. Through these figures, he explored ideas of motherhood, resilience, cultural identity, and intergenerational connection.
Mother and Child (2009) is one of the works that reflects this theme, placing the relationship between family and Palestinian identity at its centre.
Other familiar symbols also found their way into Sliman’s paintings. Orange trees and Jerusalem became part of a visual language that allowed recognisable details of Palestinian life to carry wider meanings of home and belonging.
One example is Lost Sea II (2015), which draws on these familiar elements while reflecting the deeper emotions attached to place and memory.
Yet among all of Sliman’s paintings, one painting would become particularly powerful and widely recognised: Jamal al-Mahamel (Camel of Hardships).
The painting depicts an elderly porter carrying Jerusalem on his back, making the city feel like a weight he can physically carry.
Over time, the image became associated with Palestinian memory, longing and endurance and was reproduced widely, from posters to homes and shops.
Sliman remembered
Reflecting on Sliman’s legacy, Barjeel Art Foundation founder Sultan Sooud Al-Qassemi paid tribute to him following his death, remembering how widely his work had come to be recognised.
"Sliman's figurative style was immediately recognised by all Palestinians and was adapted into posters, t-shirts, tattoos and mobile phone wallpapers. When Palestinians wanted an image of love, life, or resilience, they were very likely to opt for a painting by Sliman. We lost a giant of modern Arab art,” Al-Qassemi shared.
"Sliman captured a universal Palestinian spirit. His artworks are also among the most recognisable in the Arab world, even to people who aren't very interested in or knowledgeable about art.
"Sliman was part of a group of Palestinian artists who, in the wake of the First Intifada of the 1980s, defied Israeli restrictions on Palestinian life by adapting the materials they used to make art, switching from oil on canvas to locally sourced materials. He became known for his works using mud and straw," he added.
"Using earth to make art was for Sliman also a reflection of Palestinian connectedness to their homeland. Sliman worked from within Palestine and witnessed the harshness of the occupation on a daily basis. His paintings captured this reality, but more importantly, they offered symbols of perseverance to all Palestinians.
"Although Sliman was well known throughout his career, social media brought his work and legacy to a new generation of Palestinians and Arabs. An entire generation of young Palestinian artists was shaped by his legacy, and his work will live on through the countless artworks he produced throughout his career.
"His most famous painting, Camel of Burdens, has been reproduced countless times, whether as a poster or through recreations by other artists. The painting represents the burdens Palestinians carry with them, whether they are in Palestine or in the diaspora.
"For many Arabs, Sliman was able to convey the wide range of emotions we felt towards Palestine, from joy to sadness. As a Palestinian who lived and practised in Palestine, his works were lost, destroyed and confiscated by Israeli authorities, and yet he persisted nonetheless.
"In recent years, his work also achieved significant commercial success, with his paintings selling for hundreds of thousands of dollars at auction. Sliman also drew from both Christian and Islamic heritage in his artwork."
That ability to create paintings that stayed with people was part of what made Sliman so influential among younger Palestinian artists, many of whom came to his work through images that had already become familiar parts of Palestinian life.
Palestinian-American artist Saj Issa had hoped to meet Sliman for years. Whenever she visited Palestine, she would message him about coming to see him, but his declining health meant he eventually stopped receiving visitors.
Her connection to his work, however, began much earlier, through a painting hanging in a neighbour's home in Beitin. The scene was an olive grove, which reminded her of the one near her grandfather’s home.
"The tree is synonymous with Palestinian identity, and Sliman was one of the pioneers in giving Palestinians a visual language and motifs to grasp onto," Issa told The New Arab.
That sense of connection was also evident in the way Sliman portrayed Palestinian women, Issa said, particularly in their relationship with the land and the work they did within their families and communities.
"His paintings of Palestinian women showed them at their best: tending to our land, adorned with the fruits of their labour, and as breeders of life," she said.
While Sliman's use of colour has sometimes been described as having a Fauvist influence, Issa said his paintings also brought back vivid memories of her own childhood in Palestine.
"I feel as if I’m experiencing the loss of my own grandparent as he transitions into the next life, because I’m going to miss a wise storyteller of an idealised Palestine very dearly," she shared.
Even when Sliman turned to pain and suffering, Issa said, there was a sense of nostalgia in his imagery that reflected the resilience passed down through Palestinian generations.
Palestinian artist Rasha Eleyan also remembers Sliman's work from childhood, when she first encountered one of his most famous paintings.
She recalls seeing Jamal al-Mahamel on posters in people's homes and shops, an image so widely known that its meaning was understood even outside art circles.
“To me, that artwork embodied our struggle,” Eleyan tells The New Arab. "It was such a powerful and popular image that everyone seemed to know it."
Her memories of Sliman went beyond his paintings. He was a close friend of her father, Nasr Abdelaziz, and later of her mother, and Eleyan remembers him as generous with his time and advice.
“I will always remember his humility and how generous he was with his advice whenever I asked for it,” she said.
“He will be deeply missed, but a great artist never dies.”
Eleyan reflects on how Jamal al-Mahamel has taken on a different meaning for her with age, but its ability to speak to Palestinians has not faded. She believes its message will continue to resonate with generations to come.
Sliman's influence as both an artist and teacher is echoed by Palestinian visual artist and calligrapher Alaziz Atef, who described his death as a deeply personal loss.
"He was my extraordinary teacher, the teacher no school ever assigned to me and whose lectures no university required me to attend. He was the teacher I chose to seek out because I wanted him to teach me," Atef tells The New Arab.
"He placed the light of art in my eyes, ignited an intellectual fire in my mind and planted deep within my heart a profound reverence for Palestine and for humanity. Sliman was not merely an artist whose mastery of colour or captivating painting style could astonish you," Atef adds.
"He possessed an exceptional artistic mind, with a rare depth of thought and vision. I spent five years with him, five days a week, eight hours a day and often more. That is why this loss feels so immense and so deeply personal. I have lost the teacher who taught me what a painting truly means. And, in return, I taught him what it meant to have a devoted student and a close friend.
"Over time, our relationship grew to the point where I would offer my thoughts on his paintings, and nothing made me happier than when he was persuaded by something I had said and allowed my idea to find its way into his work," Atef continues.
“What we have lost is immense: a human loss, an Arab loss and a Palestinian loss. Yet today, I grieve for myself even more than I grieve for Palestine. Palestine will always give birth to creators, as it has done before — giving us Sliman Mansour, Mahmoud Darwish and Ghassan Kanafani."
As for Palestinian artist Bashar Alhroub, he remembered Mansour not only as a major figure in Palestinian art, but also as a friend, colleague and mentor whose influence extended across generations of artists: "Sliman Mansour was much more to me than simply a major figure in the history of Palestinian art. He was a friend, a colleague, and an artist whose presence had a profound impact on generations of Palestinian artists, including myself. I will always remember him not only through his works and images, which have become icons of Palestinian visual memory, but also through his humanity, humility and deep connection to Palestine and its people.
"The significance of Sliman’s practice lies in his ability to transform the Palestinian experience, with all its loss, displacement, resilience and sense of belonging, into a visual language that reached far beyond Palestine. His images of the land, its people, Jerusalem and exile have become part of our collective visual memory. Through his practice, he demonstrated the power of art to preserve identity and memory in the face of attempts at erasure," Alhroub tells The New Arab.
"I believe Sliman’s legacy for future generations of artists lies in this profound commitment to place and history, and in his ability to be deeply Palestinian while speaking to a universal human experience. He taught us that artistic practice need not be separated from an artist's responsibility to society and collective memory," Alhroub adds.
"Sliman Mansour's work will remain an essential part of Palestine's visual history, and his legacy will continue to live through the memory and practice of generations of artists. His passing is not only a profound loss for Palestinian art and culture, but also a great loss for Arab art. His artistic and human presence extended far beyond Palestine and left a lasting impact on the wider Arab art world."
Zainab Mehdi is a British Iraqi journalist and the Associate Features Editor at The New Arab. She holds a BSc in Modern History and International Relations from the University of Essex and an MA in Near and Middle Eastern Studies from SOAS

U.S. military attacks alleged drug-smuggling boat in Caribbean, killing 4 people
Washington — The U.S. military attacked a boat suspected of being used to smuggle drugs in the Caribbean Sea on Tuesday, killing four people, as the Trump administration continues its monthslong campaign against alleged traffickers in Latin America.
The latest attack brings the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the U.S. military to at least 227 in 68 strikes since the Trump administration began targeting those it calls "narcoterrorists" almost a year ago. As with most of the military's statements on strikes in the eastern Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea, U.S. Southern Command said it targeted the alleged drug traffickers along known smuggling routes.
The military didn't provide evidence that the vessel was ferrying drugs, but said on X that "confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking." A video in that same post on X showed an image of what appeared to be a moving boat followed by a flash.
Tuesday's strike came just two days after the U.S. military carried out a strike on a vessel in the eastern Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of trafficking drugs. That action came after a pause of more than two months in the U.S. campaign against alleged smugglers.
The Trump administration is pursuing deals with allied nations to extend its offensive to land across multiple Latin American countries. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said during a visit to Panama this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to let the U.S. carry out joint military operations against criminal groups on their soil. Guatemala denied reaching such a deal. Ecuador launched similar missions with the U.S. in March.
President Trump has said the U.S. is in "armed conflict" with cartels in Latin America and has justified the attacks as a necessary escalation to stem the flow of drugs into the United States and fatal overdoses claiming American lives. But his administration has offered little evidence to support its claims of killing smugglers.

Israeli settlement sanctions plan deepens divisions within UK Labour Party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
08:36:18 UTC
17:36:18 KST

Ahmet Gencturk
26 August 2026•Update: 26 August 2026
- Prime Minister Andy Burnham reportedly considering tougher measures in response to Israel’s E1 project
 
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s plans to impose tougher sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank have deepened divisions within the governing Labour Party, local media reported Tuesday.
More than 140 Labour lawmakers, roughly a third of the parliamentary party, have signed a letter calling on the government to ban trade with Israeli settlements, according to The Times.
Supporters are also preparing to submit a motion at Labour’s annual conference next month. Burnham is expected to announce his position before the gathering to prevent the issue from overshadowing his first party conference as leader.
Labour Friends of Israel, however, warned that distinguishing settlement products from other Israeli goods would be “practically impossible” and that the measure could become a de facto boycott of Israel.
The group said it strongly opposed Israeli settlements and supported “calibrated” action against extremist settlers and settler organizations, but argued that a trade ban could harm Britain’s national interests, the British Jewish community, and Palestinian workers.
Burnham wants Britain to adopt a “far more robust” stance than his predecessor, Keir Starmer, in response to Israel’s plans to construct around 1,200 additional settler homes, the newspaper reported, citing a senior government source.
The measures under consideration reportedly include a ban on trade with Israeli settlements and sanctions against individuals involved in settlement activity.
Officials have also warned of difficulties in separating products originating in settlements from those produced within Israel’s internationally recognized borders. They said legitimate Israeli businesses and Palestinian companies operating in the occupied territories could also be affected.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said Israel’s E1 settlement project would effectively divide the occupied West Bank and eliminate prospects for a two-state solution.
The Israeli government recently issued construction tenders for the project, drawing condemnation from Britain and several other countries.
In a joint statement last week, international leaders said the E1 project would “drive a wedge through the West Bank,” undermine Palestinian territorial continuity, and further diminish prospects for a two-state solution.

FACTBOX: Aftermath of Ukrainian drone attack on Russian regions, 426 neutralized UAVs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
08:34:02 UTC
17:34:02 KST

MOSCOW, August 26. /TASS/. On-duty air defenses intercepted and destroyed 426 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over Russian regions overnight, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
The drone attack caused a fire at a Wildberries e-commerce logistics center in Kotovsk, Tambov Region, that covered more than 100,000 square meters.
Two people were killed after a private home caught fire following a drone crash in the Lipetsk Region.
TASS has compiled key information on the attack’s aftermath.
Scale
- Air defense systems detected and destroyed a total of 426 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles over Russian regions between 8:00 p.m. Moscow time (5:00 p.m. GMT) on August 25 and 7:00 a.m. Moscow time (4:00 a.m. GMT) on August 26, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
- According to the Defense Ministry, drones were brought down over the Belgorod, Bryansk, Kursk, Oryol, Kaluga, Tula, Lipetsk, Voronezh, Tambov, Ryazan, Nizhny Novgorod, Volgograd and Rostov regions, the Moscow Region, the Krasnodar Region and the Republic of Crimea.
- Local authorities issued drone danger alerts from midnight to 8:00 a.m. Moscow time (5:00 a.m. GMT) in 11 Russian regions across three federal districts, according to TASS calculations.
- Governor Andrey Klychkov said 43 drones were destroyed over the Oryol Region overnight.
- About 40 Ukrainian drones were downed in Taganrog and seven districts of the Rostov Region overnight, Governor Yury Slyusar said.
- Governor Vladislav Shapsha reported that 27 drones were destroyed over the Kaluga Region overnight.
- Another 27 drones were detected and destroyed over Voronezh and eight districts of the region, Governor Alexander Gusev said.
- Tula Region Governor Dmitry Milyaev reported the destruction of eight Ukrainian drones.
Attack on Wildberries warehouse in Tambov Region
- The town of Kotovsk came under a massive Ukrainian attack overnight on Wednesday, Tambov Region Governor Yevgeny Pervyshov said.
- The drone strikes caused a fire at a Wildberries logistics center.
- The fire spread across more than 100,000 square meters, Pervyshov said.
- Earlier reports put the fire area at 40,000 square meters.
- Staff evacuated the facility immediately after the alarm sounded, which saved lives and prevented injuries, Pervyshov added.
- Preliminary reports indicate that a Wildberries employee suffered a concussion from the blast wave.
- The Tambov Region prosecutor’s office is overseeing the protection of citizens’ rights following the Ukrainian drone attack on Kotovsk, the agency’s press service said.
Aftermath
- A Ukrainian drone crash caused a house to catch fire at one of the cottage communities in the Tambov Region, Pervyshov said.
- A man and a woman suffered moderate injuries in a Ukrainian drone attack in a suburb of Voronezh, a city in central Russia, and received hospital treatment, Gusev said.
- The drone attack also set three outbuildings on fire in another district of Voronezh, but firefighters quickly put out the blaze.
- A man was injured when drone debris fell in the Tula Region, Milyaev said.
- A drone crash caused a private home to catch fire in the Lipetsk municipal district in western Russia, Governor Igor Artamonov said.
- A man and a 14-year-old child died in the fire.
- Two women were hospitalized and received all necessary medical care.
- The prosecutor’s office is overseeing the protection of victims’ rights following the attack near Lipetsk, its press service said.

DOHA, August 26. /TASS/. Negotiations to end the conflict between Iran and the US have reached an impasse, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty stated.
"There is a problem, and as you know, there is currently neither peace nor war," he told the Emirati newspaper The National. The top diplomat added that the situation appears to be at an impasse.
Abdelatty also emphasized that Egypt "continues to maintain contact" with Tehran and advocates for a swift end to the conflict based on an agreement that would include provisions on the nuclear program, the lifting of US sanctions, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and a ceasefire.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran, with Islamabad acting as mediator, signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, in the early morning hours of July 8, the US resumed large-scale strikes against Iran, accusing it of violating the terms of the agreements reached on the Strait of Hormuz.

Poland reveals President Nawrocki's wishes for Ukraine on Independence Day
Polish President Karol Nawrocki sent his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy a congratulatory letter to mark the 35th anniversary of the restoration of Ukraine's independence, wishing Ukraine victory in the war.
Source: Marcin Przydacz, Head of the Polish President's International Policy Bureau, in an interview with RMF24, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Przydacz said Nawrocki had sent Zelenskyy a letter on the occasion of Ukraine's Independence Day in which he mentioned "points of tension" in the relations between the two countries.
Quote from Przydacz: "In the letter, the president essentially wished Ukraine victory in the war against Russia, while noting that there are a number of points of tension that we would like to gradually reduce... The most important thing is that Poland values good-neighbourly relations. They must be based on certain fundamental principles, and one of those principles is historical truth."
Details: Przydacz also said that dialogue between the Ukrainian and Polish presidential offices is continuing. However, there are currently no plans for Karol Nawrocki to visit the Ukrainian capital.
While on the subject of relations with Kyiv, Przydacz also referred to the law establishing Ukraine's National Pantheon. He was critical of the initiative.
Quote: "I believe this will not help improve relations not only with Poland, but also with other countries and Western Europe as a whole. If I were in the Ukrainians' position, I would not insult the historical memory of victims or glorify criminals. If Ukraine does this, it must expect those actions to have negative consequences."
Background:
- Earlier, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk congratulated Ukraine on the 35th anniversary of its independence.
- Polish President Karol Nawrocki has previously said that he believes support for Kyiv in its fight against Russian aggression should continue, as Ukraine's success is in Poland's strategic interests.

India and China to continue to seek political settlement of border issue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
08:31:52 UTC
17:31:52 KST

India and China to continue to seek political settlement of border issue
India and China agreed to continue to seek a political settlement of their border dispute in talks between top officials held in Beijing on Tuesday.
Indian National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, the designated special representatives for the border talks mechanism, “had a candid and in-depth exchange of views on the India-China boundary question, and agreed to continue their work in seeking a political settlement of the boundary question in the context of their overall and long-term interests,” the Indian Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
It said the two sides expressed satisfaction at the steady resumption of people-to-people and cross-border exchanges, including the ongoing Kailash Manasarovar pilgrimage and resumption of border trade through the Himalayan passes.
The special representatives noted the progress made in implementing the consensus reached between Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Kazan, Russia on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in October 2024, and again in Tianjin, China in August 2025 on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit.
ICYMI: Doval, Wang Yi Hold 25th Round Of India-China Boundary Talks 
New Delhi and Beijing agreed to continue working towards a “fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable” settlement of their boundary question, while stressing the importance of maintaining peace along the border.… pic.twitter.com/L0jbSFQcjd
Kazan was the first formal bilateral meeting between Modi and Xi in four years, since a skirmish in the Ladakh region of the Himalayas in 2020 left 20 Indian soldiers and at least four Chinese soldiers dead.
At Kazan, Modi and Xi agreed to use the special representatives mechanism and foreign minister dialogues to seek solutions to the border question and maintain peace in border areas.
The Beijing talks were held under the strategic guidance of Modi and Xi and in a constructive and forward-looking spirit, the statement said, adding that India highlighted the importance of maintaining peace and tranquility in the border areas for the continued development and progress of bilateral relations.
Doval and Wang also discussed bilateral, regional, and international issues of mutual interest, as the two neighbors prepare for this year’s SCO summit next week in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan and the BRICS summit next month in New Delhi.
Xi is expected to attend the BRICS meeting with a large delegation, according to reports.
Doval also called on Chinese Vice President Han Zheng before the special representative talks.

China’s multilateral pitch is finding an audience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
08:30:07 UTC
17:30:07 KST

As Washington increasingly turns away from the multilateral order it once helped build, Beijing is emerging as an advocate of international cooperation and 
rules-based stability
. For some, the real surprise is that China’s rise is not challenging the world order but that its interests align with preserving it.
When I met Foreign Minister Wang Yi in the corridor of a congress centre in Myanmar, he had just finished addressing more than 50 foreign ministers, emphasising the need for a multilateral, cooperative approach to our shared future. It was 2017, and the message was what you would expect in a ceremonial speech. Few in that hall could have imagined that less than a decade later, serious Western leaders would regard China as one of the foremost advocates of the international order.
The years that have passed since then have left the world more volatile than it has been in decades, and the behaviour of its strongest actor has not worked in favour of stability. The United States, the chief architect of the post-war order and once the proud protector of international law, has been showing signs of losing its edge in more areas than it can peacefully accept. Washington’s 
increasingly erratic behaviour
 on the international scene has been met with disbelief by even its allies.
There is a vacuum forming in global leadership. US withdrawals from a 
multitude of international organisations
 and US President Donald Trump’s tariff war against practically half the world made this obvious lately. The US is not isolating itself – it is as active internationally as ever. But instead of building coalitions and upholding well-established standards, it acts without any multilateral constraint, disintegrating said standards across the board.
While Europe is weighed down by structural problems and its 
lack of a common voice
, the Global South is gaining momentum. Still, China is not rushing to take the vacated spot of a global hegemon.
On the contrary, it is calling for an end to this world order that has long been defined by domination. In Beijing’s view, the future is written through multilateral cooperation, respect for the international legal order and finding win-win solutions to all major global dilemmas.

In Donetsk region, the occupiers announced an early start to the pseudo-elections to the Russian State Duma
Kyiv • UNN
The occupation "authorities" of Donetsk region announced early voting for the Russian State Duma starting on August 30. The Center for Countering Disinformation called this preparation for falsifications.
The occupation "authorities" in the seized territory of Donetsk region announced that the pseudo-voting for the State Duma of the Russian Federation will begin on August 30 - 21 days before the official election date. Security and allegedly concern for the population are cited as the reason. This is reported by the Center for Countering Disinformation of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine, reports UNN.
Details
According to the CCD, the occupation "authorities" of Donetsk region announced that the pseudo-elections to the State Duma of the Russian Federation in the temporarily occupied territories will begin on August 30 - 21 days before the official date. Local representatives of the occupation "authorities" explain the early start of voting by "security considerations and the need to take care of the population."
In reality, the occupation "authorities" seek to create more convenient conditions for the uncontrolled stuffing of ballots and the use of other mechanisms to falsify the results of the "expression of will." Russian propaganda, creating the illusion of massive public support for the occupation, is attempting in this way to legitimize it. However, organizing such "elections" in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine violates the norms of international law, and their results are legally null and void
We remind you
Russia plans illegal elections to the State Duma in the occupied territories of Ukraine, ensuring turnout of more than 65–70% and support for "United Russia" of at least 70%. Andrii Kovalenko, head of the Center for Countering Disinformation of the National Security and Defense Council, said that this is being done to legitimize the occupation.

According to the regional department of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine, fires broke out in different parts of the city overnight after enemy drones struck their targets. Petition to Cabinet on regulation of psychological counseling collects only 32 votes
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
11:27:10 EEST
17:27:10 KST

A petition on the website of the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine calling for the introduction of legislative regulation of psychological counseling and psychotherapeutic practice in Ukraine has failed to gather the required number of votes for consideration.
According to the platform on the government website, the petition was submitted on May 25 and as of August 26 has collected only 32 votes out of the 25,000 required.
"In Ukraine, the number of individuals providing psychological consultations, psychotherapeutic services, and working with people’s mental state without proper specialized education, clinical training, supervision, and professional responsibility is growing rapidly," the petition said.
The author of the petition states that currently there is effectively no clear state regulation regarding: the use of professional titles "psychologist," "psychotherapist," "consulting psychologist," "therapist"; the activities of individuals working with psychological trauma and mental health of the population; and liability for providing psychological services without proper qualifications.
In her view, because of this, Ukrainian citizens may become victims of unprofessional help, psychological manipulation, imposition of dangerous practices, and pseudotherapy by individuals who: have completed only short-term courses; lack a basic psychological education; have not undergone clinical practice; lack supervision and ethical control; and actually exert psychological influence without proper professional training.
The author emphasizes that practice without appropriate qualifications is especially dangerous when working with: people in crisis states; military personnel and veterans; children and adolescents; victims of violence; people with PTSD; depressive and anxiety disorders; people with suicidal ideation; and persons who have experienced loss, occupation, and the consequences of war.
She states that in most European countries, psychological and psychotherapeutic practice is regulated by law: education requirements exist; professional certification; ethical standards; professional liability; and client protection mechanisms.
"At the same time, in Ukraine, anyone can position themselves as a ‘psychologist’ or ‘therapist,’ actively promote their services on social networks, and work with vulnerable people without proper competence verification," according to the petition.
In this regard, the author requests: drafting and adopting legislative norms regarding the regulation of psychological and psychotherapeutic practice in Ukraine; establishing clear qualification requirements for individuals entitled to provide psychological and psychotherapeutic services; legislatively regulating the use of professional titles: psychologist, psychotherapist, consulting psychologist, clinical psychologist; creating a state or official professional registry of certified specialists; establishing liability for misleading citizens through the unauthorized use of professional titles and the provision of psychological services without proper qualifications; and legislatively separating the concepts of: psychologist; psychotherapist; coach; consultant; mentor; personal development trainer.

Rare saker falcon attracts hundreds of twitchers to West Flemish Polders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
08:26:12 UTC
17:26:12 KST

Since last Thursday, hundreds of birdwatchers have been flocking to the polders of Uitkerke in the seaside resort of Blankenberge. A rare saker falcon has been spotted. The saker falcon is a species of large falcon that normally lives in Eastern Europe and Asia. According to Frank De Scheemaeker of the Mergus birdwatching group, the bird accidentally strayed off course and has remained in the polders, low-lying land behind the coastline that is protected by a dike, because plenty of food is present.
The saker falcon is normally found only in Asia and Eastern Europe, in countries such as Romania and Bulgaria. But even there, the species is becoming increasingly rare because it is under threat. Bird experts estimate that there are now only around 500 breeding pairs left.
The fact that the bird has now also been spotted in Flanders is exceptional news, which since last week has been attracting around a hundred birdwatchers to the polders of Uitkerke every day.
A rare, impressive bird
If you want to see the bird, you’ll have to make a bit of an effort, says Frank De Scheemaeker of the Mergus birdwatching group. “It’s not like a heron or a wader that just sits obediently on a puddle,” he explains. “The saker falcon flies around the wider area. You’ll easily have to spend a whole day out in the field to stand a chance of spotting it. I’ve been out looking for it twice so far without success.”
Twitchers who are patient will be richly rewarded, says De Scheemaeker. “Not only is it a rare bird, but it is also very impressive. Measuring 55 centimetres in length and with a wingspan of up to 1.30 metres, it is much larger than the falcons we normally see in Flanders. It is not clear whether it is a male or a female. Females are always larger than males, but it is still a young bird that is probably not yet fully grown.”
Polders provide the perfect habitat
It is uncertain how the saker falcon ended up in Uitkerke. “It probably strayed off course by accident and decided to stay in the polders for a while,” says De Scheemaeker. “It is, after all, an ideal habitat: an open landscape with plenty of mice and other small mammals.”
De Scheemaeker and other bird experts expect the falcon to remain in the polders for a few more weeks due to the abundant food supply. After that, it is likely to continue its migration via France, in the hope that it will find its way back to Romania or Bulgaria. “As the bird is not ringed, we will never know for certain whether that will happen. However, previous ringing records of other bird species have shown that some stray birds do eventually return to their original habitat.”

Breaking: Macquarie Group dumps KPMG from audit contract
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
08:24:41 UTC
17:24:41 KST

Macquarie Group has announced it will drop KPMG as an auditor, amid an ongoing scandal relating to its handling of confidential information.
Macquarie announced on Wednesday afternoon that its board held concerns over the firm's auditing practices, amid ongoing scrutiny of KPMG.
"The decision follows continued scrutiny of KPMG Australia's audit practice, including information exposed by the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Corporations and Financial Services," the statement said.
"It also follows Macquarie's formal enquiries of KPMG to consider its capacity to deliver the audit, as well as the nature and impact of ongoing issues at KPMG Australia."
The board said it would instead recommend incumbent auditor PwC auditor at the company's annual general meeting.
KPMG also released a statement acknowledging the decision.
"While disappointed by the outcome, KPMG respects the decision taken by Macquarie," the statement read.
KPMG chief executive John Sams said Macquarie's announcement was "a clear reminder that the consequences of our past failings are real".
"Rebuilding trust will require sustained action, transparency and time. I am committed to leading this change with honesty, transparency and urgency," he said.
Whistleblower raised concerns 'through the appropriate channels'
KPMG has faced scrutiny over the alleged misuse of client data and misconduct after a whistleblower brought their complaints forward in 2024.
Public documents released by the parliamentary committee, shared with the whistleblower's consent, detail the nature of the allegations, including claims the firm mishandled the whistleblower's initial complaints.
The whistleblower told the committee said they attempted to address the issues with the KPMG partners, the head of audit, senior leadership and independent directors, before reaching out to KPMG International's whistleblower hotline and global leadership.
They ultimately turned to ASIC and Senator Deborah O'Neill, which triggered the parliamentary inquiry.
Among the more serious allegations were claims KPMG had stored confidential board papers and "used in the pursuit of major audit tenders," the statement read.
The whistleblower told the committee these were not "minor employment matters" and further claimed in one instance partners offered access to clients internal audit papers along to with a Telstra-issued laptop.
The next public hearing is slated for September 4, 2026, in Sydney.

About 400,000 oysters stolen from Australian farm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
08:21:51 UTC
17:21:51 KST

Faisal Mahmud
26 August 2026•Update: 26 August 2026
Australian police have launched an investigation after about 400,000 juvenile oysters were stolen from aquaculture leases on the New South Wales Mid North Coast, local media reported Wednesday.
Some 320 aquaculture bags containing the oysters were taken from Latitude 31 Oysters’ property at Scotts Creek on Oxley Island, according to ABC News.
Farm owner Ryan Freeman discovered the theft Tuesday morning when he visited the leases in the Manning River near Old Bar to prepare the oysters for the Christmas season.
“We noticed our floating gear and tumblers were missing,” Freeman said.
Police estimated the oysters’ value at approximately 350,000 Australian dollars ($233,000), while Freeman said the stolen stock and equipment could be worth as much as 400,000 AUD ($266,000).
Around 80% of the stolen oysters had been intended for sale during Christmas, when the business typically sells between 35,000 and 40,000 dozen oysters, he added.
Freeman said the thieves may have targeted the stock because it was approaching marketable size and could be sold during the festive season.
The theft wiped out roughly one-third of the farm’s livestock, with insufficient time remaining to secure replacement stock.
Police urged anyone with relevant information or surveillance footage to contact investigators.

Son of Uganda's president says he will stand for top job in 2031
NAIROBI, Aug 26 - Uganda's military chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of the country's long-ruling President Yoweri Museveni, said he would run for president in 2031.
Kainerugaba, 52, has long been touted as a possible successor to his ageing father and is well known for his fiery social media posts including threats to behead the leading opposition leader Bobi Wine.
He played a key role in securing his father's re-election in the last polls in January by ordering a crackdown on opponents and cutting the internet.
"I will stand for the highest office in the land in 2031. And we will win by the grace of Almighty God," Kainerugaba said in one of a series of posts on the X platform late on Tuesday.
"With my great father, Mzee's, support I will get 90% in the elections in 2031," he added using an honorific reference to his 81-year-old father.
Kainerugaba, who leads a political pressure group called the Patriotic League of Uganda, had previously declared he would stand in the last election in January but ultimately backed out.
Museveni, who heads the ruling National Resistance Movement, has ruled Uganda since 1986 and critics have accused his government of a range of human rights violations including torture, kidnappings and arbitrary detentions. The government denies the allegations.
The country's main opposition leader, Bobi Wine, fled to the U.S. earlier this year, saying he feared for his life. Another veteran opposition figure, Kizza Besigye, has been in prison since 2024 and is on trial for treason.
When asked if Museveni would seek another term, government spokesman Alan Kasujja told Reuters, "as has been the case over the years, President Museveni and the party he leads will make that decision when the time comes." REUTERS

Trump’s Korean gambit exposes a shifting East Asian order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
08:18:55 UTC
17:18:55 KST

Trump’s Korean gambit exposes a shifting East Asian order
Trump’s transactional approach is deepening uncertainty over US commitments and accelerating regional recalculation.
When President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to cut the annual United States-South Korea Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS) military exercise planned for mid-August from 11 days to five, he laid bare the transactional logic of his approach to East Asia. The move blindsided Seoul and drew a calculated rebuff from Pyongyang, underscoring how growing doubts about the US defence umbrella are reshaping strategic calculations across the region.
Trump framed the reduction as a goodwill gesture towards Kim Jong Un, whom he described as a leader he “knows very well” and with whom he has a “very good relationship”. He claimed the drills sent a “totally inappropriate and hostile” signal to Pyongyang and linked the decision directly to Seoul’s refusal to join the US war effort in Iran, declaring that America “can’t go around and protect all of these countries, especially when they’re not there to help us”.
Pyongyang’s response to Trump’s overture was carefully calibrated. Kim Yo Jong, Kim Jong Un’s sister, stated she was “unaware” of any communication between the two leaders, contradicting Trump’s claim of a “very positive” exchange. Yet she reaffirmed her brother’s “personally good memories and feelings” towards the US president, signalling that Pyongyang remains open to engagement, but on very different terms: Washington would have to accept North Korea as a nuclear-armed state and abandon what Pyongyang calls its “hostile” policy. Those demands remain fundamentally at odds with Washington’s insistence on complete denuclearisation, raising the prospect that any November meeting could amount to little more than political theatre unless one side changes its position.
China’s response to the renewed prospect of US-North Korea engagement was more restrained, but no less revealing. Beijing was more circumspect about the prospect. Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Lin Jian declined to comment on a possible Trump-Kim meeting. China’s broader position, however, emerged more clearly when Foreign Minister Wang Yi visited Seoul. He urged South Korea to pursue“genuine strategic autonomy” and avoid “bloc confrontation or taking sides”, while calling for accelerated negotiations on the second phase of the China-South Korea Free Trade Agreement and expanded cooperation in AI, the green transition and the digital economy. More significantly, Wang made no reference to denuclearisation and did not endorse Seoul’s multiparty peace initiative, instead speaking of “peaceful coexistence” on the peninsula. The formulation appears to move Beijing closer to accepting the reality of two separate Korean states, rather than continuing to centre denuclearisation as the organising principle of peninsula diplomacy. Notably, Washington appears to be moving in parallel: in the August 25 readout of the Cho Hyun–Marco Rubio call, the US State Department conspicuously omitted any reference to denuclearisation — a term that had appeared routinely in previous trilateral statements as recently as July 22.
Wang also warned against “Japanese right-wing forces’ attempts to reverse the course of history”, urging that “Japanese militarism never be allowed to rise again”. His warning points directly to the speed and scale of Tokyo’s military transformation. Japan under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is moving rapidly to entrench that process. Trump’s latest move did not start this, but it reinforces the logic behind greater Japanese strategic autonomy. On July 31, Tokyo inaugurated its National Intelligence Bureau, strengthening the prime minister’s control over intelligence coordination across government. Japan’s core defence budget has reached a record 9.04 trillion yen ($56.7bn), while Japan says broader defence-related spending has reached its benchmark of 2 percent of gross domestic product ahead of schedule. The buildup is also being embedded in fiscal policy through new defence-related taxes. The pace of this shift has drawn Pyongyang’s wrath: Kim Yo-jong warned Japan that any “wrong choice” would bring “an immediate and unsurvivable, annihilating strike”.
For Beijing, however, the deeper concern is the autonomy of Tokyo’s drive. Japan is seizing the uncertainty surrounding Washington’s commitments to institutionalise military normalisation. Relaxed weapons export rules and deepening symbiosis with defence contractors Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Kawasaki Heavy Industries and IHI, whose combined defence order backlogs reach 6.25 trillion yen ($39.2bn), signal a Japan building the institutional scaffolding for greater independent action. For Beijing, this is the nightmare scenario: A rapidly remilitarised Japan operating not merely as a US proxy, but as an independent great power asserting its own sphere of influence as US credibility frays.
Seoul, too, is recalibrating. On August 18, after Trump ordered the UFS cut, President Lee Jae Myung renewed his push to regain wartime operational control of South Korean forces and accelerate plans for nuclear-powered submarines, arguing that stronger independent defence capabilities should complement the US alliance.
At the centre of this emerging order is a geopolitical triangle: A US treating alliances as transactional commodities, a Japan racing towards permanent military emancipation amid growing uncertainty over US commitments, and a China stabilising its periphery while pushing back against Tokyo’s rightward turn. South Korea, caught in the middle, is increasingly forced to navigate Washington’s unpredictability, Beijing’s economic gravity, and Tokyo’s accelerating militarism.
The uncertainty is profound. If Trump’s rapprochement with Pyongyang produces only theatre, North Korea’s nuclear programme will continue to advance as Beijing and Moscow shield Pyongyang from meaningful external pressure. If Washington’s pressure on Seoul succeeds, South Korea may be dragged deeper into America’s wars, from the Strait of Hormuz to a Taiwan contingency. If Tokyo’s remilitarisation proceeds unchecked, the post-war regional security architecture could be irrevocably altered.
The APEC summit in Shenzhen this November may offer the first real diplomatic test of this emerging order. The prospect of Trump, Xi Jinping, the Japanese and South Korean leaders, and possibly Kim Jong Un converging in one Chinese city would give Beijing an unusually prominent opportunity to shape the diplomatic response to this disorder. Whether it can broker a stabilising understanding, or the summit becomes another stage for competing nationalisms, could help determine East Asia’s trajectory for the decade to come.
The old certainties are eroding. The US alliance system that has anchored the region for three-quarters of a century is being weakened from within. Japan is exploiting the resulting ambiguity to shed post-war constraints. China, preferring a stable periphery and appearing increasingly willing to accommodate a permanent two-state reality on the peninsula, finds itself managing a level of regional uncertainty not seen since the Cold War.
No single summit can arrest the forces driving this transformation. East Asia is entering a new order in which Washington’s ability to set the terms is diminishing, its allies are testing the limits of their dependence, and its rivals are seeking to shape what comes next.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

What to pack for a child’s school lunchbox and what to avoid — recommendations from the Ministry of Health
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
11:17:19 EEST
17:17:19 KST

What to pack for a child’s school lunchbox and what to avoid — recommendations from the Ministry of Health
Kyiv • UNN
Half of the lunchbox should consist of vegetables, fruits and berries, and another quarter of protein-rich and whole-grain foods. The Ministry of Health recommends water and advises avoiding sweets.
A school snack should help a child remain energetic and focused throughout the day. A balanced lunchbox can be assembled without complicated dishes if vegetables and fruit, a source of protein, whole-grain products, and healthy fats are combined correctly. This is reported by the Ministry of Health of Ukraine, as UNN reports.
Details
A school snack affects a child’s concentration, energy reserves and mood throughout the day. Parents often get lost among the advice and eventually put in the lunchbox whatever will simply "last" until lunch—sweets or sandwiches. In fact, preparing a tasty and healthy snack is not difficult if you follow the principles of the healthy eating plate
In particular, the ministry recommends using vegetables, fruit, and berries as the basis of a snack. They should make up approximately half of the entire lunchbox.
Give preference to seasonal products and make sure there is variety: the more colors, the better
Another quarter should be allocated to foods rich in animal and plant protein. "baked chicken, stewed beans, boiled chickpeas, or homemade unsalted hummus, thick "Greek" yogurt without sugar, and so on. Adding plant-based protein to the diet is a simple way to diversify one’s diet and reduce the consumption of saturated fats, which meat dishes are often rich in
The remaining quarter can consist of whole-grain products: bread, crispbreads, homemade oatmeal cookies with minimal sugar content, or a small portion of porridge, no larger than a child’s fist. This can be oatmeal, buckwheat, pearl barley, brown rice, or quinoa. Such products contain complex carbohydrates and help keep children full longer, unlike fast simple carbohydrates (sugar).
Nuts or seeds can also be added to a snack—they support the health of the cardiovascular system, brain, and skin and promote the absorption of vitamins. At the same time, it is best to give a child a bottle of plain water to drink. Unsweetened tea or compote without sugar are also suitable.
What is better not to put in a lunchbox
The Ministry of Health advises against putting the following "to take along":
-  Foods that spoil quickly: eggs, fish, fatty meat,
soft cheese, and cream pastries. Products that require refrigeration must not be left at room temperature for a long time; 
-  Sauces (mayonnaise, ketchup, etc.): depending on their composition, they may contain a lot of fat, salt, and added sugar, and they also accelerate food spoilage; 
-  Foods high in salt: sausages, frankfurters, pâtés, processed cheeses, canned foods, etc.; 
-  Store-bought sweets: pastries, candies, and bars. It is
better to replace them with fresh fruit or berries. You can also add a small portion of dried fruit, homemade cookies with a minimal amount of sugar, or a few pieces of dark chocolate; 
-  Drinks with added sugar.  
Let us remind you
Experts from Harvard University developed the "Healthy Eating Plate" model, which is a simple guide for forming a daily diet.

Taiwan CEC chair against combining referendum questions on ballot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
08:15:55 UTC
17:15:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Central Election Commission Chair You Ying-lung (游盈隆) on Wednesday strongly opposed putting multiple referendum questions on one ballot, warning the change could disrupt elections.
CNA reported that the legislature could pass the proposed Referendum Act amendment on Friday. You urged lawmakers to delay it, saying the CEC had identified 11 major problems.
The proposal would place several referendum questions on one ballot instead of using a separate ballot for each question. Supporters say this could reduce the number of ballots voters collect and make voting more efficient, per UDN.
You said fewer ballots would not necessarily make voting or counting faster. Election workers would still need to count each referendum question separately.
He also rejected comparisons with the US, where multiple questions and candidates can appear on one ballot. You said the US uses different ballot designs, optical scanners, electronic counting systems, worker training, and voting procedures, per TTV News.
Taiwan cannot adopt only one part of the US system without changing the equipment and procedures that support it, You said. He warned the proposal could create more problems than it solves.
The commission said the change could increase invalid ballots, make some voting choices harder, and create difficulties for visually impaired voters. It could also complicate vote monitoring, recounts, decisions on ballot validity, and storage of election materials.
Local election commissions have also raised concerns about the proposal. You said Taiwan has less than 100 days before the Nov. 28 election and not enough time to make the necessary changes, per TVBS News.
Rushing the new system into use could increase the risk of election errors, he said. You added that the issue was not simply technical, but whether Taiwan’s election system could safely and effectively carry out the change.

Taiwan’s MediaTek completes latency test with Ericsson, AT&T
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
08:15:52 UTC
17:15:52 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — MediaTek, Ericsson, and AT&T have completed North America’s first real-world test of technology designed to reduce data interruptions when devices switch between mobile base stations.
The trial tested Ericsson’s L1/L2 Triggered Mobility (LTM) technology in a live network, with Ericsson serving as the radio access network supplier, per CNA. The company said LTM can reduce handover interruption times by up to 40% by triggering data transfers between base stations more quickly.
Handover interruption time refers to the brief loss of data connectivity that occurs when a device moves from one base station to another. Ericsson said reducing these interruptions could improve user experience and help prevent security risks and disruptions.
Ericsson has contributed to the development of LTM technology through 3GPP, the global organization responsible for mobile communications standards. The company said seamless handovers are becoming important as AI applications require predictable latency.
Ericsson explained that extended reality scene reconstruction, edge-assisted sensing, and industrial automation could benefit from reliable connections as devices move between networks.

Taiwan extends employment support for 9 manufacturing sectors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
08:15:45 UTC
17:15:45 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Workers in nine industries who have their hours reduced for at least 30 days can receive up to NT$11,500 per month in wage-gap subsidies under an extended government support program.
The Ministry of Labor said the employment stabilization measures will apply retroactively from Aug. 1 through Oct. 31, extending support for another three months as industries recover at different rates, per Liberty Times. The ministry cited a 10% US Section 301 tariff rate recently set for Taiwanese goods under a forced-labor trade investigation, while a separate investigation into structural excess capacity remains unresolved.
Employer-worker reduced-hours arrangements are generally reported in three-month periods, matching the length of the extension, per UDN.
Workers qualify after spending at least 30 days under a reduced-hours agreement that has been reported to local labor authorities. Payments cover 70% of the gap between their pre-reduction average monthly insured salary and the salary received under the new arrangement.
The nine sectors are: textiles, electrical equipment, automobiles and auto parts, machinery and equipment, food and animal feed, other transportation equipment and parts, fabricated metal products, plastic products, and rubber products.
Applications can be submitted monthly or for three months at once through a Workforce Development Agency branch or TaiwanJobs.
For first-time reduced-hours cases, the 30-day qualifying period must be completed by Oct. 31. Anyone starting after Oct. 2 will miss that cutoff, but may still receive up to NT$16,300 (US$512) per month in training support through the Reduced Working Hours Worker Recharging Program.

Morgan Stanley raises Taiwan’s GDP growth forecast to 11.6%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
08:15:34 UTC
17:15:34 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Morgan Stanley has raised its forecast for economic growth from 8.9% to 11.6%, which would be the highest in nearly 40 years.
The Wall Street bank also lifted the nation’s 2027 growth forecast from 4.7% to 7.5%, per UDN. Taiwan’s GDP grew 15.43% year over year in the first quarter and 12.92% in the second quarter, averaging 14.15% in the first half.
Morgan Stanley said the upgrade reflects strong AI-driven technology exports, increased semiconductor and supply-chain investment, and improving private consumption. Growth is no longer driven solely by net exports, with rising domestic investment and consumption showing that the AI and semiconductor boom is benefiting the broader economy.
Taiwan’s exports rose 44.7% year over year in the first seven months of the year, marking 33 consecutive months of annual growth, UDN reported. July exports rose 32.9%, while export orders jumped 61.9% to a record NT$3.11 trillion (US$97.9 billion), driven by demand for integrated circuits, electronic components, and information and communications technology products.
Morgan Stanley forecasts Taiwan’s exports will grow 20.7% for the full year, with shipment growth slowing from about 28% in the first half to about 13% in the second half. It said the slowdown mainly reflects a higher comparison base and shipment timing, with no clear signs yet of a meaningful downturn in the semiconductor cycle.
The report said semiconductor export growth may have peaked by the end of 2025, but the share and value of advanced chips in exports continue to rise, while global AI capital spending remains strong, per CNA. As a result, shipments of technology products and nominal exports are expected to remain resilient.
The bank forecasts the consumer price index will rise 2.1% in 2026 and 2.2% in 2027, with headline and core inflation likely to remain slightly above the Central Bank’s 2% threshold, per SET News. It cited fuel prices, weather-related food costs, higher technology prices amid the AI boom, recovering consumption, and elevated wage expectations as sources of inflationary pressure.
The report also noted that Taiwan plans to distribute another NT$10,000 cash payment to each person in 2027. If approved, the program could add about 0.3 percentage points to GDP growth, although the expansionary budget could also increase demand-driven inflation.

Ukrainian Suppliers to International Corporations Need Transparent Business Identification - D&B
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
11:13:44 EEST
17:13:44 KST

Ukrainian companies seeking to become suppliers to international corporations face formalized supplier onboarding procedures. For a large customer, receiving a commercial offer is not enough — it must unambiguously identify the legal entity, verify its owners, banking details, country of registration, and basic risks.
As a result, transparent business identification is becoming one of the practical barriers to Ukrainian suppliers entering global procurement chains. A company may meet technical requirements but lose time because of discrepancies in its name, address, registration data, or international profile.
“A supplier to a large corporation must not only be competitive but also easy to verify. The procurement officer must quickly understand exactly which legal entity stands behind the offer, who controls it, and whether the data match across different systems. For Ukrainian business, this is one of the elements of professional preparation for working with global clients,” said Maksym Urakin, Director of Development and Marketing at Interfax-Ukraine, Head of the D&B–Interfax-Ukraine business unit, PhD in Economics.
Before registering in a supplier system, a company should verify its official English-language name, legal address, information about its director and owners, contact details, banking information, and international identifiers. If a D-U-N-S Number has already been assigned, it should ensure that the profile linked to it is up to date.
For an international corporation, such standardization reduces the risk of duplicate suppliers, fraud, erroneous payments, and sanctions violations. For a Ukrainian company, it speeds up the customer’s internal procedures.
Dun & Bradstreet works with a global system of business identification and corporate data used in supplier management, due diligence, and procurement processes. In Ukraine, the relevant services and support are provided by D&B – Interfax-Ukraine.
For Ukrainian manufacturers, IT companies, engineering enterprises, and service providers, a transparent business profile can become one of the basic tools for integration into the procurement chains of international groups.
Dun & Bradstreet is an international provider of business data and analytical solutions whose history began in 1841. D&B works with company data worldwide and provides tools for business identification, counterparty verification, assessment of credit and commercial risks, compliance, and supply chain management.
The official representative of Dun & Bradstreet in Ukraine is the Interfax-Ukraine News Agency. The specialized D&B – Interfax-Ukraine unit provides Ukrainian companies with access to international business data, helps verify foreign counterparties, and supports work with D&B tools.
Questions can be submitted through the specialized D&B resource — dnb.ua, by email at [email protected], or by phone at +38 (044) 270-65-74.

Instagram CEO denies hiding data on platform’s impact on teens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
08:11:48 UTC
17:11:48 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
26 August 2026•Update: 26 August 2026
Instagram CEO Adam Mosseri rejected allegations from US prosecutors that the company withheld damaging information from the public, as he took the stand in a major federal trial over social media’s impact on young people.
“I am not trying to encourage my team to hide anything,” the CEO, Adam Mosseri, told a California courtroom on Tuesday, according to The Guardian.
Prosecutor Jason Slothouber questioned Mosseri about Instagram’s “Take a Break” feature, introduced to encourage teenagers to step away from the platform after long periods of scrolling. Slothouber pointed out that only 1.8% of teens had signed up, while Mosseri publicly promoted it without disclosing that figure.
“I’ve definitely said publicly that the opt-in rates are low,” Mosseri responded. “I don’t know if I’ve said numbers.”
The testimony came during a federal jury trial in Oakland, California, where US states accuse Meta of deliberately designing addictive products that harmed young people’s mental health and contributed to anxiety, depression and suicide. The states also allege that Meta collected information from children under 13 without parental consent, violating federal and state laws.
If Meta is found liable, the company could face up to $200 billion in damages and be ordered to change its products to strengthen protections for children. Meta has denied the allegations and called the states’ potential damages claim an “outlandish payout.”
Mosseri, who has led Instagram since 2018, has faced repeated scrutiny over the platform’s effect on teenagers. On Tuesday, Slothouber questioned him about a blog post published a day before Mosseri’s 2021 Senate testimony announcing the Take a Break feature. Mosseri said the company wanted to show the public it was making progress on safety.
The prosecutor also asked Mosseri about “drumbeat messaging,” a strategy of repeatedly communicating the same idea to build awareness. Mosseri defended the approach, saying safety tools needed to be repeatedly highlighted to parents.
“We need to repeat it to raise awareness of those tools.”
The jury has also heard from former Meta safety engineer and whistleblower Arturo Bejar, who accused the company of following a “don’t ask, don’t tell” approach to child safety. Psychologists and other former employees have also testified.
The trial is expected to continue through September, with Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg among those scheduled to testify.

The blaze began in the early hours of Wednesday and engulfed the ward at Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences, the biggest state hospital in Islamabad.

Kamal suggested that the blaze had been caused by an air conditioner but investigators were still at the scene and authorities have not confirmed the cause. Repair works and construction were ongoing at the hospital.
