Swiss to vote on whether to tighten neutrality, end peacetime cooperation with NATO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:38:58 UTC
14:38:58 KST

Swiss to vote on whether to tighten neutrality, end peacetime cooperation with NATO
ZURICH, Aug 26 - Swiss voters will decide in a referendum next month whether to approve a more restrictive form of neutrality that would block their country from imposing economic sanctions or cooperating with NATO.
Posters featuring doves of peace and asking voters to reject war have appeared across the Alpine nation in a campaign that has won the backing of the Kremlin but has raised fears that it could isolate Switzerland from its European neighbours.
Opinion surveys suggest voters will reject the proposal, with one recent poll showing 62% against to 36% in favour, but with campaigners for change outspending supporters of the status quo, the gap could narrow, said pollster Fabio Wasserfallen.
Swiss neutrality, internationally recognised since 1815 and part of the country's constitution since 1848, kept Switzerland out of both world wars.
But this status is under threat after Switzerland imposed sanctions on Russia over its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, said Christoph Blocher, a veteran politician and backer of the right-wing Swiss People's Party (SVP) which supports the campaign.
"Switzerland has not had a war for 200 years because it has remained permanently armed and neutral," Blocher told Reuters in an interview.
CAMPAIGNERS SAY SWISS NEUTRALITY IS BEING ERODED
The terms of Swiss neutrality are not explicitly spelled out in the constitution. Its scope is defined by the 1907 Hague Convention, which says neutral countries must not allow military use of their territory and be impartial between belligerents.
Blocher, who has led successful campaigns against closer ties with the European Union, said neutrality was being undermined, with Russia now seeing Switzerland as a party to the conflict because of the sanctions.
"A third world war may not be that far away, and then it will matter whether we are credibly neutral or not," he said.
Russia's foreign ministry has weighed into the debate, with spokeswoman Maria Zakharova criticising Switzerland in a social media post for aligning its sanctions with those of the EU.
"In legal terms, 'flexible neutrality' means no neutrality at all," said Zakharova, who is herself under Swiss sanctions.
The campaign wants the constitution to stipulate that Switzerland cannot join or cooperate with any military or defence alliance, unless attacked, and that it refrain from joining any sanctions unless approved by the United Nations.
OPPONENTS OF PROPOSAL SAY NO CHANGE IS NEEDED
The Swiss government and most political parties apart from the SVP oppose the proposal, with Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis saying it would harm national security and prevent it from training with NATO.
"We'd only be able to issue verbal condemnations but take no concrete action, that would certainly cause a major problem with our neighbours," Cassis told a press conference.
The government's legal experts said there was no need to change what they call a successful formula, which recently has seen Switzerland ban overflights by U.S. military aircraft during the Iran conflict.
"Neutrality is clearly defined and understood around the world," said Franz Perrez, head of international law at the foreign ministry. "Implementing these measures would not make Switzerland more neutral."
Laurent Goetschel, a political scientist at Basel University, said the campaign's posters saying "No to war, yes to neutrality" could sound attractive to voters who may not fully understand how neutrality was applied.
"Neutrality is not a dogma," he added. "It makes sense for Switzerland to be neutral, but the way it handles it should be up to the discretion of the government and not fixed in the constitution."
The referendum will take place on September 27. REUTERS

China Focus: China's cotton know-how takes root in Central Asia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:30:39 CST
14:30:39 KST

URUMQI, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Several hundred kilometers from Tashkent, the capital of Uzbekistan, cotton plants in a 1,000-mu (about 66.67 hectares) demonstration field are approaching one meter in height, each bearing 8 to 10 bolls.
For Song Meizhen, chief scientist of a high-quality cotton research team at the Institute of Western Agriculture under the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, the crop is developing as expected.
"Given the current growth and field management, the field is well on track to exceed the target of 550 kilograms of seed cotton per mu this year," Song said.
This high-standard cotton seed breeding demonstration field is jointly operated by Xinjiang Huaxing Investment Group and the institute. From surveying the land and selecting varieties before spring planting to designing cultivation methods and setting technical standards for sowing and field management, Chinese researchers have been involved throughout the process.
They have also provided regular video guidance and remote technical support.
The project combines high-quality cotton varieties with a range of techniques already widely used in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, including drip irrigation under plastic film, denser planting designed to improve light use, and mechanized harvesting.
Song said the cooperation endeavor is aimed at introducing a package of Chinese cotton-growing technologies and management practices to Uzbekistan.
Xinjiang is China's largest cotton-producing region. In 2025, it produced 6.17 million tonnes of cotton, accounting for 92.8 percent of the national total. The region's cotton sector is already among the world's most mechanized, with an overall mechanization rate for cultivation and harvesting surpassing 97 percent.
At a smart cotton field jointly developed by the Xinjiang Changji National Agricultural High-tech Industry Demonstration Zone and the institute, weather stations and soil-moisture sensors collect field data around the clock, helping growers manage irrigation, fertilizer and other field operations more precisely.
According to the institute, the system can save more than 10 percent of water and nearly 20 percent of fertilizer per mu while increasing yields by over 10 percent.
Similarities in climate, water and soil conditions between Xinjiang and Central Asian countries have laid the groundwork for cross-border adoption of improved cotton varieties, cultivation techniques and agricultural machinery.
Shadman Namazov, an academician of the Uzbek Academy of Sciences who has visited the Changji demonstration zone several times, said Chinese cotton-growing techniques have brought improvements in planting density, water use, yields and quality compared with traditional local practices.
He cited precision irrigation and fertilizer use, mechanized operations and modern field management, saying these technologies were scientifically grounded and could be replicated on a wider scale.
Namazov added that the use of Chinese techniques in Uzbekistan has helped raise cotton yields while reducing production costs, contributing to higher incomes for local growers.
These cooperation efforts are also translating into stronger demand for Chinese cotton seeds and agricultural machinery in Central Asia.
Hilltide, a Xinjiang-based seed industry company, sells cotton seeds and provides related technical services in Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan and Kyrgyzstan. Company executive Lu Yang said its cotton seed exports to Central Asia rose from 800 tonnes during the sales season from late 2024 to early 2025 to 1,500 tonnes during the season from late 2025 to early 2026.
Lu revealed that the company's cotton seeds have maintained a market share of more than 70 percent in its Central Asian markets, attributing the growth to high-yield, stress-resistant varieties and technical services provided in addition to the seeds.
Chinese cotton pickers are gaining ground in Central Asia as well.
The Xinjiang branch of China Railway Construction Heavy Industry Co., Ltd. dispatched a batch of new four-row box-type cotton pickers to Central Asia in early July. The company said its cotton pickers have been developed to suit planting patterns and harvesting conditions in Central Asia, and orders from the region account for more than 70 percent of its production capacity this year.
At Xinjiang Boshiran Intelligent Agricultural Machinery Co., Ltd., Vice President Feng Guang said Chinese high-end cotton pickers can match leading international products in harvesting efficiency while costing about half as much as comparable European and U.S. machines.
Feng said a high level of domestically produced components, shorter delivery times and more timely after-sales service have also helped Chinese machines meet demand in Central Asian markets. The company has seen a sharp increase in overseas orders since last year, he added.
Alongside business exchanges, research cooperation has also deepened. Since 2023, Chinese institutions have worked with agricultural research institutes across all five Central Asian countries on joint research and technical training in cotton breeding, high-yield cultivation and water-saving irrigation, while promoting standardized technical guidelines in English and Russian.
The Uzbek demonstration field is one place where the results of this cooperation can be seen in the crop itself. Across Central Asia, Chinese cotton expertise is increasingly arriving not as a single product, but as a combination of seeds, farming techniques and machinery. ■

Across China: "China can set an example": U.S. delegation seeks lessons on aging, healthcare reform
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:30:36 CST
14:30:36 KST

Members of the exchange program "Harvard Healthcare China Trek 2026" pose for photos while visiting Peking University in Beijing, capital of China, Aug. 19, 2026. (Xinhua)
BEIJING, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- China can set an example for the world in confronting demographic change, a U.S. public health scholar said, as a 25-member American delegation tours the country to learn from its healthcare reform, biotech innovation and artificial intelligence application.
David Crumpacker, assistant professor at Texas A&M University and a master of public health graduate from Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, stressed the importance of learning from Chinese experience, such as primary care infrastructure, and efforts to manage the intersection of economic development with population health.
"These are insights that are not fully reflected in global health literature. We want to understand those insights from the people who generate them," he said.
The delegation, comprising scholars, medical professionals and students from Harvard University and other leading U.S. institutions, has been in China since Aug. 16.
They have visited the National Healthcare Security Administration and a national artificial intelligence medical pilot base in Beijing, as well as hospitals in Shanghai. They are also scheduled to tour health companies in Shenzhen, a global tech hub in southern Guangdong Province, and the Boao Lecheng International Medical Tourism Pilot Zone -- the country's sole medical special zone -- in Hainan Province.
China is racing to upgrade its healthcare system to meet the needs of an aging society. With more than 300 million people aged 60 and above, it has the largest elderly population of any country in the world.
By the end of 2025, the national basic medical insurance program covered 1.331 billion people, with the participation rate remaining stable at over 95 percent.
"Over one billion people means over one billion patients," said Jennifer Miles-Thomas, vice chair of integration and innovation at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago.
She said China and the United States are "very aligned" in the goal of delivering the highest quality care, but the U.S. faces challenges with expensive healthcare and incomplete insurance coverage. "I'm here to observe and to receive information and ideas about what we can do better," she said.
The exchange program, "Harvard Healthcare China Trek 2026," is hosted by the China Center for International People-to-People Exchange under the Ministry of Education, with support from Peking University Health Science Center and Fudan University Shanghai Medical College. It is part of a broader initiative to invite 50,000 young Americans to China over five years for study, research and dialogue.
During a visit to the BioPark in Beijing, Khaoula Belahsen, a 28-year-old master's student at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and an AI researcher at Harvard Medical School, was impressed by the scale and speed of the pharmaceutical and biotechnology hub. First announced in October 2025, the BioPark has drawn nearly 5,000 medical and healthcare companies, including global leaders Eli Lilly, Pfizer, Bayer, AstraZeneca and Medtronic.
"I've always dreamed of coming to China. The country has so much history, but also so much progress economically and scientifically," Belahsen said.
Morgan Moncada, 35, a Harvard graduate and founder of an AI digital health company, said strong incentives exist for medical companies to engage with the Chinese market, citing lower costs and vast reach. "China is open to collaboration, and that is really exciting," he said.
China is pushing artificial intelligence deeper into healthcare, with a roadmap to bring AI-assisted diagnosis to all primary-care clinics by 2030. Major hospitals are already using AI for imaging analysis and treatment planning.
Noting that his company uses AI agents to help people manage chronic diseases such as sleep apnea and diabetes, Moncada expressed his hope to introduce the technology they're building in the U.S. to China and adapt it for the Chinese population.
"I think something that we're really interested in is how we can contribute to China's healthcare system and how we can learn from China's healthcare system to improve healthcare in the United States and other countries around the globe," Moncada added.
In the Boao Lecheng pilot zone, patients can access innovative drugs and medical devices not yet approved on the mainland -- a policy that has benefited nearly 280,000 people and spared many costly overseas medical trips. The zone also uses real-world patient data to accelerate regulatory approvals, helping more products reach the wider Chinese market faster.
"We're very interested in seeing how this special zone actually helps, and how all those incredible medical technologies take effect," said Ze'ev Drukker, a 26-year-old bioengineering graduate from Tufts University who is applying for a master's program at Tsinghua University in Beijing.
As the delegation explores China's healthcare landscape, they are also building bridges of understanding between the younger generation of U.S. and Chinese health professionals, paving the way for joint efforts to advance global public health.
"What I like about healthcare is that it's something shared between all people, and across all countries. We all face the same challenges, and all want to integrate innovation to save people's lives and reduce burdens," Belahsen said. "It's really inspiring to come to China and see what innovation looks like here." ■

Syria's Kurdish-led group announces dissolution
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:30:34 CST
14:30:34 KST

Mazloum Abdi, commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), speaks at a press conference at the People's Palace in Damascus, Syria, Aug. 25, 2026. Abdi announced Tuesday the dissolution of the force following the completion of its integration into Syrian state institutions, ending a decade-long chapter in which the U.S.-backed group controlled large parts of northern and northeastern Syria.
Abdi also announced the dissolution of the Kurdish-led Autonomous Administration and affiliated military and civilian formations, following their full integration into state institutions. (Xinhua)
DAMASCUS, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Mazloum Abdi, commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), announced Tuesday the dissolution of the force following the completion of its integration into Syrian state institutions, ending a decade-long chapter in which the U.S.-backed group controlled large parts of northern and northeastern Syria.
"Today, we announce the end of the mission of the Syrian Democratic Forces, and we responsibly announce its dissolution as a military force," Abdi said at a press conference at the People's Palace in Damascus, according to Syria's state-run Al-Ikhbariya TV.
Abdi also announced the dissolution of the Kurdish-led Autonomous Administration and affiliated military and civilian formations, following their full integration into state institutions.
He described the move as the beginning of a new chapter focused on peace, stability and rebuilding Syria after years of conflict.
The transition should mark a genuine shift "from the battlefields to the fields of construction," said Abdi, calling for the building of a unified country encompassing Syria's different communities.
He also raised the issue of Kurdish cultural and linguistic rights, saying he had sought an open position from Syrian interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa regarding the right to education in one's mother tongue.
Tuesday's announcement caps months of difficult negotiations and intermittent military confrontation between Damascus and the SDF over the future of northeastern Syria and the shape of the country's post-war state.
The two sides initially agreed in early 2025 to integrate the SDF and the Kurdish-led administration's civilian institutions into the Syrian state. Implementation, however, became bogged down amid disagreements over the structure of the integration, military command arrangements and the degree of autonomy Kurdish authorities would retain.
Tensions subsequently escalated, including clashes in Kurdish-held neighborhoods of Aleppo, before developing into a broader military confrontation in January this year.
Government forces advanced into SDF-held territory in northern and eastern Syria, substantially reducing the territory controlled by the Kurdish-led force.
On Jan. 18, Damascus and the SDF reached a ceasefire and integration agreement providing for an immediate halt to fighting, the withdrawal of SDF formations to areas east of the Euphrates River and the transfer of administrative and military authority in Raqqa and Deir al-Zour provinces to the central government.
A more comprehensive agreement followed later that month, setting out the phased integration of the SDF's military and administrative structures.
The arrangements included the deployment of Interior Ministry security forces in Hasakah and Qamishli and the incorporation of SDF fighters into formations operating within the Syrian military structure.
Implementation continued over the following months. Damascus assumed control over key state institutions and facilities in the northeast, including Qamishli airport and major oil fields, while government security forces entered Hasakah and Qamishli.
Yet disagreements persisted over the SDF's ultimate status, particularly whether it could retain a distinct command structure within the Syrian military. As recently as early August, dissolution remained a key issue under negotiation between Abdi and al-Sharaa.
Abdi announced on Aug. 20 that the integration of the Kurdish administration's military, security and civilian institutions into the Syrian state had been completed, paving the way for Tuesday's formal dissolution.
Tuesday's announcement also came one day after Washington formally removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, ending a designation that had lasted since 1979.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that the decision was part of Washington's effort to give Syria a path toward prosperity.
Washington also revoked the designation of Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), a former al-Qaida-linked rebel group that played a dominant role in the formation of Syria's new government, as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organization.
Since its formation in 2015, the SDF had been backed primarily by the United States and served as Washington's main local partner in the fight against Islamic State militants.
But following the fall of the former Syrian government in December 2024, Washington increasingly supported efforts to bring Syria's institutions and armed groups under a unified state framework while building closer ties with the new authorities in Damascus. ■

People gather at a hospital following a fire incident in Islamabad, Pakistan on Aug. 26, 2026. At least 14 infants were killed when a fire broke out in the gynecology ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences here on Wednesday, police sources said. (Xinhua/Ahmad Kamal)
ISLAMABAD, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- At least 14 infants were killed when a fire broke out in the gynecology ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences here on Wednesday, police sources said.
The fire broke out at around 6:40 a.m. local time (0140 GMT) in the gynecology ward area on the third floor of the hospital, where children were present, the sources told Xinhua on condition of anonymity.
The hospital administration launched rescue operations, while fire brigade personnel, ambulances and police rushed to the scene. Several children were reportedly rescued from the ward.
The sources said that initially nine children died on the spot, while the others later succumbed to their injuries after being shifted to the children's ward.
Rescue operations were still underway, while police were ascertaining the cause of the fire and exact details regarding the casualties. ■

Kyrgyzstan's central bank keeps key interest rate unchanged at 12 pct
China
Unknown Publisher

14:30:29 KST

BISHKEK, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- The Board of the National Bank of Kyrgyzstan has decided to keep its key interest rate unchanged at 12 percent, the bank's press service said on Tuesday.
Since the beginning of 2026, consumer prices have risen by 7.3 percent, while annual inflation has reached 11.7 percent. Rising fuel and lubricant prices, as well as higher food prices amid volatility in global food markets, have been among the main drivers of inflation.
At the same time, economic activity remains strong, with real GDP growing 11.1 percent in January-July 2026. Growth has been supported by high investment activity, particularly in construction, as well as increased domestic consumption.
The National Bank said persistent external inflationary risks require maintaining tight monetary conditions. Keeping the key rate at its current level will help contain secondary inflationary effects and create conditions for a sustainable decline in inflation over the medium term. ■

City Tower One is a 358-meter-tall (1,175 ft.) tower in Dubai designed by Pelli Clarke & Partners. The 93-story mixed-use skyscraper completed construction and launched for leasing in June 2026. The building is located in the Trade Centre First neighborhood, on a site connecting Sheikh Zayed Road to Al Badaa Road along Eleventh Street, and includes 608 residential units across from Hazel Wong's Emirates Towers and Killa Design's Museum of the Future. The building's presence in Dubai's skyline and everyday urban life was recently captured by local photographer Ahmad Alnaji, founder of SARAB Art Production and a contributor to the visual identity of landmark buildings across the region, including projects by architecture practices such as Foster + Partners, UNStudio and Killa Design.
Pelli Clarke & Partners' City Tower One comprises a mix of residential units ranging from studios to four-bedroom penthouses and duplexes, together with office and retail space. With nearly half of all residential units being three-bedroom homes, the tower has low-density floors, with eight to nine homes per floor. Indoor amenities include a gym, a movement studio, a residents' multi-purpose lounge and children's play areas. A dedicated residential amenity deck, linked to the main tower by a skybridge above a nine-story parking structure, provides additional indoor and outdoor shared facilities. Outdoor amenities include an infinity pool, a tennis court, landscaped lounge areas, children's play areas, and a specialty café.
Particularly noticeable in the photographs, the tower's champagne hue shimmers in the desert sun. A grand-scale, expansive and light-filled entrance space is defined by mashrabiya-inspired aluminum screens that dapple and modulate light. A rooftop amenity deck, designed by the firm as "an oasis for leisure and wellness," sits atop the parking structure. The deck stretches wide, offering views of the Gulf and the Burj Khalifa, alongside a full-service fitness facility, a yoga studio, a residential lounge, and a pool and recreation area for children. The photographs place these design elements within the context of everyday urban life, presenting the tower as an integral part of Dubai's skyline and a recognizable landmark at all hours.
 Architecture is rarely just building. The UAE, in particular, has deliberately used architecture and cities to state who it is. Photographing that architecture as art rather than as product is a way of taking it seriously on its own terms. — Photographer Ahmad Alnaji

BRUSSELS – Russia is expanding its campaign of hybrid attacks against countries that supply weapons and money to Kyiv and has caught Europe without a plan to respond.
From cyberattacks to armed drones and mysterious cases of arson, tensions are rising across the continent as the war in Ukraine is set to enter its fifth winter.
Poland said in August that it thwarted an attempted assassination of a US citizen originally from Ukraine that was ordered by Russia, while Estonia accused Moscow of being behind a fire at a drone maker.
Meanwhile, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Aug 25 that those responsible for hybrid attacks “will pay the price” after an explosive-laden drone was discovered at an airport in Leipzig near a Ukrainian cargo plane, raising speculation that Moscow was involved in an attempted strike.
European officials have been anticipating for months that Russia may escalate its aggressive campaign against the continent.
But the bloc has yet to change its fundamentally defensive posture, according to people familiar with how the institutions gauge outside threats, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
That has likely encouraged Moscow to probe how far it can go in trying to intimidate and wear down Western allies as it remains locked in a war of attrition with Ukraine.
“NATO, European and national responses have largely been reactive and defensive,” said Agnia Grigas, a non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council in Vilnius.
“They have focused on detecting and countering individual provocations, but have not built a record of effective deterrence by consistently dissuading Moscow from continuing or escalating them.”
That lack of preparedness comes as Europe has taken on the primary role in supporting Ukraine, with the US shifting away from the continent.
While NATO’s mutual defence clause commits member states to help one another in case of an attack, Russia’s alleged actions have so far fallen short of what would become a trigger for such a response.
Moscow has increasingly relied on recruitment via social media to carry out arson or other sabotage attacks after large-scale expulsions of its diplomats following the invasion of Ukraine.
Two Ukrainian nationals were handed prison sentences in Britain in June after a jury found them guilty of conspiring to commit arson attacks on a car and property linked to then Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
The prosecution said during the trial that one of the perpetrators was recruited online by a Russian-speaking Telegram user.
Lithuanian prosecutor-general Nida Grunskiene said last week that the drone attack in Germany has “links” to an ongoing investigation into an attempt to detonate a parcel on a DHL cargo plane in 2024.
Lithuania has charged five in the attempted sabotage, allegedly hired by Russia’s military intelligence.
While Germany has not singled out Russia as being behind the armed drone or the recent discovery of a cache of weapons on the outskirts of Berlin, a slew of investigative media reports have pointed the finger at Moscow.
It also added to fresh warnings that Europe’s biggest economy must grapple with the new dimensions of asymmetrical risks.
There are indications that Russian intelligence and security services are looking at hybrid warfare operations against the Baltic states and Poland, an intelligence official told Bloomberg earlier in August.
Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Moscow is weighing a potential false flag operation using captured Ukrainian drones to strike critical infrastructure in the Baltic region.
“Russia’s ongoing hybrid warfare in Europe is a highly coordinated, sub-threshold campaign aimed at destabilising Western political systems, fracturing NATO and EU unity, and eroding support for Ukraine,” said Alex Kokcharov, geoeconomics analyst at Bloomberg Economics in London.
“To achieve these goals, the Kremlin maintains plausible deniability by exploiting anonymity and utilising proxies to obfuscate direct state attribution.”
Some European Union members have called on the bloc to respond by adopting the sanctions that have been blocked, including seizing assets, a ban on transporting Russian liquefied natural gas and restricting visas, according to people familiar with the matter.
The EU is preparing another package of sanctions on hundreds of individuals and entities, which it aims to adopt in the fall, they said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
But as previous such measures have failed to restrain Moscow, it is unlikely they will do now.
“Russia is willing to use kinetic means because until now, they have been unsuccessful in discouraging support for Ukraine,” said Marek Kohv, head of the security and resilience programme at the Tallinn-based International Centre for Defence and Security.
“It is directly connected to how Russia is doing on the front line.”
NATO members have pledged US$80 billion (S$101.5 billion) in military aid to Ukraine for 2026 and “at least the equivalent levels” in 2027 at the alliance’s July summit in Ankara.
The money is overwhelmingly coming from Europe.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham handed over cruise missile blueprints to Kyiv in a visit on Aug 24.
He also compared Ukraine’s fight with Britain’s resistance to the Nazis in World War II, drawing a response from Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.
He accused Britain of “methodically and regularly adding fuel to the fire” and “methodically and regularly plotting to prevent any progress in the peace process” in his remarks to reporters on Aug 24.
Russia has also warned that Britain would face “consequences for which it will have to answer” after reports that Kyiv used drones made by British companies to carry out strikes inside Russian territory.
In August, the Estonian authorities said they were investigating Russian involvement in a fire at Milrem Robotics, a drone manufacturer that supplies Ukraine.
A Latvian charity for Ukraine said its warehouse was the subject of an arson attack in July.
“Russia is clearly seeking to escalate the situation – not through direct military escalation, but perhaps by influencing Western countries, particularly those supporting Ukraine,” Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in Helsinki on Aug 24. “But it is not working. South Korea said on Wednesday it had scrambled fighter jets in response to Russian military aircraft entering its air defence zone, the second such incursion in weeks.

An air defence identification zone is not sovereign airspace but a buffer area where countries require foreign aircraft to identify themselves for security purposes.

Cyclone from Balkans and anticyclone from Scandinavia affect weather - forecast for August 26
Kyiv • UNN
On August 26, rain and thunderstorms are expected in some regions of Ukraine, while the rest of the country will remain dry. Temperatures will reach 30°C during the day.
The weather in Ukraine on August 26 will be influenced by a cyclone from the Balkans and an anticyclone from Scandinavia; it will be rainy in some places and dry in others, while daytime temperatures will reach 30 degrees Celsius, the Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center reported, writes UNN.
On August 26, an atmospheric front from the cyclone over the Balkans will bring unsettled weather to the central regions, Zakarpattia, Chernivtsi, and, during the day, most southern regions, while also affecting the southern districts of Kyiv region. Weather without precipitation in the rest of the country will be determined by a high-pressure field from an anticyclone centered over southern Scandinavia. Moderate northeastern winds will prevail, bringing cool air to Ukraine; its influence will be most noticeable in the northern part, especially at night
According to the forecast, today will be partly cloudy.
In the central regions, Zakarpattia, Chernivtsi, during the day also in most southern regions and in Kyiv region, there will be moderate, locally heavy rain and thunderstorms; elsewhere, no precipitation.
The wind will be predominantly northeastern, 5–10 m/s.
Temperatures will be 14–19° at night, 8–13° in the northern part; 21–26° during the day, and 25–30° in the southeast of the country.

Iceland to vote on reopening EU membership talks in close referendum

Iceland to vote on reopening EU membership talks in close referendum
Icelanders will vote in a referendum on Saturday whether to resume entry talks with the European Union amid growing global insecurity. Voters are not being asked to decide just yet if they want to join the 27-member bloc – only whether they want their government to negotiate possible terms.
Icelanders are to vote Saturday on whether to resume entry talks with the European Union amid growing global insecurity, in a referendum seen as going down to the wire.
Icelanders are not being asked to decide just yet if they want to join the 27-member bloc – only whether they want their government to negotiate possible terms, including on the highly sensitive fishing issue.
"This is an opportunity, it's not a final decision," Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir told AFP, arguing that the referendum paved the way for a "risk-reducing 'Yes'".
"This way you get a deal on the table, you're able to see all the questions, the answers to all the questions we get here," she said.
She was speaking to AFP after a "listening meeting" in Selfoss, one of the many small towns the Social Democratic leader has visited to hear Icelanders' questions and concerns on the issue.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
On Saturday, voters will be asked to answer "Yes" or "No" to the question: "Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?"
Implied is the question of whether the country of 400,000 inhabitants ultimately thinks it best to remain the captain of its own ship, or hitch its cart to the EU.
If the "Yes" side wins, an accession agreement negotiated with Brussels would be put to a new referendum and likely require a change to Iceland's constitution, as well as ratification by EU member states.
The north Atlantic island applied to join the bloc in 2009, a year after the 2008 financial crisis led to the collapse of its banks and economy.
Membership negotiations began in 2010 but were suspended in 2013 after a eurosceptic government came to power.
The world has changed radically since then.
Read moreIceland to hold EU referendum 'in the coming months', PM says
"The EU is looking around, it's finishing deals with India, with Mercosur. We're seeing changes in the global climate when it comes to how people are using tariffs as weapons," Frostadottir noted.
Divisive question
While Iceland's economy is flourishing again – albeit with a volatile currency – households are struggling with rising inflation and soaring interest rates, with the central bank raising rates three times so far this year to eight percent. This makes the euro an attractive option to indebted households.
On the global stage, the return of war in Europe with Russia's invasion of Ukraine has shaken established security doctrines.
US President Donald Trump's threats to take over neighbouring Greenland have added to Icelanders' concerns. Their island is strategically located in the sub-Arctic, has no military and depends on NATO and a 1951 bilateral agreement with the United States for its defence.
"The geopolitical upheaval that we have seen recently is not the root cause of this referendum. But obviously, those concerns are impacting the debate," Bifrost University professor Eirikur Bergmann told AFP.
"Mainly the aggression towards Greenland has caused great concern in Iceland and caused many people here to pause and reassess where Iceland belongs."
Opinion polls suggest Icelanders are deeply divided on the EU question.
Office worker Vilborg Inga Magnusdottir said she saw no reason to change the status quo.
"Why would we want to enter the European Union? What would we benefit from it when things are already good?" the 33-year-old told AFP.
Unlike her, Hrafnkell Gudnason plans to vote "Yes".
"It's getting more dangerous for a small country to stand outside the EU," the 59-year-old consultant and horse-breeder said.
"I think it's safer to be a part of a bigger family."
Compromise on fishing?
In a country where seafood products account for around 40 percent of exports of goods, fishing – an integral part of Iceland's national identity – would inevitably be the key issue in EU negotiations.
Half a century after the last "Cod Wars" with Britain, many Icelanders are reluctant to yield even the tiniest bit of control of their hard-won national waters to Brussels.
Even Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir, a staunch europhile, has made it clear that in any future negotiations Reykjavik would insist on retaining "sovereign control over all fisheries".
That would be difficult to reconcile with the EU's current Common Fisheries Policy.
Brussels has stayed out of the fray ahead of the referendum, but has sent positive signals, even on the sensitive fisheries issue.
For the EU, the prospect of welcoming a wealthy, stable country already largely integrated in the single market through its membership in the European Economic Area would provide a strong showcase for its enlargement policy and strengthen its presence in a coveted region.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Several oil companies to avoid using ships on Iran's blacklist over security concerns, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:18:14 UTC
14:18:14 KST

At least three Indian oil refiners and a global energy major plan to stop using vessels on Iran's new blacklist, including for ship-to-ship transfers, due to security concerns, four sources with direct knowledge of the matter said this week.
Tehran announced on Sunday a blacklist of 45 ships it said had broken its rules for crossing the Strait of Hormuz, and would take action against any vessels transferring loads with them, escalating its threats over the key waterway for global energy supplies six months into the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Iran's announcement appears designed to impede the so-called shuttle runs Gulf oil producers such as the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia have undertaken with dedicated tankers to move oil from the Gulf through Hormuz for unloading through STS transfers in the Gulf of Oman onto ships to end-users.
The shuttle runs have kept alive oil flows from the Middle East that have been curtailed by Iran's clampdown on shipping through the strait because of the war.
The named vessels could be fined, detained, and have their cargoes confiscated, according to a post on social media site X/Twitter from the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, a new body Iran set up to manage the strait.
"We will avoid our chartered vessels dealing or STS or anything to do with non-compliant ships for Middle Eastern cargoes," said one of the sources, who works at an Indian refinery.
The sources declined to be identified because of the sensitivity of the issue.
Some of the tankers Iran listed are owned or chartered by Saudi Aramco and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co (ADNOC). The ships have been used for shuttling crude, refined products and liquefied natural gas (LNG) out of the Gulf for STS transfer off Fujairah in the UAE or Sohar, Oman, according to shipping data.
Saudi Aramco and ADNOC declined to comment.
Ana Subasic, a trade risk analyst at shipping tracking firm Kpler, said the most compliance-sensitive buyers are expected to avoid these vessels moving forward, but the trade is more likely to reroute through alternative tonnage, counterparties or transfer locations than disappear altogether.
Internal discussions
Several charterers and shipping firms are discussing internally whether to continue their STS operations or not and are evaluating Iran's warning, multiple other trade and shipping sources said, with one of them, a Gulf crude buyer, saying it would be safer to buy oil on a delivered basis shipped to a final destination instead of free-on-board at STS locations in the Gulf of Oman.
Those sources also declined to be identified because of the sensitivity of the matter.
"Our internal departments are still in discussion on how to proceed with crude deliveries from the Strait of Hormuz via ship-to-ship transfers in the long term,” said Formosa Petrochemical Corp President KY Lin.
Iran has previously attacked several of the tankers, including the Wedyan, Mombasa B and Al Bahyah.
Two crude ships no longer giving location
Two of the 12 very large crude carriers on Iran's blacklist were no longer giving their location through their automatic identification systems (AIS) by Tuesday after the list was released, while the rest have had their AIS transponders switched off for weeks.
"The key issue is contagion," Kpler's Subasic said.
"If Iran follows through on threats to penalize vessels that conduct STS transfers with blacklisted tankers, that should narrow the pool of willing shipowners, charterers and buyers, particularly among firms with material Gulf exposure, while increasing due-diligence requirements and potentially freight, insurance and risk premia."

SpaceX to build $100 billion Starship rocket complex in Louisiana
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:17:20 UTC
14:17:20 KST

SpaceX unveiled plans on Tuesday to build its largest rocket launch complex yet in southern Louisiana, a $100 billion effort to transform coastal wetlands into a critical base for the company's Starship and AI satellite launch ambitions.
The 125,000-acre (50,585-hectare) site on Pecan Island, which SpaceX named Starbase Louisiana, is an expansion of the company's Starship launch operations beyond South Texas and those planned for Florida as its next-generation rocket remains in late-stage development.
The company's second Starbase campus will eventually launch thousands of Starship flights a year, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said, reiterating its goals for an ambitious cadence contingent on solving steep engineering challenges and regulatory hurdles.
Construction will begin next year with the first Starship launch in 2029, SpaceX said. Shotwell detailed the plans near the proposed site in Louisiana's Vermilion Parish at an event with Governor Jeff Landry and other senior state officials.
The "self-sustaining" spaceport envisioned by SpaceX will include its own methane production for propellant, power generation, deep-water shipping capabilities to transport Starships from Texas, vehicle processing facilities, and probably an airport, Shotwell said.
The marshland site is more than eight times the size of Manhattan. Shotwell said "very large portions" of the land will remain natural wetlands with no infrastructure, while an animated SpaceX video showed the area dotted with several launch pads surrounded by greenery.
Site at center of ExxonMobil lawsuit
The site had been at the center of a decade-long lawsuit against ExxonMobil brought by local parishes alleging the oil major's coastal drilling and canal dredging contributed to the state's wetland loss. The state reached an agreement with Exxon to settle the lawsuit in June, prompting its dismissal the following month, a court order shows.
That cleared the way for SpaceX's launch plans for the 18-mile (29-km) coastal strip, which the company had been discussing with the state since February, Louisiana Economic Development Secretary Susan Bourgeois said.
SpaceX has significantly expanded its southern US footprint in recent years, having built Colossus AI data centers in Tennessee and Mississippi and Starlink facilities in Austin, Texas. It is planning a chip plant in central Texas.
"This project means more than just steel, technology, and capital," Landry said. "It represents jobs for our families. It represents momentum for our communities, and it represents protection for our coast."
SpaceX said the Louisiana site will add more than 3,000 jobs to the region. The governor's office said those jobs are expected to pay an average salary of $92,600, or 192% higher than the average wage in Vermilion Parish.
Second starbase
The launch site, which will be SpaceX's fourth in the US, appears to replicate, at a larger scale, its widening footprint in South Texas, the site of its first Starbase rocket campus. However, the Louisiana site will not have rocket production facilities.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk sees Starship as central to the company's goals of expanding its Starlink constellation and eventually deploying up to 1 million AI data-processing satellites in orbit. The rocket also plays a key role in NASA's Artemis moon program.
Pecan Island is situated in a geographically convenient location for Musk's satellite ambitions. It allows a rocket to launch south over the Gulf waters and into a sun-synchronous orbit that offers plenty of sunlight for solar-powered AI satellites.
Starbase Texas is Starship's only active launch site as the rocket remains in development, while SpaceX builds two Starship pads in Florida next to its flagship Falcon 9 launch pads. The company also has Falcon 9 launch facilities at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.
As SpaceX developed Boca Chica, Texas, into the company town of Starbase with support from local government officials, it has faced resistance from residents concerned about water, environmental, and noise pollution and pressure to sell their land.
Shotwell highlighted environmental plans and outlined efforts to restore Pecan Island's receding marshlands and coastline, which act as a natural buffer to protect inland areas from flooding during heavy rainfall.
Pecan Island is a protected hub for dozens of migratory bird species seasonally traveling throughout the Western Hemisphere. At Starbase Texas, Starship launches have blasted shorebirds and their nests with gravel and debris, according to environmental groups.
"The birds might fly away during a launch, but I guarantee they come back," Shotwell said, prompting applause from state officials. "As soon as the rocket's gone, the birds come back. It's not like months later."
She said SpaceX will help fund environmental "protection, restoration, and stewardship" while the launch site is constructed.

Anatolia’s giant pyramids defy the passage of time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:16:31 UTC
14:16:31 KST

Studies indicate that the Bintepeler tumuli were built through extensive planning and sophisticated engineering, rather than simply by piling up soil.
The Bintepeler tumulus field in the western province of Manisa’s Salihli district, known as the “Pyramids of Anatolia,” sheds light on ancient history with its monumental royal tombs and vast necropolis.
Located next to Sardes, the capital of the ancient Lydian Kingdom, the site is considered one of the largest tumulus burial grounds in the world.
Among hundreds of tumuli of various sizes in the area, the most striking is the monumental tomb of King Alyattes, father of the famed Lydian ruler Croesus. Standing about 70 meters high and measuring approximately 300 meters at its base, the tumulus is regarded as the largest known tumulus in the world.
Its enormous scale has drawn comparisons with the pyramids of Egypt. Ancient historian Herodotus also praised the monument in his writings, describing the Alyattes Tumulus as one of the largest monuments built by humans. Its imposing silhouette can still be seen from kilometers away across the Gediz Plain.
Archaeological and geological studies indicate that the Bintepeler tumuli were not created simply by piling up soil. Their construction involved extensive planning and sophisticated engineering.
Different types of soil were deliberately brought from various geographical areas and geological layers to create a stable structure and prevent collapse and erosion. The soils were blended and compacted layer by layer, helping the monumental tombs withstand natural disasters and the passage of thousands of years.
The world’s largest cemetery
Nicholas Cahill, the excavation director of the ancient city of Sardes, said around 125 tombs have survived in the Bintepeler area, while historical evidence indicates that the site once contained about 160. Covering approximately 73 square kilometers, the necropolis is considered the world’s largest cemetery.
“There are three very large tumuli here. The Alyattes Tumulus is the largest tumulus in the world. There is no larger monument anywhere,” Cahill said, noting that the monument is about 70 meters high and 300 meters wide.
He added that Herodotus also mentioned the burial grounds, saying that apart from the monuments of Babylon and Egypt, the largest monument was in Lydia and was the Alyattes Tumulus.
Cahill said studies by Teoman Yalçınkaya, the Turkish representative of the Sardes excavations, suggest that the tumulus was built by a workforce of about 300 people over approximately 15 years.
“Very little machinery was used. About 300 people and a few carts were involved in the construction,” Cahill said, emphasizing that large amounts of water were needed to compact the soil.
He noted that different layers of soil have been identified inside the tumulus, including black soil and sandy soil, indicating that construction teams brought soil from different regions and used the materials in successive layers.
With its vast scale and architectural significance, Bintepeler represents an important part of the cultural heritage not only of Manisa but also of the wider world. Viewed from above, its monumental burial mounds resemble giant pyramids scattered across the plain, preserving evidence of the burial traditions and displays of status associated with Lydian kings and aristocrats.

Seljuk stone bearing name of Prophet Muhammad found at Ani
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:15:36 UTC
14:15:36 KST

The name of Prophet Muhammad is repeated six times in Kufic script around an eight-pointed star motif at the center of the stone. (AA photo)
A decorated stone bearing the name of Prophet Muhammad six times in Kufic script has been discovered at the Seljuk Cemetery at the UNESCO-listed Ani Archaeological Site in eastern Türkiye, Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy has announced.
Ersoy said the artifact was unearthed during archaeological excavations that have been ongoing at the Seljuk Cemetery since 2021.
“We found a unique artifact in Ani, where Sultan Alparslan’s conquest in 1064 opened the door to Turkish-Islamic history in Anatolia,” Ersoy said.
The 51-by-21-centimeter stone was carved using the relief technique. The name of Prophet Muhammad is repeated six times in Kufic script around an eight-pointed star motif at the center of the stone. Since only half of the artifact has survived, three of the six inscriptions are currently visible.
The stone is believed to be an architectural element from one of the Seljuk tombs in the cemetery.
“The name ‘Hz. Muhammed’ appears three times in the inscription band surrounding an eight-pointed star-shaped motif at its center,” Ersoy said. “This artifact, believed to have belonged to a Seljuk tomb, is a centuries-old stone testament to the deep love our ancestors held for the Prophet Muhammad.”
According to the Culture and Tourism Ministry, the artifact provides tangible evidence of Ani’s Turkic-Islamic identity, the religious beliefs of the period and the region’s burial culture.
Archaeological findings indicate that the Seljuk Cemetery at Ani is the earliest known Turkic-Islamic cemetery and Turkish martyrdom site in Anatolia.
Ani, conquered by Sultan Alparslan in 1064, is considered one of the key starting points of Turkish-Islamic history in Anatolia. The site also holds particular significance for the region’s architectural heritage, with monuments described as the first conquest mosque, first mosque and first masjid in Anatolia.
Similar decorative designs can be seen at the 1191 Mama Hatun Tomb in Tercan, the 1224 Grand Mosque of Malatya, the Eşrefoğlu Mosque in Beyşehir and the Tahir and Zühre Mosque in 
Konya.

Divers exploring the Princes’ Islands off Istanbul encountered rare species including tope sharks and angular roughsharks, revealing a thriving underwater ecosystem in the Marmara Sea despite environmental pressures.
Dives at Viranbağlar, Yelkenkaya, Kurşun Burnu, Sivri Ada, Kalpazankaya, Hastane Altı, Terk-i Dünya and At Mezarlığı captured returning species. While exploring At Mezarlığı, south of Büyükada facing Sedef Island, divers found large horse bones mingling with active marine life, dive instructor Mehmet Karail said.
Divers spotted a 60-centimeter tope shark and three John Dorys during a single night dive, welcoming the chance to observe species rarely seen in recent years, Karail said. He said they observe lobsters and octopuses frequently.
The region hosts extensive biodiversity. Cameras recorded starfish, swimming crabs, pipefish, sea hares, blennies, scorpionfish, gobies, hermit crabs, tub gurnards, red-lipped gobies, peacock’s tails, warty crabs, combers, crabs, sea pens, anemones, rocklings, stingrays, corals, squids, wrasses, pen shells, flounders, weevers, sea cucumbers, rays, green anemones, feather stars and sponges.
Observations of egg-carrying scorpionfish indicate ongoing breeding cycles.
The Marmara Sea sustains diverse habitats at various depths due to converging waters from the Mediterranean, Aegean and Black Seas, Karail said.
Human activities like heavy fishing and urban waste threaten this ecosystem.
“We do not want to say to our children and grandchildren, ‘This used to be a sea,’” he said, urging the public to stop polluting the waters.
The Marmara Sea, an inland body of water entirely within Türkiye, connects the Black Sea to the Aegean Sea. It has faced severe ecological challenges recently, including a massive marine mucilage outbreak in 2021 caused by agricultural runoff and untreated wastewater.

Türkiye’s ageing population puts pressure on nursing homes

Türkiye’s ageing population is increasing demand for residential care, with nursing homes struggling to keep pace, particularly in major cities.
The share of people aged 65 and over has risen to 11.1 percent of the country’s total population, according to data from the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK), highlighting growing pressure on elderly care and accommodation services.
Family and Social Services Minister Mahinur Özdemir Göktaş said in a statement that 15,263 people are currently receiving care at 178 nursing homes and elderly care and rehabilitation centers operated by the ministry. There are also 290 privately run nursing homes and 18 facilities operated by other public institutions.
Göktaş said applicants to nursing homes have an average age of 78, while capacity expansion efforts are continuing. Six new care facilities with a combined capacity of 710 people are planned, while construction is underway at 24 nursing homes. Fourteen of those facilities are expected to be completed in 2027.
The ministry is also conducting feasibility and project studies for 26 additional nursing homes. Facilities whose projects are completed are expected to be proposed for inclusion in the 2027 Presidential Investment Program.
Waiting lists are particularly long in major cities and at certain facilities, Göktaş said. Preferences for single rooms, as well as climate, dietary habits and a desire to remain in the city where people were born and raised, are among factors contributing to longer waits.
The ministry also plans to expand day care centers and develop community-based care models, allowing older people to receive support while remaining connected to their homes and social surroundings. The approach offers alternatives to institutional care as the country’s demographic profile continues to change.

Academics map Istanbul gravestones to preserve heritage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:15:04 UTC
14:15:04 KST

A state-backed project launched two years ago has academics mapping and cataloging historic gravestones across Istanbul’s iconic mosque courtyards, safeguarding centuries of architectural and historical data.
The Islamic Inscriptions and Gravestones Inventory Project operates under the auspices of the Presidency with support from the Culture and Tourism Ministry and the General Directorate of Cultural Heritage and Museums.
An eight- to 10-person team conducts active fieldwork in the Üsküdar district, photographing each stone, recording precise measurements and capturing GPS coordinates immediately upon entering a site.
Data from headpiece types, plan and section features, decorations and script forms is entered into the ministry’s Museum National Inventory System after a detailed expert examination process. Istanbul Medeniyet University art history faculty member Professor Kadir Pektaş coordinates the work.
He told state-run Anadolu Agency the gravestones should not be viewed merely as grave markers, but rather as vital historical records and significant artworks. “We clarify their locations by taking coordinates with GPS,” he said. “We are essentially taking the title deed of the artifact.”
He said the stones are as important as the Ayazma Mosque where they stand, providing direct dates, names, naive craftsmanship and aesthetic features revealing the deceased person’s profession and social status through their headpieces.
Çanakkale Onsekiz Mart University theology faculty research assistant Betül Eser said gravestones feature symbols representing the afterlife, such as fruit bowls symbolizing heaven’s blessings and cypress trees representing eternity.
She said classical Ottoman gravestones carry phrases of surrender to God, while 19th-century Westernization introduced expressions of worldly attachment and lamentation like scorching death and scorching separation.
“Even if these gravestones occupy a 1- or 2-square-meter area, they are artifacts reflecting the entire belief and social situation of their era,” she said.
Marmara University geography faculty member Assistant Professor Emre Duman said they use geographic information systems to map spatial and attribute data, preventing future losses of relocated or damaged artifacts.
These enclosed burial areas, traditionally reserved for state officials, religious figures and local notables in the Ottoman Empire, are scattered throughout the city’s older districts.
The ministry’s centralized database allows researchers and authorities to track Türkiye’s cultural heritage assets, monitoring their conservation status and preventing the illegal sale of historical artifacts.

“Armenia must first submit an official application for EU membership,” he said, adding that preparations would probably begin “in the near future.”

On the proposed EU application, Peskov pointed to Türkiye and other countries whose accession processes have continued for decades.

Kocharyan, who leads the opposition Armenia Alliance, has denied wrongdoing. His allies described the investigation as politically motivated.

Scientists turn plastic bottles into protein-rich cookies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:03:30 UTC
14:03:30 KST

Scientists turn plastic bottles into protein-rich cookies
Scientists at Southern Illinois University Carbondale (SIU) have developed a way to make 3D-printed cookies using genetically engineered yeast to produce protein and nutrients from plastic and agricultural waste.
The project aims to tackle two of the planet’s crises: plastic waste accumulation and food insecurity.
The team first set out to develop ways to make use of waste plastics, Lahiru Jayakody, an associate professor of microbiology at Southern Illinois University said in an interview with the American Chemical Society (ACS) published on Monday.
“We thought, why not focus on making food? Because plastic is carbon and food is carbon,” he said.
The process starts by breaking down plastic and plant waste with water and oxygen under high temperature and pressure. Genetically engineered yeasts then consume the resulting compounds and produce proteins, fats, and acids. With the addition of fiber, starch, and sweetener, the resulting mix is fed into a 3D printer which molds the paste into any desired shape.
With this technology, the scientists created small protein-rich cookies they dubbed “µBites” or “microbites.” They are waiting for the safety go-ahead from their university to actually taste-test them, however.
The novel technology could be useful in hostile environments, according to Jayakody.
“If you want to produce food in a very extreme environment using the resource you have, carbon resource waste like Arctic, or the desert, and potentially one day in the Mars or the lunar surface, microbeids can do that job,” he told Reuters.
SIU researchers have been developing the technology since 2021, when their µBites concept was selected for NASA’s Deep Space Food Challenge.
The news comes as scientists are paying closer attention to how plastic already unintentionally enters the human food chain.
Researchers have reported microplastics and even smaller nanoplastics in human tissues. A 2025 study published in Nature Medicine detected them in the liver, kidneys, and brain, while a 2026 review published last month said particles had also been found in blood, placenta, and heart tissue.
The particles could pose health risks, with studies linking exposure to inflammation, oxidative stress, cell death, and disruptions to metabolism and immune function. However, researchers say more evidence is needed to determine the effects of long-term exposure in humans.

Two years in limbo: the residents still paying mortgages on flats destroyed in east London fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:00:36 UTC
14:00:36 KST

Sarah Williams vividly remembers the night in 2016 when she camped overnight in a car park to put down a deposit on a flat in the newly completed Spectrum Building in Dagenham, east London.
“People started queuing for those flats 24 hours before they went on sale,” she said. “It was basically the only flat I could afford in London. This was a year before Grenfell, and the flats market in London was completely crazy.”
Four years later, her flat became unsellable when they realised it was covered in dangerous, flammable cladding. Another four years and it, like Grenfell Tower in west London in 2017, had burned down.
It has been two years since the fire at the Spectrum Building on 26 August 2024, which left more than 80 people homeless. They were forced to flee a blaze that broke out in the early hours of the morning, fuelled by the scaffolding that covered the building while the cladding was replaced.
Williams, like many leaseholders, is stuck in a legal limbo, paying the mortgage on a flat that no longer exists, with no idea how much she will get back.
The building’s freeholder, Arinium Ltd, went bankrupt shortly after the fire, and administrators are now responsible for distributing any remaining money, including insurance payouts for loss and damages.
“We still haven’t got our money, and we have no idea whether it will even cover the value of the flats,” said Williams, a charity worker. “We don’t know when we’re going to get it. We’ve still got to pay our mortgages. We’ve still got to pay our rent.
“So many people have told us: ‘It’s terrible what happened to you, and this is a priority for us.’ But our lives are still on hold.”
Insurance payouts are covering emergency accommodation for leaseholders for three years – no one knows what will happen if compensation hasn’t been awarded by then, and people are left to pay both rent and a mortgage.
James Allchurch, who owned two flats which burned down in the fire, said the arduous legal process was compounding the trauma many experienced that night. He and his partner ran from their third-floor flat when he woke up by chance and saw embers and blue flashing lights outside the window.
“We just grabbed whatever clothes we had and ran out the building, leaving everything behind. Because the last thing you think is, we’ll never go back in our flat,” he said.
“It wears you down. I still have nightmares about the fire, I have nightmares about watching our building being demolished, losing everything. There’s an underlying sense of anxiety that has been with me most days since that fire.”
Leaseholders are also concerned that if the freeholder is prosecuted over any fire safety breaches and ultimately fined, that money could come out of the pot of money that would otherwise be distributed to them.
“You want some justice, you want to feel that someone’s taking responsibility and there’s accountability,” Allchurch said. “But the result of that might be that we’re all thousands of pounds worse off.”
As well as frustration at the delays in getting any money back, residents are angry at what they describe as the painfully slow pace of work to replace flammable cladding on buildings across the country.
The day after the fire, the then deputy prime minister, Angela Rayner, told reporters at the site that cladding remediation was going “far too slowly” and vowed to “speed up the process”. But the number of buildings in need of cladding remediation where work has started or been completed has only increased from 50% to 53% in the past two years.
“I don’t want anybody else to go through this,” said Williams. “Do not stand in front of my smouldering building saying this is a priority then fail to follow up on that. I expected fast and urgent action, but I haven’t seen that for the residents of Spectrum and I haven’t seen that for the country.”
Giles Grover, from the End Our Cladding Scandal campaign group, said they were still waiting for Labour to keep its manifesto commitments on building safety.
“Progress has been very slow in the last couple of years,” he said. “There’s been a couple of small steps forward, but it’s piecemeal.
“It feels like Labour prioritised building 1.5m homes, and that’s meant they’ve swept ending the building safety crisis under the carpet. But this fire was a warning, and they need to heed it. There’s hundreds of thousands of people still living in unsafe buildings.”
A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: “The residents of the Spectrum Building must be fully and urgently compensated so they can start to rebuild their lives – and we urge the building’s administrators to resolve the insurance settlements as quickly as possible.
“More broadly, we’re speeding up cladding removal to bring the building safety crisis to an end, and introducing a new legal duty to remediate, to force those responsible to fix unsafe buildings or face criminal prosecution.”

A Tamil summer vegetarian feast: Cynthia Shanmugalingam’s cucumber yoghurt curry and gooseberry pickle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:00:35 UTC
14:00:35 KST

This lovely summery “curry” is a cold, refreshing dish from Karnataka in India, and is eaten widely in Tamil Nadu, just 20 miles across the Palk Strait from my ancestral Tamil homeland in north and eastern Sri Lanka. Along with chefs Louis and Seb in our development kitchen, we decided that smacking the cucumbers helps give them a silky texture, and means the fragrant yoghurt base can get into all the nooks and crannies. It’s wonderful with plain rice and a side of fenugreek-heavy hot Tamil pickle, made with English gooseberries rather than superfood nelli, both of which are said to make your skin shine and hair bouncy.
Hot gooseberry pickle
Prep 10 min
Cook 10 min
Pickle 10 min
Chill 2 hr+
Serves 4
250g gooseberries
  250ml apple cider vinegar
  1 tbsp caster sugar
  1 tsp salt
  1 tsp fenugreek seeds
  1 tbsp mustard seeds
  4 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed
3 tbsp vegetable oil
4 tbsp Kashmiri chilli powder
  Some salt
Wash the gooseberries well, then spread them out on a cloth and leave to dry.
Put the vinegar, 250ml water, the sugar and salt in a saucepan and cook on a high heat until the sugar and salt have dissolved and the liquid is simmering. Add the gooseberries, turn off the heat and leave to pickle for 10 minutes.
In a small frying pan, dry roast the fenugreek for about 60 seconds, until fragrant, then leave to cool. Tip the cooled fenugreek into a small spice grinder or mortar, add the mustard seeds and crushed garlic, then blitz or grind to a paste. Scrape the mix into a small bowl, add the drained gooseberries, the oil, chilli powder and salt, then cover and put in the fridge for at least two hours.
Cucumber yoghurt curry
Prep 15 min
Cook 10 min
Serves 4
2 cucumbers
80g desiccated coconut (frozen or freshly grated), soaked in water for 15 minutes, then drained
2 green chillies, roughly chopped
  4 garlic cloves, peeled and roughly chopped
30g fresh coriander, stalks and leaves
  ½ tsp black peppercorns
  2 tsp sesame seeds
  100g natural yoghurt
  Salt, to taste
Boiled white rice, to serve
For the temper
4 tsp vegetable oil, or coconut oil
10 fresh curry leaves
1 tsp fenugreek seeds (optional)
2 tsp mustard seeds
  2 tsp cumin seeds
  3 dried red chillies, ideally cascabel
First, make a coconut-cucumber paste. Peel the cucumbers, reserving the skins. Wrap each cucumber in clingfilm, then bash them lightly with a rolling pin. Remove the clingfilm, keeping the seeds, and cut the flesh on a slight diagonal into 1cm slices. Put a few of the chopped cucumbers, the cucumber seeds and skins into a blender, add the drained coconut, green chillies, garlic, coriander, black peppercorns and sesame seeds, then blitz smooth.
Put the yoghurt in a medium bowl, and whisk until smooth, then beat in enough water, if need be, to get it to a pouring consistency. Add salt to taste, stir in the cucumber paste and remaining chopped cucumber, then pour into a serving bowl and put in the fridge to chill.
When you’re ready to eat, make the temper. Put the oil in a small frying pan on a high heat, add the curry leaves and, after about 30 seconds, when they’re sizzling, stir in the fenugreek (if using), mustard seeds, cumin seeds and red chillies – stand well back, because the spices will probably splutter. Pour the hot temper, oil and all, over the cucumber yoghurt curry and serve with plain boiled white rice.
- 
  Cynthia Shanmugalingam is chef/proprietor of Rambutan, London SE1

Iran seeks to criminalise all contact with foreign media in latest ‘chilling’ crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:00:35 UTC
14:00:35 KST

Iran has taken the first step towards criminalising contact with foreign media, in a move human rights groups have said attempts to “sever the entire Iranian society from the rest of the world”.
For journalists, researchers and even ordinary citizens, the proposed law being discussed by Iranian lawmakers this month could make speaking to international audiences and groups a potential criminal act and restrict coverage of events such as January’s mass anti-regime protests.
Even social media platforms that the regime considers to be “financed” by another country, such as Instagram and X, would fall under the bill, said Moein Khazaeli, an Iranian human rights lawyer at Dadban, a legal counselling centre for Iranian activists.
“It means any kind of interview, contact, or sending photographs to them [foreign media or organisations] could lead to six months to two years’ imprisonment. Not just the US and Israel, but any contact with foreign media in any country could be considered a crime if one doesn’t inform the intelligence ministry beforehand,” said Khazaeli.
Among the recent examples of the risks facing Iranian journalists is the case of Yalda Moaiery, an acclaimed photographerwho was sentenced this month to 15 years in prison in Tehran for documenting the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Although Moaiery was charged under the espionage law introduced after last year’s 12-day war between Iran and Israel, Khazaeli said the new bill signalled a broader effort to regulate and punish contact between Iranians and foreign media and institutions. “It could move [Iran] to a North Korea kind of situation,” he said.
Moaiery, 44, has spent two decades covering the harsh realities faced by people in Iran, including the nationwide Woman, Life, Freedom protests in 2022 and the anti-regime protests that led to thousands being killed in January.
She came to international prominence in 2019 after criticising Trump’s use of one of her photos of a woman at a demonstration near Tehran University, saying Trump’s sanctions were damaging Iranian lives, including those of her friends and family. “This image shows my people and is for my people, and shouldn’t be abused by these men in Washington,” she wrote.
Now, in a cruel irony, Moaiery said she had been sentenced in absentia for her work covering the US-Israeli war in Iran and accused of media activity deemed to strengthen and aid Israel and the US.
“I have been a critic of Israel and its policies all my life. I am not an Israel supporter, never, ever. And I have always been a critic of American politics. It was like something that you are against, and they want to stick it to you. So it’s hard. It’s super hard,” she told the Guardian.
 Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI), said the new law on media contact risked turning Iran into an “isolated black hole”.
“It is not simply an attack on journalists and citizen journalists; it is an attempt to sever the entire Iranian society from the rest of the world by criminalising the free flow of information itself.
“It sends a chilling message and threatens to turn ordinary academic, professional and civic engagement into a potential national security crime,” she said.
Moaiery was arrested and sentenced to eight years in prison in 2022, but later received an amnesty. This time, however, she fears her sentence could be upheld and she might be jailed.
“Of course, I am scared,” she said. “The only thing that I’m worried about is wasting my life if I have to be there for 15 years. When I get out, I’ll be 60 years old.”
  She also criticised foreign journalists who travelled to Tehran to cover the funeral in July of the late supreme leader, Ali Khamenei.
“I have one word for them: shameful. They just want to say, ‘We were in Tehran.’ OK, but what did you do? They didn’t go and ask people about the economic situation or talk to the families of the thousands who died in January. Why were you here? To participate in their propaganda?”
