====================================================================================================

Sledgehammer sovereignty: Zvi Sukkot’s vigilante stunt hurts Israeli security, law - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
03:13:14 UTC
12:13:14 KST

There are reasons for Israel to oppose monuments that glorify terrorists. That does not justify a Knesset member taking a sledgehammer into a Palestinian village and deciding that he is the law.
Religious Zionist MK Zvi Sukkot entered the West Bank village of Madama near Nablus on Tuesday during an IDF-escorted tour and participated in destroying a monument that appeared to honor members of the al-Aqsa Martyrs Brigades and Palestinians killed during the intifada. Sukkot argued that such memorials glorify those who murdered Jews and encourage others to follow their example.
There is a serious argument there. Societies reveal their values through those they choose to honor, and Israel should not ignore incitement or the glorification of terrorism.
But that is not the issue here.
According to the IDF, Sukkot requested military protection for what was presented as a tour of monuments. Soldiers were diverted from operational duties to provide security. The army says Sukkot and those accompanying him then acted outside the approved plan and began destroying the monument without authorization.
Self-appointed judge, enforcer, demolitionist
The IDF called their conduct deceitful and manipulative.
A member of Knesset does not acquire executive authority because he believes the authorities have failed to act. If Sukkot believed the monument was illegal or constituted incitement, he had every right to demand its removal. He could appeal to the IDF, the Civil Administration, the government, or the courts. He could raise the issue in the Knesset.
What he could not do was appoint himself judge, enforcement officer, and demolition crew.
That is not governance. It is vigilantism.
The principle matters beyond one monument. Israel is a sovereign state because it possesses institutions that exercise authority according to law. Its army uses force under orders. Its police enforce laws. Its courts settle disputes. Elected officials make policy, but they do not carry it out with sledgehammers when the state does not move quickly enough.
Once such distinctions disappear, every group can claim its cause is righteous enough to justify bypassing the law.
There is a security cost.
A day earlier, Central Command chief Maj.-Gen. Avi Bluth reportedly warned that nationalist crime could be the “match” that ignites a broader West Bank escalation. The army is stretched across multiple fronts. Troops should be protecting Israelis and preventing terrorism, not diverted to provide cover for political stunts.
Sukkot says his actions were about protecting Jews. Yet consuming military resources and inflaming a volatile arena does not make Jews safer.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office called the incident unacceptable. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said such monuments should be removed but stressed that the IDF alone should do so.
That distinction matters.
Existence of Israel, institutions bestows responsibility on Jews
The episode deserves more than a political rebuke because it touches something deeper about Jewish sovereignty.
For centuries, Jews knew what it meant to live without power, dependent on rulers who might protect them one year and persecute them the next. The creation of Israel changed that. Jews now possess an army, a government, courts, police, and the ability to defend themselves.
That power carries responsibilities.
Jewish sovereignty was not created so that Jews could enjoy the privilege of lawlessness.
Strength does not mean acting without restraint. It means having the power to act while choosing to remain within the law.
Israel’s enemies portray the Jewish state as motivated by vengeance, domination, and contempt for Palestinians. Those accusations are often dishonest and politically motivated. Israel should reject them forcefully.
But it should also refuse to provide images that reinforce that caricature.
What lesson does an Israeli child learn from seeing an elected lawmaker participate in destroying a monument while soldiers stand nearby? That laws matter only until someone believes strongly enough that he is right? That Jewish sovereignty gives individuals permission to use force whenever institutions disappoint them?
That cannot be the message.
Israel has every right to confront incitement and prevent the glorification of terrorism. The IDF says it removes monuments and symbols deemed incitement when authorized to do so.
The Jewish answer to lawlessness cannot be Jewish lawlessness.
Sukkot’s actions represented neither Jewish strength nor responsible leadership. Jewish power means the ability to defend ourselves while remaining governed by law.
That is a far stronger answer to our enemies than any sledgehammer.

Another post on the social media platform contained an image of a map with “Lake Ontario” crossed out and “Lake America” spelled out in gold letters with the American flag.
Trump bashes Canada in social media flurry
The posts came amid a flurry of claims by the president against Canada, including that it has been “ripping off the US for decades” by charging US farmers more than 400% in tariffs, driving companies out of business, and causing the US to lose an average of $60 billion a year.

Lake Ontario sits on the border between Canada and the US, although around 53% of it is Canada. It is the smallest and easternmost of the five Great Lakes of North America.

Australia’s royal commission on antisemitism to conclude hearings after Bondi Beach attack

2026-08-26
03:12:59 UTC
12:12:59 KST

Australia's Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion held its final day of hearings on Wednesday, wrapping up months of testimony from Australians in the aftermath of the 2025 Bondi Beach mass shooting.
Established in the wake of the ISIS-inspired attack on a Hanukkah event at Bondi Beach in Sydney, where Sajid and Naveed Akram allegedly murdered 15, the commission has heard from hundreds of Jewish community members, policy experts, and security officials.
The commission has also reportedly received over 20,000 submissions.
Some of the key witnesses include survivors of the massacre, Holocaust survivors, and the head of Australia's national security agency.
Chabad of Bondi director Rabbi Yehoram Ulman is scheduled to be among the last to testify on Wednesday. Ulman's son-in-law, Rabbi Eli Schlanger was killed in the attack.
Royal commission was initially rejected, only formed after public pressure
Some in Australia have called for the commission's duration to be extended to allow for a more thorough investigation. New South Wales Premier Chris Minns told the press he would call for an extension to get “the fundamental truth of what happened” out.
“If we need to for a couple of weeks longer, given that most of the expense was spent setting it up, that would seem to be money well spent because both the federal and the state government are relying on these recommendations to shape some of our policy,” News.com.au reported him as having said.
MP Julian Leeser, who has Jewish ancestry, submitted a motion in Parliament to extend the commission, though it was defeated.
Following the attack, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese initially rejected calls for a royal commission. Weeks later, after calls from Jewish organizations, individuals, and politicians, he announced the formation of the commission.
From its formation, the commission was tasked with four main areas: Investigating antisemitism, making recommendations to assist security services to respond to antisemitism, examining the circumstances surrounding the Bondi attack, and making recommendations to strengthen social cohesion in the country.
Wednesday's testimony focused on social cohesion.
Following the conclusion of testimony, the commission, headed by former High Court justice Virginia Bell, will convene to draft the final report, expected around the December anniversary of the attack.
The commission released an interim report in April, which found that Australia's legal and regulatory frameworks hadn't stopped security agencies from preventing or responding to the attack.
Among the recommendations of the interim report were calls to expand protection for Jewish communities during holiday events and services, updating the counterterrorism handbook, and a national gun buyback plan. Other recommendations weren't made public due to the security aspect of the commission.
Albanese's government pledged to adopt the interim recommendations.
Mathilda Heller and Reuters contributed to this report.

Taiwan’s CPO supply chain broadens as Nvidia's light-based technology enters mass production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
03:12:54 UTC
12:12:54 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s co-packaged optics (CPO) supply chain is expanding beyond component manufacturing as the technology moves into mass production, CTEE reported Wednesday.
CPO is a packaging technology that integrates light-based components with computing chips in the same package, shortening signal paths to reduce power consumption and transmission delays. Nvidia’s Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics platform, which incorporates CPO, entered full mass production earlier this month.
TSMC, Siliconware Precision Industries Co., and Foxconn are among the Taiwanese companies already involved in the supply chain. Analysts have also identified Fiber Optic Communications Inc., Browave Corp., Ezconn Corp., and Mpi Corp. as potential beneficiaries, with businesses covering fiber array units, high-speed connectivity, and testing equipment.
TSMC manufactures light-based components, including photonic integrated circuits (PICs). The chipmaker can also leverage its advanced packaging technology to combine them with electronic integrated circuits (EICs).
Siliconware Precision handles wafer-level packaging, assembly, and testing. Foxconn integrates CPO switches into complete network systems that can be deployed in data center racks.
On the optical side, Fiber Optic Communications and Browave provide fiber array units. They act as precision optical interfaces that connect chips with external fiber networks, according to Sinotrade.
The supply chain also extends to other forms of high-speed connectivity. Mpi provides components and modules used in optical communications, as well as high-frequency radio-frequency (RF) connectors.
Testing is another key part of CPO mass production, as inspection must move beyond final testing to the wafer and individual chip stages. The process involves checking how well light is generated and transmitted, including its wavelength and signal loss, as well as whether electrical signals remain intact.
Taiwanese testing interface suppliers include WinWay Technology Co. and Chunghwa Precision Test Tech Co. Msscorps Co., meanwhile, provides materials and failure-analysis services to help identify problems that may arise during the development and production of CPO components.
Nvidia said its Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics is five times more energy-efficient than traditional networks that rely on separate, pluggable optical parts. By built-in connections that place optical parts closer to the main switch chip, it allows AI applications to run for five times longer and speeds up data center setups by 30%.

Alarming study reveals Israeli teachers lag behind global peers substantially in all metrics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
03:12:15 UTC
12:12:15 KST

Israeli teachers scored below their counterparts in the countries examined in literacy, numeracy, and problem-solving, according to a new study that also found a substantial skills gap between academically educated teachers and other Israeli workers with academic degrees.
The study, released on Wednesday and conducted by Yael Melzer of the Shoresh Institution for Socioeconomic Research, analyzed data from the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) 2022-2023 Program for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC).
Israeli teachers scored below the average for the 18 comparison countries across all three areas examined. Among teachers with academic education, Israeli teachers also scored below the comparison-country average in every age group.
PIAAC does not directly measure classroom performance or teaching ability. Rather, it assesses adults’ literacy, numeracy, and adaptive problem-solving skills - their ability to process information and deal with everyday and work-related tasks.
The findings came against the backdrop of the wider 2022-2023 PIAAC results, in which Israeli adults scored below the OECD average across all three areas.
International gap tied to multiple factors
Melzer’s study focuses specifically on teachers.
Part of the international gap may be connected to formal education. Some 37% of Israeli teachers in the study held master’s degrees, compared with 49% among teachers in the comparison countries.
But the difference did not disappear when teachers with similar levels of education were compared. Instead, the gap was concentrated among those with academic degrees.
Among Israelis with academic degrees, teachers scored lower than degree-holders working in other professions. The pattern was reversed among Israelis whose highest level of education was upper secondary: Teachers scored higher than similarly educated workers outside teaching.
The divide was particularly pronounced among men.
While teachers and other workers with academic degrees in the comparison countries recorded broadly similar results, academically educated male teachers in Israel lagged considerably behind Israeli men with degrees working in other professions.
The study found a smaller, though still visible, gap among women.
A similar pattern emerged among teachers with academic backgrounds in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics.
In the comparison countries, people with academic backgrounds in STEM were generally among the highest-skilled workers.
In Israel, teachers with STEM backgrounds recorded the lowest skill levels among academically educated teachers in literacy and problem-solving, while their numeracy skills were similar to those of other academically educated teachers. They also lagged markedly behind Israelis with similar academic backgrounds working outside education.
Melzer interpreted the pattern as evidence that the education system has greater difficulty competing for highly skilled workers with academic degrees. The study argued that while teaching appears relatively successful in attracting skilled workers from among people without academic degrees, it has more difficulty recruiting and retaining highly skilled academics.
The data showed an association rather than establishing why those workers choose other professions. Melzer pointed to greater rewards for skills in the private sector as one possible explanation, particularly for the pronounced gap among men.
Substantial differences within the system
Substantial differences also appeared within Israel’s education system.
Teachers in the Arab education stream recorded markedly lower scores than teachers in all other streams examined.
Ultra-Orthodox (haredi) teachers also scored below teachers in the secular and religious non-haredi systems in literacy and numeracy.
The study noted that those differences do not exist in isolation. Melzer pointed to lower investment and shortages of infrastructure and resources in Arab education and noted that the difference between spoken and written Arabic may also affect PIAAC performance in a way that cannot be fully separated from the skills being measured.
The other particularly weak point was early-childhood education.
Upper-secondary teachers recorded substantially stronger skills than teachers working with younger children across all three areas measured. Primary-school teachers also performed better than preschool teachers in literacy and problem-solving.
The findings came as the Education Ministry moved to recruit additional teachers ahead of the coming school year. The ministry this month opened a temporary employment track allowing schools to recruit up to 8,000 teachers through personal contracts, including professionals without previous teaching experience, with full-time salaries that can reach roughly NIS 20,000 a month depending on their experience and professional background.
Shoresh recommended changes aimed at attracting more highly skilled candidates into teaching.
The study proposed raising admission requirements for teacher training, including a model in which future teachers first complete a degree in the subject they intend to teach and only afterward undergo shorter pedagogical training.
It also recommended changing compensation structures to make teaching more competitive for highly skilled graduates, alongside targeted efforts in Arab and early-childhood education.
“The findings show that Israel’s education system is struggling to attract and retain highly skilled academics,” Shoresh president Prof. Dan Ben-David said, arguing that the gaps both with other countries and within Israel require changes to how teachers are recruited, trained, and compensated.
Ben-David said particular attention should be directed toward Arab and early-childhood education, warning that without broader reforms, “it will be difficult to narrow the gap with the leading countries and improve the quality of teaching in Israel.”
The study’s broader concern was not only the number of teachers entering classrooms but also the education system’s ability to attract highly skilled people into the profession.

Hird has chance to finally deliver true unity Essendon seeks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
03:10:54 UTC
12:10:54 KST

analysis
Essendon is seeking unity under Mark McVeigh and James Hird has the chance to deliver it
When new Essendon coach Mark McVeigh was flanked by president Andrew Welsh and CEO Tim Roberts at his introductory press conference on Wednesday, there was a clear theme emanating from the day: unity.
Unity is the thing Essendon has strived for, and failed to find, for the last two decades as it has cycled through players, coaches and administrators in a bid to end an infamous finals drought.
Welsh hopes that by hiring McVeigh he is able to kill two birds with one stone.
The process to find its next coach acted as a litmus test for Essendon to actually show it had changed as a club after years of saying it with no actions to follow.
When Brad Scott was ousted midway through the season and James Hird launched his candidacy on national TV in the same week, the consensus was that Hird's return to the Bombers coaches box was a fait accompli.
The lack of belief or trust in Essendon as a sporting organisation left candidates pulling out, believing the club's trumpeted 'process' was actually a sham designed to deliver Hird the role.
It proved to be anything but, as Hird himself revealed after being beaten by McVeigh, leaving both he and Essendon at a potentially pivotal crossroads.
This rejected bid to be Essendon's coach is completely different to Hird's last rejection, when he finished second behind Brad Scott.
There was something symbolic in Hird, one of Essendon's favourite sons, being beaten out by Scott, a nemesis of his from the Brisbane Lions heyday.
Scott winning the coaching race was reminiscent another occasion where he'd famously got one over Hird, overpowering the under-cooked then-Essendon skipper on the wing during a key period in the 2001 grand final.
Scott, having arrived from the AFL and being selected by an independent panel, appeared a choice that was an aggressive attempt to get away from the fabric of Essendon.
Scott's regime brought a lot of change, and while his decisions may eventually age well, they left Essendon's diehards feeling more disillusioned with every loss that followed.
Hird wasn't exactly forbidden from returning to Essendon while Scott was in charge, but he also wasn't welcomed with open arms.
This time around is different as both McVeigh and Welsh prepare to launch full-court presses to get Hird back through the doors, just not as the coach.
While the knock on Hird's coaching bid was his lack of experience in a recent AFL coaches box, what cannot be disputed is his knowledge of the game.
If Hird is able to get past the itch of being the coach, he could prove to be an incredible asset as either a football boss, or as a developmental coach. The opportunities are endless, given Essendon has basically wiped out its entire football department.
Having held the belief that McVeigh would have come with him had he been successful, as he also pledged to do in 2022, Hird now has the chance to repay the favour.
Welsh has hinted at Essendon bolstering its football department with key appointments in the coming months as it looks to surround McVeigh with a strong staff. It could do worse than bringing Hird back into the fold.
It is notable that Hird, while not receiving the job he wanted, mentioned he has experienced healing during the process in the form of mending fences with individuals he had fallen out with over the club's supplements scandal.
Hird is smart enough to know what his decision from this point on has the potential to do to his beloved club.
As Essendon desperately seeks unity, Hird's return would guarantee it, and he knows that. It is hard to see him turning his back on Essendon to try and coach elsewhere, even if that means he never gets to coach again.
At the front of Hird's mind will be two scenarios: winning Essendon's next premiership, but not as the coach, or winning a premiership elsewhere as the coach. He must figure out which of those will make him happiest.
The benefits of the McVeigh hire are two-fold for Essendon.
He has spent significant time in the coaches' boxes of two teams that have enjoyed deep September runs, albeit without winning the whole lot.
McVeigh's history of working with both the Allies and the Swans Academy was a major selling point given Essendon's list demographic.
Critics suggesting McVeigh's hire was simply a case of jobs for mates were disrespectful to both his decade of coaching reps as well as Welsh's ability to be a professional.
Contrary to all the hysteria about Essendon only hiring "Essendon people", McVeigh is the first Essendon person to be hired as the club's senior coach since Hird's departure in 2015.
The coaches that have followed Hird — John Worsfold, Ben Rutten and Scott — have all enjoyed success at other clubs like McVeigh has, but lacked an ability to truly connect with the club and its fans.
That is McVeigh's superpower. He connects, and he connects with all generations.
It was not by accident that the club filmed McVeigh being greeted at The Hangar by Ken Fraser, the captain of Essendon's 1965 premiership side.
It was also not by accident that both McVeigh and Welsh continually referenced the goal for Essendon to be "one club", making a pointed note to invest in the club's AFLW program.
McVeigh even appeared on a podcast with some of Essendon's biggest content creators from outside the club, a stark difference from Scott, who gave off the vibe of an untouchable CEO fans could never really connect with, rather than your friendly local head coach.
It is no surprise that McVeigh's arrival has already seemingly caused a change in tune from both Hird and fellow Essendon icon, Matthew Lloyd.
Since his retirement at the end of 2009, Lloyd has mostly stayed away from the club while becoming one of the AFL's most prominent media figures.
Lloyd is uncompromising when it comes to his views on Essendon, annoying segments of the club's fanbase who wonder why he has not stepped in to help fix the problems he keeps highlighting.
As McVeigh's appointment grew closer, Lloyd curiously changed his tune and said he would like to go back to club land.
It would be no surprise to see him in an official role at Essendon in the coming years as McVeigh builds out his staff.
All of this brings us back to Hird and Essendon's seemingly never-ending quest to find unity.
The basic pitch from Hird's supporters is that he is the only one who can truly bring unity back to what has been a broken club.
The pitch just missed one thing.
Who says Hird can only bring unity as Essendon's coach?

A US federal judge has blocked plans to auction more than 100 artifacts recovered from the wreck of the Titanic, siding with the US government and preservationists who raised concerns about the proposed sale and the care of the historic collection, The Washington Post reported Tuesday.
District Judge Rebecca Beach Smith in Norfolk, Virginia ruled Monday that the auction must be put on hold. She rejected an argument by RMS Titanic, the company that holds exclusive salvage rights to the wreck, that the artifacts were outside the court’s jurisdiction, the Post said.
Smith said any sale of the artifacts would require court approval. She also raised concerns about the condition of RMS Titanic’s collection, pointing to the company’s financial difficulties.
The judge ordered the company to provide the court with an inventory of the artifacts and information about their condition, said the report.
RMS Titanic had proposed auctioning more than 100 items recovered during a deep-sea expedition decades ago. The collection includes gem-studded jewelry, tableware and a bronze cherub that once decorated the Titanic’s grand staircase.
The proposed auction faced opposition from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration as well as historians and archaeologists who argued that the artifacts should be preserved and maintained as a collection.
The French government also protested the sale because France participated in the expedition that recovered some of the artifacts.
The Titanic sank in the North Atlantic in April 1912 after striking an iceberg on its maiden voyage from Southampton to New York. More than 1,500 people died in the disaster.

Too small for fries: Drought shrinks Belgian potatoes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
03:05:00 UTC
12:05:00 KST

Too small for fries: Drought shrinks Belgian potatoes
- Belgian potato farmers face a severe drought causing potatoes to shrink, making them unsuitable for traditional fries despite the flavour remaining intact.
- The Comijn family relies on stored 2025 potatoes to meet supply contracts but expects a shortfall and lower-quality varieties must be used.
- Fry vendors warn that potato shortages could raise fry prices, affecting 4,500 shops and causing concern among consumers in Belgium.
AI generated
AMAY – Mathieu Comijn inspected rows of potatoes in a field of cracked earth and browned leaves, pulling from the ground tubers barely the size of ping-pong balls.
“How do you expect to make fries out of these?” asked the Belgian farmer in frustration, as he uprooted another plant and examined it.
“Normally, they should be at least four times this size.”
Like many Belgian farmers this summer, Comijn’s harvest in Amay, near the eastern city of Liege, has been hit by a devastating combination of weather extremes.
First, a spate of heavy rain and storms at the end of spring weakened the soil. Then, as elsewhere in Europe, exceptionally hot and dry conditions followed – blamed by scientists on man-made climate change.
That caused the soil to harden into compact clumps in which potatoes “cannot breathe properly” and struggle to grow, the farmer explained.
“It’s a disaster,” the 30-year-old told AFP. “I’ve never seen anything like it.”
The problem for Comijn is that all these rows of Bintje potatoes, a prized variety in Belgium, were destined to become long, golden fries – a beloved staple in a country dotted by “friteries” or “frituren”, street stalls specialising in the stuff.
Yet with just a month to go before the harvest, set for around Sept 20, none are larger than the palm of his hand. The only silver lining is that their flavour has not been spoilt by their diminished size.
‘Too painful’
Comijn’s father Stephane has been so distressed by the situation that he refused to visit the field for several days.
“It’s too painful,” said the septuagenarian, wiping his forehead. The former head of the family farm struggles to remember weather this dry in the region – except, perhaps, during a historic heatwave in 1976.
But good harvest or bad, the Comijn family, who grows 500 hectares of potatoes, still have supply contracts to meet.
As the world’s top exporter of frozen fries, Belgium applies strict rules to its potato trade.
Before the harvest, growers and processors negotiate both delivery volumes and prices.
To help fulfil part of their commitments, the Comijns will draw on stocks from 2025, when the harvest was exceptionally abundant.
“We had started throwing some of them away,” Stephane Comijn explained, to make space for the 2026 crop.
“But now they’re worth money,” he said, standing in front of a refrigerated warehouse kept at 10 deg C, where mountains of 2025 potatoes remain in storage.
Supply crunch
But Stephane Comijn knows using the 2025 stocks will not be enough.
“We’re going to have to use varieties that aren’t as good,” he lamented. “People at the fry shops complain. You can explain to them that it’s because of the drought, but they don’t understand.”
Bernard Lefevre, the president of the national union of fry vendors, sought to put things into perspective.
“There’s always a problem,” said Lefevre, who has worked in the sector for a quarter-century.
“Either there are too many potatoes, like last year, and prices collapse, so producers say it’s a catastrophe, or it’s the opposite extreme.
“And yet, year after year, we manage to get through it.”
But with supplies under pressure, fry prices are likely to heat up too – and for Lefevre, who represents 4,500 fry shops across Belgium, that is no small matter.
“Aside from illness in the royal family, the second-worst piece of news a Belgian can hear is that the price of a cone of fries is going up,” he said. AFP

At least 25 pct former NFL players have degenerative brain disorder: study

12:01:08 KST

LOS ANGELES, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- At least one in four former National Football League (NFL) players who died between 2016 and 2021 had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disorder, according to a new study published Tuesday in the British Medical Journal.
Researchers from Mass General Brigham, Boston University and the Concussion & CTE Foundation examined 235 donated brains from 878 former players who died between 2016 and 2021.
In that sample, 215 brains were diagnosed with CTE, meaning that, to take those who didn't donate their brains into account, at least 24.5 percent had the disease.
Dr. Leah Croll, a neurologist at Maimonides Medical Center, said repeated head impacts -- a dominant feature of American football -- are associated with an abnormal buildup of tau protein that damages brain cells and may eventually contribute to problems with memory, thinking, behavior and mood.
"The true number could be substantially higher, and even this minimum estimate suggests that CTE is not a rare outcome among former NFL players," she told ABC News.
In a statement, the NFL Players Association called the study "a sobering reminder that football carries real risks," noting that the findings should spur broader action to advance research, improve access to care, develop treatments and support affected players. ■

WASHINGTON – Meta Platforms and state attorneys-general have discussed a possible mid-trial settlement of a blockbuster case accusing the company of deliberately designing Facebook and Instagram to get teenagers addicted, people familiar with the matter said.
The trial, now in its second week in federal court in Oakland, California, poses an enormous risk for Meta as the top legal officers of 29 states are seeking both massive financial penalties on behalf of the public and mandatory changes to how the platforms operate.
The people familiar with settlement talks asked not to be identified due to their sensitivity.
A spokesperson for Meta had no immediate comment.
A representative of the attorney-general’s office in California declined to comment.
Representatives of the other three states leading the case – Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey – did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The states have alleged violations of state consumer protection and federal privacy laws, which carry fines that add up quickly when multiplied by millions of young Instagram and Facebook users.
Meta has denied the states’ allegations and accused the attorneys-general of seeking unreasonable design changes and an “outlandish payout”. By Meta’s own calculations, a loss at trial could saddle it with penalties of as much as US$1.4 trillion (S$1.8 trillion), an amount close to its market capitalisation and unheard of in the annals of legal history.
A settlement would likely amount to a far smaller sum.
During the first week of testimony at the trial, jurors heard from Instagram head Adam Mosseri, as well as a collection of current and former Meta employees who helped design its social media platforms and study how teen users interact with tools designed to cut down on problematic use.
Lawyers have said they also expect to call Meta founder and chief executive officer Mark Zuckerberg to testify.
The four attorneys-general spearheading the case alleged under their separate state laws that Meta knowingly designed features that encouraged compulsive and prolonged use of its platforms by young people, while simultaneously misleading consumers about safety features.
The broader bipartisan group of 29 states accused Meta of collecting data from users under 13 years old in violation of the federal Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act.
Social media companies are facing a global backlash over concerns that they profit at the expense of young users, for whom a growing body of research shows that excessive screen time is dangerously unhealthy.
While the authorities from Australia to Europe have enacted or proposed outright bans for youths in the last year, legislative crackdowns in the US have had limited success, turning the courts into a pivotal battleground.
Meta, Alphabet’s Google, Snap and TikTok all face billions of dollars in potential exposure from more than 3,000 personal injury claims by individuals and families in the US and about 1,300 more lawsuits by public school districts across the nation. BLOOMBERG

SEOUL, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's retail sales rose in single digits in July, driven by strong online demand for groceries and solid offline demand for luxury brands, government data showed Wednesday.

Revenue of online retailers mounted 8.5 percent, and sales by offline retailers swelled 3.2 percent.

Grocery purchases in cyberspace advanced 10.4 percent last month, but food demand in offline stores retreated 2.6 percent.
Online demand for services, such as travel, food delivery and e-coupon purchase, surged 17.5 percent, while offline sales of foreign luxury brands soared 28.9 percent.
Online sales of home appliances increased 11.4 percent, propelled by high demand for air conditioners and cooling equipment. ■

CANBERRA, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) said on Wednesday that the Australian consumer price index (CPI) rose by 3.5 percent in the 12 months to July, down from 3.8 percent in June and the lowest annual figure since November 2025.
Despite the fall in headline inflation, the ABS noted that the annual trimmed mean, the measure of underlying inflation preferred by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), remained steady at 3.6 percent in July.
Economists from the Commonwealth Bank of Australia had forecast that CPI growth would fall to 3.2 percent in July and the trimmed mean would ease to 3.5 percent.
The ABS said that housing prices were the biggest driver of headline inflation in the 12 months to July, rising by 5.0 percent, followed by a 3.2 percent rise in food and non-alcoholic beverage prices.
Rachael McCririck, head of price statistics at the ABS, said that new dwelling prices rose by 5.7 percent in the year to July as builders passed on higher costs for materials and labor.
She said that automotive fuel prices were 7.5 percent higher in July than in June due to higher global oil prices and the federal government winding down fuel tax relief measures.
The latest forecasts from the RBA projected that annual trimmed mean inflation would drop to 3.3 percent in December before falling within the central bank's 2-3 percent target range in 2027. ■

Chinese envoy calls for cessation of hostilities to ensure food production
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
11:00:23 CST
12:00:23 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese envoy on Tuesday called for greater efforts to end hostilities and create a secure environment for food production.
Fu Cong, China's permanent representative to the United Nations, made the remarks at a Security Council open debate on the council's role in mitigating global and local food crises.
"Raging conflicts displace people, destroy farmland and disrupt food production, and are an important driver of humanitarian crises and hunger," said Fu.
"The Security Council bears the primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security. It should make promoting political solutions to conflicts a priority, actively engage in mediation and good offices, encourage the parties to resolve their differences through dialogue, and work for an early and lasting ceasefire to create the basic conditions for restoring agricultural production," he said.
International humanitarian law is a fundamental baseline that must be respected, Fu said, stressing that hunger must never be used as a weapon of war.
Parties to conflict should always put the protection of life first, protect agricultural infrastructure, avoid disrupting agricultural activities, and ensure the unimpeded delivery of humanitarian assistance, including food aid, he said.
In the context of economic globalization, food production and supply are closely linked to the international situation, particularly the global logistics and transportation system. In the face of intensifying geopolitical rivalry and regional conflicts, the international community should ensure the safe and unobstructed operation of land and sea trade routes and the normal flow of essential goods such as food and fertilizer, Fu said.
China welcomes the UN initiative to establish a time-bound mechanism for the Strait of Hormuz and supports a greater role for the United Nations, he said.
At the same time, all parties should further uphold open and transparent market policies, deepen international cooperation on food supply, and promote the rational allocation of food resources globally, he said.
Food security governance is a global issue that requires coordinated action and a collective response from all countries. It cannot be dictated by a handful of countries or interest groups, Fu said.
All parties should firmly support the United Nations in playing a central role, while the representation and voice of emerging market economies and developing countries in international organizations dealing with food-related issues should be effectively enhanced, he said.
"We should uphold the principles of extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits, promote a more equitable, reasonable, inclusive and effective global food security governance system, and safeguard the common interests of all countries," Fu said.
As the world's largest grain producer, China feeds more than 1.4 billion people with less than 9 percent of the world's arable land. Through its own efforts, China has achieved basic self-sufficiency in grain supply and absolute security of staple food, Fu said.
"This is not only a great achievement in China's development, but also a major contribution to safeguarding global food security," he said.
China has always been committed to strengthening international cooperation, helping improve global food security and contributing to global poverty reduction, Fu said.
China stands ready to continue upholding the vision of building a community with a shared future for humanity, work with all parties, and make greater contributions to the complete eradication of global hunger and to world peace, security, development and prosperity, he added. ■

Writing the rulebook? China to steer world’s first solid-state battery standards
As next-gen EV tech accelerates, the global standard agency’s nod could allow Beijing to export its domestic testing benchmarks worldwide
A Chinese-proposed international standard for automotive solid-state batteries has been approved as a new work item by the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) – marking the first of its kind for the advanced power systems and the nation’s latest effort to shape rules in emerging industries.
Led by China, with input from technical experts in France, Japan, South Korea and other countries, the proposal outlined application guidelines, items and conditions for testing rechargeable lithium-ion solid-state batteries used in electric vehicles (EVs), according to an official statement by the State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR).
The governmental agency said the framework would draw on domestic research and development benchmarks to standardise testing specifications for solid-state batteries, which are widely viewed as the next frontier for EV power systems.
Announced by the SAMR last week, the China-led proposal comes amid intensifying global competition in advanced technologies, as major economies increasingly leverage standard-setting to secure long-term industrial influence.
“When Chinese products go to an overseas market, they will more easily meet the requirements – there will be few major changes in parameters, production processes and so on,” said a veteran Chinese researcher on international standardisation, who spoke on condition of anonymity. This would place China in the position of setting benchmarks that others followed, she noted.

NMC orders monthly reporting of student suicides by medical colleges

NMC orders monthly reporting of student suicides by medical colleges
Anuja Jaiswal / TNN / Updated: Aug 26, 2026, 10:54 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
For each suicide or unnatural death, colleges have to report the student's course/year, date and place of occurrence, police intimation, FIR status, institutional inquiry and corrective measures.
NEW DELHI: The National Medical Commission (NMC) has directed medical colleges to maintain updated records of student suicides and unnatural deaths and submit a certified Action Taken Report (ATR) every month, following Supreme Court directions on student mental health and safety. It has also asked institutions to fill vacant faculty and key administrative posts within four months.The commission has marked the compliance exercise “MOST URGENT” and asked institutions to accord it top priority.The move comes amid a rise in student suicides. On this issue, Dr Om Prakash, Professor of Psychiatry and Head, Department of Geriatric Mental Health, sharing NCRB data, said 14,488 student deaths by suicide were recorded in 2024, up 4.3% from 13,892 in 2023. The number rose from 8,068 in 2014 to 14,488 in 2024, an increase of around 80% over the decade. More than 1.15 lakh student deaths by suicide were recorded during 2015-24.For each suicide or unnatural death, colleges have to report the student's course/year, date and place of occurrence, police intimation, FIR status, institutional inquiry and corrective measures.The NMC has also sought department-wise details of sanctioned, filled and vacant faculty posts, non-teaching vacancies and key administrative positions, including dean/director, medical superintendent, registrar, wardens and counsellors.
Colleges have been given four months to fill vacant faculty and key administrative posts, with special recruitment drives for reserved posts. The compliance format also requires 24x7 access to qualified medical assistance on campus or within 1 km.
The IHBAS presentation highlights the role of faculty as “gatekeepers”, who can often notice changes in attendance, academic performance, withdrawal or behaviour. Faculty are advised to recognise warning signs, approach distressed students, ask directly about suicidal thoughts, facilitate referral and follow up, without taking on the role of therapists.It also cautions against attributing suicide to a single trigger such as examination failure, relationship problems or social media. Academic pressure, fear of failure, bullying, ragging or harassment, discrimination, social isolation and financial difficulties are among the factors identified as contributing to vulnerability.The NMC said information submitted by institutions will be consolidated to monitor compliance with the Supreme Court's directions and submitted to the Ministry of Education as required.

She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Sen. Darline Graham won Tuesday’s Republican primary runoff for the South Carolina Senate seat previously held by her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham.
 
Darline Graham, 62, defeated Rep. Ralph Norman 52.5% to 47.6%. 
 
The two had emerged as the top candidates in a crowded Republican primary earlier this month. Neither candidate had secured enough votes to win the Aug. 11 contest outright, sending the race to a runoff.
 
The victory puts Darline Graham on track to appear on the November ballot as the Republican nominee for a full six-year Senate term. She will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews.
 
Lindsey Graham, 71, died unexpectedly in early July after more than two decades in the Senate. He had won the Republican nomination for another term in the initial June primary before his death.
 
South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Darline Graham to temporarily fill the vacant Senate seat. She subsequently announced her campaign for a full term and received the backing of President Donald Trump.
 
In her victory speech, Graham said she "humbly" accepts the nomination to serve as the Republican nominee for the upper chamber.

Norman, for his part, said he “hates it for the state" and "never understood" why Trump got involved.
 
"He has that right, that's his prerogative ... his policies are good, I never understood why he got in this race to beat but it is what it is, and I'll accept it," he said.

In the race to replace Oklahoma Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt, who cannot run for re-election due to term limits, there will be a runoff between Trump-endorsed former state Sen. Mike Mazzei and Gentner Drummond. The winner will face Cyndi Munson, who won the Democratic primary, beating her two opponents with 74.9% of the vote.

South Carolina Republicans voted to try to keep one of the state’s U.S. Senate seats in the Graham family, as Darline Graham Nordone, who was appointed to fill it temporarily, has won the runoff for the special Republican primary election to replace her late brother Lindsey Graham on the ballot in the November general election.
The Associated Press called the race at 9:01 p.m. ET, as Nordone led with about 52.5% of the vote.
Nordone said in a speech after securing the nomination that she has mixed emotions about her primary victory and that she misses her brother.
“There is still a big hole in my heart,” Nordone told supporters at a rally, “but I know he’s looking down right now very proud of everyone in this room.”
She then added that her nomination is merely “the starting line for an even bigger fight which lies ahead.”
Nordone will next face off against the Democratic candidate Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who won her primary in June. The upper chamber seat, though, is unlikely to flip in Democrats’ favor; the Cook Political Report rates the race as “Solid Republican.”
In June, Graham won the Republican primary race to compete for his fifth term as Senator, but after his death the following month, a special primary election was called for Aug. 11. While Nordone, who was appointed by South Carolina’s Governor to serve out the remainder of her brother’s term, earned the highest share of the vote on Aug. 11, she fell short of the majority she needed to win the race, triggering the runoff. Nordone earned nearly 33% of the vote on Aug. 11, while her opponent, U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman, came in second, with nearly 25%, sending both candidates to the runoff race.
President Donald Trump had championed Nordone in the race, publicly encouraging her to run for a full term before she had even announced her plans to do so. In a Truth Social post in July, Trump called Nordone “a spectacular person, and a true American Patriot.”
“Lindsey was one of the greatest people and Senators I have ever known, and his sister shares his deep love of our Country, and the State of South Carolina,” Trump said in his post. He added that he asked Nordone to run for a full term, saying, “I hope Darline does this, in that there would be nobody better to honor the legacy of her beloved brother, Lindsey. Darline, who comes from an absolutely incredible family, has been a WINNER all of her life and, should she accept, has my Complete and Total Endorsement in the Special Election for U.S. Senate in South Carolina.”
Although Nordone was a strong supporter of her brother’s political career over the years, she had never before held elected office. Her lack of political experience was the subject of scrutiny during her campaign, particularly after a debate against Norman leading up to Tuesday’s runoff. When asked during the debate if Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues for the U.S., Nordone replied: “I’m just going to be honest here … I’m not that informed on national security, so.”
Her opponents were quick to criticize her for the remark. Nikki Haley, Trump’s former U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. who endorsed Norman in the race, shared a clip of Nordone’s response to the debate question on X, saying, “Lindsey Graham was well informed on the United States’ national security. Darline Graham admits she’s not. This is not something you inherit. And it’s critical in the U.S. Senate.”
Nordone responded to the backlash in an interview on Fox News.
“I tripped up on one question last night,” she said. “But you know, I’ve said many times, I’m not a politician, certainly not a career politician. I don’t speak politician. You know, I was just honest, and I think that’s kind of a foreign concept.”

Kiev’s terror, Orthodox Church persecution and Moscow-Vatican ties: Key points from Lavrov’s meeting with Holy See’s envoy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
02:37:52 UTC
11:37:52 KST

Kiev’s terror, Orthodox Church persecution and Moscow-Vatican ties: Key points from Lavrov’s meeting with Holy See’s envoy
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov discussed the Ukraine conflict, Kiev’s persecution of the Ukrainian Orthodox Church, and restrictions on the Russian language during talks with the Vatican’s top diplomat, Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher.
Gallagher, who heads the Holy See’s diplomatic service, arrived in Moscow on Monday for a four-day visit.
The talks also covered the Middle East, Africa, and other global hotspots, according to the Russian Foreign Ministry. Moscow and the Vatican also found common ground on protecting traditional values and discussed emerging issues such as AI.
Here are the key takeaways from Lavrov’s remarks following the meeting:
Ukraine conflict
Moscow praised the Vatican’s “balanced position” on the Ukraine conflict and briefed Gallagher on Russia’s approach to ending the hostilities by addressing the “root causes.”
President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Russia was forced to launch the military operation in Ukraine to protect civilians in the largely Russian-speaking Donbass. Moscow has also long described Kiev’s deepening military cooperation with NATO as a major threat to Russian national security.
Lavrov also praised the Vatican’s involvement in humanitarian efforts linked to the conflict, including work to reunite children separated from their families.
‘Blatant cruelty’
Lavrov noted the “blatant cruelty” of Ukrainian attacks on Russian civilians. He accused Kiev of striking civilian targets “on a daily basis,” including facilities where children are present.
Lavrov said another wave of Ukrainian strikes on several southern Russian regions early Monday killed three minors and injured six others at a childcare center in Krasnodar.
“We will [also] never forget and will seek justice for [Ukrainian leader Vladimir] Zelensky’s bloody terror attack in Starobelsk,” Lavrov said, referring to a drone strike in May on a college dormitory in the Donbass city. The attack killed 21 people, most of them teenage girls.
Russian language crackdown
Lavrov accused Kiev of waging an unprecedented campaign against the Russian language and Russian culture.
Ukraine is the only country to have outright banned Russian, he stated, arguing that no other state has gone as far in targeting Russian speakers.
“We discussed how Ukraine treats the Russian language, Russian education, Russian media, and Russian culture in general,” Lavrov said. He expressed hope that Vatican diplomats would raise the issue directly with Kiev.
Plight of Ukrainian Orthodox Church
Gallagher was also given a copy of its latest report on Kiev’s persecution of the canonical Ukrainian Orthodox Church. The report details “unlawful actions” against the church, the clergy, and parishioners and has already been submitted to the UN and the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), Lavrov said.
The Ukrainian authorities are “legislatively pursuing the destruction of the canonical Ukrainian Orthodox Church,” he warned, urging the Vatican to take a closer look at the issue.
Zelensky’s government has targeted the Ukrainian Orthodox Church for several years, accusing it of maintaining ties with Moscow despite the church declaring independence from the Russian Orthodox Church in 2022.
The crackdown has included monastery raids, property seizures, and dozens of criminal cases against clergy on collaboration charges. Kiev also supports the rival Orthodox Church of Ukraine, which the Russian Orthodox Church considers schismatic.
Moscow-Vatican ties
Despite deep geopolitical divisions elsewhere, Russia and the Vatican have managed to keep their relationship “trustworthy, friendly and pragmatic,” Lavrov said.
He praised the Holy See for favoring diplomacy and peaceful solutions and said Moscow remains ready to work closely with the Vatican on humanitarian issues.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said the two sides discussed defending traditional spiritual and moral values, family reunification, prisoner exchanges, and the protection of Christian communities around the world.

SpaceX to build $100 billion rocket launch facility in southern Louisiana
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
02:36:40 UTC
11:36:40 KST

SpaceX to build $100 billion rocket launch facility in southern Louisiana
SpaceX unveiled plans on Tuesday for a $100 billion rocket launch complex in southern Louisiana, its largest yet, aimed at supporting Starship and AI satellite missions. The 125,000-acre Starbase Louisiana site on Pecan Island could eventually handle thousands of Starship launches annually, the company said.
SpaceX unveiled plans on Tuesday to build its largest rocket launch complex yet in southern Louisiana, a $100 billion effort to transform coastal wetlands into a critical base for the company's Starship and AI satellite launch ambitions.
The 125,000-acre (50,585-hectare) site on Pecan Island, which SpaceX named Starbase Louisiana, is an expansion of the company's Starship launch operations beyond South Texas and those planned for Florida as its next-generation rocket remains in late-stage development.
The company's second Starbase campus will eventually launch thousands of Starship flights a year, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said, reiterating its goals for an ambitious cadence contingent on solving steep engineering challenges and regulatory hurdles.
Construction will begin next year with the first Starship launch in 2029, SpaceX said.
Shotwell detailed the plans near the proposed site in Louisiana's Vermilion Parish at an event with Governor Jeff Landry and other senior state officials.
Read moreAstrophysicist Jonathan McDowell explains why we need an international space traffic control agency
The "self-sustaining" spaceport envisioned by SpaceX will include its own methane production for propellant, power generation, deep-water shipping capabilities to transport Starships from Texas, vehicle processing facilities, and probably an airport, Shotwell said.
The marshland site is more than eight times the size of Manhattan. Shotwell said "very large portions" of the land will remain natural wetlands with no infrastructure, while an animated SpaceX video showed the area dotted with several launch pads surrounded by greenery.
The site had been at the center of a decade-long lawsuit against ExxonMobil brought by local parishes alleging the oil major's coastal drilling and canal dredging contributed to the state's wetland loss. The state reached an agreement with Exxon to settle the lawsuit in June, prompting its dismissal the following month, a court order shows.
That cleared the way for SpaceX's launch plans for the 18-mile (29-km) coastal strip, which the company had beendiscussing with the state since February, Louisiana Economic Development Secretary Susan Bourgeois said.
SpaceX has significantly expanded its southern US footprint in recent years, having built Colossus AI data centers in Tennessee and Mississippi and Starlink facilities in Austin, Texas. It is planning a chip plant in central Texas.
"This project means more than just steel, technology, and capital," Landry said. "It represents jobs for our families. It represents momentum for our communities, and it represents protection for our coast."
SpaceX said the Louisiana site will add more than 3,000 jobs to the region. The governor's office said those jobs are expected to pay an average salary of $92,600, or 192% higher than the average wage in Vermilion Parish.
Read moreSchool-bus-sized chunk of SpaceX rocket believed to have crashed into the Moon
Second Starbase
The launch site, which will be SpaceX's fourth in the US appears to replicate at a larger scale its widening footprint in South Texas, site of its first Starbase rocket campus. However, the Louisiana site will not have rocket production facilities.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk sees Starship as central to the company's goals of expanding its Starlink constellation and eventually deploying up to 1 million AI data-processing satellites in orbit. The rocket also plays a key role in NASA's Artemis moon program.
Pecan Island is situated in a geographically convenient location for Musk's satellite ambitions. It allows a rocket to launch south over the Gulf waters and into a sun-synchronous orbit that offers plenty of sunlight for solar-powered AI satellites.
Starbase Texas is Starship's only active launch site as the rocket remains in development, while SpaceX builds two Starship pads in Florida next to its flagship Falcon 9 launch pads. The company also has Falcon 9 launch facilities at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.
As SpaceX developed Boca Chica, Texas, into the company town of Starbase with support from local government officials, it has faced resistance from residents concerned about water, environmental and noise pollution and pressure to sell their land.
Shotwell highlighted environmental plans and outlined efforts to restore Pecan Island's receding marshlands and coastline, which act as a natural buffer to protect inland areas from flooding during heavy rainfall.
Pecan Island is a protected hub for dozens of migratory bird species seasonally traveling throughout the Western Hemisphere.
At Starbase Texas, Starship launches have blasted shorebirds and their nests with gravel and debris, according to environmental groups.
"The birds might fly away during a launch, but I guarantee they come back," Shotwell said, prompting applause from state officials. "As soon as the rocket's gone, the birds come back. It's not like months later."
She said SpaceX will help fund environmental "protection, restoration, and stewardship" while the launch site is constructed.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

Search expert details exhumation of Polish Army soldiers in Lviv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
02:32:00 UTC
11:32:00 KST

Search expert details exhumation of Polish Army soldiers in Lviv
Liubomyr Horbach, head of the Pamiat Society for the Search for War Victims, told Ukrinform.
According to him, the Ukrainian side is represented by a team from the Pamiat Society, while the Polish team includes specialists from Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance and Wroclaw Medical University. The Ukrainian and Polish teams include search experts, archaeologists and anthropologists. About 30 specialists will work at the site in total.
“Based on search operations conducted in 2010 and 2019, 110–120 individual graves of Polish Army soldiers were discovered at the cemetery. They were killed in battles against German military units that had encircled Lviv from the west and south in September 1939. The graves include Poles, Ukrainians and representatives of other nationalities who served in or were mobilized into the Polish Army,” Horbach said.
The graves are arranged in three rows. The area where the Ukrainian and Polish specialists will work measures 40 by 12 meters. Some of the graves have been flooded by groundwater, which will have to be pumped out. The teams initially plan to excavate five graves per day.
“We will work manually because using machinery would be impractical in this case. Once the remains are uncovered and recovered, anthropologists will examine them. In particular, they will collect samples for DNA testing. The soldiers buried here are officially listed as missing. Work is underway in Poland to locate their relatives and obtain their DNA so that we can establish the identities of the soldiers buried here. Items found in the graves may also help with identification, including military identification tags, if they have survived,” Horbach said.
According to him, the exhumed remains will be reburied at a cemetery in Mostyska, where the remains of about 200 Polish soldiers were reburied in 2015–2016 and again in 2025.
As reported, the exhumation of the remains of Polish Army soldiers has begun at Holoskivske Cemetery in Lviv. The exhumation research is being carried out in accordance with agreements reached through the Ukrainian-Polish Working Group on National Remembrance.

Three takeaways from Tuesday's South Carolina Republican Senate primary
WASHINGTON, Aug 25 - South Carolina Republicans on Tuesday nominated Darline Graham to run in November's general election for her late brother's U.S. Senate seat, as she defeated Representative Ralph Norman in a primary runoff.
Here are some takeaways from the result:
TRUMP ENDORSEMENT PAID OFF
President Donald Trump didn't just endorse Graham – sharing a stage with her in South Carolina on Friday, he declared that he too was "on the ballot."
A day before the primary runoff, he appeared to hedge his bets: For "a few" of the candidates he endorsed it was "almost impossible for them to win," he posted on Truth Social, but he felt "obligated" to back them. He did not specify which candidates he was referring to, though the post came amid concerns about the viability of Graham's campaign.
By late Tuesday, however, it was clear she had pulled it off. While Norman performed well in his home base of Greenville, Graham outperformed him in much of the rest of the state – including a resounding win in the area surrounding Myrtle Beach, where Trump campaigned with her last week.
It was a much-needed win for Trump, facing mounting public concerns over inflation, the conflict with Iran and an escalating trade war with Canada.
Only 33% of Americans approve of his performance, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll, but Tuesday's result shows he still has singular influence among Republican voters.
The president's ability to boost turnout among his party faithful will be a key factor in determining whether Republicans are able to retain control of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate in November's midterm elections.
MAGA INC. MEGA MONEY
A political action committee, MAGA INC., established to support Trump, spent $827,711 to bolster Graham's campaign, according to reports filed with the Federal Election Commission.
While Trump has given his vocal endorsement to Republicans in races across the country, his PAC has rarely contributed to their campaigns.
It appears to have paid off for Trump, and could embolden MAGA INC. to keep the money flowing to the president's favored candidates in key races going forward.
GRAHAM AN UNLIKELY REBEL IN THE SENATE
The late Senator Lindsey Graham became a close ally of Trump's after a rocky start in 2016 when, as a candidate in the Republican presidential primaries, he referred to Trump as a "bigot" and "complete idiot."
He would go on to become a frequent golfing companion of the president and one of his most loyal supporters in Congress.
Darline Graham so far has followed in her brother's footsteps, and would appear to be another ally in the making for Trump. It is still unclear, however, whether Republicans will be able to hold onto their slim Senate majority next year.
Whether they do or not, Graham is looking like she could be in the mold of many first-term senators who have held to another tradition, keeping their heads down during their maiden year and following their leadership's desires. REUTERS

He accused them of historically favouring the ancient text over the document adopted by the country.Owaisi made the remarks during his address at the Jalsa-e-Rahmatul-lil-Alameen at Darussalam .n Hyderabad on the occasion of the 1501st Eid Milad-un-Nabi. He targeted the RSS over its reported opposition to the Constitution drafted by Dr BR Ambedkar and contrasted the organisation's position with that of Muslim freedom fighters during British rule."I am asking those associated with the RSS about Manusmriti. Is it not true that on November 26, 1949, we adopted the Constitution? Yet, four days later, on November 30, a mouthpiece of the RSS published a complaint against it, stating that it wasn't a constitution at all and that it should have been the Manusmriti. They had issues with the Constitution drafted by Babasaheb Ambedkar," Owaisi said.
The AIMIM chief also attacked Hindutva ideologue VD Savarkar, referring to his correspondence with the British during his imprisonment in the Andaman cellular jail.
"Savarkar was in support of Manusmriti. While he was in Andaman jail, he was writing letters to the British, saying, 'I am with you, please release me.' But what were we doing? Allama Fazl-e-Haq Khairabadi was also in jail; he endured hardships but never wrote a 'love letter' to the British. Instead, he issued a fatwa for Jihad against them. Even today, his grave stands in the Andaman as a testament," he asserted.Owaisi further sought to highlight the role of Muslim figures in India's freedom struggle. He claimed that the first prisoner sent to the Andaman Islands was Maulvi Alauddin, the Imam of Hyderabad's Mecca Masjid."Listen, BJP and RSS people, who was the first prisoner in Andaman? It was not your father, grandfather, or ancestor. It was Hyderabad's Maulvi Alauddin, the Imam of Mecca Masjid. He was the first prisoner," Owaisi told the gathering.His remarks come amid an intensifying political confrontation between the BJP and Congress over the Manusmriti and its place in India's social and constitutional discourse.The BJP has recently targeted Congress leader and Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi over his criticism of the Manusmriti. It accused Rahul of making statements that undermine India's traditions, cultural heritage and democratic institutions. Several BJP leaders, including chief ministers, have alleged that Rahul Gandhi's remarks sought to "belittle" India's civilisational values.
At an event titled 'Chhatron ki Goonj' in Pune, Rahul Gandhi criticised a passage attributed to the Manusmriti concerning women's independence."This is a direct quote from the Manusmriti, and these words are a shame, because these words should never ever have been spoken," Gandhi said after quoting the passage: "In childhood, a female belongs to her father. In youth, she belongs to her husband. When her lord is dead, she belongs to her sons. A woman must never be independent."Rahul also called for an end to patriarchal structures, telling female students that the country needs to "smash the prevailing patriarchy" to achieve genuine empowerment for women.The exchange has brought the Manusmriti back into the centre of a wider political debate over constitutional values, social equality and competing interpretations of India's cultural and political history.

Taiwan wholesale revenue hits record NT$1.76 trillion in July
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
02:21:46 UTC
11:21:46 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan's wholesale revenue reached a record NT$1.7573 trillion (US$55.16 billion) in July, surging 56.4% from a year earlier, according to a Ministry of Economic Affairs press release on Tuesday.
The July total was the highest monthly wholesale revenue on record and marked the 18th consecutive month of year-on-year growth. Demand for AI, high-performance computing, and cloud services drove shipments across related supply chains.
Wholesale revenue for the first seven months rose to NT$10.7905 trillion, up 36.2% from the same period last year and a record for the first seven months. At the current pace, wholesale revenue could surpass the annual record set in 2025 as early as September, according to MOEA Department of Statistics Deputy Director-General Chen Yu-fang (陳玉芳).
Retail revenue also reached a record for July, totaling NT$418.3 billion, up 7.7% year on year. Revenue for the first seven months reached NT$2.881 trillion, up 4.6% from the same period last year and a record for the January-July period.
The automotive and motorized two-wheel vehicle sector grew 12.6% year on year, while department stores rose 9.6% and information and communications technology and home appliance retailers increased 12.5%. Hypermarkets and convenience stores also posted gains of 10.3% and 4.2%, respectively.
Chen said the automotive and motorized two-wheel vehicle market benefited from summer promotional campaigns and the introduction of new models, contributing to growth for a second consecutive month. However, she cautioned that major purchases typically slow during Ghost Month, which falls in August this year.
Food services revenue reached NT$88.7 billion in July, up 2.5% from a year earlier and the highest July figure on record. Revenue for the first seven months totaled NT$642.2 billion, up 3.9% year on year and also a record for the period.
Restaurant revenue increased 0.8%, while beverage shops posted a 9.7% increase as summer vacation boosted dining out and group meals. Catering and group meal contracting services rose 7.7%, supported by continued cross-border travel and increased demand for in-flight catering.
Chen said the number of days affected by typhoons in July was greater than expected, weighing on retail and food-service revenue growth. While supermarkets and hypermarkets benefited from increased demand for supplies ahead of storms, some businesses were hurt by typhoon-related closures and cancellations.
Regarding the impact of the Central Union Oil food-safety incident on July retail and food-service sales, Chen said the availability of substitute products meant the overall impact was not significant. The ministry attributed the weaker-than-expected growth primarily to typhoons.
Looking ahead, the ministry expects retail sales in August to benefit from Father's Day and Chinese Valentine's Day promotions, while food services are expected to receive support from summer travel, dining out, festive gatherings, and demand for cold beverages amid high temperatures.

Instead, she focused her remarks on domestic issues, including Trump’s immigration clampdown and anti-abortion advocacy.
She had never held public office until her appointment to the Senate, having previously held positions advocating for persons with physical disabilities.
South Carolina has overwhelmingly embraced Trump in all three of his runs for president and is not likely to play a role in the battle for the control of Congress.
Norman, 73, a long-time real estate developer, has spent nearly a decade in the US House.
His defeat on Aug 25 comes on the heels of an unsuccessful bid for governor.
He has been a leading member of the right-wing House Freedom Caucus, but endorsed the more moderate Nikki Haley, a former governor of South Carolina, in her 2024 failed presidential bid.
Earlier in August, Graham and Norman were the two top vote-getters in the Republican primary’s 10-candidate field, but neither garnered enough support to avoid Aug 25’s run off. REUTERS

Productivity Commission slams political attacks on integrity after GST report
In short:
WA Premier Roger Cook called the Productivity Commission "east coast clowns" over its interim findings on GST, with a senior federal minister casting doubt over the report's validity.
The interim report recommended changing the current GST arrangements, saying they were a "costly mistake" and the only state better off was WA.
What's next?
Angela Jackson told the ABC the commission welcomed debate ahead of their final report, which she stressed would not be influenced by politics.
The Productivity Commission says the WA premier "crossed a line" with his criticisms of the body's interim report on GST, adding that political commentary from federal government ministers undermines the commission's integrity.
The report, released earlier this month, was tasked with looking at GST distribution reforms put in place in 2018. It described those arrangements as a "costly mistake" that had forced Australian taxpayers to foot the bill of almost $23 billion, and the only state better off was WA.
WA Premier Roger Cook lashed the report authors as "east coast clowns" and described the commission's proposals for change as "dodgy, deceitful, and quite frankly dumb".
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese labelled the findings as an "economic rationalist" position, while Resources Minister Madeleine King sympathised with the WA premier's comments and cast doubt on the report's methodology.
Within days of the interim report's release, Mr Albanese stood with Mr Cook in Perth, pledging not to unwind any deal for WA while he was prime minister.
Productivity commissioner and economist Angela Jackson, who co-authored the report, said the body welcomed public debate, but the WA premier's remarks went too far.
"Our view is that a line was crossed in terms of the nature of those comments," she told ABC Radio National.
"To undermine and, I guess, attack our integrity, I think, is an additional bridge too far.
"We want to call this out as being unacceptable as a result. But that said, in doing that, we welcome ongoing dialogue with Western Australia."
Mr Albanese this week distanced his party from the commission's report, pointing out the previous Morrison government commissioned it.
"This report was commissioned by the Morrison government, not us," he said.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers, who wrote the terms of reference for the report, said today the Productivity Commission is "full of really good people ... publicly-spirited people".
"I want them to know just how much I value their work," he said.
"I don't consider what the PM said to be inappropriate, but I think some of the other commentary around it has been unfortunate," Mr Chalmers said.
"I think you can disagree with the conclusions of the Productivity Commission without denigrating them."
Commission says it is 'above politics'
Dr Jackson said the prime minister's comments were "disappointing" but added that most economists would take being described as "economic rationalists" as a "badge of honour".
She said the findings were part of an interim report and were subject to consultation and change.
The productivity commission was independent and would not be swayed by politicians' views, she added.
"We often refine our recommendations. We may well change our recommendations in some instances, depending on the feedback we receive," she said.
"It's important for us to indicate that that process will not be influenced by the prime minister's comments,"
"We are above politics."
Dr Jackson's comments come after her co-author, Alex Robson, told The Australian Financial Review (AFR) he was disappointed by senior Labor member's comments, which he called inappropriate.
"I totally reject those comments and the language used. It doesn't advance the policy debate at all," he told the AFR.
Other government ministers have declined to condemn Mr Cook's remarks.
Industry Minister Tim Ayres today told the ABC his "east coast clowns" comment was "colourful language" but insisted Labor welcomed debate and MPs did not have a "glass jaw".
Ms King, who hails from WA, said Mr Cook's comments were "fair enough", although she would not use that language herself.
"I don't actually quite agree that it [the Productivity Commission] has gone through it as methodically as it might have," she told ABC's Radio National on Tuesday.
"I respect the work of the commissioners. And I also note there are no Western Australians on the Productivity Commission."
The Productivity Commission is the independent research and advisory body for the Australian government, undertaking research in areas like housing supply, childcare subsidies and hospital funding and carrying out ongoing work on Closing the Gap.
