- The US is cautiously restoring some Middle East diplomatic missions and threatening sanctions on countries trading with Iran, while oil prices drop and US public support for the conflict declines.
AI generated
CAIRO – Iran said it had restarted talks with neighbour Oman to manage the Strait of Hormuz as it faces heightened economic pressure from US President Donald Trump in the wider conflict.
Iran and Oman have been in on-and-off talks for weeks about controlling traffic through the strategic waterway, which handled one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the war began in February.
Most shipping has been shut down since then.
The two countries said on Aug 25 that they discussed “a joint temporary navigational corridor” through the strait and agreed to clear it of mines.
Trump said all mines in the strait had been cleared, repeating comments that he has previously made.
Though active hostilities between the US and Iran have largely subsided, diplomatic efforts to reach a peace deal have stalled and passage through the waterway remains perilous.
An oil tanker was struck on Aug 25 by an unidentified projectile and disabled about nine nautical miles north-east of Oman’s Ash Shishah, which lies at the entrance to the strait, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said.
Separately, the US Secret Service said on Aug 25 that it was aware of a video broadcast by Iranian state television discussing a potential plot to assassinate Trump’s youngest son, Barron.
A three-minute video broadcast by Iranian state TV discussed a potential plot to assassinate Barron Trump, 20, claiming that he was being monitored and alleging that a US$10 million (S$12.7 million) bounty had been offered for his killing.
Sanctions
Despite the ongoing tensions, the US is beginning to send personnel back to some diplomatic missions in the Middle East that were evacuated or downsized amid tensions with Iran, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
The move suggests Washington sees a lower risk of the conflict with Iran escalating in the near term, though some embassies will initially operate below full capacity.
In an effort to hobble Iran’s economy, the US earlier this week threatened to punish countries that continue to do business with Iran, but said it would not impose penalties immediately.
Oil prices fell for a second day as traders brushed off the impact of the US sanctions, while Iran denounced the US effort to isolate its economy as an act of “gross lawlessness”, expressing confidence that many countries would not join the pressure campaign.
US public approval of the war has fallen to its lowest level since the conflict’s early days, and Trump’s popularity is likewise at a record low ahead of congressional elections in November, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling.
Thousands of people have died in the conflict, most of them in Iran and Lebanon, while the US and Israel have degraded much of Iran’s conventional military capacity.
The exact state of Iran’s nuclear programme, which the US and Israel aim to dismantle, remains unknown. REUTERS

Russia may lose two more «Rassvet-3» satellites due to problems with a Starlink analogue
Kyiv • UNN
Two Russian «Rassvet-3» satellites are descending in orbit without engine correction. Their loss will complicate the plan to deploy the constellation.
The Russian satellite constellation "Rassvet-3" has encountered new problems — two spacecraft from the second batch may deorbit and burn up in the atmosphere. This is reported by Defence Express, which analyzed data from monitoring services, writes UNN.
Details
These are the satellites with NORAD numbers 100083 and 100089, which have not activated their engines for orbital corrections even once since their launch on July 19. Their current average altitude is about 290 km, while the lowest point of their orbit is approximately 277 km and is gradually decreasing.
The first "Rassvet-3" satellite has already deorbited and burned up in the atmosphere on June 6. At the same time, even the functioning spacecraft in the constellation have not yet reached the planned altitude of 800 km — most of the satellites from the first batch are at an altitude of approximately 500–550 km.
Another problem for Russia could be the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ strike on the Progress Rocket and Space Center in Samara on August 15. The facility produces Soyuz-2.1b launch vehicles, which are used to launch Rassvet-3 satellites.
Russia planned to deploy a constellation of approximately 300 Rassvet-3 satellites by the end of 2027. Problems with the spacecraft already launched and possible disruptions in the production of launch vehicles could complicate the implementation of this plan.

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Aug 26, 2026
CIA director Ratcliffe visits Russia: US media
US Central Intelligence Agency director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow on Aug 25 for meetings, in what would be his first known visit to Russia as CIA head, US media reported.
The purpose of the reported visit was not immediately clear, and there was no immediate comment from the CIA or the White House when contacted by AFP.
CBS News quoted sources familiar with the matter as confirming Ratcliffe’s trip, while Axios separately reported on the visit quoting two US officials.
Data from tracking site Flightradar24 had earlier shown a US military C-17 travelling from the United States to Latvia and then on to Moscow’s Vnukovo airport. The data showed the same plane leaving Moscow several hours later.
Charges for major who called for Trump impeachment
A US military service member who called for President Donald Trump and Vice-President J.D. Vance to be impeached is facing charges under the military justice system, his lawyer and the Air Force said on Aug 25.
The active-duty officer, Major Jason Watson, denounced Trump and Vance in July for actions including going to war with Iran without congressional authorisation, according to a video of the protest event posted online.
In the video, the US Capitol Police can be seen detaining Watson, who held a protest sign calling for their impeachment, conviction and removal.
SpaceX announces plans for $100 billion ‘spaceport’
Elon Musk’s SpaceX announced plans Aug 25 to build a US$100 billion (S$126 billion) facility in the southern US state of Louisiana to launch its highly anticipated Starship megarockets, currently being developed at the company’s Texas Starbase.
“A spaceport on the Louisiana Gulf Coast enabling a multiplanetary future,” declared the SpaceX website.
The new facility will be built in Vermillion Parish, about 180km west of New Orleans.
Williams, Alcaraz advance in US Open mixed doubles
Serena Williams made a triumphant return to the US Open on Aug 25 partnering with Carlos Alcaraz to beat Erin Routliffe and Lloyd Glasspool 5-3 4-1 in the opening round of the mixed doubles, while top seeds Novak Djokovic and Aryna Sabalenka crashed out.
The 23-times major winner had not competed at Arthur Ashe Stadium since her tearful farewell from the sport in 2022 and the crown jewel of American tennis erupted in deafening cheers as their queen took the court again.
The 44-year-old Williams had an easy rapport with Alcaraz, who is 21 years her junior, as the partners grinned and giggled their way into the quarter-finals, where they will meet Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli later on Aug 25.
US country music legend Dolly Parton dies aged 80
Dolly Parton, the American country music singer who rose from poverty in Tennessee to become a US cultural giant with hits like Jolene and 9 To 5, has died at 80, her family said on Aug 25.
“Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus,” her nephew Bryan Seaver said in a video on social media.
He said the multiple award-winning artist had “opened doors for generations of singers, songwriters, musicians, and dreamers from every walk of life.”

The U.S. Supreme Court allowed Trump to advance restrictions on voting by mail
Kyiv • UNN
The court lifted the block on key provisions of Trump’s executive order but did not declare them lawful. The states fear chaos ahead of the November 3 election.
The U.S. Supreme Court overturned a federal court ruling that had blocked key provisions of President Donald Trump’s executive order restricting voting by mail. Bloomberg reports, UNN writes.
Details
The court’s conservative majority agreed with the Justice Department that the lower court had prematurely blocked Trump’s initiative. At the same time, the Supreme Court did not determine whether the future restrictions themselves are lawful.
The decision creates legal uncertainty ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. More than a dozen states are already due to begin sending mail-in ballots to voters in September.
States fear election problems
Under the new rules, the U.S. Postal Service may return ballots if they do not meet the established requirements. States may also need to change the design of ballots, retrain election officials, and inform voters.
Trump’s opponents said they would continue challenging his executive order in court. California Attorney General Rob Bonta said that the fight against the administration’s actions “is far from over.”
Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson criticized the majority’s decision, saying that it “introduces chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections.” The dispute over voting rules is expected to return to the Supreme Court.

'I don't support the rally': Zohran Mamdani opposes RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat's Madison Square event
Edited by: Rajeev Singh / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 26, 2026, 03:46 IST

Mamdani was responding to questions about the RSS, the proposed event and protests against Bhagwat's appearance.
NEW DELHI: New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani has said he does not support a planned event featuring RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat at Madison Square Garden, while noting that the city may not have the legal authority to stop the private gathering.Bhagwat is scheduled to address around 5,000 members of the Indian diaspora at the iconic New York venue on August 29. His visit to the United States is part of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh's centenary-year global outreach programme."I don't support the rally, but I don't know if the city has any jurisdiction on cancelling a private event,” Mamdani said at a news conference on Tuesday.Mamdani was responding to questions about the RSS, the proposed event and protests against Bhagwat's appearance. He was also asked whether the gathering should be cancelled.The mayor, who is the first Indian-American to hold the post in New York City, said his views were influenced partly by his family background.“I also stand here as the first Indian-American Mayor in our city's history, and my mother's family is all still in India," Mamdani said.He said his understanding of India was based on the idea of a society where people of different backgrounds could belong equally.
He said the vision of India that he was taught by his family and the one that he grew up being very familiar with was that of "a pluralistic society, of a secular republic that believed in the belonging of each and every person who was from India".Mamdani said he was opposed to what he described as an increasingly exclusionary political movement.“And it has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision of any country, frankly, and so it is one that I find myself in deep opposition to, not only as an Indian-American but also as the Mayor of a city that believes deeply in the belonging of each and every person, no matter their colour, their creed, their religion, their faith, wherever they're from,” Mamdani said.
Protests planned over Bhagwat event
The planned appearance has faced opposition from several interfaith and civil rights organisations. Groups including Hindus for Human Rights, the Indian American Muslim Council and the Interfaith Centre of New York held a press conference outside New York City Hall and called for the event to be cancelled.
Bhagwat arrived in the US on Tuesday as part of the RSS's centenary-year outreach. During his stay in New York, he is also expected to participate in the Universal Oneness programme.The event is being organised by AHEAD Forum, which said in a social media post that Bhagwat would attend the Universal Oneness Celebration in New York on August 29.“The event carries a timeless and universal message: 'The world is one family'. It calls upon us to look beyond artificial divisions and differences, recognise the bonds that unite humanity, and embrace a spirit of mutual respect, harmony, and oneness,” the post said.Bhagwat's wider international tour includes the US, Canada and the UK as part of the Sangh's centenary-year global outreach programme.

SpaceX plans to build a $100 billion spaceport in Louisiana
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
22:09:01 UTC
07:09:01 KST

Elon Musk is continuing his push into the Southern U.S. with SpaceX, his aerospace and tech conglomerate, planning a $100 billion launch facility in Louisiana.
In a joint statement, the Louisiana Economic Development office said on Tuesday that SpaceX will establish its Starbase in Vermilion Parish, Louisiana, at a former Exxon property to, "support thousands of launches annually."
SpaceX stock rose about 2% to close at $137.95.
Once built, Starbase, LA will serve as the main launch facility for Starship, SpaceX's in-development rocket that's the largest ever built and designed to be fully reusable.
Musk has aspirations to massively expand SpaceX's Starlink satellite network, to launch orbital data centers and to someday colonize Mars. Those ambitions, and justification for SpaceX's nearly $2 trillion market cap, hinge on the success of Starship.
SpaceX said, in a video posted to its website on Tuesday, that the search for a site to build launch pads and have access to ample fuel for its operations took about seven years. Musk said in the video that the company would bring "probably 10,000 really exciting jobs" to Louisiana with the spaceport.
A fact sheet posted online by the state of Louisiana said SpaceX is expected to generate an estimated "3,000 direct new jobs over the next 10 years" in the state, and "8,100 indirect new jobs."
SpaceX said it would work on a "historic coastal restoration" in Louisiana, in partnership with the state to "bring the marsh back" and ensure the wetlands around its new facility will have "storm protection."
Earlier this year, Republican Governor Jeff Landry signed bills, that became law in May, exempting some aerospace projects in Louisiana from public review, and making unauthorized entry into a spaceport a felony. They also offered financial incentives to aerospace manufacturers.
SpaceX previously faced community backlash, lawsuits and fines following environmental violations at its first Starbase facility in Boca Chica, Texas, in the company town now known as Starbase.
In its first test flight of Starship in April 2023 in Texas, energy from the rocket caused SpaceX's concrete launchpad to explode and its spacecraft to blow up in midair. Chunks of concrete were flung into a nesting and migration site important to some endangered species and a fire chewed through around 4 acres of Boca Chica State Park Land south of the Texas launchpad.
In 2024, SpaceX was also found to have violated the Clean Water Act at the Texas launch facility by repeatedly releasing pollutants into or near bodies of water in Texas, a state agency said in a notice of violation focused on its water deluge system.
SpaceX's work in Louisiana follows Musk's move from California into Texas, Tennessee and Mississippi. The company said Louisiana was its fourth launch site.
Musk's AI venture, now known as SpaceXAI, built out its Colossus data centers and a power plant in Greater Memphis. Before that, Musk relocated the headquarters of his automaker, Tesla, from California to Austin, Texas. Tesla now operates a massive vehicle assembly plant in Austin and is testing its driverless, Robotaxi service and Cybercab vehicles in the region.
Tesla and SpaceX, in partnership with Intel, also plan to build a massive AI chip factory in Grimes County, Texas.
— CNBC's Kif Leswing contributed to this story.
Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that SpaceX will establish Starbase, Louisiana in Vermilion Parish. A previous version misspelled the name of the parish.

Brazil fines TikTok $30m for child data privacy violations

Brazil fines TikTok $30m for child data privacy violations
Owner ByteDance ordered to erase illegally obtained child data in Brazil as crackdown on tech giants intensifies.
Brazil’s data protection authority has fined TikTok’s parent company, ByteDance, nearly $30m for the alleged mishandling of children and teenagers’ personal data, in the nation’s latest move against social media companies.
The regulatory body said in its ruling that TikTok had breached data privacy laws across both logged-in accounts and guest browsing sessions by collecting and processing young users’ personal information without a valid legal basis or adequate safeguards.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Brazil’s president says Amazon oil is ‘passport to the future’
- list 2 of 3Brazil bus crash kills at least 23 and injures five in Parana state
- list 3 of 3Brazil launches AI supercomputer push while balancing US and Chinese tech
The regulator estimated that TikTok may have processed the data of at least 8 million children, highlighting what they said were systemic deficiencies within the platform’s age-verification mechanism.
The company can still appeal the decision in the next 10 days, according to the regulator.
The ruling also includes an order for TikTok to erase all data amassed illegally.
Brazil’s regulatory authority also mandated the company to formulate an improved comprehensive youth-protection framework, stressing that TikTok’s “logged-out feed”, which allows users to browse content without creating an account, enables widespread use of the platform by minors while bypassing age-verification checks.
According to the regulator, the feature is available in Brazil but not in the United States or Europe, where access is solely restricted to registered users.
Earlier this month, the regulator ordered the social media platform Discord to suspend its livestreaming feature across the country, accusing the platform of failing to protect children and teenagers. The move came after a 13-year-old girl died by suicide following a livestream in which authorities say she was encouraged to harm herself.
The voice and text chat app, hugely popular with gamers, launched in 2015.
Brazil’s government, under President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and the Supreme Court have tried to regulate internet use by minors, with mixed results so far, at a moment when countries such as Australia, Canada and Indonesia are undertaking similar efforts.

What's next?
The main draw of the US Open gets underway from August 30 at Flushing Meadows in New York.
Bernard Tomic's seemingly unending quest to fight his way back into another grand slam main draw has fallen short once again at Flushing Meadows despite one more worthy scrap from the veteran Australian.
The last time the 33-year-old managed to battle into a main draw of a major was at his home Australian Open in 2021.
In the five years since, he has entered 10 more qualifying events in the slams and failed to negotiate his way through any.
Alas for the former teenage wonder boy who got to number 17 in the world a decade ago, that drought continued on Tuesday afternoon, local time, in New York as he fought back in his first-round match against South African Lloyd Harris only to be outplayed in the final stanza.
No-one can possibly fault the effort of world number 179 Tomic, who was once perceived as being a talented but undisciplined figure who did not really care enough about the sport, as he has since battled on in the lower reaches of the game around the world, tirelessly seeking another day in the sun.
But Harris, a former world number 31 himself who is still dangerous even if his ranking has fallen to 139, just had a little too much for the Gold Coast veteran, who staged a second-set fightback before going down 6-2, 5-7, 6-2.
It was the same story for a couple of other Australians in first-round action, as teenager Emerson Jones fought valiantly to peg back Dutch world number 164 Suzan Lamens in a tight second-set tiebreak, only to succumb in the decider 7-5, 6-7 (7-9), 6-2 after two hours and 25 minutes.
With another veteran, Alex Bolt, losing 7-6 (7-3), 7-5 to Spain's Pablo Llamas Ruiz, it meant that Australia were still looking for their first winner of the week in qualifying after James McCabe's loss on the opening Monday.
At least one Aussie was guaranteed a place in the second round of qualifying as Storm Hunter took on her friend Maddison Inglis later in the day.

A visiting US delegation has sharply rebuked a senior Israeli official over illegal settlers' violence in the occupied West Bank, Israel's Channel 12 reported.

Increased violence

According to figures released by the Palestinian Colonisation and Wall Resistance Commission, illegal settlers have killed 25 Palestinians since the start of 2026, 61 since October 2023 and 87 since 2019.

In FocusNo immunity: how Xi’s anti-corruption fighters are zeroing in on fresh targets
China’s anti-graft push has expanded to those who once felt shielded, from retired cadres and local bosses to the investigators themselves
It used to be an easy choice for senior Chinese officials deciding between a local government position and a post at the same level in Beijing.
Most would choose the assignment outside the capital, as fewer supervisors around meant more clout and a bigger say in local affairs. As the Chinese saying goes: “The mountains are high and the emperor is far away.”
In fact, according to a tally by the South China Morning Post, among the most senior tier of officials targeted in the anti-corruption campaign between 2013 and 2025, 60 per cent were taken down while in regional government roles.
The SCMP looked at all publicly known officials targeted by the Communist Party’s Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. Most of them belonged to a pool of officials known as “centrally managed cadres”, meaning they typically held ranks at the deputy ministerial level or above. A smaller number of them held slightly lower ranks but occupied sensitive positions in important sectors.

‘Darth Vader’ Wants You to Know He Definitely Supports Flock Surveillance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
21:51:32 UTC
06:51:32 KST

At the San Diego City Council’s most recent budget meeting, Sith Lord Darth Vader had some points to make. Between gasping breaths, Vader praised the council’s recent votes to renew its contract with the surveillance company Flock Safety, which has been making headlines recently as more and more stories of police officers abusing its tools have continued to come out—and as a WIRED review of code for a new AI tool already in use by some police departments has made clear that it is watching far more than just license plates.
“The emperor is a fan of Flock. And we must continue utilizing Flock technologies so that we can follow and surveil the rebel scum as they move from playground to playground, from playground to pool, from pool to gymnasium.”
The recording of the video has gone viral, reaching millions of people on TikTok and Instagram.
The man behind the stunt is Anthony Ralphs, a San Diego-based DJ, event producer, and agriculture consultant who has spent the better part of the past year advocating against the city’s support of Flock’s use by the San Diego Police Department.
Initially, Ralphs thought about keeping his identity hidden behind the Vader mask—a 2004 Hasbro model. But he says that as the video has picked up more and more steam, he decided to “take ownership” of the stunt that put Flock and surveillance technology on the minds and feeds of millions of people around the world.
WIRED spoke to Ralphs about advocacy, crafting a costume, and the role that art can play in civic engagement.
This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.
VITTORIA ELLIOTT: How did this start for you? Was this your first city council meeting?
ANTHONY RALPHS: No. My first time attending a city council meeting was sometime last summer or last fall. But really the most consequential city council meeting that I attended, that really got me in the fold of starting to regularly participate in my civic duties, was this issue of Flock. It was my third, or maybe my fourth, city council meeting back on December 9th, and the city council was putting this up to a vote, whether to continue to use Flock.
The story back then was that the city council didn't exactly know what the technology was. The police were touting it as a force multiplier. There were over 300 people at that vote, the meeting room was completely full, and I would say 95 percent of the people there were saying they didn’t want Flock. But the council voted for it anyway. It was extremely discouraging, and it really lit a fire under me to start going and regularly participating.
I came to the following city council meeting, and I was one of maybe five people in the city council chambers, and there had been close to 300 just a couple of weeks prior. That moment was eye-opening. I realized not everyone can be there all the time to do this, and that's what we need. We need consistent advocacy. So I took time off of school to be able to do that.
Why did this feel so critical?
Our city's $120 million deficit. They cut several arts programs, and while they did that, they also provided the $2.2 million for Flock's contract, even when people in those communities that are being most heavily policed say that they don’t want this. And now, we have the case of Hugo Parra, a local San Diegan who was falsely imprisoned and sat in prison for 30 days due to an erroneous tag by the Flock cameras. [Flock did not immediately respond to a request for comment on this matter.]
He and his friend, who was also arrested, are both suing this city for $1.5 million. So by the time the city ends up settling those two lawsuits, it will probably add another million dollars to that contract.
What were you studying?
I was taking classes at San Diego Mesa College and San Diego City College, I had been studying theater and labor studies, and I got my certificate in labor studies. As a student, I interned for the American Federation of Teachers, the local chapter here in San Diego. Our job was to organize and we would get real hands-on training going to strike lines and showing solidarity. We would canvas for candidates, and we were doing phone banks, so we got a really comprehensive experience of what it's like to participate civically in the real world. I would DJ for the people on the picket line once a week before school, and that really showed me the power of art specifically to make a political impact.
What ultimately led to the choice to attend the council meeting as Darth Vader?
I was always interested in guerrilla theater, I studied it in a playwriting class in school. But this was really a last resort. I had been going to meetings for months, and I have a lot of sympathy for these representatives, because I am the vice chair of my local planning group. I know what it’s like to sit there and get dunked on by random people. So, I did my homework on all of them. I learned what they voted for, what they've voted against, the progressive policies that they had enacted that I could support. I went so far as to bring them flowers.
But at a certain point, it felt like we've exhausted all of the efforts. We did it the right way, and they still continued to ignore their constituents.
I was in the shower one day and it hit me. I was trying to think of how I could satirize their points, because I realized they seemed to have a lack of self-awareness. I realized we're not getting through to them, and they are not listening to us and there's no consequences for them not listening to us. So, maybe we need to show them how silly they're being.
How did you prepare?
I am a huge Star Wars fan. I used to watch the movies almost every day as a kid. In the lead-up to the meeting, I rewatched all the movies again, the original ones, trying to get his gesticulations down. I got a silk cape, I think it was from Turkey. I found the original 2004 Hasbro helmet, and I chose this one because it had a voice changer in it. But I had been told the voice changer was a little bit gimmicky, so I thought “I'll just replicate his voice myself.” I wasn’t able to get everything I wanted for the costume, but I knew that the August 19th meeting was going to be the big one, because the ACLU was going to be at that committee meeting. So I pulled together some stuff I already had, and I think it turned out well.
The helmet actually came in handy, because there were buttons on it to make noises. At certain points, I'd stand up to go to the bathroom and I'd hit the breathing button—you know, the Darth Vader breathing sound. At one point I turned around, and I'm right within earshot of the chief of police, and I pushed the button and it said, “Your powers are weak!”
What do you hope this achieves?
I want to make it cool to engage in one's civic responsibility again. City council meetings don't have to be stale rooms with boring thoughts presented in unoriginal ways. They can be places where we bring our own art, where we bring the strength of our intellect and our moral fortitude with our talent and creativity.
This sparked a global conversation about luxury surveillance and living under Big Brother, and in Orwellian-digital, fully surveilled hellscape. Some people didn't know what Flock was a week ago. We've reframed the narrative from “this is a ‘necessary evil’” to “if Darth Vader finds it a ‘necessary evil,’ that should make us pause and reflect on whether or not we need it.”

‘Fascinating and shocking’ book about Putin’s private life wins prize
Exiled Russian journalists awarded Prix Strasbourg for taboo-breaking work based on hundreds of interviews with witnesses who later vanished
A taboo-breaking book about Vladimir Putin’s rise to power and private life, written by two exiled Russian journalists, won a newly established French literary prize on Tuesday.
The book, titled The Tsar in Propria Persona: How Vladimir Putin Deceived Us All, draws on more than two decades of investigative reporting by journalists Roman Badanin and Mikhail Rubin.
The work won a newly established literary award called the Prix Strasbourg awarded by EBRA, France’s largest regional newspaper group, and its parent company, Credit Mutuel Alliance Federale.
The book is due to be published in France next month.
It reads “like a spy novel”, the jury said, describing the book as a “fascinating and shocking work about a figure who is himself fascinating and shocking”.
“It is the result of several hundred interviews with witnesses, some of whom later disappeared under tragic circumstances.”
Badanin is the founder and editor-in-chief of Proekt, an investigative media outlet created in 2018.

PRAIA, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Unpaid work in Cabo Verde has an estimated economic value equivalent to 9.6 percent of the country's GDP and continues to be disproportionately undertaken by women, according to a report presented Tuesday by the Cabo Verdean Institute for Gender Equality and Equity (ICIEG).
The report shows that 88.4 percent of women aged 10 and above engage in unpaid work, compared with 67.9 percent of men. In care work involving children, the elderly and people with disabilities, the participation rate stands at 36 percent among women and 18.8 percent among men.
David Matern, Resident Representative of UNDP, UNICEF and UNFPA in Cabo Verde, said that if such work were included in national economic accounts, its economic value would amount to approximately 9.6 percent of GDP.
Matern stressed that domestic and care work constitutes an "economy" that takes place every day in households and communities, but "remains practically invisible in national accounts."
According to ICIEG President Marisa Carvalho, the overall volume of unpaid work has decreased by more than 50 percent compared with 2012, but the difference between women and men in performing this work remains above 20 percentage points.
Adelsia Almeida, Minister of Family, Inclusion, Social Development and Labor, said the figures show that care constitutes a "true economic asset" of the country, adding that the government intends to progressively strengthen the National Care Policy by expanding services such as childcare centers, home-based support, day centers for the elderly and services for people with disabilities. ■

Feature: Gaza children swim to reclaim joy, childhood lost to war
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:48:01 CST
06:48:01 KST

GAZA, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- For seven-year-old Camelia Hadi, swimming is more than a sport. It has brought her a moment of joy and a chance to feel like a child again after years of war.
The laughter of Hadi rang out as she swam among dozens of children in the sea off Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip. For a few hours, she looked like any other child her age, enjoying the water and learning to swim with her peers.
For Hadi, however, such moments are rare.
She was four when the war began in October 2023 and has since been displaced more than 20 times after her family lost their home. The hardship has also forced her to take on responsibilities beyond her years, including helping her family obtain water and bread.
"When I am here, I feel like a normal child," she said. "I laugh, I play and I learn to swim. I hope we can always come to the sea and live without fear."
Hadi was among hundreds of children who took part in "Swim With Gaza," a swimming event organized by the Gaza-based Tantish Swimming Academy and running through the end of this month.
The initiative seeks to give children an opportunity to participate in sports and recreational activities while helping them develop swimming skills and regain a sense of normality after years of war.
Among the participants was 11-year-old Farah Hassan Abu Halima, who said she initially felt frightened and uneasy about joining the swimming lessons. Her feelings changed after she arrived at the event.
"At first, I was afraid and uneasy, but when I heard about the courses, I was encouraged to register," said Halima. "When I arrived, I found a wonderful atmosphere. The swimming coaches and the activities made us happy and lifted our spirits."
Amjad Tantish, head of the Tantish Swimming Academy, said that more than 2,500 children had learned to swim since the current season began in June, when the initiative was relaunched after being suspended during the war.
According to Tantish, "Swim With Gaza" week has also drawn participants at dozens of locations worldwide in solidarity with Gaza's children. He said the initiative aims to help children cope with the difficult circumstances they have experienced.
"These swimming lessons are not only about sport. They give children a chance to play, have fun and escape the harsh conditions around them."
He said that swimming skills also have practical importance in Gaza, where many children spend time near the sea. He added that the initiative also honors six swimming instructors who were killed during the war, including his brother.
The need for such activities is underscored by the toll of the war on Gaza's children. Since October 2023, over 21,500 Palestinian children have been killed, with many others injured, orphaned or displaced, according to the Hamas-run Gaza government media office in July.
Abdullah al-Jamal, director of Gaza's psychiatric hospital, described the psychological situation as "catastrophic," especially among children with moderate to severe war-related disorders. "Children feel insecure and afraid, negatively impacting their lives and risking long-term trauma and disorders," al-Jamal said.
A 2024 survey showed that 96 percent of children in the surveyed households in Gaza felt that death was imminent, while 92 percent struggled to accept their new reality.
Ismail Qudaih, 12, from Khan Younis, said taking part in the swimming activities had given him moments of joy and helped him temporarily escape the painful memories of the war, in which he lost his mother and three siblings.
"When I get into the water, I feel different. For a while, I stop thinking about the war and everything that happened to my family. I can swim, play and laugh with the other children," he said.
His father, Ibrahim Qudaih, said the most significant change was seeing his son smile and enjoy himself again.
"Children in Gaza need spaces where they can feel safe and where they can simply be children. They need to play, exercise, laugh and meet other children. These things may seem small, but for a child who has lost his mother and siblings, they can make a very big difference," the father said. ■

During the ceremony, Majdalani highlighted China's support and stressed the importance of investing in children and young people as an investment in the future of Palestinian society.
Sun Zhen said Chinese assistance to Palestine was rooted in the friendship between the two peoples, describing "voluntary support" and "hope" as two keywords for Chinese aid.
Sun expressed hope that the participating children would grow into active contributors to their homeland and ambassadors of friendship between the Chinese and Palestinian peoples. ■

Risk of falling behind on AI most profound in developing economies: IMF chief
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:47:56 CST
06:47:56 KST

WASHINGTON, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- The future impact of artificial intelligence (AI) is clouded by "significant unknowns," International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said Tuesday, noting that the risk of falling behind on AI is "most profound" in developing economies.
At a roundtable with reporters in Washington, D.C., Georgieva said in her opening remarks that the global economy is like the ship in Christopher Nolan's new movie The Odyssey. "It is resisting powerful headwinds from high debt levels, stubborn inflation, and trade tensions," she said.
The IMF chief noted that thus far, the global economy has weathered the energy shock caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz better than the IMF feared, due to a combination of factors: drawdowns of oil and gas reserves, increases in non-Gulf supply, more renewable energy capacity, a partial shift back to coal in some places, as well as reductions in demand, which are more impactful than originally projected.
Besides these factors, Georgieva continued, the global economy is also benefiting from the tailwinds of an AI investment boom, noting that those plugged into the AI supply chain are among the first to benefit.
"We have literally a tug of war between the negative supply shock from the Middle East and the positive demand shock from AI," she said, adding that the net impact of these two forces is asymmetric across countries.
"It depends on their exposure to energy disruptions, macroeconomic vulnerabilities, and their position in the AI chain," said the IMF chief.
Georgieva noted that countries are facing mounting fiscal pressures, as evidenced by rising bond yields and a stalled disinflation process, while shrinking oil and gas reserves mean that "the energy shock is not over."
Moreover, she noted that the future impact of AI is "dogged by significant unknowns," including possible risks to financial stability. "Should the outlook deteriorate, it will further widen the dispersion of growth prospects around the world," she said.
"The risk of falling behind on AI is also most profound in developing economies. All this leaves no room for complacency," she added.
The IMF chief joined the media roundtable weeks before the 2026 Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group, scheduled to take place in Bangkok, Thailand, in October.
Looking ahead to the event, Georgieva said that this year's annual meetings are set to take place in Asia, the most important source of global economic growth, but also a region that has played an important role in AI development and has been significantly hit by the energy shock.
One of the two main topics would be resilience, she said. "What more can we do to create the conditions for successful navigation in an uncertain environment?"
The other topic will be dynamism, she continued. "We should not forget the fact that growth has been somewhat underwhelming. What can be done, and how can it be done to reduce divergence in economic fortunes?" Georgieva said. ■

BRATISLAVA, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said on Tuesday that the European Union (EU) should pursue "friendly competition" with China rather than treat the country as an enemy and put up barriers.

Fico said Slovakia was concerned about the EU's ability to compete globally, arguing that greater competitiveness should not mean imposing new tariffs or barriers, but rather striving to do better and outperform others.
"I have a different view about relations between the EU and China. I don't think we should fight China by putting up barriers and treating it as an enemy," Fico said. "China is a country with which we should compete in a friendly spirit and strive to do better."
On the EU's next long-term budget, Fico said Slovakia supported maintaining a strong cohesion policy to reduce regional disparities across the bloc.
"We're even saying that some extra funding should be found for countries in the eastern part of the EU, which, for example, share borders with Ukraine," he said, adding that a strong agricultural policy is another key Slovak priority.
The two leaders also discussed EU enlargement. Fico reiterated Slovakia's support for countries seeking membership, but said all applicants must meet the required criteria.
"That means no exceptions and no shortcuts. And that also applies to Ukraine," he stressed.
Fico said Ukraine should not be allowed to overtake countries such as Montenegro, Albania or Serbia in the accession process, arguing that they had been preparing for EU membership for much longer. ■

====================================================================================================

Ghanaian expert urges Africa to partner with China for cheaper energy development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:47:40 CST
06:47:40 KST

Benjamin Boakye, Executive Director for Africa Center for Energy Policy (ACEP) is pictured during the 2026 Future of Energy Conference in Accra, Ghana, on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Seth/Xinhua)
ACCRA, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- A Ghanaian expert on Tuesday called on Africa to form a strong partnership with China on energy development for cheaper electricity that will help the continent realize its vision of industrialization.
Benjamin Boakye, Executive Director for Africa Center for Energy Policy (ACEP), said during the 2026 Future of Energy Conference in Accra the Ghanaian capital, that the continent may not be able to realize its value addition and industrialization aspiration and the continental free trade agenda if energy costs remain high on the continent.
Whereas in other jurisdictions, industries pay about six cents per kilowatt-hour (kWh) for electricity, the opposite is the case in Africa, where power costs about 14 to 16 cents per kWh, making products from the continent uncompetitive, due to the energy cost component in their pricing, according to Boakye.
"For industrialization and free trade to succeed on the continent, it is not about importing to sell, but manufacturing at scale and at a competitive cost, so that products in Ghana, for instance, can be exported to other African countries at competitive prices," he highlighted.
The causes of the high cost of energy in Africa, Boakye said, include corruption, sole-sourced contracts, and the high political risk cycle, which makes some investors seek to recover their investments and make profit within the shortest possible time.
The energy expert cited China as an important player in the energy system, which Africa needs right now to deal with the high cost of power on the continent.
In the area of renewable technology, Boakye said "the most affordable technologies available in the world come from China, and that is why we need that level of continental engagement with China on how we reduce the cost of energy."
He said the continent already has untapped resources for cheaper electricity generation, including hydro and solar resources.
"We are seeing imposition of the VAT on export of solar panels and also on battery storage. But that can go off, by intervention. In that proposed conversation, the African Union and its organs should ensure that China partners Africa in a dispensation of cheaper electricity, which is a critical step we need to take immediately," Boakye urged. ■

1,1000-year-old statue of human riding leopard unearthed in SE Türkiye
China
Unknown Publisher

A stone sculpture depicting a human figure sitting on the back of a leopard is pictured at Karahantepe, Sanliurfa province, Türkiye, on Aug. 25, 2026. Archaeologists have uncovered an 11,000-year-old stone sculpture showing a human figure seated on a leopard at Karahantepe, a neolithic site in southeastern Türkiye, Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said Tuesday. (Mustafa Kaya/Handout via Xinhua)
ANKARA, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Archaeologists have uncovered an 11,000-year-old stone sculpture showing a human figure seated on a leopard at Karahantepe, a neolithic site in southeastern Türkiye, Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said Tuesday.
In a social media post, Ersoy said the 70-cm sculpture, which was unearthed at Karahantepe near the city of Sanliurfa this year, was found on a bench against the wall of a circular structure about 3 meters in diameter.
Minister Ersoy called the find a "unique sculpture" and said its artistic style had not previously been identified at the prehistoric settlement.
Karahantepe is part of an archaeological site that encompasses a group of Neolithic sites dating back more than 10,000 years.
In the Neolithic period, communities in the region were transitioning from mobile hunter-gatherer lifestyles toward more settled forms of life. Excavations in the region have revealed monumental structures and sophisticated artwork, providing evidence of complex social and ritual practices long before the emergence of cities and written records.
"I believe this discovery, which opens the door to new questions about the earliest periods of human history, will resonate widely in the scientific community," the Minister added. ■

NASA, ESA astronauts complete spacewalk to install space-to-ground antenna
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26

LOS ANGELES, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- NASA astronaut Anil Menon and European Space Agency (ESA) astronaut Sophie Adenot concluded a spacewalk outside the International Space Station on Tuesday, successfully installing and connecting a spare space-to-ground antenna.
During the 6.5-hour spacewalk, Menon and Adenot installed the antenna, a critical link that enables high-speed data transmission between NASA's Mission Control Center in U.S. Houston and the orbital complex, according to NASA.
They then secured the failed antenna, which had been removed and temporarily stowed during their Aug. 18 spacewalk, to a spare-parts platform on the station's truss structure.
Initial checkouts of the newly installed antenna showed good power and data transmission, NASA said. Flight controllers on the ground will continue testing the antenna overnight to ensure its full functionality.
The spacewalk was Menon's third and Adenot's second. It was also the 283rd spacewalk in support of space station assembly, maintenance and upgrades. ■

Canadian student wins water prize for AI plastic-cleaning robot
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:47:18 CST
06:47:18 KST

HELSINKI, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- A Canadian student has won the 2026 Stockholm Junior Water Prize for developing an autonomous robot that uses artificial intelligence (AI) and magnetic technology to remove plastic from water while minimizing harm to aquatic life.
Moroti Adegboyega of Canada, selected from national winners representing more than 40 countries and regions, received the award from Sweden's Crown Princess Victoria at a ceremony on Tuesday evening in Stockholm.
Adegboyega's project, Ecoferroquatics, combines AI, robotics and a specially developed ferrofluid-based magnetic suspension to detect and collect plastic particles from water.
According to the Stockholm Water Foundation, which hosts the annual competition, the project offers an alternative to existing cleanup methods such as nets, trawlers and filters, which can be labor-intensive and may harm marine organisms.
Tests showed the system outperformed a simple sieve in collecting small particles, including microplastics that can pass through conventional screening methods.
Plastic debris can break down into smaller particles, be ingested by wildlife and carry harmful chemicals through the food chain, the foundation said.
The jury also awarded its Diploma of Excellence to Laura Ivanka of Hungary for DIVE&CLEAN, a project using specially designed underwater bins along recreational diving routes to collect plastic waste before it breaks down into microplastics.
The People's Choice Award went to Basmala Diab of Egypt, whose project uses activated carbon made from rice and corn straw to improve microbial fuel cells that treat wastewater while generating electricity.
Held annually since 1997, the Stockholm Junior Water Prize is an international competition for young people working on water-related research and innovation, with national competitions involving tens of thousands of students worldwide. ■

ABUJA, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- At least 50 children have been killed and several others hospitalized in an outbreak of diphtheria in Nigeria's northwestern state of Kano, the state legislature said Tuesday, calling for swift emergency measures to assist affected communities.
The Kano State House of Assembly called on the government to invoke the state's Health Protection Law to contain the outbreak and directed its committee on health to engage relevant authorities on the public health issue affecting several local government areas.

Other lawmakers at the plenary said the outbreak had spread to other communities and towns across six local government areas, including Rano, Tudun Wada, Kibiya, Bunkure, Bebeji and Kiru.
Diphtheria is a disease caused by a bacterium that affects the upper respiratory tract, and sometimes the skin. It also produces a toxin that damages the heart and the nerves.
According to a 2025 report by the World Health Organization, at least 884 diphtheria-related deaths were reported in an outbreak that affected about 240 local government areas across 30 of Nigeria's 36 states.
The global health body had previously urged Nigeria to increase vaccination coverage to at least 80 percent to ensure community protection and prevent future outbreaks in the country.
In Nigeria more than 2 million children are under-immunized, including those with zero-doses, highlighting the high risk of further spread. ■

World faces historic population decline – study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
21:41:04 UTC
06:41:04 KST

World faces historic population decline – study
Global fertility may have fallen below replacement level for the first time in human history, putting the world population on course for decline within roughly one generation, a new study has warned.
The paper, Terra Incognita: The Economics of a Shrinking World, published earlier this month by economics professor Jesus Fernandez-Villaverde of the University of Pennsylvania and Northwestern University researcher Patrick Norrick, warns that prolonged low fertility could shrink workforces, rapidly age societies, and strain economies and welfare systems.
The researchers estimate that humanity is likely already below replacement fertility – the average number of children per woman needed for each generation to replace itself. The global threshold is around 2.2, while the study puts the current rate at no higher than 2.19, suggesting the world may have only just crossed it.
“As of 2026, humanity is likely to be below replacement level: we are having fewer births than we need to keep population constant in the long run… this has never happened before in our history as a species, not even during wars or pandemics,” the authors stated.
The analysis covers 236 countries and territories from 1950 to 2023, with fertility declining in 219. On average, countries have lost around 0.062 births per woman annually, and there is little evidence the trend is leveling off, authors note.
The global population is not shrinking yet because large generations born in previous decades are still having children, but the researchers estimate this effect could sustain growth for only another three decades, with population peaking at around 9 billion in 2056 before declining.
The authors note the trend has spread well beyond rich countries, with fertility rates in 2025 estimated at just 0.87 in Thailand, 1.01 in Colombia, 1.35 in Iran and 1.52 in Brazil. They say there is no automatic mechanism driving fertility back toward replacement level because there is no single explanation for falling birth rates: while housing and childcare costs, economic insecurity, contraception, and changing social norms may all contribute, none fully explains the global trend.
The economic consequences of the looming population decline could be far-reaching, the study warns. Smaller generations mean fewer workers supporting growing elderly populations, straining pensions, healthcare, and public finances while slowing growth. In the US, the authors estimate that 2% annual productivity growth combined with a 0.5% contraction in the workforce would reduce long-term GDP growth to roughly 1.5%.
UN demographic forecasts have also shifted sharply downward over the past decade. In 2015, the organization projected more than 11.2 billion people in 2100, with no peak before the end of the century. Its 2024 revision instead projected that the population would peak at around 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s before declining slightly to about 10.2 billion by 2100.
The world’s population crossed the 8 billion mark in 2022, according to UN estimates, and currently stands at approximately 8.3 billion.
Musk weighs in
US tech billionaire Elon Musk, who has repeatedly warned about falling birth rates, reacted to the study after an X user described its findings as an “existential crisis.” “I’ve been warning about this for years,” he wrote.
I’ve been warning about this for years https://t.co/kHFPFjNkE7
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) August 23, 2026
Musk, who has 13 children, has repeatedly described declining birth rates as one of the greatest threats to civilization. In 2022, he wrote that “population collapse due to low birth rates is a much bigger risk to civilization than global warming.” Last year, he warned that “Low birth rates will end civilization” and called for the issue to be treated as a national emergency, while suggesting Europe could “die out” unless birth rates recover.
Last weekend, commenting on a paper outlining ancient Rome’s attempts to boost its population, Musk wrote: “The reason Rome fell was because they stopped making Romans.”
Russia’s demographic challenge
Russian officials have long warned about the country’s demographic challenges. According to state statistics agency Rosstat, Russia’s total fertility rate fell to around 1.305-1.374 children per woman last year, alongside some of the lowest monthly and quarterly birth figures in modern Russian history.
Moscow has introduced childbirth payments, expanded maternity benefits and other family support measures to reverse the trend. It has also revived the Soviet-era “Mother Heroine” title, which provides financial rewards to women with ten or more children, and discouraged the promotion of “child-free” lifestyles.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly stressed the importance of improving economic and social conditions in order to promote larger families and make parenthood a widely supported choice. He has backed a national family support service and established a presidential council on family and demographic policy in 2024.

Syria's Kurdish-led SDF dissolves as part of integration with Damascus
The Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces has been dissolved, the armed militant group's leader said on Tuesday, a major step in the integration plan agreed on earlier this year with the Islamist-led government in Damascus.
"We announce today the end of the mission of the Syrian Democratic Forces and announce with full responsibility its dissolution as an independent military force," SDF commander Mazloum Abdi said in a televised speech.
The government and the group, which helped defeat the Islamic State with U.S. backing and held parts of northern and eastern Syria, agreed in January to a phased integration of Kurdish fighters into the state, a plan Washington called a "historic milestone".

Abdi said that the announcement followed an agreement with Sharaa after the integration of the group's forces into the army.
The Kurdish People's Protection Units, which formed the core of the SDF, had already been integrated within state forces with its commander, Sipan Hamo, appointed in March deputy defence minister for the country's eastern territories.
The SDF dissolution comes as the new leaders in Damascus seek to resolve internal strife and rebuild Syria, with support from Washington, after nearly 14 years of civil war and decades of isolation under former President Bashar al-Assad's rule.

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Tuesday granted interim protection from arrest to Abhishek Upadhyay who claimed he was vindictively booked under SC/ST Act by Ghaziabad police for an alleged road rage incident just because he had exposed embezzlement of donations offered by devotees at the Ram temple in Ayodhya.Appearing for the petitioner, senior advocate Pradeep Rai told a bench of CJI Surya Kant that Upadhyay was the whistleblower and the first to report the alleged misappropriation of monies donated by devotees at the Ayodhya temple.He said since UP Police is vindictive, investigations into the alleged road accident case lodged against him coupled with charges under SC/ST Act should be transferred to an independent agency such as CBI or Delhi Police.

Asking police to furnish a copy of the FIR to the petitioner to enable him to take remedial steps in accordance with the law, the bench said, “As soon as a copy of the FIR is received by the petitioner, he shall be at liberty to approach the jurisdictional high court for seeking relevant relief.”

US judge blocks Ohio law requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
21:32:00 UTC
06:32:00 KST

US judge blocks Ohio law requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote
The amended law was an attempt by state Republicans to crack down on unproven claims of voting by noncitizens.
A United States federal court has temporarily blocked an Ohio law that required proof of US citizenship from residents who wanted to register to vote while they obtained a driver’s license.
In his ruling on Tuesday, US District Judge Solomon Oliver Jr granted a preliminary injunction against the law, saying it likely violates the US National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) because it requires more information than necessary to determine a resident’s eligibility to vote.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US Supreme Court sides with Trump administration on mail voting
- list 2 of 3Key takeaways from Donald Trump’s controversial speech on election security
- list 3 of 3Did China steal 2020 US election data, as Trump claims?
“Election officials do not need documentary proof of citizenship to assess a voter registration applicant’s citizenship because signed attestation of citizenship is enough,” Oliver wrote.
The judge also pointed to a clause in the act that says each US state’s driver’s license application “shall serve as an application for voter registration with respect to election for Federal office unless the applicant fails to sign the voter registration application”.
Oliver said that Ohio must offer applicants the opportunity to register once they’ve submitted their driver’s license application, not after it’s been approved by the state’s Bureau of Motor Vehicles (BMV).
“To interpret this section of the NVRA otherwise would allow States to make registering to vote at the BMV more onerous, and could result in fewer voter registrations because the opportunity to apply was not proactively offered to otherwise eligible citizens,” Oliver added.
In 1995, Ohio passed a so-called “motor-voter” law that allowed residents the opportunity to register to vote when they applied for a driver’s license
But that law was amended last year by the state’s Republican-controlled legislature in an attempt to crack down on unproven claims, pushed in part by US President Donald Trump, that noncitizens were voting in the state’s election. US law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections.
The ruling marks a victory for voting rights advocates like Red Wine & Blue, which sued Ohio’s secretary of state, Frank LaRose, over claims that the law disenfranchised eligible voters and violated the NVRA.
One of the group’s lawyers, Ben Stafford, praised the ruling, calling it “a win for Ohio voters.”
“With the registration deadline just weeks away, eligible Ohioans will now have the opportunity to register to vote at the BMV without having to produce unnecessary paperwork that is not required by federal law,” Stafford, an attorney at Elias Law Group, said in a statement.
LaRose said his office disagrees with the decision and will appeal.

SpaceX to expand beyond Texas Starbase with new Louisiana spaceport dedicated to Starship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
21:28:59 UTC
06:28:59 KST

Elon Musk’s SpaceX is ready to expand its horizons beyond its Starbase in South Texas. On Tuesday the company announced it will build a spaceport in Louisiana dedicated to launching its Starship megarocket. The effort is aimed to up SpaceX’s flight cadence to thousands of launches per year, according to the firm.
SpaceX, which became a public company earlier this year with a $1.77-trillion valuation, plans to put at least $100 billion toward the spaceport, which will be situated on Pecan Island in southern Louisiana. The area, which sits within Vermilion Parish, is known for its coastal marshlands. In a video statement, Musk said the new spaceport could lead to thousands of new jobs for the local community; some 57,000 people lived in Vermillion Parish as of the 2020 U.S. Census.
SpaceX also promised to support the site's surrounding wetlands—the company has faced pushback in the past in the form of lawsuits alleging environmental violations and damage to homes near its Texas Starbase.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The new spaceport, which SpaceX has named Starbase, Louisiana, will be the “biggest launch site on Earth,” according to Musk. Dedicating the site to Starship could help launch that vehicle more frequently without compromising the Falcon 9, SpaceX’s current workhorse rocket, or the Falcon Heavy. Eventually, SpaceX hopes to use Starship’s high cargo capacity to rapidly build out its satellite Internet constellation, Starlink, and to construct an orbital artificial intelligence data center. Currently, SpaceX launches its rockets from its Texas Starbase or from facilities in Florida or California.
The move comes days after U.S. President Donald Trump announced an executive order promising the “Golden Age” of spaceflight. Under the order, the administration hopes to boost rocket launches and reentries to more than 1,000 per year by 2030. Part of that effort involves making it easier for space companies to build infrastructure for launch and to grow “a vibrant commercial space economy.”

Canada unveils retaliatory tariffs on about $20 billion of U.S. goods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
21:26:01 UTC
06:26:01 KST

Canada on Tuesday announced retaliatory tariffs against the United States, matching "dollar for dollar" the 50% duties that President Donald Trump imposed over the weekend after a breakdown in trade talks.
Ottawa's new tariffs encompass more than 700 U.S. goods and are worth about $20 billion, mirroring the size of Trump's latest import taxes on Canadian wine, cement, hockey sticks and more.
The counter tariffs range from 15% to 50% and target a wide array of Canadian imports from the U.S., including dairy, seafood, appliances, wood and paper products, and clothes.
Among the most significant are 50% tariffs on American steel and aluminum, doubling the current rate. The duties on metals and wood were chosen to respond to previously imposed U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum, lumber and other products.
The new tariffs are set to take effect Sept. 8. Canada also unveiled an additional $7.5 billion package to support businesses and workers being harmed by the U.S. tariffs.
"When the United States of America asked too much and offered too little, we made a choice. We chose Canada," said Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne at a news conference Tuesday morning.
The new duties would have been averted if the two sides struck a trade deal before they took effect on Saturday. Trump had claimed earlier that week that a deal was all but complete — but Canada suspended negotiations on Friday evening, contending that the U.S. made unreasonable demands and "last-minute changes." The Trump administration has likewise accused Ottawa of blowing up the talks by seeking last-minute changes to the deal.
Trump, asked in a call with CNN about Canada's claim that the U.S. made eleventh-hour demands, said, "That sounds like me."
When pressed to clarify that he does not deny Canada's account of the collapse in trade talks, Trump said, "No, no, I don't deny anything," CNN reported Tuesday afternoon
"So no, they have to pay a fair amount. And if they don't pay a fair amount, we won't make a deal. That's fine," Trump said, according to CNN.
The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on CNN's report.
The collapse of the negotiations has opened a bitter new chapter in the top allies' trade war, raising tensions that were already inflamed by Trump's heavy use of tariffs and inflammatory comments toward Canada.
The new tit-for-tat tariffs could also exacerbate widespread concerns about high costs, as businesses warn they will cause major uncertainty and could make it prohibitively expensive for some sellers to trade across the border.
Prime Minister Mark Carney, in a speech following the failed trade talks, acknowledged that the decision to retaliate "will raise costs and reduce choice for Canadians."
Carney, who became prime minister last year after previously leading the Bank of Canada, has expressed a desire to diversify his country's economy in order to reduce dependence on the U.S., which he says has "changed" under Trump.
Trump has placed tariffs at the center of his agenda throughout his second term in the White House, though his use of the economic tool has faced some major legal setbacks and stoked heated pushback from other countries.
Trump lashed out at Canada on Tuesday morning, suggesting on Truth Social that the U.S. would halt business with Ontario, and repeatedly floating the prospect of renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America."
In more Truth Social posts, Trump accused Canada of targeting U.S. farmers, and complained about America's trade deficit with Canada — though that is primarily due to the U.S. making heavy purchases of Canadian crude oil.
"I deal with many countries, and Canada is easily the most difficult and unreasonable," Trump wrote in one post.
Canada's trade minister, Dominic LeBlanc, told CNBC's "Squawk Box" earlier Tuesday morning that Ottawa did not want to abandon trade talks with the U.S.
"Our preference was to find a deal that benefits both countries," he said. "We still believe that's possible. But in the meantime, we're not waiting by the phone."

NATO surveillance drone flies 25 hour mission
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
22:25:07 BST
06:25:07 KST

A NATO RQ-4D Phoenix has returned to Sigonella in Sicily after a sortie lasting around 25 hours, most of it flown without appearing on public flight tracking.
The aircraft, using the callsign MAGMA10 and carrying the registration MM-AV-SA-0017, departed Sigonella late on the evening of 24 August and landed on the night of 25 August.
It reappeared on tracking at 58,000 feet over Greece as it headed back towards Sicily.
NATO
Operated by Italy Air Force 🇮🇹
RQ-4D Phoenix #33FD5E/MM-AV-SA0017/MAGMA10
Tracking NE out of Sigonella.@Borrowed7Time @blackswanadria @Intel_Sky pic.twitter.com/Jd3W5tb6SD
— 1776Girl (@sipjack1776) August 24, 2026
Sorties of that length are within the design endurance of the type but sit at the upper end of what is routinely observed. The RQ-4D is NATO’s variant of the Global Hawk Block 40, capable of remaining airborne for more than 30 hours at altitudes above 50,000 feet, and the airframe is built around persistence rather than speed.
The Phoenix fleet forms the Alliance Ground Surveillance force, one of the few capabilities NATO owns and operates directly rather than relying on contributions from individual members, alongside the airborne early warning fleet at Geilenkirchen. The aircraft are based at Sigonella and flown by a multinational unit, having reached initial operating capability in 2021.
Their sensor is the Multi-Platform Radar Technology Insertion Program radar, which combines synthetic aperture imaging with a ground moving target indicator mode. In practice that allows the aircraft to build a radar picture of terrain and structures and to detect vehicles and formations moving across it, from a standoff distance and without entering the airspace it is watching.
Since 2022 the fleet has flown extensively along NATO’s eastern flank, with regular missions over the Black Sea, Romania, Poland and the Baltic states, and over the eastern Mediterranean. Flights are frequently visible on public tracking, which is a deliberate feature of the way NATO conducts much of its surveillance, though aircraft do periodically operate without broadcasting.
As we reported on Tuesday, a United States Air Force C-17A Globemaster III, serial 07-7191 and using the callsign REACH 4555, flew from Riga to Moscow Vnukovo, arriving mid-morning. The aircraft had routed from Joint Base Andrews to Latvia two days earlier. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was aboard for meetings in the Russian capital, according to CBS News senior White House reporter Jennifer Jacobs, in what appears to be his first known trip to Russia since taking the post.
Neither Washington nor the Kremlin explained the flight while it was in the air, and military aircraft generally require approval before entering another country’s airspace, which is what made the Riga to Moscow leg notable.
NATO does not comment on individual intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance sorties, and no link between the two movements has been established. Alliance Ground Surveillance aircraft fly routinely over the Black Sea, the eastern flank and the eastern Mediterranean, and a long mission on any given day is not in itself unusual for the type.
Alliance Ground Surveillance sits under Allied Air Command and delivers its product into NATO’s intelligence structures rather than to any single nation. The programme was funded by fifteen member states, with Britain not among the original contributors, though the United Kingdom operates its own strategic ISR fleet including the RC-135W Rivet Joint from RAF Waddington, which flies missions along the same frontier.
One of those aircraft flew a patrol around Kaliningrad on 7 August, and a substantial allied air package including a NATO E-3A Sentry operated over the Baltic region on 18 August, with further flights on the two days following.

Spain speeds up the return of migrants from Ceuta to Morocco
Kyiv • UNN
Spain has approved measures to return migrants who remained in Ceuta after the mass influx from Morocco. There are 3,500–7,000 people in the enclave.
On August 25, the Spanish government approved measures to speed up the return of thousands of migrants who remained in the enclave of Ceuta after the mass influx from Morocco. LRT reports, according to UNN.
Details
At the end of July, more than 70,000 migrants arrived in Ceuta, most of whom subsequently returned to Morocco. Authorities estimate that between 3,500 and 7,000 people remain in the enclave, including unaccompanied minors.
The Spanish authorities must establish the migrants’ identities and determine whether they are entitled to international protection. Those who are not entitled to it may be returned to Morocco in accordance with Spanish law.
To speed up the process, the government created a “single leadership” for Ceuta headed by Minister for Territorial Policy Ángel Víctor Torres.
The priority is to return and repatriate as many people as possible, adults and minors, in accordance with Spanish law and human rights
At the same time, Spain will continue providing humanitarian assistance to asylum seekers and unaccompanied minors. Last week, the government also announced the creation of reception centers for 1,800 migrants.

Expert witnesses challenge claim that Lindsay Clancy experienced psychosis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
21:23:43 UTC
06:23:43 KST

One more day of rebuttal testimony was expected this week in the trial against Lindsay Clancy, followed by closing statements likely on Thursday.
The jury, which will likely begin deliberations on Friday, will decide whether the Massachusetts mother was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she killed her three children in January 2023.
On Tuesday, prosecutors put two expert witnesses on the stand who challenged the arguments made by Clancy’s defense team – specifically, that Clancy committed the acts while suffering from postpartum psychosis – a mental illness that can cause hallucinations, mood swings, delusions and more, and was hearing a voice compelling her to do it. Her attorney Kevin Reddington has also claimed Clancy had bipolar disorder and was overmedicated.
Tuesday’s testimonies capped off more than a month of testimony in a trial that has largely depended on opposing views from experts about Clancy’s mental health and her ability to understand the gravity of what she was doing. 
 It’s not disputed that she strangled the children – Callan, 8 months, Dawson, three years old, and Cora, five years old, before she allegedly jumped from a second-floor window, which left her paralyzed from the waist down. But the outcome of the trial hinges on questions surrounding Clancy’s mental state at the time of the children’s deaths. The burden of proof is on the prosecution to show Clancy was not suffering from “a mental disease or defect” and that she had enough capacity to understand “the wrongfulness or criminality of her conduct”.
Kirk Heilbrun, a forensic psychologist hired by prosecutors, initially took the stand on Friday and continued his testimony on Tuesday morning. He told the court he “did his best to have an open mind”, when he evaluated Clancy in April and that he believed she was “criminally responsible” for the deaths.
“She retained an awareness of the illegality of killing others, including her children,” he said. “Her moral awareness of this killing was influenced by her strong desire to die and, if she was dead, not to leave her children behind.”
Over nearly three days of testimony, the prosecution also focused on the timeline of events during the killings, asking Heilbrun to identify whether each step Clancy took was a decision – including her action to take the children down to the basement – in an attempt to convince the jury that these were planned murders. For each, he answered that they did.
Under cross-examination, Heilbrun’s told the court he had been paid roughly $54,000 for the 180 hours he has worked on the case on behalf of the state, and that he will likely be paid more as the trial goes on. He also told Reddington that he didn’t have experience with postpartum mental health conditions.
A recess was called at one point, after several heated exchanges between Heilbrun and Reddington during which Clancy’s attorney accused the psychologist of not reading her medical reports.
Heilbrun’s testimony on Monday prompted a request for a mistrial from Reddington after the psychologist mentioned Clancy’s Catholic faith. The request was denied, but Judge William Sullivan admonished Heilbrun for the comment and instructed the jury to disregard the reference to “the religion that the defendant was raised with”, calling it “an absolutely inappropriate area of testimony”.
After Heilbrun left the stand on Tuesday afternoon, prosecutors called forensic psychiatrist Gregory Saathoff, who is affiliated with the FBI and University of Virginia. Unlike Heilbrun, he claimed he was not paid for his testimony and had treated several women who have killed their children.
Saathoff told the court that it was unusual that Clancy hadn’t reported hearing voices before the killings and that the voices ceased afterwards. He also said he found several inconsistencies in Clancy’s account of what happened.
It is well documented that Clancy needed treatment for a mental health condition, and admitted herself to McLean, a psychiatric hospital in Massachusetts, a few weeks before the murders. Testimony from expert witnesses who were called by the defense had very different conclusions about her mental state.
Dr Phillip Resnick, a forensic psychiatrist and expert in filicide, testified on Friday that Clancy was “clearly psychotic” on the day she killed her children and was not in control of her actions.
“It was almost like she was a puppet and someone else was pulling the strings,” he said.
That echoed another defense witness, Paul Zeizel, the psychologist who concluded Clancy “had no appreciation for the wrongfulness of her act”.
Before the court adjourned for the day on Tuesday, Judge Sullivan told the jury that the presentation of evidence would conclude on Wednesday and that closing arguments would likely follow on Thursday. Deliberations are expected to begin on Friday. He encouraged jurors not to form their own conclusions until the very end.
“You’ve heard a lot of evidence, but you haven’t heard all of it, right? And like I said before, you haven’t heard the closing arguments of the attorneys,” Sullivan said. “You haven’t heard the law that you’re going to have to apply to this. So you still have to keep an open mind.”
