NEW DELHI: The cost of the Ahmedabad-Mumbai bullet train has been revised to around Rs 2.1 lakh crore, nearly double the original cost of approximately Rs 1.1 lakh crore. The proposal to seek approval for the revised cost of the 508-km high-speed rail line was placed before the Cabinet Tuesday, TOI has learnt.Sources said the railway ministry has cited the time taken in land acquisition in Maharashtra and delay in getting the train sets from Japan as among the main reasons for the cost escalation. They added the project is likely to be completed in 2030 and the first leg of the corridor is scheduled to be operational in Aug 2027.
Sources said most of the additional funding would come from budgetary support. So far, the funding of Rs 1.1 lakh crore has been from Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) and budgetary allocation. They added that Railways has said high-speed trains will be manufactured in India and each of these would cost around Rs 390 crore to Rs 400 crore. There was no official briefing on the decisions of the Cabinet meeting chaired by PM Narendra Modi.In Jan, railway board chairperson Satish Kumar had said the project cost had increased by around 83% to Rs 1.98 lakh crore. The project has faced time and cost overruns due to many reasons, including delay in land acquisition, statutory clearances and finalisation of the trains.

NMC pushes old doctors to re-register, but can’t net new ones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
21:14:36 UTC
06:14:36 KST

Based on MBBS seats and pass rates, at least 68,000 new doctors should have registered to practice.
National Medical Commission (NMC) is seeking to re-register around 11 lakh doctors to create an updated national medical registry, yet it has failed to register even fresh entrants to the profession despite many state registries sharing records every year, reports Rema Nagarajan.Based on MBBS seats and pass rates, at least 68,000 new doctors should have registered to practice, but only 44,400 entries were recorded in 2025 with at least 24,000 graduates missing in Indian Medical Register. The gap points to potential failure of NMC to sync state and national registries, as required under NMC Act.
NMC pushes old docs to re-register, but can’t net new ones
The National Medical Commission (NMC) is pushing a regulation to make about 11 lakh doctors re-register to create an updated national medical registry, but it has failed to even register fresh entrants to the profession despite many state registries sending it new entries every year.With over 91,000 MBBS seats available in 2020-21, even with an estimated 75-90% pass percentage, at least 68,000 MBBS graduates should have registered to practice in 2025. Yet the Indian Medical Register shows just over 44,400 entries. That means at least 24,000 of those who graduated just last year are missing from the registry.If thousands of foreign medical graduates who register each year are included, the number of freshly minted doctors missing from the registry would be even more.
For instance, in 2023, over 10,000 foreign medical graduates passed the qualifying exam, after which they have to complete a mandatory one-year internship before receiving permanent registration that would make them eligible to practice in India. So, most of these 10,000 would have registered in 2025. Thus, the total number of doctors registering in 2025 would be roughly 80,000, but just over half the number (55%) have been added to the registry.Most of the doctors would have registered with state medical councils. However, new entries in state medical council registries are not being reflected in the national registry as the NMC is yet to synchronise all state registries with the national registry. The NMC Act, 2019, had mandated such synchronisation. It is yet to happen, almost six years after the NMC was constituted in Sept 2020. Neither is NMC adding the new entries that many state councils send every year.
Take Assam Medical Council, for instance. It is a state with only govt medical colleges. In the national registry, there are a total of 25,722 registrations from the state council. It shows only one entry for 2025, zero for 2024 and 2023, 106 entries for 2022 and 353 in 2021. The website shows 890 registered in 2024. There were over 720 seats in Assam in 2015 and 1,000 seats in 2020. How is NMC accepting zero entries in 2023 and 2024, or only 106 in 2022?Similarly, NMC’s registry has a total of 67,142 entries from Kerala with just seven entries in 2025 and 17 in 2024. In 2014, Kerala had 3,650 MBBS seats, which increased to 4,500 by 2020. “We are sending details every year... In the name of a new updated NMR, they are not updating the existing one,” said KSMC chief Dr Harikumaran Nair.If the NMC were to register only those who became doctors in the last five years, including foreign medical graduates, it would have had an updated registry of over 3.5 lakh doctors (32%) of the estimated 11 lakh who are said to be available.

They also posted pictures of him meeting with representatives from Chinese community organisations, including groups which are linked to the Chinese government's influence operations.
Strictly speaking this was a breach of protocol, because Liu hasn't yet presented his credentials to the Governor-General, and he's not yet officially ambassador.
Yesterday the department's ever-vigilant protocol branch sent a rather stern note to all diplomatic missions in Canberra reminding them that "ambassadors-designates should avoid media engagement, commentary, advocacy and other activities that could create the impression they have assumed the functions of head of mission".
"Where a public reference is necessary before credentials are presented, missions should use the title of ambassador-designate" it reads.
There was no direct reference in the note to China, or to Ambassador Liu (apologies! Ambassador-designate Liu).
But it's not very hard to guess who the note might have been aimed at.
What is net overseas migration (NOM) and why are politicians fixated on it?
Three letters are defining the latest migration debate in Australia and catching out political parties.
Net overseas migration, or NOM, has become a de facto measure on how tough each party is on migration but the term is widely misunderstood.
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson this week was again forced to clear up the party's NOM target, after their newest MP, David Farley, suggested the party's figures were "not too different" to Labor's.
Labor, the Coalition and One Nation are all saying they will cut back on net overseas migration, although how exactly each party plans to achieve this remains scant on detail and policy.

Consumer inflation running at annual pace of 3.5pc in July, slowing down from 3.8pc in June
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 3.5 per cent in the 12 months to July 2026, down from 3.8 per cent in the 12 months to June, according to the latest data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).
The largest contributor to annual inflation in July was Housing, which rose by 5.0 per cent.
The next largest contributors were food and non-alcoholic beverages, rising 3.2 per cent, and recreation and culture, which rose 2.6 per cent.

Coalition report calls for $30 reduction to pack of cigarettes
A Coalition report has recommended an 80 per cent cut to the tobacco excise, a move that would go further than One Nation's plan to slash the tax on cigarettes.
If the cut were to be implemented, it would lead to a more than $30 reduction in the price of a 25 pack of legal cigarettes sold in Australia.
The report, authored by Liberal MP Mary Aldred and Senator Richard Colbeck, says the excise regime needs to be overhauled to prevent an entirely black market for tobacco and nicotine products.
It also calls for a "highly regulated" licenced framework for businesses to legally sell vapes in Australia.
Tax revenue from tobacco has collapsed between $7.7 billion and $11.8 billion in revenue in the past financial year, in part because of the rise in illicit tobacco sales.
"The strategy of increasing prices to encourage people to quit smoking has been undermined by organised crime and effectively wiped out, and the organised crime price comes with none of the requirements of a regulated market — including selling to children," Colbeck says.
"Our central recommendation is blunt: drastically reduce the tobacco excise, and do it now, because until the price gap closes, no amount of enforcement alone will fix this catastrophic market failure."
Trucking industry launches bid to hold supermarkets accountable for supply chains
The transport union is demanding Aldi and other supermarkets be held accountable for alleged illegal truck contracting in their supply chains, claiming workers are being stripped of their rights while delivering goods to retailers who wilfully turn a blind eye.
Union officials and the Australian Road Transport Industrial Organisation have lodged an application with the Fair Work Commission seeking to force major retailers to audit their contracts with transport companies.
The push comes amid a crackdown by the Australian Taxation Office on so-called sham contracting, a practice in which workers are falsely classified as contractors, denying them entitlements including workers' compensation and superannuation.
The union claims the practice gives trucking companies an unfair cost advantage, allowing them to cut wages and offer retailers transport at a much cheaper rate.
They're turning an accusatory finger to supermarket giant Aldi, which they say has refused to engage in talks about safe supply chains and regularly contracts companies known to have used sham contracting.
"Sham contracting is an illegal and reprehensible scourge on the transport industry, and it is time wealthy transport clients were held accountable for stamping it out," TWU secretary Michael Kaine says.

Hi Peter,
It's easy for everyone to forget that the headline CPI number is an average of all of the consumer prices in the economy, and that underneath that average, some major prices are increasing at much faster rates than the average.
The other day, before today's data was released, I had a look at the general price level.
It told me that, in the last five years, consumer prices have jumped by 24%. But if prices had kept increasing at their 2014-2019 rate, prices would have only risen by 8.8%.
That big space between the old trajectory for prices, and our current price level, is where everyone is living (and hurting). It's where insurance premiums, council rates, and rego costs are making us feel claustrophobic.

Hi Maurie,
When it comes to house prices, the consumer price index captures the prices of new dwellings (new builds and major renovations), rather than property prices per se.
The major prices it collects under its "Housing Group" is new dwellings, rents, and utilities.
And this is what the data says for July:
New dwelling prices:
Rose 5.7% in the 12 months to July 2026, down from a 5.8% rise to June 2026. The rise was driven by project home builders raising base prices to pass through higher labour and materials costs over the year.
Rents:
Rose 3.6% in the 12 months to July 2026, unchanged from the annual rise to June and May 2026.
Utilities:
The annual rise of 6.1% in electricity costs is largely due to the ending of Commonwealth and State Government electricity rebates. This is down from a 22.4% rise in the 12 months to June 2026 mainly due to the timing of rebate payments in 2025.
In monthly terms, prices for Water and sewerage (+5.8%) and Gas and other household fuels (+2.8%) rose following annual price reviews. Prices for Electricity fell 1.6% in monthly terms following annual price reviews.

Trump threatens to demolish Kennedy Center if $250m renovation not done
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
21:10:51 UTC
06:10:51 KST

The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts could be demolished if repairs are not carried out, the Trump administration warned in a court filing on Monday.
Lawyers for the US president said the national arts complex in Washington DC must undergo a $250m renovation or risk facing the wrecking ball.
“Without those efforts, the Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years,” they argued.
The warning came as Donald Trump leaves a trail of destruction in Washington, demolishing the East Wing of the White House to make way for a $600m ballroom and ordering a renovation of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool that resulted in algae blooms and a peeling liner.
The court filing represented the first time that Trump’s allies have raised the prospect of knocking down the Kennedy Center – a 100ft-high complex with a concert hall, opera house and theatre – as the dire alternative to closing it for two years of improvements. Such an aggressive move would be sure to face legal challenges, protests and an outcry from historic preservation groups.
The threat emerged on Monday as the administration urged a federal judge to reject a fresh legal challenge to Trump’s efforts to put his name on the Kennedy Center. The dispute has become part of a months-long battle over the president’s attempt to alter the memorial created by Congress in honour of John F Kennedy, the 35th US president, who was assassinated in 1963.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
A federal judge ruled in May that only Congress has the power to change the Kennedy Center’s name. But the centre’s board, now largely made up of Trump appointees, voted 20-3 on 13 August to change the building’s signage to read “The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J Trump”. It also voted to name the grounds the “President Donald J Trump Plaza”.
The administration argued the latest proposal did not breach the court’s injunction because the building would still formally be called the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. The words “Restored and Renovated by” merely acknowledge Trump’s role, lawyers said, comparing the inscription to acknowledgments of major donors at other cultural institutions.
The filing was made in response to a request by Joyce Beatty, a Democratic congresswoman from Ohio and a member of the Kennedy Center board by virtue of her position in Congress, to stop Trump’s name being restored to the facade.
Beatty sued last year after the centre altered its white marble facade to read “The Donald J Trump and John F Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts”. In May, Judge Christopher Cooper ordered Trump’s name removed, ruling that the venue “must be named for, and is meant to honor, President Kennedy alone”.
Cooper added: “Congress named the Kennedy Center and only Congress can change it.”
Trump’s name was removed from the facade in June and a big tarpaulin has covered the affected section of the building since then. An appeals court last month rejected the administration’s request to keep the name in place while it challenges Cooper’s ruling.
Nathaniel Zelinsky, a lawyer for Beatty, described Monday’s filing as legally baseless and said it “reads like it was written personally by Donald Trump”. Judge Cooper is due to hear Beatty’s request for an injunction at a hearing in federal court in Washington on Thursday.
The Kennedy Center was established by Congress as a living memorial to Kennedy and opened in 1971. It has hosted stars ranging from Frank Sinatra and Beyoncé to Robert De Niro and Lin-Manuel Miranda. It has been limping artistically and commercially since Trump took over last year, culling staff and declaring war on “woke” programming.
On Tuesday, the Washington Post reported that ticket sales, already down since Trump seized control, plummeted further after his board of trustees voted in December to rename the complex after him and put his name on its marble facade.
Norm Eisen, a former White House “ethics czar” and co-founder of the nonpartisan group Democracy Defenders Action, posted on social media that “the administration is now threatening in federal court to LEVEL the Kennedy Center if Trump does not get his way. His path of destruction knows no bounds & he will answer for it in court.”
John Larson, a Democratic congressman from Connecticut, condemned Trump’s threat. “No one is surprised that someone with an ego as big as Donald Trump’s believes their name should be above John F Kennedy’s on our beloved former president’s living memorial,” said Larson. “I wish President Trump were more focused on ending the illegal war he launched in Iran than he is on destroying the Kennedy Center and building his taxpayer-funded ballroom.”
Hands Off the Arts, a group of more than 2,800 activists opposed to government censorship of the arts, said in a statement: “President Trump today issued the judge and American people a threat: ‘Allow me to hijack JFK’s memorial or I will turn it into a crater.’ As Americans, we have already watched in anger the obliteration of the East Wing to satisfy Trump’s vanity – we won’t let it happen again to the Kennedy Center. This is the people’s memorial to honor JFK, and we refuse to let it be desecrated or demolished.”

Trump administration ‘aware’ of the case

“We are aware of reports of an American detained in the West Bank,” the spokesperson said. “The Trump Administration takes its commitment to assist Americans abroad seriously and we are tracking the situation. When Americans are detained abroad, the Department advocates for their access to adequate medical care, proper treatment, and regular consular visits.”

US law demands more than advocacy. Under the Foreign Assistance Act and the Leahy Law, prolonged detention without charge is a gross violation of human rights, and Washington must cut all military aid to the Israeli units responsible for holding her.”

SOUTHCOM Conducts First Drug Boat Strike Under New Counter-Cartel Task Force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
21:06:17 UTC
06:06:17 KST

U.S. Southern Command recently announced its first lethal strike on a suspected narco-trafficking vessel in two months, and the first under a newly formed permanent counter-cartel task force. The U.S. is also reportedly planning to transfer MQ-9 drones to Colombia to bolster its counter-cartel efforts.
On Aug. 23, Joint Task Force-Western Hemisphere “executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific,” according to a SOUTHCOM social media post. The strike happened in the Eastern Pacific and killed two alleged narco-terrorists.
“When I ordered the establishment of Joint Task Force-Western Hemisphere, it was precisely for this purpose: to accelerate, synchronize, and execute lethal actions against these destabilizing narco-terrorist networks,” Marine Corps Gen. Francis L. Donovan, SOUTHCOM commander, said in a statement. “We are committed to imposing total systemic friction on narco-terrorists—disrupting their operations, dismantling their leadership, and eliminating cartel terror across the region.”
A SOUTHCOM spokesperson declined to comment on the strike, citing operational security reasons. An Air Forces Southern spokesperson did not immediately respond to a query.
As of this most recent attack, there have been 67 strikes since Sept. 2, 2025, killing 223 people. Many of the videos released by SOUTHCOM appear to be from drones, and MQ-9s are known to be stationed in the region. SOUTHCOM has declined to say what assets it has used in the strikes.
This first strike under the new task force comes just a few days after the Colombian newspaper El Colombiano reported Aug. 18 that the U.S. will transfer three MQ-9 Reaper drones to Colombia for use in its escalating war on cartels in the country.
“This transfer will also most likely require significant U.S. assistance on the training and doctrine side to allow Colombia to effectively integrate these platforms into their joint operations,” Henry Ziemer, a fellow with the Americas Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Air & Space Forces Magazine
The benefit of Colombia operating its own MQ-9s would be freeing up more assets for SOUTHCOM, Special Operations Command-South, and the 12th Air Force to conduct the backbone of the combatant command’s work in the region—intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance, retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Norm Seip, former Air Forces Southern commander, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Having the drones under Colombian control also widens the U.S. intelligence network in the region, as they’ll likely be coordinating their flights with AFSOUTH’s 612th Air Operations Center, which recently hosted Ecuadorian Air Force intelligence officers for the first time during the region’s largest military exercise, PANAMAX, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported.
SOUTHCOM still has other strike assets for the region, such as the AC-130J gunships located at Comapala, El Salvador, which has been reported as a hub for the Eastern Pacific air campaign against cartels, Ziemer said.
Larger Moves
The drone transfer news came shortly after Colombia, a previous holdout, agreed to join the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition—a 19-member group aligned with U.S. objectives in the region to combat cartels.
This marks the first known time that a Latin American nation has been armed with the MQ-9. Colombia did begin arming its military’s smaller, tactical drones in response to criminal gangs conducting more than 200 drone attacks on military personnel since 2024.
The move to put SOUTHCOM on a more aggressive footing under JTF-WH follows President Donald Trump’s shifting of the National Security Strategy and National Defense Strategy last year to prioritize Western Hemisphere operations.
On Aug. 12, during PANAMAX in Panama, students from the U.S. Naval War College’s Maritime Advanced Warfighting School presented an update to a report requested by Donovan to the commander and Panamanian Minister of Public Security Frank Alexis Ábrego on developing “a joint, combined and interagency defense of identified strategic terrain in the region,” according to a NWC release.
Siep said the report itself wasn’t unusual and likely also stood as another “optic” for the region.
“It sends a couple of messages,” Seip said. “One, to those that are thinking that it’s business as usual with regard to what they may be doing, that is not in line with how SOUTHCOM wants to do business. We’re out there looking at the strategic level of various things that are of our interest to the command there, as well as certainly advertises to the United States taxpayers that, ‘hey SOUTHCOM is growing their game with capability, and here’s one way that we’re doing that’ from a standpoint of intellectual capital that’s being expended for this particular project.”
Though the “strategic terrain” was not identified in the release, Ziemer believes that since it was presented in Panama during the major exercise, it likely relates to the Panama Canal and other critical infrastructure.
“It does reflect a growing interest in SOUTHCOM’s area of responsibility from a U.S. defense planning perspective,” Ziemer said.
Effective Strikes
Donovan testified to Congress in March that while the drug boat strikes will be a part of the overall strategy to counter cartels, they might not be the most effective.
“Putting total systemic friction from point of production to point of delivery … I believe that actually kinetic strikes will be one of the many tools, and probably not the most effective tool, when we actually look at it as more of a campaign approach,” Donovan said at the time.
Seip said he agreed strikes are not the most effective tool, but they have a place in the overall mission to create the systemic friction that Donovan is seeking.
“It may be that these types of strikes, whether you have a positive or negative opinion of them, but these types of strikes may fit into what he’s trying to accomplish,” Seip said.
Part of that is not only hitting those specific boats but also sending a message: “You will not be allowed to operate and roam freely in the waters of South and Central America without consequences,” said Seip, president of the D.C. think tank American Security Project.
While experts say the strikes have not made a large impact on drugs flowing to the United States, the strikes are likely to continue.
“Neither the White House nor SOUTHCOM wants to foreclose the option to carry out future strikes against trafficking targets at sea, even as they recognize this strategy has not had the desired effect on drug trafficking flows,” Ziemer said. “Going forward, I would expect to see these kinds of strikes continue, albeit more sporadically.”

US targets 1,000-plus Tomahawks a year
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
22:00:42 BST
06:00:42 KST

Raytheon has received a seven-year contract worth $22.9 billion to sharply increase Tomahawk cruise missile production, with annual output planned to rise above 1,000 weapons for the US Navy and allied customers.
The United States is moving to raise annual production of Tomahawk long-range cruise missiles to more than 1,000 weapons under a seven-year contract awarded to Raytheon, according to the company.
The RTX news update values the agreement at $22.9 billion, approximately £16.8 billion, and says it will support a major expansion of manufacturing capacity for the US Navy and allied customers. Raytheon described the award as part of the Department of War’s wider “Arsenal of Freedom” effort to increase production of high-demand weapons.
Tomahawk is a long-range, subsonic precision-strike cruise missile used primarily to attack targets on land from substantial stand-off distances. In US naval service it can be launched from surface warships and submarines, giving commanders the ability to strike fixed and other designated targets hundreds of miles from the launch platform without placing crewed aircraft directly over the target area. Newer versions of the weapon have also expanded the missile’s targeting and maritime strike capabilities.
Raytheon President Phil Jasper said, as quoted in a news update: “Tomahawk is the Navy’s most important strike weapon, able to target hostile forces hundreds of miles away without ever risking the lives of our sailors.”
He added: “We are making significant investments in our workforce, technology, supply chain and facilities to dramatically boost production capacity and meet surging demand.”
The scale of the planned production increase is substantial. RTX said the new contract supports an annual manufacturing rate exceeding 1,000 Tomahawks, together with associated support. The company did not state that production is already running at that level, instead describing the figure as the target of the multi-year production ramp.
RTX has already been increasing deliveries. According to the company, Raytheon delivered three times as many Tomahawk missiles during the first half of 2026 as it did during the equivalent six months of 2025. The seven-year arrangement is intended to provide greater certainty to the manufacturer and its supply chain as production expands further.
Hundreds of small and medium-sized suppliers across the United States are expected to contribute to the programme. Long-term contracting can allow manufacturers further down the weapons supply chain to invest in machinery, staff and production capacity with greater confidence than under smaller annual orders, particularly where specialist components can otherwise become bottlenecks as final assembly rates increase.
Tomahawk has been in US service for decades and has been repeatedly used in combat for long-range conventional strikes. The weapon has undergone successive upgrades rather than being replaced outright, with later variants introducing changes to communications, targeting and mission flexibility while retaining the basic role of delivering precision effects at extended range.

====================================================================================================

The ‘polite’ face of Germany’s far right: Where can he take the AfD?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

Germany’s most dangerous man or a ‘polite’ face of the far right?
- Ulrich Siegmund, a popular AfD figure, could become Germany's first far-right state premier, as the AfD leads with over 40% in Saxony-Anhalt polls, threatening traditional parties.
- The AfD promotes radical policies including mass deportations, scaling down public broadcasting, favouring Russian gas, and overturning Germany's current political and social order.
- The party's rise exploits eastern Germany's economic and political frustrations, raising fears of authoritarianism, economic harm, and social division among the people.
AI generated
JERICHOW, Germany – On a warm afternoon in the small east German town of Jerichow, Ulrich Siegmund looked less like a political firebrand and more like a polite neighbour.
Slender, with neatly parted hair, and wearing an approachable smile, the 35-year-old moved easily across the central square.
He shook every hand and patted dozens of backs. He asked about family, remembered names and patiently posed for smartphone wefies with anyone who asked.
By the time the town’s “AfD Barbecue” reached its peak, more than 300 locals had gathered under the blue-and-white banners of the Alternative fur Deutschland (AfD). They ate grilled sausages, drank beer and cheered.
Yet, behind this staged picture of rural normalcy lies a profound political earthquake.
Siegmund could soon become the first far-right state premier in post-World War II German history.
In the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, elections are scheduled for Sept 6 – and the AfD is polling at over 40 per cent.
Under favourable circumstances, even slightly more than 40 per cent could be enough for the party to secure an absolute majority of seats in the regional Parliament.
It would allow the AfD to govern alone – without Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the Social Democrats or any other traditional party that has governed Germany since 1949.
Siegmund’s primary rival is Sven Schulze, the current prime minister of Saxony-Anhalt and leader of the state’s CDU. However, in the opinion polls, the CDU garners only between 22 and 24 per cent.
Eighty-one years after the fall of Adolf Hitler’s Nazi regime in 1945, a party whose Saxony-Anhalt state organisation is classified by the state’s domestic intelligence service as a confirmed right-wing extremist organisation stands on the precipice of real state power.
Siegmund’s speech that afternoon in Jerichow lasted barely five minutes. But the audience were not there for policy details. They were there to rub shoulders with him. He merely repeated well-worn populist tropes.
He claims that free speech no longer exists in Germany, demands the abolition of public broadcasting accused of ideological and political bias, calls for mass deportations of immigrants and condemns German aid to Ukraine.
Siegmund has cultivated the image of a political pop star. In July, he led a roaring convoy of 400 vintage East German Simson mopeds through the countryside, invoking nostalgia for a vanished socialist state. When Der Spiegel, Germany’s leading news magazine, put his face on its cover with the headline, The Most Dangerous Man In Germany, Siegmund did not hide.
He autographed copies of the magazine on camera and broadcast the video on Instagram as a badge of honour.
Gone are the days when voting for the AfD was a source of shame. Today, people openly flaunt it.
However, beneath the polished social media presence lies an apparatus deeply rooted in radical networks. Investigative reports reveal that Siegmund’s parliamentary staff includes former leaders of the Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend, a neo-nazi youth organisation banned by the German government in 2009.
Key strategic positions in a potential AfD administration – including the chief of the state chancery and senior justice officials – have been discussed for candidates with ties to banned right-wing groups.
Siegmund’s campaign operation also has links to activists and entrepreneurs from the Identitarian milieu. The Identitarian movement is a far-right European network that promotes the idea that white, European cultures are under threat from mass immigration and globalisation.
What would an AfD government look like?
Ronald Glaser, a prominent AfD lawmaker in Berlin, leaves little doubt about the party’s radical ambitions.
“A mildew has hung over Germany, essentially since the days of Helmut Kohl,” he said in an interview with The Straits Times, referring to the chancellor of Germany from 1982 to 1998.
The late Kohl was also former chancellor Angela Merkel’s mentor.
“Nothing has changed for the better, everything just kept getting worse”, Glaser, 52, said.
“There are far too many checks and balances in Germany that produce a reform backlog. Now a new party needs to step in and push things through.”
The AfD’s priorities reflect a fundamental overhaul of German domestic and foreign policy: ending subsidies for renewable energy in favour of nuclear power; reducing public broadcasting to a drastically scaled-down, tax-funded Grundfunk – or basic – broadcasting; arguing that Germany has already fulfilled its humanitarian obligation to Ukraine by taking in refugees, and restoring cheap Russian gas imports.
“Countries have interests, not friends,” Glaser argued. “We want to do business with the Russians because they have cheap gas and are an important, powerful neighbour.”
He does not deny Russia’s responsibility for the invasion of Ukraine. “Of course the invasion was wrong,” he said. “But if we’re going to talk about it, then we also have to talk about the whole history leading up to it.”
He was echoing the Russian narrative that the country was encircled by NATO and had no other choice but to invade Ukraine.
On immigration, the AfD’s stance is uncompromising. Glaser, who was a staff writer for the right-wing weekly Junge Freiheit, called for a “wave of deportations”.
Siegmund himself openly uses the term “remigration”, which is a far-right political concept that advocates for the forced removal of migrants and, in some formulations, even citizens with a migration background.
Why right-wing populism resonates in eastern Germany
To understand why this message resonates so strongly in eastern Germany, one must look at the political and social legacy of the past.
When the Berlin Wall fell in 1989 and East Germany was integrated into the Federal Republic, millions expected rapid prosperity.
Decades later, despite vast economic investments, many formerly from East Germany still feel disenfranchised.
“The feeling of political powerlessness is widespread in the east, as is the feeling of being second-class citizens,” Benjamin Hohne, a political science professor at the University of Chemnitz, explained to ST.
“East Germans remain vastly underrepresented in the civil service, universities, the judiciary and the media. Right-wing populist parties specialise in unearthing deep-seated resentments that other parties try to overcome.”
Hohne noted that in rural eastern provinces, civil society is fragile. “In rural areas, civil society structures are often weak or barely existent,” he said. “In some places, there may be little more than the volunteer fire brigade or a football club. The AfD exploits these gaps, including through its so-called citizens’ forums, which can attract considerable numbers of people.”
“For quite a few East Germans, this was never their Federal Republic, never their Constitution,” he added. “It came from the outside. It was the political order of West Germans. Many have turned away from democracy altogether, drawn towards a strong leader who will finally clean things up.”
Hohne does not reject Germany’s political firewall against the AfD. Rather, he argued that it has often been too unstable.
Established parties on the centre-right, like CDU, have at times adopted AfD positions on issues such as migration and security, while local politicians have occasionally cooperated with the AfD in municipal councils.
The aim, he said, is often to win back voters who drifted to the AfD.
But the strategy can backfire by making the AfD’s positions appear more legitimate and familiar, and “in the end, people vote for the original”, he explained.
AfD’s rise has become a national phenomenon
The AfD’s appeal is by no means confined to eastern Germany. The party has become a nationwide political force, drawing support from voters across the country and from different social groups.
This authoritarian pull alarms historians like Ilko-Sascha Kowalczuk, author of the book Fascism Is Not An Opinion.
The real fear was that Germans may no longer be able to maintain the high level of prosperity they have become accustomed to, Kowalczuk recently said in an interview with Super Illu, founded in 1990 after the fall of the Berlin Wall as a “magazine of unity”.
However, he rejects the idea that Germany’s problems justify the AfD’s increasingly radical politics. To him, the mild explanations offered by political analysts fail to grasp the severity of the moment.
“I have no time for the soft interpretation that while the AfD is far-right, its voters are not,” Kowalczuk said.
“The AfD strives for authoritarian state structures based on racist ideas. That makes it a fascist movement, and its electorate a fascist electorate. Whoever votes for fascists is a fascist.”
Kowalczuk, who grew up in East Germany, dismisses the AfD’s claim that it represents the legacy of the 1989 Peaceful Revolution that brought down the Berlin Wall.
“The 1989 revolution was a revolution for freedom, an uprising for an open society and human rights,” he said. “The AfD seeks the exact opposite: exclusion and disintegration. It is a travesty for the AfD to invoke the values of 1989.”
Far-right forces are growing globally
Kowalczuk also sees the rise of radical right-wing populism as a global phenomenon stretching from Washington to Rome.
“There is an extreme sense of insecurity caused by rapid digitalisation and globalisation. Extremists offer one simple promise: security through a romanticised, fake past.
“I fear we are standing on the threshold of a new authoritarian era worldwide.”
The AfD has also gained an international network of supporters. US President Donald Trump and his administration have openly embraced the party. The richest man in the world, Elon Musk, also publicly endorsed the AfD.
Still, there is little evidence that American support has directly translated into additional votes. Even among many AfD voters, the erratic Trump is highly unpopular.
The AfD is meanwhile attracting more younger voters, particularly young men. At the 2025 federal election, roughly one in five voters under 35 backed the party.
Still, the AfD’s strongest support comes from middle-aged voters, while younger Germans remain divided between the far right and the far left.
Some economists warn that a victory by the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt could inflict serious economic damage on the state.
A study by the Halle Institute for Economic Research estimated that the AfD’s fiscal proposals for the state would create an annual financing gap of €2.2 billion (S$3.3 billion).
The party proposes an expansion of costly public benefits and infrastructure spending, while pledging to lower taxes and reject any new government borrowing.
Furthermore, in a country suffering from acute demographic decline, anti-immigrant rhetoric threatens to cut off the inflow of skilled foreign labour essential for high-tech industries, green energy transformation, and healthcare.
German business organisations and economic leaders have increasingly warned that the AfD’s policies could undermine international cooperation, investment and access to skilled labour.
In Jerichow, as the afternoon sun began to dip, Siegmund posed for his final batch of wefies. Before doing so, he made sure that no one is left without a picture.
Across from the barbecue party, a group of protesters had gathered, holding anti-AfD signs.
Siegmund approached them and asked: “Is there anything I can do to change your mind?” Minutes later, he was seen engaging in a conversation with them.
When asked if she was worried about the AfD’s rise, 44-year-old Franziska, who was standing nearby, said: “I have a young child, and of course I’m worried.
“The AfD is growing more and more. And if they actually get into power, we have no idea what’s in store for us,” she added, declining to provide her full name for fear of reprisal.

Nigel Farage wants to scrap GDPR for the UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

LONDON — Reform UK on Tuesday night outlined plans to scrap the U.K.’s data protection regime as part of a broader package of measures designed to help small businesses.
The U.K. decided to incorporate an amended version of the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) privacy laws into British law post-Brexit. Reform UK says it would replace the U.K. version of GDPR with a “light-touch” privacy law modeled on New Zealand’s approach to data protection.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said small businesses have had to deal with “suffocating EU red tape” and the package, which includes abolishing GDPR, is a “bold, common-sense rescue plan.”
Advertisement
“[T]he GDPR has strangled small businesses and tech firms alike in a web of unnecessary regulation ... Ten years after the Brexit referendum we should not still be following ridiculous EU privacy laws that hurt British businesses,” Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick said in a statement.
The EU GDPR provides for a wider set of individual rights around personal data (including the “right to be forgotten”) than New Zealand's Privacy Act does.
However, Reform UK stressed in its press release that following the New Zealand model would preserve the U.K.'s EU data adequacy status, meaning personal data would still be allowed to flow freely between the U.K. and EU.
The European Commission only grants adequacy to countries that provide an essentially equivalent level of data protection to that of the EU.
The U.K. has already diverged from Brussels on privacy laws with the passage of the Data (Use and Access) Act last year, which relaxed some aspects of the U.K. GDPR in a bid to boost economic growth.

A book about Putin’s rise to power and personal life has received a literary award in France
Kyiv • UNN
A book about Putin by Russian journalists in exile Roman Badanin and Mikhail Rubin has won the Prix Strasbourg. The winner receives 20,000 euros.
The book about Vladimir Putin by Russian journalists in exile Roman Badanin and Mikhail Rubin has received the newly established French literary prize Prix Strasbourg. LRT reports this, writes UNN.
Details
The book "The Tsar in His Own Person: How Vladimir Putin Deceived Us All" became the winner of the prize, which is presented by the French newspaper group EBRA and its parent company, Crédit Mutuel Alliance Fédérale.
The work is based on more than two decades of journalistic investigations and hundreds of interviews. According to the jury, the book reads like a spy novel and is "an intriguing and shocking work about a man who is himself intriguing and shocking."
The book's authors are the founders and investigative journalists of the publication "Proekt." Badanin and Rubin live in the United States after coming under pressure from the Russian authorities.
In the book, the authors examine Putin's path from a former KGB agent to the leader of Russia, as well as his personal life. In particular, they describe extramarital affairs, cronyism, and ties to organized crime.
Prix Strasbourg was established in 2026. The winner receives 20,000 euros, while the prize's total purse amounts to 55,000 euros. The laureates' award ceremony will take place in Strasbourg in September.

Third Drone With Traces of Explosives Found Near Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport
German investigators have discovered another drone carrying traces of explosives that may have been connected to an incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The drone, the third reportedly linked to the incident, was found in a field near the airport in the municipality of Kabelsketal on the evening of August 14, ten days after the first drone was discovered, according to Süddeutsche Zeitung on August 25.
Investigators examining the site detected a substance that, according to preliminary assessments, could have been traces of an explosive mixture containing RDX, a powerful military-grade explosive.
The discovery comes amid growing concerns in Germany over drone-related security threats. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said recent incidents indicate that the country is increasingly becoming a target of hybrid operations and that Berlin intends to strengthen its response.
According to Ukrinform on August 25, Merz said the events of recent weeks had heightened public concern over security threats, pointing to the August 4 incident at Leipzig Airport as evidence that hybrid actors are increasingly willing to risk significant property damage, injuries, and even loss of life. Despite the heightened threat, he stressed that Germany remains a safe country overall.
The latest discovery follows an earlier incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport involving a Ukrainian cargo aircraft. A drone believed to have been fitted with an explosive device was found near a Ukrainian An-124 transport plane overnight on August 5.
According to German newspaper Bild, the drone was discovered on the airport apron shortly before midnight, directly beside the Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft.

Dolly Parton’s Enduring Gift of Books
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
20:52:53 UTC
05:52:53 KST

Dolly Parton, who rose from poverty to become the nation’s most beloved country music legend and a unifying literacy hero, died today at her home in Nashville, according to a family statement.
Thirty years ago, in honor of her father, Robert Lee Parton, who could neither read nor write, she launched Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library in Sevier County, Tennessee, the Appalachian community where she grew up. The goal was simple: put carefully selected, age-appropriate books into children’s homes before kindergarten, every month, at no cost to families.
Three decades later, that local initiative has become an international program to promote early literacy that mails free books to children from birth to age five through partnerships with the Dollywood Foundation, local program partners, states, communities, and donors. It operates in English-predominant countries—the US, Canada, the UK, Australia, and the Republic of Ireland, but it has expanded its reach to include bilingual Spanish-English options in some states, as well as audio and Braille books.
Recent program reports count more than 300 million books gifted and more than 3 million books mailed each month.
Parton’s philosophy was to treat literacy as a birthright for everyone. A child enrolled from birth can receive a home library of up to 60 books, each arriving in the child’s name.
Learn more at https://imaginationlibrary.com/. Supporters can contribute directly at https://donate.imaginationlibrary.com, where gifts help local partners keep books moving from shelves to doorsteps.

Dolly Parton, queen of country music, dies at 80
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
20:49:13 UTC
05:49:13 KST

‘She never saw a door she couldn’t open’: Singer Dolly Parton was more than just a music icon
Dolly Parton was around six when she wrote her first song Little Tiny Tasseltop, an ode to her corncob doll with corn-silk hair. Her mother stored it preciously in a shoebox.
“I loved that little doll,” Parton wrote decades later. “I expressed myself and my feelings through writing – I’m sure what I was thinking was, ‘Well, Tasseltop has to have a song about her’.”
Parton never stopped making music after that. The irrepressible American country music singer, songwriter and actress whose charisma, heartfelt lyrics and business acumen captured the public’s imagination for nearly six decades, died on Aug 25 at the age of 80, her family said in a statement.
No cause of death was disclosed, but her publicist said she died peacefully in Nashville. People magazine reported the star fought a “brief battle with cancer”, citing her representatives. Days earlier, she had told People that she was dealing with unspecified health issues but planned to keep working.
“By her example, we believed anything was possible,” her nephew Bryan Seaver said in a video message. “She never saw a door she couldn’t open, and the doors she opened made and changed history.”
With classic songs including Coat Of Many Colors (1971), Jolene (1973) and I Will Always Love You (1974), Parton became one of the best-selling female artistes of all time, with over 100 million records sold. She won 11 Grammys, including a Lifetime Achievement Award.
Parton’s wholesome personality, combined with her towering blonde hairdos, flamboyant costumes and giddy delight at holding centre stage, endeared her to Americans of all backgrounds and helped introduce country music to international audiences.
Over the years, she hosted a TV variety show, starred in movies, and even created a theme park, Dollywood, a popular tourist spot in her home state of Tennessee – all in addition to her lauded work as a songwriter.
But the quality that gave her enduring star power was her ability to connect with people. Coming from a self-described “dirt-poor” family, Parton often stood as a symbol of the working-class American and regularly threw her name and money behind causes she believed in.
In response to the Covid-19 pandemic, she donated US$1 million to vaccine research at Vanderbilt University in 2020, making her an early sponsor of Moderna’s vaccine development.
She conducted a literacy programme for pre-school children across the United States, as well as in Canada, Britain, Australia and Ireland, and provided scholarships to high school students in the Tennessee county where she was born.
The county erected a life-size statue of her in front of the courthouse in appreciation, though she declined another proposed statue of her in Nashville in 2021, saying: “Given all that’s going on in the world, I don’t think putting me on a pedestal is appropriate at this time.”
It was this ability to stay true to her roots, combined with her drive to work hard and her non-partisanship, that fuelled her appeal among conservatives and liberals in a politically polarised America.
US President Donald Trump ordered flags to be lowered across the country, and New York’s Empire State Building was to be lit in pink at 9.25pm local time – a nod to Parton’s hit song and movie 9 To 5 (1980).
He called her passing a “true loss for millions of people”.
“There has never been anyone like her, and never will,” Trump posted on his Truth Social network. “Rest in peace, Dolly! The world loves you.”
‘Mama had this haunting voice’
Dolly Rebecca Parton was born on Jan 19, 1946, in Pittman Center, Tennessee, and grew up in a one-room cabin in nearby Locust Ridge. One of 12 children of tobacco farmer Robert Lee Parton, her difficult childhood gave credibility to her often personal songs trilled in a distinctive soprano.
Her mother, Avie Lee, would sing constantly – songs from England, Ireland and Wales that told a story. “Mama had this haunting voice, and Lord you would feel it,” Parton wrote in her 2020 book Dolly Parton, Songteller co-authored with Robert K. Oermann.
Parton got her first real guitar when she was eight. Her mother would say, whenever she had guests: “I want you to hear this song this little thing has made up. It’s really good.” Parton loved the attention.
She was singing on a local radio station by age 11, and at age 13, was appearing on the Grand Ole Opry, a weekly country music concert in Nashville, Tennessee.
After graduating from high school, she moved to Nashville to pursue a music career and began a famous partnership with country music singer Porter Wagoner, which would include a years-long stint on his TV show and 14 top 10 duets.
She penned her hit song I Will Always Love You as a farewell to Wagoner when she decided to pursue a solo career.
On the first day Parton arrived in country music’s capital, she met Carl Dean, an asphalt paver. They would marry two years later, in 1966. The couple had no children and he died in 2025.
Throughout their long marriage, Dean shunned the spotlight and did not tour with her, though he would be a muse for many of her greatest hits, including Jolene, which was inspired by a red-haired bank teller’s crush on Dean.
‘The Dolly image’
Her own appearance was the object of intense interest. Initially embarrassed, she eventually found the humour in frequent questions about her extravagant dress sense and generous figure.
She dismissed rumours that her breasts were insured and laughed off periodic rumours that she was bedridden due to their weight, telling People magazine: “Well, they are heavy, but they haven’t crippled me yet.”
Parton patterned her signature look on a woman she would see walking around her Tennessee home town in tight skirts and high heels, with red nails, red lipstick and peroxided hair.
“I thought she was beautiful. But everybody said, ‘She’s trash!’” Parton wrote in her 2023 book Behind The Seams: My Life In Rhinestones.
“I laughed and said, ‘Well, if that’s trash, that’s what I want to be when I grow up!’”
But as much as she embraced her signature look, she also viewed it as distinct from herself.
“I look one way and am another,” she told Ladies’ Home Journal in 1982.
“It makes for a good combination. I always think of ‘her’, the Dolly image, like a ventriloquist does his dummy. I have fun with it. I think, what will I do with her this year to surprise people? What’ll she wear? What’ll she say?”
She also expressed the wish that her appearance would serve to sell, rather than overshadow, her talent.
‘I want to paint a picture’
Her music gained a following not only among the public but also with fellow singers who widely covered her songs – perhaps most famously pop diva Whitney Houston’s rendition of I Will Always Love You.
Some of Parton’s most beloved covers and duets were with her goddaughter, American singer-actress Miley Cyrus and Cyrus’ father, country music star Billy Ray Cyrus.
Jolene was covered by artistes as varied as Beyonce and rock duo The White Stripes.
While Parton was a force onstage and an accomplished vocalist, what set her apart from her peers was her talent with words.
She wrote every one of her hit songs. All told, she penned an estimated 3,000 throughout her life, though she recorded only about 450 of them.
“I love to write poetic songs and sing flowery words,” she wrote in Dolly Parton, Songteller.
“I like to make you see something visually, so I want to paint a picture.
"And I love to come up with clever lines, not just like a songwriter, but like a poet.”
‘The songs are my legacy’
Parton made her movie debut in 9 To 5, starring alongside Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin, with the title tune earning Parton an Oscar nomination for songwriting. She got another Oscar songwriting nomination in 2006 for Travelin’ Thru, written for the 2005 film Transamerica.
Her other movie acting roles included The Best Little Whorehouse In Texas (1982), Steel Magnolias (1989), Rhinestone (1984) and Straight Talk (1992).
Twenty-five of her songs reached No. 1 on the Billboard Country charts and she was a member of the Songwriters Hall of Fame, receiving its highest honour, the Johnny Mercer Award, in 2007. She was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022.
Parton received her first Grammy award in 1978 for her song Here You Come Again. In 1988, she won the People’s Choice Award for favourite all-around female entertainer.
But despite all her accolades and achievements, Parton found the greatest meaning in her art.
“I feel like I’m closest to God when I write,” she wrote in Dolly Parton, Songteller. “A great line will just come to me, and I’ll go, ‘Hey, thank You, Lord. I know I didn’t think of that.’
“At the end of the day, I hope that I will be remembered as a good songwriter. The songs are my legacy.” REUTERS

The SG said Centre was not seeking review or modification of the judgement.
NEW DELHI: Seeking two years to frame creamy layer criteria for OBCs, Centre Tuesday requested Supreme Court for an early hearing on its application against retrospective implementation of SC’s March 11 judgement, which disallowed this classification of OBC candidates based on the salaries of parents employed in PSUs or the private sector.Solicitor general Tushar Mehta requested a bench led by CJI Surya Kant to list the application seeking certain clarifications on the March 11 judgement in the Rohit Nathan case. This was opposed by advocate Varun Thakur, who said the law was settled by SC.The SG said Centre was not seeking review or modification of the judgement but wanted to apprise the court of field-level difficulties in retrospective implementation. The SG said this would require changing the status of older batches of creamy layer OBC candidates to non-creamy and warrant change in cadre, post and service in civil services. It would also necessitate corresponding changes for an equal number of candidates who had long been serving in a cadre and service like IFS, IAS and IPS, and result in chaos.Mehta said he was only requesting early listing before a bench of Justices P S Narasimha and R Mahadevan.
CJI agreed to list the applications on Sept 1.In its application, Centre said, “On account of the serious challenges and implications with the implementation of the directions of SC, govt is committed to bring out a policy which will effectively address the observations made by SC, while also ensuring that the direct and indirect impact of the policy is fair and just.”If the March 11 judgement is implemented without suitable policy intervention it will have a far-reaching impact on govt recruitments and admissions in higher education institutions undertaken by central as well as 18 state/UT govts, it said.Govt said major bodies/employers — like Railways, banks, the department of posts and paramilitary — would also be flooded with hundreds of thousands of representations/litigations seeking retrospective reclassification of the creamy layer.
Following the Indra Sawhney judgement in 1992, govt had issued an office memorandum on Sept 8, 1993, prescribing the criteria for identifying the OBC creamy layer who would be excluded from reservation benefits.In its March 11 judgement, SC had also observed that the determination of the creamy layer status must be based on the occupational categories specified in the 1993 office memorandum and the income of parents employed in private sector organisations could not automatically lead to the conclusion that the candidate belonged to the creamy layer.

Trump says China is driving opposition to US data centres. These residents disagree

Trump says China is driving anger at US data centres. These residents disagree
Community living near AI facility in Virginia reports invasive levels of noise, fumes and gas turbines – and it’s not Chinese propaganda
On the tree-lined streets of Sterling, northern Virginia, Lindsay Shaw’s home sits across from an industrial neighbour that has consumed the past several years of her life: a data centre.
When Shaw sits outside, she can hear its constant hum. At night, the security lights blaze through her window, making it harder to sleep. Gas turbines, diesel fumes, and 24/7 industrial noise have choked Shaw’s neighbourhood since the data centre moved in.
“It’s not China telling us anything. It’s not Russia telling us anything,” Shaw said. “It’s truly living next to it is what it is.”
Shaw came to this view gradually. She did not initially oppose the project. Shaw and her husband had worked in cybersecurity and understood the need for data centres to power cloud infrastructure and artificial intelligence.
Their concerns only emerged after the facility was approved, when eight gas turbines were added to power it while it awaited a connection to the electrical grid – a process that can take years. It was not until it was up and running that the constant noise, occasional smoke and nightly lights came.

Meta reaches $17 billion settlement with US states over social media harm to teens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Meta reaches $17 billion settlement with US states over social media harm to teens
Meta Platforms on Wednesday agreed to pay $17 billion to settle claims, filed by 47 US states, that the company designed Facebook and Instagram to deliberately make teens addicted to their products while deceiving the public, according to state attorneys general. The company agreed to add child-safety measures as part of the settlement.
Meta has agreed to pay $17 billion and add child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms to end a landmark trial over teen social media addiction and settle claims filed by 47 states, state attorneys general announced Wednesday.
California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey were among 29 states that sued the tech giant in 2023, but the deal cuts short the trial, which was expected to see CEO Mark Zuckerberg take the stand before a jury in federal court in California.
The agreement is worth $353 million in Virginia alone and is one of the biggest in state consumer protection history, Attorney General Jay Jones said in a statement.
Read moreMeta sued by US states for hooking and exploiting kids in pursuit of profit
“For years, Meta intentionally deceived the public about the addictive and harmful design features that have wreaked havoc on youth mental health," Jones said. The settlement "will put an end to these dangerous practices and deliver meaningful relief that will protect children from online harm”.
Meta did not respond immediately to a request for comment. The $17 billion settlement is a fraction of the company's 2025 revenue of $201 billion.
The lawsuit accused Meta of contributing to the youth mental health crisis by deliberately designing features that addict children to its platforms and hiding them from the public. It also argued that Meta violated federal laws by routinely collecting data on children under 13 without their parents’ consent.
The trial kicked off last week in Oakland, California, with US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers overseeing the proceedings. Adam Mosseri, the head of Instagram, began his testimony late Tuesday and defended Meta’s record and progress on child safety and privacy.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The cases in other states had been expected to go to trial later. In addition, nine attorneys general filed lawsuits in their respective states.
Under the proposed settlement, Meta agreed to adopt a series of safety features, including a “hard cap” on daily time limits and pauses for children using Instagram and Facebook.
It will eliminate push notifications during weekday school hours and bring in “robust” age-assurance measures and “age-appropriate” content controls to prevent bullying and harmful material about eating disorders and self-harm.
There will be stronger and more user-friendly parental controls and limits on social comparison features such as “like” counts.
The federal lawsuit was the result of an investigation led by a bipartisan coalition of attorneys general from California, Florida, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Nebraska, New Jersey, Tennessee, and Vermont. It followed newspaper reports, first by The Wall Street Journal in 2021, that found that the company knew about the harm Instagram can cause teenagers – especially teen girls – when it comes to mental health and body image issues.
Meta has since added a host of safety features to Instagram, including separate accounts for teenagers with stronger protections around messaging and privacy, along with content restrictions.
But child safety experts, along with some former Meta employees, have long contended that the features are little more than window dressing.
Read moreFacebook and Instagram must stop ‘addictive’ features like infinite scroll, EU tells Meta
Arturo Béjar, a former Meta engineering director, said during his testimony last week that Meta consistently prioritised profits over safety in designing its products, focusing on how often and for how long people used them, even if it was detrimental to their mental well-being.
“If you step away from the product, they are not going to make any money,” he said.
While the four states in the Oakland trial did not officially say how much they had been seeking, Meta said in a court filing that financial penalties in the case could amount to as much as $1.4 trillion – a figure legal experts said was unlikely, if not impossible.

Investor competition for commercial real estate sees strongest growth in a year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
20:44:51 UTC
05:44:51 KST

A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.
Investors are flooding back into the commercial real estate market, powered by a steep rise in liquidity from sources across the finance spectrum. That's despite stubbornly high borrowing rates.
Bidding for properties in June posted its strongest monthly improvement in a year, according to quarterly bidding and credit indexes released Tuesday from JLL. Also, July saw the second highest count of unique bidders in the index's five-year history. Competition among lenders is also well above previous record highs, according to JLL.
"An interesting finding with the most recent data in this index is the lessening divergence between the credit intensity index and bid intensity index," said Lauro Ferroni, JLL's head of capital markets research for the Americas. "We've actually found that the credit intensity index is a leading indicator for the bid intensity index, because credit availability sets the tone for liquidity."
Even though macro uncertainty and volatility continue to show up in the broader economy, bidding keeps rising. Ferroni said that's likely because the weight of active capital in the market is counteracting and potentially working as a stronger force than that ongoing volatility.
Credit is now flowing more freely from commercial mortgage-backed securities, insurance companies, government agencies and debt funds. This was not the case in the first few years following the pandemic, thanks to distress in several CRE sectors and then higher interest rates starting in 2022.
"It's because they like real estate. They want to increase their real estate books. In some cases, they can generate more of a yield there," Ferroni said. "They've seen how the sector has played out. There was not a big wave of distress or defaults or anything like that. So they're coming back into the sector."
Specifically, investors are flooding into retail and industrial. Retail is a newer phenomenon, as it had been one of the worst performing sectors due to the growth of e-commerce during the pandemic. Retail is getting more competitive because owners like the returns they're getting and therefore have no interest in selling, according to JLL.
Industrial has already been strong for several years, due to the explosion of e-commerce, but also because of recent reshoring and reindustrialization. Companies are moving or expanding manufacturing closer to the U.S. to shorten lead times, reduce supply-chain risk and, in some cases, reduce tariff exposure, according to a midyear report from CBRE. The report shows manufacturing leasing was up 27% year over year.
The weakest sector for bidding and credit activity continues to be multifamily. The sector is still working its way through a historic supply of new construction. Vacancies are finally falling nationally, but that is largely driven by new properties. Stabilized vacancies, which strip out properties still in lease-up, were up 34 basis points in the second quarter of this year, according to CoStar.
Ferroni said he doesn't see any major warning signs for competition in overall CRE. The U.S. Treasury Department's move last week to buy long-term bonds could help those currently underwriting property transactions. It also boosts confidence among investors that they can be more competitive in their bidding.
"There's quite a bit of gas left in the tank for further growth, and we think it'll be gradual, not explosive momentum," Ferroni said. "It doesn't appear to be frothy at all."
Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that bidding for properties in June posted its strongest monthly improvement in a year, according to JLL. A previous version misstated the time frame.

The U.S. just recorded its first two deaths from measles for 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
20:42:22 UTC
05:42:22 KST

Two people who were not vaccinated against measles died of the disease in Pennsylvania, public health officials said on Tuesday—these are the first measles fatalities in the state in 35 years. The deaths have come as the number of measles cases across the U.S. has exploded, with 36 outbreaks recorded so far this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Both people were residents of Lancaster County. State health officials said no other details would be released to protect the privacy of the victims and their families.
So far, 2026 has seen 2,777 confirmed cases of measles, an increase from 2,289 cases for the whole of 2025, according to the CDC. This year the Pennsylvania Department of Health has reported 393 cases so far; last year Pennsylvania reported just 16 infections.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Measles is a preventable disease; the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine effectively protects against infections—in fact, it has done such a good job of lowering measles incidence that, in 2000, the U.S. was declared to have eliminated the disease entirely. Now, as vaccine rates drop as a result of increased skepticism toward the shots, infections are back on the rise, and public health experts expect the nation will soon lose its elimination status.
That matters for public health: Measles is the most contagious human virus we know of. It has a fatality rate of one to three deaths per 1,000 cases in the U.S. And it can cause severe health issues, including pneumonia and brain swelling. Some 20 percent of people who contract the disease require hospitalization. Children and pregnant women are among the most at risk of severe disease; measles can also harm unborn fetuses.
Pennsylvania’s secretary of health Debra Bogen encouraged residents to get vaccinated against the disease in a statement. Nationwide, inoculations have been declining: New data from the CDC show the proportion of kindergarteners who received the MMR vaccine has fallen from 95 percent to 92.4 percent over the past decade.
“Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness,” Bogen said. “We want to ensure every Pennsylvanian has the information they need to protect themselves, their loved ones and their communities. As a physician, I want to make sure that people understand that the MMR vaccine is safe and provides the best protection we have against measles.”
The two deaths from measles were confirmed just weeks after President Donald Trump signed an executive order aimed at altering the childhood vaccine schedule, particularly by splitting the MMR vaccine into three separate shots. When announcing the order, Trump falsely claimed the MMR vaccine can be “lethal.” Members of his own administration made efforts to walk the pronouncement back: In an interview on Sunday, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services administrator Mehmet Oz said the MMR shot is not, in fact, “a lethal vaccine.” The overwhelming evidence shows the MMR vaccine is safe and effective, with a very low risk of serious side effects.

WASHINGTON - Elon Musk’s SpaceX announced plans Aug 25 to build a US$100 billion (S$126 billion) facility in the southern US state of Louisiana to launch its highly anticipated Starship megarockets, currently being developed at the company’s Texas Starbase.
“A spaceport on the Louisiana Gulf Coast enabling a multiplanetary future,” declared the SpaceX website.
The new facility will be built in Vermillion Parish, about 180km west of New Orleans.
“We’re committed to investing at least US$100 billion and creating more than 3,000 new jobs at Starbase, Louisiana,” the company said, with construction to begin in 2027.
SpaceX says the buildout will go beyond mere launch pads and include all the infrastructure necessary to support “thousands of Starship flights per year,” with the first expected in 2029.
Starship is the company’s megarocket, still under development, which it plans to use for missions to the Moon and Mars.
“Starbase Louisiana will ultimately have over a dozen launch towers, enabling more than 30 Starship flights per day and making it the biggest launch site on Earth!” Musk wrote on X, which he also owns.
Musk, the world’s richest man, is known for his grandiose promises and highly optimistic timelines.
The Louisiana Economic Development agency said the average salary of workers at the facility would be 192 per cent more than the region’s current mean wage.
SpaceX also said it would undertake significant efforts to preserve the coastline and protect local wildlife.
The company is currently developing its Starship rocket at a facility in Texas that is near protected areas, drawing opposition from several environmental groups.
The US Geological Survey estimated in 2017 that Louisiana has more coastal wetland loss than the combined total of all other states in the contiguous US. AFP
