- He is charged under Article 88 for contempt towards officials, with the Air Force confirming pre-trial confinement and due process rights.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - A US military service member who called for President Donald Trump and Vice-President J.D. Vance to be impeached is facing charges under the military justice system, his lawyer and the Air Force said on Aug 25.
The active-duty officer, Major Jason Watson, denounced Trump and Vance in July for actions including going to war with Iran without congressional authorisation, according to a video of the protest event posted online.
In the video, the US Capitol Police can be seen detaining Watson, who held a protest sign calling for their impeachment, conviction and removal.
Watson's lawyer said in a statement that the airman would face charges under three articles, including Article 88 - a rarely used provision which accuses him of contempt towards officials.
“Major Watson acted knowing the risks to his career and his liberty,” said Christopher Mutimer, counsel for Watson.
“It is my hope that other Americans who feel powerless in this moment will take some measure of courage from his willingness to speak and to stand by his convictions,” Mutimer said.
The Air Force confirmed Watson had been charged and said he would continue to be held in pre-trial confinement and be afforded the right to due process.
Laws governing US military service members place restrictions on their political activities, particularly while in uniform.
Article 88 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice prohibits officers from using “contemptuous words against the President, the Vice-President, Congress” and other US representatives. REUTERS

What we have seen so far looks much more like an expansion of the existing sanctions regime than a fundamentally new economic weapon," he said.

"The real question now is how aggressively Washington is prepared to enforce secondary sanctions against Iran’s remaining trading partners. China is the key. Iranian crude exports have already fallen sharply because of the blockade, and Beijing is essentially the only significant buyer left. Unless China materially reduces purchases further, the additional impact on Iranian oil revenues could be relatively limited," he said.
"Washington is trying to turn the military blockade into a much broader economic blockade. But after decades of sanctions, Iran has developed a highly resilient survival economy," Leon added. "More economic pain does not necessarily translate into political capitulation," he concluded.

The US would be prepared to impose secondary sanctions on any countries refusing to comply with new restrictive measures against Iran, Bessent said. Is this movie high art or dangerous filth? It took Australia decades to decide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Is Salò high art or dangerous filth? It took Australia decades to decide
There's a new Halloween game coming out next month, but Australians and New Zealanders hoping to cosplay as Michael Myers may be disappointed.
It's because Halloween: The Game has been "refused classification" by the Australian Classification Board, not because of the presence of a violent killer, but because in the game the consumption of cannabis can alert players to Myers's location.
In a statement, the Australian Classification Board gave its reasons: "Games containing illicit drug use related to incentives or rewards cannot be accommodated within the R18+ classification category and must be Refused Classification under the Guidelines."
This means the game cannot legally be sold in Australia, and it's not the first piece of media to be caught in Australia's classification net.
Existing in some form for more than 100 years, the Australian Classification Board (ACB) consists of a director, deputy and a revolving set of board members who assess every film, video game and publication submitted for public distribution against legally enshrined classification guidelines.
The ACB does not directly censor media, but its decisions can lead studios and production companies to alter their product.
When a piece of media receives a restrictive classification or is refused classification in Australia, studios and distributors have two basic options: Accept it's been restricted, or alter the content and reapply to the ACB in the hopes of receiving a new rating.
That's what happened with Greta Gerwig's Oscar-winning drama Ladybird back in 2018 when the ACB gave it a MA15+ rating for "brief strong nudity", restricting it to those over 15 — not exactly ideal for a coming-of-age movie.
So, distributor Universal cut the offending scene — a fleeting shot of a penis on the back of the magazine — and the ACB agreed to a lowered M rating.
"Neurotic" is how professor and author of The Money Shot: Cinema, Sin and Censorship Jane Mills describes Australia's relationship with media classification.
"There's all these euphemisms and mealy-mouthed sort of words used to describe what is very paternalistic at its least bad," she tells ABC Arts.
"But at its worst, I think it's denying people the right to know and make informed judgement, which is the basis of democracy."
Innocence and ignorance
Halloween: The Game is far from the first piece of media cast out into Australia's refused-classification wasteland.
In 2003, a dozen police officers raided Sydney's Balmain Town Hall and arrested five people, including movie critic Margaret Pomeranz, over an illegal screening of Larry Clark's Ken Park.
The psychological thriller had been refused classification over "actual sex, sexualised violence and what appeared to be child sex abuse". It remains illegal to stream, rent, buy or screen Ken Park in Australia.
"I think there's often a confusion between innocence and ignorance. We keep people ignorant in the interest of keeping them innocent," Mills says.
"People should be allowed to see, hear, read what they want when we consider that they're of an age to make that decision. One might not necessarily like what one hears or reads, but the right of someone to write it or speak it, I think, is a crucial thing to protect.
"It makes us different from fascist countries."
Pier Paolo Pasolini's Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom, has one of the most storied censorship journeys in Australian film history. Banned shortly after its Australian release in 1976, the controversial political art horror was submitted for appeal in 1993 and rated R for theatrical release, turning the film into a political football as it bounced around Australian cinemas.
A campaign to have the film re-banned, led by Christian figureheads like then-National Party senator Julian McGauran, succeeded in 1998, and the movie was once again refused classification. After another failed distributor application in 2008, a 2010 DVD release was submitted again, this time with 176 minutes of 'contextual material'. The application was successful, drawing the ire of McGauran and the Australian Christian Lobby.
Forty years after it was banished from Australia, Salò is set to be screened as a centrepiece of Sydney's Festival of Dangerous Ideas' inaugural Dangerous Films slate.
"Being the first year, we had to do Salò because it's the one that, if people go, dangerous ideas, banned films, films that are really hard to watch — that's the one," festival director Danielle Harvey tells the ABC.
"It's been quite the journey for me even to be able to watch it, to know exactly what I'm going to be subjecting people to.
"Subjecting, I think, is the right word because it is unwatchable and everyone should watch it."
Shock and awe
Salò's infamous scenes of rape, abuse, coprophilia, violence and murder, along with the furious debate around its legality, have seen it detached from the deep political analysis lurking beneath its cruelty.
Set in 1944 in fascist-controlled Italy, the film centres on four wealthy, powerful men — the Duke, the Bishop, the Magistrate and the President — as they collect lower-class victims upon which to unleash their reckless depravity.
"It's not just shocking for its own sake. That's the first thing. It's a very serious argument about power, about fascism, about consumerism, and it puts the audience in a really uncomfortable position to get them to think about these things," Harvey says.
"There is no titillation to this. It is absolute horror, but horror because it is talking about what humans let happen to other humans, and that is fascism, that is consumerism."
Mills, who edited a 2023 retrospective of Pasolini's work, has seen Salò three times — first closer to release in a "dirty" London cinema ("it must have been illegal"), once for the retrospective and a third time to prepare to introduce it for The Festival of Dangerous Ideas.
Every viewing brought a new appreciation for Pasolini's intent.
"I was actually surprised by how well made it is. Pasolini only took 37 days to film it. It's supremely intellectual and cleverly thought out. I was very, more impressed by it than shocked," she says.
"The set designers and the set decorators need Oscars. It's got this incredibly beautiful, elegant 1930s art deco decor, that elegance in the context of the barbarity of some of the sex and violence and you can't really distinguish where it begins and ends."
Who can hack it?
Harvey says it wasn't easy to track down a copy of Salò — the film isn't streaming, and physical copies are hard to come by — but the effort was worth it.
"It's been this hilarious journey of finding the last Blu-ray player in Sydney for me to watch it ahead of time and to make sure that I'm not doing something stupid in showing this film," she says.
"It stands up as incredibly audacious filmmaking. Inviting people to come and experience this in a communal setting and watch these really young people be absolutely brutalised incessantly — it is a big statement, but at the same time, where else are you going to see this?
"It's the idea of how do we talk about power and what power is, and as humans, how do we allow bad things to happen to other humans? Of course that's in my mind right now. It's in everybody's mind."
Mills says that beyond Salò, the banning of film, books, video games, and even social media often boils down to moral panic.
"The masses can't get hold of something very dangerous because we don't want the masses to have access to ideas about individual freedom and choice," she says.
"I think the only way one can counteract this is by saying, well, people must be allowed to see, read, hear what they like to judge for themselves."
Ultimately, Harvey is excited about the opportunity to screen Salò, not just to share an important piece of art with a wide audience, but for what it represents for other pieces of media that have been refused classification and can't make it into an arts festival.
"Banning a film just makes it less available. It doesn't mean that it ceases to exist. What you're doing is you're encouraging a form of elitism in who can and can't access art, and that is really problematic," she says.
Harvey says there is a difference between banning a film because the content breaks laws, like in the extremely rare case of snuff films, and prohibiting a film because of what it represents.
"A film that is using artistic trickery and storytelling gets banned because it's trying to say something, then by banning it, you're also making a statement about who can cope with these kinds of ideas," she continues.
"That to me is much more interesting. Why do we think that audiences are so feeble that they can't cope with the hard facts about things or be pushed into uncomfortable territory? What are you saying about people?"
Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom, will screen as part of the Festival of Dangerous Ideas on August 29.

Can you eat too much tinned tuna?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Can you eat too much tinned tuna?
Tinned tuna is a lunch box staple for many people. It's affordable, high in protein and doesn't need cooking, making it a nutritious and convenient option for busy days.
But if you're eating tuna most days, you may have wondered whether it's possible to have too much. Or perhaps you've watched your child happily eat a tuna sandwich every day for a week and wondered if that's too much of a good thing.
The concern usually comes down to mercury. Mercury can be harmful in high amounts, particularly during pregnancy and early childhood. But the amount of mercury in seafood varies considerably between species — and that's where much of the confusion begins.
For most Australians, the evidence on tinned tuna is reassuring. Let's unpack this.
Why does tuna contain mercury?
Mercury is a naturally occurring element in the environment. It enters rivers and oceans through natural processes, such as volcanic activity and weathering of rocks, as well as from some industrial activities.
In water, bacteria convert mercury into a form called methylmercury. Fish absorb it from the water and food they eat.
When larger fish eat smaller fish, the mercury builds up inside them over time. Because bigger fish usually live longer, they often contain more mercury than smaller fish.
This isn't unique to tuna. Large fish such as shark (flake), swordfish and some marlin can also contain higher mercury levels because they are larger predatory fish.
Is all tuna the same?
No. Most tinned tuna sold in Australia comes from smaller tuna species, such as skipjack and yellowfin. Because these are generally younger and smaller than the species commonly sold as fresh tuna steaks, they typically contain much lower levels of mercury.
This is why health advice distinguishes between tinned tuna and larger predatory fish.
How much mercury is safe to eat?
Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ) uses international safety guidelines to estimate how much mercury people can consume over time without increasing health risks. This limit is called the provisional tolerable weekly intake (PTWI).
For most people, the PTWI is 3.3 micrograms (µg) per kilogram of body weight per week. For pregnant women, the limit is about half that, at 1.6µg per kilogram of body weight per week.
To put this into perspective, a person weighing 70kg would have a PTWI of about 231µg of mercury per week. But if pregnant, that drops to 112µg of mercury a week.
Limited research has specifically examined mercury concentrations in canned tuna products sold in Australia. So evidence from international studies is often used to indicate expected mercury concentrations. But levels may vary between countries, species and products.
A 2025 Spanish study analysed 60 cans of tuna and found an average mercury concentration of 0.138mg/kg.
Based on these findings, a small 95g can of tuna could contain about 13µg of mercury.
For a person of 70kg, this means:
- one can of tuna per week may provide roughly 13µg of mercury, or less than 6 per cent of the recommended weekly limit
- one can of tuna every day for a week may provide about 92µg of mercury per week, or approximately one-third (40 per cent) of the recommended weekly limit.
For a typical four-year-old who weighs 20kg, they can eat up to 66µg of mercury per week. One can of tuna may use up about 20 per cent of a four-year-old's weekly mercury allowance.
This means two to three cans of tuna a week, which is what you'd use to make a week's worth of tuna sandwiches, is unlikely to be a concern.
But overall, children have a much lower mercury limit than adults because they are smaller and weigh less.
What is mercury poisoning?
Mercury poisoning occurs after prolonged exposure to high levels of mercury.
Depending on the amount and duration of exposure, symptoms can include numbness or tingling in the hands and feet, muscle weakness, problems with coordination, changes in vision or hearing, and difficulties with memory or concentration.
These symptoms are extremely unlikely to occur from eating the amounts of tinned tuna typically in an Australian diet.
What about other fish?
Some Australian fish contain much higher levels of mercury than canned tuna, and their intake should be limited. It's recommended you consume no more than one serving of shark (flake), swordfish, broadbill or marlin per week and avoid other fish during the same week.
Should I eat the same protein every day?
Even though tinned tuna is a healthy choice, eating the same food every day isn't ideal. Not because of mercury, but because no single food provides every nutrient we need.
Fish provides omega-3 fats and iodine.
But there are health benefits from other sources of protein:
- eggs are rich in choline (a nutrient important for metabolism)
- legumes provide fibre and plant protein
- lean meats contribute iron and vitamin B12
- tofu provides plant protein and can also be a source of calcium
- nuts and seeds provide healthy fats, fibre and a range of vitamins and minerals.
Including a variety of these foods across the week makes it easier to meet your nutritional needs than relying on any single food.
The bottom line
Tinned tuna is a nutritious, affordable and convenient source of protein.
For most Australians, eating tinned tuna regularly, even every day, is unlikely to result in unsafe mercury exposure.
Rather than avoiding it because of concerns about mercury, it's best enjoyed as one of a variety of protein-rich foods that together make up a healthy, balanced diet.
Lauren Ball is Professor of Community Health and Wellbeing at the University of Queensland and Emily Burch is an accredited practising dietitian and lecturer at Southern Cross University. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

25 years since the Tampa affair: How 'stop the boats' changed the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

How 'stop the boats' changed the world
In 2001, Australia was criticised on the world stage for its unprecedented hardline policy on asylum seekers. Twenty-five years later, governments around the world are following suit.
August 24, 2001. The Palapa, a small Indonesian fishing boat, is stranded in the ocean.
The vessel is barely seaworthy. It's crammed with 433 asylum seekers, mostly Hazara Afghans, fleeing persecution in their home country and travelling via Indonesia to seek refuge in Australia.
The wooden boat has weathered a bad storm and now floats 140 kilometres from the Australian territory of Christmas Island.
Its occupants are exhausted, dehydrated and fearing for their lives.
They could not have imagined the next eight days would reshape Australia's politics and send shock waves around the world for decades.
After two days adrift, they were rescued when Norwegian freighter, the MV Tampa, diverted course to answer the boat's distress call.
But where to head next became an increasingly difficult question.
Upon first rescuing the asylum seekers, the freighter's captain, Arne Rinnan, set course for the Indonesian port of Merak, the closest able to dock such a large vessel.
But soon after, the Tampa's crew reported their new passengers became increasingly distressed, with some threatening suicide if they were returned to Indonesia and demanding instead that the ship take them to Christmas Island.
When Rinnan requested permission from Australian authorities to dock at the island, however, he received a firm response.
Prime minister John Howard would allow no such thing.
It was the start of a tense, days-long stand-off in the open ocean.
Frantic missives flew between Australian, Indonesian and Norwegian authorities, arguing over which nation should claim responsibility for the Tampa's human cargo.
On August 29, as conditions on the freighter worsened, the captain sent out an SOS and made the decision to enter Australian waters without authorisation.
On the mainland, Australia's leadership was plunged into political and legal turmoil. The government sent SAS troops to board the Tampa and prevent its ingress.
Meanwhile, the prime minister attempted to rush through emergency legislation to turn back the asylum seekers, but it was rejected by the Senate.
The international press lambasted Australia, especially as the ship's crew reported cases of dysentery and ailing pregnant women on board the languishing freighter.
By September 2, Howard and his minister for foreign affairs, Alexander Downer, had arranged a hasty agreement with New Zealand to accept 150 of the asylum seekers. Others, it was determined, would be sent to the small island nation of Nauru, around 4,500 kilometres from Australia.
The following day, the Tampa's passengers were transferred to the better-resourced HMAS Manoora, which set sail across the Pacific.
At the same time, a legal battle was unfolding in the Federal Court. On the morning of September 11, Justice Tony North ruled that the government was unlawfully detaining the asylum seekers en route to Nauru, and decreed that they should be brought to Australia.
Hours later, the world changed.
The shock of the September 11 terrorist attacks reverberated far beyond the United States.
In Australia, public sentiment swung in favour of Howard's tough border stance. In the minds of a nation awed by the horrors of extremist violence, those rescued by the Tampa — along with the possibility of a more porous Australian border — now represented an unacceptable risk.
Six days after the attacks, on September 17, the Full Court of the Federal Court overturned Justice North's judgment on appeal, ruling that the government was legally able to turn asylum seekers away from its shores before processing their claims.
On September 26, while the world looked to New York, parliament passed a law excising several islands from Australia's migration zone, meaning asylum seekers who landed there would not be able to settle on the mainland.
What began as an emergency response had evolved into a steadfast policy. The Pacific Solution was here to stay.
Go to glossary of key terms
'The mood of the country'
In the first half of 2001, as a federal election loomed, Howard's political future was in peril.
After two embattled terms, his government was trailing Labor in approval ratings and tipped to lose seats across the nation. It was widely believed Howard would not last another election.
He saw a reversal of fortune after the Tampa affair and 9/11.
Questions of border control and national security dominated the lead-up to the November 10 federal election. The Pacific Solution positioned the prime minister as a strong and decisive leader, and sent his approval rate soaring.
It was during this campaign that Howard uttered the now-famous words:
"We will decide who comes to this country and the circumstances in which they come."
Just weeks before the election, government officials said asylum seekers trying to reach Australia by a different boat had thrown their children overboard. By the time this was proven to be untrue, the election was decided.
"We were not willing to allow a large number of asylum seekers to make the rules, because once we did that, we were saying we no longer controlled our borders," Howard tells the ABC's Tampa: The Turning Point.
"If the view became entrenched around the world that it was easy to get into this country, we would have an enormous problem.
"I think if there'd been no Tampa, no 9/11, we still would have won, but our majority would have been smaller. That's how I felt. That was the mood of the country."
'Fortress Australia' and the Tampa legacy
That mood went on to define a generation of policy.
"Tampa changed the way that Australia understood and spoke about mass migration and irregular migration," explains Guardian journalist Ben Doherty, who has covered asylum seeker policy extensively.
"People arriving by boat were no longer 'asylum seekers', but 'illegals'. We had ministers talking about floods and waves of people; it was framed in terms of an invasion."
The idea of the "queue jumper" — which was first popularised by the Whitlam government during the influx of Vietnamese refugees in the 70s — reared its head again in the wake of Tampa.
"The concept of the queue jumper was actually created by the Australian government," says Madeline Gleeson, deputy director of the Kaldor Centre for International Refugee Law at UNSW Sydney.
"This was an incredibly powerful political concept because it created this artificial distinction between the so-called good refugee, who waited patiently far away in a refugee camp until we invited them to come to Australia, and the so-called bad refugee, who was cheating the system.
"That distinction does not reflect reality … There is no queue; there is no system where you get a number by the order in which you registered for asylum, and then you come in that order."
It wasn't only the language that hardened. The law did, too.
Australia is one of 149 countries that are part of the UN Refugee Convention, which means it's required by international law to protect asylum seekers and refugees, including not returning them to a country where they face persecution.
"Until that moment, the norm, both in Australia and internationally, was that when an asylum seeker arrived at a state party to the [UN] Refugee Convention, their asylum claim was processed in the territory of that state," Dr Gleeson says.
"What changed with Tampa in Australia is that we looked to exclude people from our territory and find ways to push them elsewhere."
Offshore processing — sending migrants to countries outside Australia for their asylum claims to be assessed — has since become a core feature of Australia's refugee policy. It has long received bipartisan support, despite critics citing exorbitant cost, human rights abuses and breaches of international law.
The Pacific Solution, which saw asylum seekers processed at Nauru and Manus Island in Papua New Guinea, lasted until 2008. After growing public pressure, Kevin Rudd's Labor government ended what it called a "dehumanising and punishing" arrangement.
In the years that followed, however, boat arrivals climbed, and the issue grew only more contentious. According to parliamentary records, unauthorised arrivals by sea jumped from five boats in 2007 to 278 in 2012.
In August 2012, the Gillard government announced the reopening of detention centres for offshore processing, claiming "too many lives had been lost" at sea.
The tough approach to asylum policy continued under subsequent governments, most visibly through Tony Abbott's Operation Sovereign Borders. Launched in 2013, it upheld the same principles as the Pacific Solution, but with a focus on stopping boats reaching Australian shores.
More than a decade later, the policy remains in force.
Since then, proponents from both sides of the political aisle have repeated familiar talking points: breaking the business model of people-smugglers, preventing deaths at sea, and encouraging asylum seekers to seek refuge elsewhere.
Shortly after Labor's most recent election victory, home affairs Minister Clare O'Neil reiterated:
"If you try to come to Australia by boat you will not make it … Operation Sovereign Borders, the policy that underpins this, is being enforced fiercely, if not more fiercely, than it was before."
As for the success of these policies, opinion is divided.
Supporters argue they have reduced the number of unauthorised arrivals and, therefore, the number of deaths at sea. Critics say they have failed to establish a safe and sustainable way to manage asylum claims, and fall foul of Australia's international obligations.
On one point, however, most agree: the "Australian model" has become a prized export.
"We've seen Australian politicians explicitly going overseas, saying, 'We've worked it out, this is what you need to do'," Doherty says.
"This idea of keeping people away, the 'Fortress Australia' mentality — we're seeing that play out all over the world, through the Mediterranean, the UK, in America.
"This is the world that Tampa created."
UK follows Australia's lead
Those paying attention to the UK's border policies in recent years might have felt a sense of deja vu.
From the early 2000s, as conflict flared in Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria and Yemen, tens of thousands of people seeking asylum attempted to reach British shores.
Amid an ongoing humanitarian crisis and fraught political landscape, UK leaders turned to Australia to inform their approach.
"Countries don't create their refugee, asylum and border control policies in isolation," explains Daniel Ghezelbash, law professor and director of the Kaldor Law Centre.
"They keep a very careful eye and monitor developments in other countries, and when one country adopts more restrictive policies … we see them spread quickly around the world."
Since 2012, when then-home secretary Theresa May promised a "hostile environment" for illegal migrants, other Conservative politicians have echoed some familiar sentiments.
In 2016, prime minister David Cameron vowed to "bust the business model of people-smugglers", while Boris Johnson later declared: "We've got to be able to control who comes into this country and the terms on which they remain".
"We really saw the 'stop the boats' messaging take off in the UK, particularly under Rishi Sunak's prime ministership," Professor Ghezelbash says.
"We saw exactly the same language, the same messaging, even the same graphics being used.
"By far the most high-profile example [of the UK emulating Australia] was the UK-Rwanda deal, which was very closely and explicitly modelled on Australia's policies, and there were actually a lot of Australians involved in making that happen."
The contentious plan, announced by Boris Johnson's government in 2022, aimed to send some asylum seekers arriving by sea to be processed in Rwanda, where, if they were recognised as refugees, they would remain.
After a protracted legal battle, the deal was stymied by European and UK courts, and was eventually cancelled by Labour prime minister Keir Starmer in 2024. Only four migrants were relocated through the program.
Advising the scheme was none other than Alexander Downer, former Australian foreign affairs minister and a key architect of the Pacific Solution, who was appointed by the UK government in 2022 to lead an independent review of the UK's Border Force.
"People coming across the channel were gaming the system," he tells the ABC.
"I was always telling them when I was the High Commissioner in London [from 2014 to 2018], 'You need to come up with an offshore processing scheme'."
But the realities of enacting "the Australian model" have proven difficult in the UK, where human rights law is more stringent.
"Australia is one of the only liberal democracies in the world that doesn't have a national-level Bill of Rights. Our Constitution is notoriously famous for being very light in terms of individual rights protections," Professor Ghezelbash explains.
"There are human rights mechanisms ... that provide additional protections in the UK and in Europe that don't apply in Australia."
EU echoes: 'We will decide'
At the height of the migrant crisis in 2015, retired Army general and former Liberal senator Jim Molan — a key architect of Operation Sovereign Borders — told media, "when [Europe is] ready to control [its] borders, come and talk to the Australian government".
A year later, then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull and immigration minister Peter Dutton took to the stage at a United Nations summit to champion Australia's border policy as "creating order out of … chaos".
Soon enough, European nations followed suit with their own raft of hardline policies.
Over the past five years, Poland, Hungary, Greece, Croatia, Bulgaria and Italy have strengthened border-control measures and expanded powers of detention and expulsion. Human rights bodies have cited evidence of pushbacks in 13 European countries, and have reported concerns over human rights abuses at borders.
Meanwhile, several countries have explored or pursued forms of offshore or third-country asylum processing, such as Italy's arrangement with Albania, the Netherlands' interest in Uganda, and Denmark's discussions with Rwanda.
Politicians have also spoken explicitly about the need for an "Australian-style" asylum policy.
Alberto-Horst Neidhardt, senior analyst at the European Policy Centre, says this momentum has been building since the Tampa affair.
"[In the early 2000s], European leaders were looking at policy initiatives elsewhere, and there were echoes of what Australia decided," he says.
"Around the same time, we started hearing the first European politicians talking about models of outsourcing responsibility to third countries, and since then, we've seen again and again attempts to make this policy more concrete."
In June 2026, the EU implemented new standardised border controls, which included mandatory security screenings, expanded powers to deny asylum, and processing centres known as "return hubs".
Critics argue these will create "human rights black holes", undermine safeguards during processing, and lengthen detention stays.
"A lot of these policies have to do with political signalling. We know that migration is a very salient political issue in most countries," Dr Neidhardt says.
"We have elections soon enough in many European countries, including in France, where migration is also a very important political issue.
"If the public does not see an effect in their day-to-day reality, then the risk is that they will choose parties that seem to offer the most effective solutions that are oftentimes simplistic."
Trump's ICE borrows from Australia
Although Donald Trump's characterisation of migrants as "animals" and "terrorists" has made headlines, hardline refugee policies in the United States long predate his presidency.
A longstanding American practice in fact inspired the Howard government policies that came out of Tampa.
"The US had been carrying out a version of offshore processing on Guantanamo Bay since the 90s," Professor Ghezelbash says.
"It also had been carrying out … pushbacks since the 80s in the Caribbean.
"I spoke to a senior US policymaker who was one of the architects of the US model, and he was providing advice around how Australia could respond [during the Tampa crisis]."
But increasingly, the student has become the teacher.
During Trump's first-ever conversation with then-prime minister Turnbull in 2017, he complimented Australia's use of detention centres for asylum seekers.
"That is a good idea. We should do that too," the President said, according to a leaked phone call.
Since then, Trump's government has implemented increasingly strict refugee policies, including offshore detention and agreements with dozens of governments to deport migrants to countries where they have no ties.
These schemes have attracted many of the same criticisms as Australia's regime, including the denial of due process and the risk of human rights violations.
Julia Morris, an associate professor of international studies at the University of North Carolina Wilmington, has seen these policies align "very much with the right-wing populist party line".
"There have been huge changes with this administration, with near-total freezes on asylum decisions and country-based bans that are very much driven by this America-first nationalism," she says.
"The Trump administration is very much focused on this 'Make America Great' mantra, … pandering to the idea that the reason why [people] are economically suffering is because of [migrants].
"This isn't necessarily new, but what is new is the pure hostility of the language."
The US and Australia are also sharing detention contractors.
"The private prison contractor who's tied to Australia's Nauru operations is now also involved in US ICE detention," Dr Morris says.
The same US company, Management & Training Corporation (MTC), also manages Australia's seven onshore detention centres through a subsidiary, Secure Journeys.
Investigations by The Guardian Australia have found allegations of serious misconduct against the company, both within Australia and abroad.
Its facilities have been the subject of damning reports by both Australia's federal safety regulator, Comcare, and the Commonwealth's National Preventive Mechanism, an independent network of bodies that monitors places of detention.
MTC has also been fined by the Australian government for performance failures, including multiple escapes of detainees.
In May, when asked about allegations regarding MTC's Australian facilities, Australian Border Force told Guardian Australia that immigration detention was "a complex operating environment", and that the "welfare, safety and dignity of people in immigration detention, as well as the safety of staff" were its highest priorities.
The future of asylum
Commentators across the political spectrum agree on one thing: the question of how to handle asylum seekers is unlikely to disappear anytime soon.
There are 117.8 million forcibly displaced people worldwide, according to UNHCR statistics.
"The reality that we see being played out is that once you start demonising and attacking certain cohorts of people like refugees and asylum seekers, inevitably it bleeds out to other cohorts," Professor Ghezelbash says.
"The risk is this race to the bottom that we've already seen play out in wealthy democracies around the world."
It seems the seed that was planted with Tampa has put down deep roots.
"The mass migration of people around the globe will be one of the defining characteristics of this century," Ben Doherty says.
"The way that wealthy countries like Australia respond to that is going to determine the shape of the world we live in."
Watch Tampa: The Turning Point on ABC iview
Glossary
Refugee: Someone who is outside their home country and is unable to return due to a "well-founded fear" of persecution
Asylum seeker: Someone who is seeking international protection but hasn't yet been legally recognised as a refugee
Internally displaced person: Someone who has fled their home but remains in their own country
Migrant: An umbrella term to describe people who live in a country other than their home country
Offshore processing: When a government sends people seeking asylum to another country to process their refugee claims
Pushbacks: When state authorities forcibly return migrants or asylum seekers across a border without assessing their protection claims
People smugglers: A person or criminal network that facilitates illegal entry into a country for a financial or other material benefit

Canada hits US goods with tariffs of up to 50% as trade war escalates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:29:30 UTC
03:29:30 KST

Canada hits US goods with tariffs of up to 50% as trade war escalates
Ottawa targets about US$20 billion in US products and unveils billions in assistance after negotiations with Washington collapse
The tariffs, which take effect on September 8, will apply to more than 700 categories of US goods at rates of 15, 25 or 50 per cent, according to the Canadian government.
The targeted products range from steel, aluminium and agricultural equipment to household appliances, clothing, cheese, seafood, cosmetics and electronics.
Existing Canadian tariffs on some US steel and aluminium products will double from 25 to 50 per cent, matching the rates imposed by Washington. Counter-tariffs on American-made vehicles will remain at 25 per cent.
Canadian Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said the measures would match the US tariffs “dollar for dollar, rate for rate” and were intended to defend Canadian workers and businesses rather than generate government revenue.
“We did not choose this conflict, but when our economic integration is used as a weapon rather than the foundation for a win-win partnership, we need to stand up,” Champagne said.

Netanyahu appoints sole Russian-speaking Likud candidate Elkin to lead party's immigrant outreach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:29:00 UTC
03:29:00 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appointed Minister Ze’ev Elkin to lead the Likud’s immigrant outreach campaign ahead of the elections, as the party seeks to regain support among Russian-speaking voters.
The appointment reflects the Likud’s decision to once again focus on the Russian-speaking electorate, while also raising questions about Elkin’s own future on the party’s Knesset list.
Elkin, the only Russian-speaking candidate on the Likud list, is currently ranked 32nd, a position that is not considered realistic at this stage. Netanyahu’s decision to place him in charge of the campaign headquarters and include him in the party’s campaign management team highlights the importance the Likud places on Elkin’s experience and standing among Russian-speaking voters.
The move could strengthen the possibility that Elkin will receive a reserved slot, allowing him to move into a realistic position when the party submits its final list in about two weeks.
“Ahead of the upcoming election campaign, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu decided to appoint Minister Ze’ev Elkin as the director of the Likud’s immigrant headquarters," the Likud Party said in a statement released Tuesday. "Minister Elkin will be a partner in the party’s campaign management team and will oversee all activity in the immigrant sector until the elections. Good luck, Ze’ev!”
Although the headquarters is officially called the “immigrant headquarters,” the main political effort will focus on Russian-speaking voters. According to updated assessments used by the Likud, this community currently represents an electoral force of around 15 Knesset seats.
Of those, around two seats are estimated to come from immigrants voting in Israel for the first time. The group includes people who immigrated in recent years, along with some who received Israeli citizenship from 2014 onward as part of what is known as “passport immigration.”
'Passport' immigrants arrived without permanent residency amid Russia-Ukraine war
These individuals did not permanently reside in Israel at the time, but arrived or settled in the country following the war in Ukraine and worsening conditions in Russia.
Another group of interest to the Likud is Russian-speaking voters who left Yesh Atid. According to assessments within the party, Yesh Atid leader Yair Lapid previously held the equivalent of around three Knesset seats among Russian-speaking voters, while today, according to Likud officials, he has slightly more than half a seat remaining.
The Likud views these voters as part of a support pool that has not yet consolidated behind a single party in this election.
The goal the Likud is setting this time differs from Netanyahu’s previous efforts. The party estimates that even during relatively weak election cycles, it receives around two Knesset seats from Russian-speaking voters, while in stronger years it has reached four or even five seats.
In 2009, when Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beytenu won 15 seats, the Likud estimates that around five of those seats came from Russian-speaking voters. In 2013, the Likud and Yisrael Beytenu ran on a joint list, and in 2015, the Likud again operated a significant Russian-language campaign, reaching, according to party estimates, around four to five seats among this community.
During the 2019 repeat election campaign, Netanyahu pursued a much more aggressive strategy. The Likud recruited figures previously associated with Yisrael Beytenu, including Robert Ilatov and Sofa Landver, in an effort to weaken Lieberman’s influence among Russian-speaking voters.
Netanyahu set an especially ambitious goal at the time, seeking to weaken Yisrael Beytenu to the point that it would fall below the electoral threshold. The effort failed. Lieberman maintained his support base, and the Likud concluded that around five seats among Russian-speaking voters represented a relatively stable base of support for Yisrael Beytenu that would be very difficult to shift.
The lessons of 2019 are reflected in the Likud’s current strategy. Rather than trying to dismantle Lieberman’s support base, the party will focus on preserving the votes it already holds and competing for undecided voters, particularly new immigrants and former Yesh Atid supporters.
In a close election, the Likud estimates that every additional seat beyond its base of around two seats could be highly significant in the battle between the political blocs.
Likud's entry into Russian-targeted campaigning follows that of its political opponents
The Likud is entering this contest after its rivals. Four political forces are currently operating campaigns targeting Russian-speaking voters: Yisrael Beytenu, the Likud, Gadi Eisenkot, and the Bennett-Lapid camp.
According to Likud sources, the immigrant headquarters of Naftali Bennett’s Together Party has been active for about a year. Eisenkot began building his own operation around a month and a half ago, including through Alex Rif. The Likud is the last of these political forces to establish a dedicated headquarters.
The Likud’s effort begins with preserving the support it already has among Russian-speaking voters. The party acknowledges that this task has grown more complicated because of its partnership with the Haredi parties and the dispute over the military draft law.
Some voters the Likud is seeking to reach are right-wing supporters who nevertheless hold strong positions against the Haredi parties and against exemptions from military service.
As a result, the Russian-language campaign is expected to emphasize a tougher stance on military service, while Netanyahu seeks to maintain his partnership with the Haredi parties.
Netanyahu has already signaled the direction of the campaign. In an interview over the weekend with Channel 9, when asked about the lack of Russian-speaking representation in realistic positions on the Likud list, he claimed that “Elkin is in a realistic position and will be in the next Knesset.”
He later even described himself, half-jokingly, as a “Russian in the Likud,” and listed achievements of his governments that he said should appeal to Russian-speaking voters.
Elkin’s appointment also highlights a contradiction the Likud will need to resolve before submitting its list. Elkin is currently the party’s only Russian-speaking candidate, yet he is ranked 32nd.
The Likud is therefore campaigning for support among a community that, according to party estimates, represents around 15 Knesset seats, while the only representative from that community on its list is not currently in a secure position.
Elkin’s status also carries significance for coalition management if the Likud forms the next government. On the current list, it is difficult to identify a candidate with more proven experience than Elkin for the role of coalition chairman.
Elkin previously held the position and is considered someone who understands Knesset operations, coalition management, and negotiations between political factions.
The list will be submitted before the Likud knows what its immigrant headquarters achieved in the election, meaning the significance of the appointment lies in the decision Netanyahu made now.
He placed Elkin in charge of the Russian-speaking electoral effort and added him to the campaign management team just two weeks before the lists are finalized.
After Netanyahu has already said Elkin will be in the next Knesset, the appointment adds weight to the possibility that a decision guaranteeing that outcome will soon follow, moving him into a realistic position on the Likud list.

YPG-led SDF dissolves as forces integrate into Syrian army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:29:00 UTC
03:29:00 KST

The U.S.-backed YPG terrorist group announced Tuesday that its so-called autonomous administration and all its military and civilian structures have been dissolved.
Ferhat Abdi Şahin, one of the group's ringleaders, made the announcement to reporters at the People's Palace in the Syrian capital.
"Following the agreement reached with President Ahmed al-Sharaa, and upon completion of the process of integrating our forces into the brigades of the Syrian army, we announce today, with a great sense of responsibility, that we are dissolving ourselves as an independent military force," said Şahin.
The YPG was established in 2015 with U.S. backing as the Syrian branch of the PKK terrorist group. Washington partnered with the group in its campaign against Daesh despite longstanding objections from NATO ally Türkiye over its ties to the PKK.
The PKK, which has waged a decades-long campaign against Türkiye, is designated a terrorist group by Türkiye, the U.S. and the European Union.
The group became Washington’s principal partner on the ground against Daesh and eventually gained control of large parts of northern and northeastern Syria, including areas containing much of the country’s oil resources.
The Syrian administration and the YPG terror group reached a new agreement Jan. 29 that provided for a cease-fire and the group’s gradual integration into state institutions.
“Circumstances have changed today, and the country has entered a new phase characterized by peace and participation,” Şahin said.
The political and military landscape shifted dramatically following the fall of ousted longtime ruler Bashar Assad in late 2024 and the establishment of new authorities in Damascus under the leadership of al-Sharaa.
Clashes between government forces and the YPG in January resulted in Damascus regaining significant territory, including areas in Raqqa and Deir el-Zour. The two sides subsequently reached an agreement to integrate military, security and civilian institutions in the northeast into state structures.
Al-Sharaa also met on Tuesday with Şahin to discuss steps for its integration into state institutions.
The meeting addressed "a number of issues related to integration within Syrian state institutions and the steps for the next phase to strengthen the state's presence and support security and stability," Şahin added.
Last month, Syrian officials said the country had integrated about 9,000 former members of the YPG forces into its national security institutions as part of a broader effort to unify the country’s armed forces, while appointing a former senior YPG official as a deputy defense minister.
The integration marked one of the most significant steps in the implementation of an agreement between Damascus and the YPG aimed at dissolving the terrorist group into Syria’s state institutions.
Roughly 5,000 former YPG fighters have joined the Syrian Defense Ministry, while another 4,000 have been incorporated into the Interior Ministry, officials said. Non-Syrian foreign fighters previously affiliated with the YPG have been removed from the country as part of the restructuring process.
Syrian authorities describe the process as a gradual, reciprocal approach sometimes referred to as a "zipper model," under which security, administrative and political measures advance simultaneously to build confidence between the two sides.
Ankara has repeatedly maintained that eliminating parallel armed structures and preserving Syria’s territorial integrity are essential for lasting stability in the neighboring country.
The YPG’s dissolution represents a significant step in Damascus’ efforts to restore central authority throughout Syria after more than a decade of fragmentation and conflict.
Türkiye’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AK Party) spokesperson Ömer Çelik on Wednesday welcomed the dissolution of the terrorist group, saying the move marked an important threshold in strengthening Syria’s internal unity and reaffirming Ankara’s support for the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
“We have always supported the protection of Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity,” Çelik emphasized in a statement on social media. “Syria must move toward the future as one and whole.”
Çelik said President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan had waged a major struggle to protect Syrians from terrorism and what he described as “imperialist attacks” during some of the most difficult periods of the Syrian conflict.
“Years and history are witnesses to this noble struggle,” he said.
Çelik said the dissolution of the YPG represented a significant development for Syria’s internal cohesion.
He also praised steps taken by the administration of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa toward what he described as inclusive governance, saying they were helping the country move beyond years of conflict and toward a more stable future.
Çelik linked developments in Syria to Ankara’s broader “terror-free Türkiye” and “terror-free region” objectives, saying the initiatives represented a determination to thwart attempts by outside actors to divide and exploit Türkiye’s neighboring region for their own interests.
He said the policy also offered prospects for a more stable future for Kurdish communities across the region.
Çelik added that Türkiye would continue to support steps aimed at strengthening the stability, security and prosperity of Syria and neighboring countries as part of what he called Erdoğan’s “politics of brotherhood.”

How will Trump's economic 'D-Day' plan impact Iran's nuclear, ballistic missile threat? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:28:20 UTC
03:28:20 KST

The Trump administration’s threat of an “economic D-Day” against Iran sounded impressive but so far appears to have dropped to a bit of a whimper.
It is not clear that any strategic change took place vis-à-vis Iran on Monday, though if Washington decides to go head-to-head with Beijing over Iranian oil, and if China moves in America’s direction on the issue, those events could impact Tehran over time. But the keywords here are “economic,” “if,” and “over time.”
The real “D-Day” (June 6, 1944) was not an economic sanctions campaign; it was one of the largest military ground invasions of all time.
Trump’s unwillingness to use ground forces in Iran, even for targeted operations, such as securing the Strait of Hormuz or removing Iran’s 60% enriched uranium, cannot be covered up by using the catchphrase “D-Day” where it does not apply.
The United States may hope to coax Chinese President Xi Jinping into reducing the oil it gets from Iran, given that it purchases an estimated 90% of that oil, but Jinping has also said “No” plenty of times, and it is unclear what Trump can offer him to sell such an arrangement.
“If” China keeps buying Iranian oil, is the US really going to use force against Chinese ships to block them from moving through Hormuz?
As it is, there is evidence that China has figured out how to dodge America’s blockade in some cases with its shadow fleet maneuvering tactics.
No matter how well this goes, it is a strategy that will only work “over time” – it takes time and patience.
Can Trump own such a long-term campaign?
This will not wear down Iran in a few days or weeks, unless its leadership suddenly completely changes its colors.
Rather, this will only work if the United States and the West are ready to go all in on this strategy for months, if not longer.
Can Trump own such a long-term campaign, which so far is crippling him politically, along with the US economy?
The key question is not whether Iran is being increasingly hurt economically; certainly it is.
Nor is it whether Trump has managed for some weeks here and there to mitigate some of the gas price pains with some of his confounding public relations; sometimes he has.
But the basic economic picture in the US is dark, and if the Americans’ threshold for suffering is much lower than the Iranian regime’s threshold, which is likely the situation, Trump may ditch the strategy before it can work.
Prior to the war, US gas prices were as low as $2.80 a gallon.
They have reached as high as $4.50 since Iran began to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, dropped as low as $3.80 in July, and are now back up to $4.05.
Before the war, an estimated 100 or more ships sailed through Hormuz daily.
At a low point during the war, this dropped to an average of 20 ships exiting per day and 10 entering.
In July, the numbers temporarily jumped to an average of 50 exiting daily and 20 entering.
Now those numbers are back down to 20 exiting and 10 entering.
That is the broader picture, and oil shipping has been even worse, with estimates of average daily shipping down to around 10% of pre-war levels.
The official numbers do not tell the whole story. Both Iran and the US are running clandestine shipping operations, but if gas prices remain as high as they are, that is the bottom line, which could undermine the US’s staying power in this “economic suffering” contest.
Let’s say Israel benefits from the best-case scenario where Trump stays the course on an economic and maximum pressure campaign over the next several months or longer.
How would that make Israel safer from the nuclear and ballistic missile threats?
Such a campaign would reduce Iran’s support of terror proxies and prevent it from getting a strategic upper hand to blackmail the US and the West by using Hormuz as its new regular point to crunch everyone.
In a general sense, having less money could also make it harder to restore its nuclear and ballistic missile programs.
But not really.
The debate around Iran's nuclear and ballistic missile program
Time and time again, Israel has seen that religious fanatics, from Iran to Hezbollah to Hamas, are ready to use any small amount of funds they receive to finance their most dangerous military options at the expense of helping their civilian populations.
Since the full-on part of the early 2026 war ended, Iran has been working at a furious speed to repair and rebuild aspects of its missile program and possibly aspects of its nuclear program.
And it has, at least in some months since the war ended, received billions of dollars from China and Russia – so there is money there.
The status of Iran’s nuclear and ballistic missiles program is hotly debated.
Israel certainly succeeded in setting Iran back on the nuclear issue in June 2025, given that 15 months have passed and the Islamic Republic is nowhere near developing a weapon in the near future.
It also set back Iran’s missile program, given that estimates were at one point that it had 2,500 to 3,000 missiles and the capacity to build 100 to 300 additional missiles per month, eventually reaching 5,000, 6,000, or even 8,000 missiles – and now it is down to under 1,000, possibly only several hundred.
Further, while how many new missiles it can produce now is debated, no one doubts that if enough time passes, and with help from China and Russia, the missiles could emerge once again as a separate existential threat from the nuclear program.
Trump’s minimum stated goal at the start of the war was to remove the Islamic Republic’s more than 400 kilograms of 60% enriched uranium.
That has not been accomplished.
How long do Israel, the US, and the West want to give the regime in Iran to figure out ways in which to charge forward on the nuclear or ballistic missile issues with whatever it has left?

"Queen of country" Dolly Parton has died at the age of 80

Country music legend Dolly Parton passes away, aged 80
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:28:01 UTC
03:28:01 KST

Dolly Parton, one of the last century’s most iconic and enduring contemporary music superstars, died on Tuesday at age 80 following a "brief battle with cancer," PEOPLE reported citing representatives for the singer.
The singer, songwriter, and actress whose charisma, heartfelt lyrics, and business and philanthropic endeavors won the hearts of her fans for nearly six decades had been in declining health in recent months.
Flamboyant and radiant, Parton possessed the talent to complement her ample public persona. She could enthrall an audience with a full-on Las Vegas revue or alone on a stage with an acoustic guitar and her unmistakable voice.
Parton rose from poverty in rural Tennessee to become one of the most successful and recognizable performers in country and popular American music, with a dazzling career that stretched across six decades and extended far beyond Nashville into film, television, business, and philanthropy.
The writer of classic songs like “Jolene,” “Islands in the Stream,” and “I Will Always Love You” (a huge hit by Whitney Houston), Parton was named to the list of the New York Times 30 greatest living American songwriters earlier this year.
She won 11 Grammy Awards, including a Lifetime Achievement Award.
In addition to her groundbreaking work as a singer-songwriter, Parton also starred in movies like 9 to 5 and Steel Magnolias.
Her husband of nearly 60 years, Carl Thomas Dean, died in March 2025.
Public figures reacted to Parton's death with surprise and sadness
"Very sad to report that Dolly Parton, one of the greatest Country singers, and far beyond, EVER, has just passed away," US President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social.
"This is a true loss for millions of people. There has never been anyone like her, and never will. In her honor, I am lowering the American flag throughout the United States for a one-week period beginning tonight at 6:00 PM. Rest in Peace, Dolly! The World loves you."
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said that "Dolly Parton did all the good she could, for all the people she could, for as long as she ever could... Dolly, we'll miss your great heart."
"It's hard for me to imagine the world without Dolly. Dolly's heart was as big as her talent," actress Cindy Lauper said following the singer's death.
'She was not only a great singer/song writer/actress/TV star, Dolly also lived her art. She used her art, her fame and her money to help so many people. I can't even tell you how many times I've thought to myself, 'What would Dolly do?'"
"She was a great role model for all of us."
"Moderna is saddened by the passing of Dolly Parton, whose extraordinary generosity touched millions of lives," said a company spokesperson.
"During the earliest days of the COVID-19 pandemic, Dolly supported critical research at Vanderbilt University Medical Center that, alongside the historic public-private partnership that accelerated the COVID-19 vaccine effort, contributed to the development of Moderna's COVID-19 vaccine. "She was an American treasure, and her generosity, optimism, and belief in science made a difference at a moment when the world needed it most. We will always be grateful to have shared a small part of her remarkable story," continued the spokesperson.
"Thank you, Lord, for Dolly. She's gonna have a blast in heaven singing all her favorite songs with all her family and friends who have gone on before her," country singer Reba McEntire said.
Actress Lynda Carter said, "Oh Dolly, I know where your heart is. These are impossible days. I send you, my sister, so much love."
Parton was born in 1946 in Tennessee
Born in 1946 in Locust Ridge, Tennessee, Parton grew up in a large, poor family in the Great Smoky Mountains. She performed as a child and appeared at the Grand Ole Opry when she was about 10 years old before eventually moving to Nashville to pursue a professional career. She became a member of the Opry in 1969.
Parton first gained national attention in the US as a singer on Porter Wagoner’s television program before establishing herself as a solo star. Her songwriting combined wit, vulnerability, and sharp observations about poverty, love, ambition, and women’s lives, helping her cross repeatedly from country into mainstream pop culture.
Parton built Dollywood, the Tennessee theme park that became a major regional employer and tourist attraction, and created the Imagination Library, a literacy program that distributes free books to children around the world.
Speaking to People magazine last week, Parton disclosed that she was “dealing with some health issues that I just didn’t pay attention to when I was watching over Carl.”
“Even though I’m still healin’, I’m still workin’,” she added, saying that she was working with companies to create “avatar performances,” and they are still in the “early stages of development.”

Mapuche communities in Argentina denounce territorial rights violations amid eviction disputes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:26:46 UTC
03:26:46 KST

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Mapuche community leaders from Argentina’s Neuquen province denounced alleged violations of their territorial rights amid evictions and disputes about ancestral lands, media reports said Tuesday.
“Democracy has an eternal debt to Indigenous peoples; they subject us to express evictions without a law,” said Lorenzo Loncan, spokesman for the Lof Paicil Antriao, according to the Pagina/12 newspaper.
“We denounce the Supreme Court, federal courts and provincial courts for failing to comply with ILO Convention 169, which requires free and informed consultation, as well as with the National Constitution,” said Loncon. “More than 40 Indigenous peoples are Argentine, like the Malvinas and the disappeared.”
The Lof Paicil Antriao is based in Villa La Angostura, a tourist town in Neuquen, and is involved in a long-running land dispute.
A Neuquen court rejected an appeal by the community in February, upholding an eviction order concerning land at the Correntoso campsite. The case has also involved property acquired by former Argentine basketball player Emanuel Ginobili.
The dispute comes as Argentina’s Congress debates changes to property laws that could allow faster eviction procedures.
The Senate approved a version of the proposed legislation earlier this month, including provisions for expedited eviction proceedings and changes to rules governing private property and expropriations.
Mapuche representatives have warned that the measures could affect Indigenous communities involved in longstanding territorial disputes.
The debate intensified after Argentina repealed Law 26.160 in December 2024. The law had declared a territorial emergency for Indigenous communities and suspended evictions while surveys of traditionally occupied lands were conducted.
Two Mapuche communities, Lof Kinxikew and Lof Melo, were evicted from territories near Villa La Angostura on Aug. 19, according to media reports.
The Mapuche communities argue that their territorial claims are protected by Argentina’s Constitution and Indigenous rights legislation.

Pakistan’s Kashmir Crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:25:00 UTC
03:25:00 KST

The Madina Market of Muzaffarabad, a major regional commercial hub, has finally reopened to economic activity following weeks of turmoil. Muzaffarabad – the capital of Pakistan-administered Kashmir, housing the Prime Minister’s Secretariat, the Legislative Assembly, and other government buildings emblematic of its on-paper autonomy – is showing signs of a return to daily life. Likewise, Mirpur, the region’s second largest city, has now resumed intracity public transportation, allowing locals to move between Pakistan and the territory Islamabad dubs as Azad, or Free Jammu and Kashmir. Nevertheless, Pakistan-administered Kashmir still has a visibly heightened deployment of security personnel.
Over the past three months, at least 80 people have been killed across the region amid the general election in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, which was held from July 27 to August 10. The election, which was widely deemed contentious owing to allegations of polling day irregularities, in addition to pre-election machinations alleged to benefit status quo parties, saw the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and Pakistan People’s Party (PPP) – which are also leading the ruling alliance in Islamabad – emerge victorious.
“The elections were a sham. No one who actually wants any betterment for the locals participated in the election. It is not an election when all the votes go to one party: the Pakistan army,” Tariq Rehman, a schoolteacher in Kotli, told The Diplomat.
Pakistan’s omnipotent military establishment has maintained arbitrary control over the region since the 1947 partition of the Indian subcontinent divided the erstwhile state of Jammu and Kashmir between India and Pakistan. Both states administer part of Jammu and Kashmir but claim the territory in its entirety, and they have fought multiple wars over it.
In August 2019, India revoked Article 370 of its constitution, which undid the special status of Indian-administered Kashmir. Since then, multiple Pakistani government sources, including military officials, have told The Diplomat that there have been plans to mainstream the Pakistani-administered Kashmir, effectively upholding the Line of Control dividing the territory as an international border. Calls to divide Pakistan’s existing provinces have also gathered pace in recent months.
While the Pakistani state makes up its mind over the status of its controlled section of Kashmir, the locals have been stuck in limbo, unsure of their relationship with the country. Whether they are a distinct autonomous region – as upheld by Pakistan’s longstanding position and internationalization of the Kashmir dispute – or just a part of Pakistan is a question that has manifested in local political, social, and cultural expressions.
“They want us to be Pakistanis when they feel like it. They want us to be Kashmiris when they feel like it. But the recent bloodshed shows that they want us to remain captives to their power games. Who kills people for demanding that we should have a say in deciding our own future?” said Mir Hamza, a Muzaffarabad-based artisan, who had participated in recent protests and was witness to security personnel firing on protestors. “My brother [cousin] is still in Rawalakot. We want to continue the movement until we can achieve our fundamental human rights.”
As the sit-in continues in Rawalakot, local authorities have made the city inaccessible, with media barred from reporting in the region. Internet blackouts have been in place to limit social media coverage, and laws have been passed requiring a No Objection Certificate (NOC) for coverage of any news.
Many international and local publications have been blocked in Pakistan. One of them is the Urdu publication Daily Jeddojehad, which has documented the deaths in Pakistan-administered Kashmir amid the recent state crackdown.
“Security agencies raided my home. In my absence, three of my family members were picked up. They told my family that my articles on Kashmir were anti-national and the raid was aimed at arresting me,” Jeddojehad editor Farooq Sulehria told The Diplomat.
“I was in London, hence I was lucky to escape. However, I am not able to return to Pakistan,” he added.
Many journalists and activists have been summoned over dissent in Pakistan-administered Kashmir in order to enforce complete censorship. “This is unprecedented. The state wants to deny the people of Jammu and Kashmir the possibility to voice their protest on social media against the violent repression. It wants to disseminate one-dimensional information and propaganda,” Sulehria said.
These measures have been put in place as part of the crackdown on the local protesters, who have been galvanized in recent years by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC).
Since September 2023, the JAAC has rallied for the locals’ right to have control over their own resources, with the committee emphasizing issues ranging from power and commodity prices to governance reforms. As part of its list of demands, a major political reform sought by the JAAC was the undoing of seat reservations for muhajirs, or immigrants from Indian-administered Kashmir. As things stand, 12 of the 53 seats in the legislature of Pakistan-administered Kashmir are allocated to such individuals – who could be residing outside the territory. JAAC members and critics told The Diplomat that this arrangement not only reduces local representation, but also allows the military establishment to maintain its political stranglehold.
“Azad Jammu & Kashmir should only be ruled by the people of Azad Jammu & Kashmir. Not those in uniform, nor their selected parties, nor those being picked for the reserved seats to toe the lines of the powers that be,” JAAC core leader Shaukat Nawaz Mir had told The Diplomat when the latest protests erupted in June.
Mir, among other JAAC members, has since been detained. The government slapped sedition charges on them following the announcement of “head money” over information pertaining to these individuals. The JAAC has been declared a terrorist organization by the Pakistani state, with many of its activists either being detained or voluntarily going underground.
While the JAAC enjoys significant support among the people of Pakistan-administered Kashmir, it has its skeptics as well. “I don’t know who they are, and whom they are fighting for. Some say they are Indian agents. All I know is that because of the violence and the internet shutdown I have lost significant business and customers,” said Mohammed Iqbal, a Chakswari-based restaurant owner.
According to Madina Market Traders Association President Raja Abrar Mustafa, most of the traders had supported the JAAC initially, but gradually the committee’s position hardened on some issues. “We have supported them over issues related to the public and economic issues. But traders shouldn’t get involved in constitutional matters,” he said.
Many of the JAAC’s critics, new and old – including those who are a part of the government machinery – nonetheless concede that most of the demands the committee had brought to the table reflected the sentiments of the majority of the local population, even if some matters might have been contentious.
“All of the committee’s demands were accepted. But they continued to fixate over one [on seat reservation], causing so much turmoil. What did all this achieve for the locals?” asked Mirpur-based PML-N leader Chaudhary Muhammad Saeed while talking to The Diplomat.
Saeed, who lost his Mirpur seat in the recent elections, said while the voter turnout was lower – around 50 percent compared to the usual 60 percent – it wasn’t different enough to suggest a widespread clash between the locals and the state. “Yes, some people are unhappy over certain issues, and yes, some political reforms are needed in Azad Kashmir. But what is more pertinent are economic reforms. There would be no need for such protests where there is financial stability,” he said.
Even so, many of the people who are “unhappy” are unable to participate in these conversations, or respond to the ubiquitous state-sponsored criticism against them. Many of the state’s critics are in jail, in exile, or have disappeared.
*Some names have been changed to protect the identities of sources.

The father of an American sailor serving aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier was released from federal custody following his detention by immigration authorities during the weekend, according to his family on Tuesday.
“Luis has been released back to our family,” the Aviles family said via the sailor Joshua Aviles' social media account.
They expressed gratitude for the public support received during the ordeal and requested privacy as they await the return of Joshua, who has been deployed for more than nine months.
Luis Manuel Aviles, originally from Nicaragua who has lived in the US for two decades, was apprehended Saturday in Key West, Florida. DHS stated that Border Patrol agents arrested Aviles because he had entered the country illegally.
The USS Abraham Lincoln is returning to the US following a prolonged deployment in the Middle East.

Russia’s AI disinformation campaign linked to Israel-based think tank: Spiegel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:21:17 UTC
03:21:17 KST

Ayhan Şimşek
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
A Russian anti-Western disinformation network that used artificial intelligence to spread pro-Kremlin propaganda is linked to an Israel-based think tank, German news magazine Der Spiegel reported Tuesday.
User accounts flagged by OpenAI’s security teams used ChatGPT to generate propaganda mainly for Telegram channels while also promoting the International Burke Institute, according to the magazine.
The institute describes itself as an “expert community” founded in 2025 and based in Israel.
Der Spiegel said online evidence connects the institute to a charity called Dor Moriah, which is run by Israelis with Russian and Ukrainian roots and has alleged ties to the Russian Foreign Ministry.
Neither the International Burke Institute nor Dor Moriah responded to requests for comment, according to the magazine.
In a statement Tuesday, OpenAI confirmed that it had banned a group of Russian-origin accounts involved in covert influence operations across several languages.
“We recently banned a cluster of ChatGPT accounts originating in Russia that were being used to promote the International Burke Institute,” the company said.
In addition to promoting the think tank, the accounts generated posts for several Telegram channels, according to OpenAI.
One of the channels, Lahme Ente, or Lame Duck, has about 20,000 subscribers and publishes content critical of the EU, the German government and Western support for Ukraine, Der Spiegel reported.
Some recent headlines included “What Is NATO Hiding From Us?” and “Europe’s Inevitable Downfall,” according to the magazine.
