US judge denies Ghislaine Maxwell’s ‘frivolous’ bid to throw out conviction
A US federal judge rejects Maxwell’s claims that newly released Epstein files could help overturn her felony convictions.
A United States federal judge has rejected the bid from Ghislaine Maxwell, former girlfriend and longtime associate of Jeffrey Epstein, to throw out her five felony convictions, calling the claims “meritless” and “frivolous”.
In a 67-page opinion made public on Tuesday, Judge Paul Engelmayer denied Maxwell’s post-conviction challenge to her five felony convictions.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Senate Democrat’s report says major banks ‘looked the other way’ on Epstein
- list 2 of 3French model recruiter with close ties to Jeffrey Epstein found dead
- list 3 of 3New Mexico sues US Justice Department for impeding Epstein probe
Maxwell, 64, is serving a 20-year sentence for helping the late financier Jeffrey Epstein recruit and sexually abuse underage girls for over a decade. She is eligible for release in 2037.
She was convicted by a jury in December 2021 on five felony counts. The Second Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the verdict in 2024, and the Supreme Court declined to hear a further appeal last October.
Maxwell, representing herself, submitted her petition under Section 2255, the federal statute allowing convicted defendants to challenge their sentences. Engelmayer, who did not preside over Maxwell’s original 2021 trial, called her filing a “lengthy and rambling petition”.
Much of Maxwell’s petition leaned on records released under the Epstein Files Transparency Act (EFTA), a law passed with near-unanimous congressional support in November 2025 that forced the US Department of Justice to make the files public.
Maxwell claims her constitutional rights at trial and sentencing were violated, and that the materials released as part of the EFTA support this claim.
Engelmayer found that the material worked against Maxwell rather than for her. “To the extent it is relevant,” he wrote, “far from exculpating her, it incriminates her or reinforces the correctness of the legal rulings Maxwell challenges.”
The judge also highlighted an apparent contradiction in Maxwell’s own account. On claims related to a sentencing enhancement, which increased her prison term because prosecutors argued she had a leadership role in Epstein’s scheme, her petition argued she had “largely exited” Epstein’s household by 2002.
But in a July 2025 interview with then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche, Maxwell described continuing to manage Epstein’s properties and staff years later.
On claims that Maxwell was unfairly singled out while other associates of Epstein went uncharged, Engelmayer noted she had not implicated any other person in the child sex abuse scheme and does not even concede Epstein’s culpability in her own filing.
Engelmayer described the case against her as “the epitome of a virtuous prosecution” and certified that any appeal of his ruling “would not be taken in good faith”.

HHS plans new FDA deputy commissioner roles for technology and drugs, sources say

Unknown Publisher

02:00:01 KST

The Department of Health and Human Services is planning to create two new deputy commissioner roles at the Food and Drug Administration, one of which would focus on technology and the intersection of health and artificial intelligence, CNBC has learned.
The other new position is for a deputy commissioner for drugs, according to two sources familiar with the plan. The agency already has several deputy commissioners, including an acting deputy commissioner for food, though it is unclear who will step into that role permanently.
HHS officials would appoint the new leaders in what some in the Trump administration view as a bid to exert greater influence over the agency, according to the sources, who asked to remain anonymous because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
No final decisions or formal announcements about the new roles have been made, the sources said.
Jared Seehafer, a senior advisor to the FDA and medical devices industry veteran, is the leading candidate for the technology role, according to three people familiar with the matter. Seehafer is a co-founder and former CEO of Enzyme, a life sciences compliance software company, and most recently worked at a venture capital firm in San Francisco before stepping into his FDA advisory role in August of last year.
Kyle Diamantas was most recently the deputy commissioner for food before stepping in as the acting FDA commissioner in May after Marty Makary's resignation over the agency's authorization of fruit-flavored vapes. It's unclear if Diamantas would return to that role.
CNBC could not learn of any specific candidates for the deputy commissioner for drugs role.
The two new positions would report to President Donald Trump's pick for FDA commissioner, Heidi Overton, who still needs to be confirmed by the Senate, according to two people familiar with the plan.
HHS did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
The new leadership structure would come after a tumultuous stretch for the FDA.
The agency has faced intense scrutiny over its handling of a multistate cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce, which exacerbated broader concerns about federal budget and staff cuts hindering the agency's ability to rein in foodborne outbreaks.
The FDA has also been under the spotlight for a series of decisions around certain new drug products.
For example, the FDA earlier this month granted accelerated approval to Replimune for its melanoma drug, Tudriqev, following a high-profile regulatory battle with the company and two prior rejections of the treatment.
In March, the FDA also drew sharp backlash from the biotech industry after demanding an extra clinical trial – including a fake or "sham" brain surgery placebo – for an experimental Huntington's disease treatment from UniQure. The agency later reversed its stance and greenlit UniQure to file for accelerated approval based on mid-stage data.
And on Monday, the FDA granted a three-month review extension for Capricor Therapeutics' experimental Duchenne muscular dystrophy drug to consider additional data, which came after an advisory committee to the agency voted 9-3 against recommending approval of that product.
Meanwhile, the FDA has increasingly turned to artificial intelligence to help employees with internal operations, including via its Elsa generative AI tool, which the agency has used for tasks such as document summarization and drafting. At the same time, FDA regulators are responsible for evaluating the safety and effectiveness of medical products that incorporate AI.
Last week, the FDA released a discussion paper outlining potential approaches for regulating generative AI-enabled medical devices. Instead of issuing formal guidance, the agency seeks input from patients, clinicians, developers and other stakeholders.
The new deputy commissioner for technology would oversee both the agency's own internal use of AI and its review of AI-enabled products, according to the people familiar with the matter.

Sánchez’s ministers clash over whether Madrid missed Ceuta migrant warnings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Sánchez’s ministers clash over whether Madrid missed Ceuta migrant warnings
The contradictory accounts of what the government knew — and when it knew it — are devastating for a government under fire for its handling of the crisis.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s efforts to quell concerns over his government’s handling of the migration crisis in Ceuta fell flat on Tuesday after two of his top ministers publicly clashed over whether vital intelligence warnings were ignored.
At the end of July, some 72,000 migrants poured into the Spanish exclave in North Africa, raising major questions about whether Spain’s intelligence services failed to detect the unusually large number of people gathering over the border — something that would have enabled the authorities to deploy more guards.
During an emergency hearing in the Spanish parliament on Tuesday, Defense Minister Margarita Robles insisted the National Intelligence Center, which handles both foreign and domestic intelligence and counterintelligence, had issued a warning to the national authorities on July 30, before thousands of migrants started flooding into the exclave.
Advertisement
“Our armed forces, intelligence services, and, of course, the National Intelligence Center carried out the work that was and is required of them, and shared and analyzed this information with the state security forces and the staff of the government delegation,” the minister told lawmakers, defending the work of the agents she oversees.
Robles’ statement directly contradicts the Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska’s version of events. For weeks, he has insisted the national government did not reinforce the border in Ceuta because it had no way of anticipating the sudden migrant surge.
On Tuesday, Grande-Marlaska hit back directly at Robles’ statement during a press conference, insisting that neither Spain’s intelligence services nor any foreign intelligence agents had detected or warned of anything unusual near Ceuta.
“There was no report that foreshadowed what ultimately transpired on July 30,” he said, adding that it was a matter of “common sense” that any warning would have been taken seriously and handled accordingly.
After lawmakers informed Robles that Grande-Marlaska had denied her statement, the defense minister doubled down and said the country’s intelligence services had warned authorities on July 29, a day earlier than she had originally stated, adding that it was “common knowledge, public knowledge, that people were swimming into Ceuta.”
Advertisement
But she conceded that her agents might have informed national authorities “verbally.”
“Intelligence services operate in many ways,” she said. “Often, handwritten reports aren’t necessary.”
Detrimental divisions
The finger-pointing between two such senior ministers is embarrassing for Sánchez.
Nearly a month after the surge, thousands of unauthorized migrants remain in the exclave, and the prime minister is under pressure to prove his government is capable of not only resolving the immediate crisis, but guaranteeing the longer-term security of Spain’s North African exclaves.
Sánchez hoped to assuage public fears by convening an emergency meeting of his National Security Council on Tuesday, during which he selected Territorial Policy Minister Ángel Víctor Torres to manage the ongoing response to the crisis. But the attempt to present a united governmental front was upended by Robles and Grande-Marlaska.
While infighting within the cabinet is always problematic, the spectacle of two of Sánchez’s longest-serving ministers publicly contradicting each other over what the government knew — and when it knew it — is potentially devastating for a government already under pressure to explain how the crisis was allowed to unfold.
Advertisement
Opposition lawmakers seized on the divisions on Tuesday to accuse Sánchez’s executive of attempting to cover up its botched handling of the crisis.
“Marlaska and Robles aren’t even bothering to hide their attempts to accuse one another of lying about the Ceuta crisis,” said Miguel Tellado, secretary-general of the center-right People’s Party.
“Spain has been attacked and the prime minister’s response has been to go sunbathing and leave his ministers to fight one another to avoid taking the blame.”
Alberto Asarta, lawmaker for the far-right Vox party, went even further and announced he would request Spain’s parliament invoke Article 102 of the constitution, which allows for the prosecution of members of the government.
“80,000 people don’t congregate near the border without the intelligence services of Spain and Morocco being aware of it,” Asarta said, adding that the ministers’ failure to protect the exclave “constitutes the crime of treason against the security of Spain.”

National Legend of Ukraine award ceremony held in Kyiv
An Ukrinform correspondent reports this.
The award ceremony was held in Kyiv in the presence of President Volodymyr Zelensky and First Lady Olena Zelenska.
“After the first ‘Legend,’ after we marked the 30th anniversary of our independence, the full-scale war began. Today, we are celebrating 35 years of independence, and we have a state, we have independence, and we have our strong warriors,” Zelensky said before presenting the awards.
He separately highlighted Ukraine’s foreign partners who support the country, including American actor Sean Penn, who personally attended the ceremony.
“We have our foreign partners here today. Sean Penn didn’t come to the Oscars in America, you see, but he came to the ‘Legend’ awards,” the President remarked.

1 / 16
The title of National Legend of Ukraine was awarded posthumously to dissident and human rights activist Levko Lukianenko and Serhii Kuzminskyi, the leader of the rock band Braty Hadiukiny.
The other recipients were Braty Hadiukiny members Pavlo Krakhmaliov, Mykhailo Lundin and Ihor Melnychuk; José Andrés, founder of World Central Kitchen and United24 ambassador; Ihor Belanov, the 1986 European Footballer of the Year; Anatolii Borychevskyi, director of the Prydniprovska Thermal Power Plant, a separate unit of DTEK Dniproenergo; Senior Lieutenant Oleksandr Dziuba, chief of a headquarters group of the Ukrainian Ground Forces’ 1st Separate Medical Battalion; sculptor and People’s Artist of Ukraine Anatolii Kushch; Colonel and Hero of Ukraine Rostyslav Lazarenko; Alla Mazur, presenter of the 1+1 TV news service; American actor, film director and screenwriter Sean Penn; Junior Lieutenant Antin Roschin, commander of a squad in a company of the Ukrainian Ground Forces’ 1st Separate Medical Battalion; artist and Taras Shevchenko National Prize laureate Tiberii Silvashi; composer and Hero of Ukraine Yevhen Stankovych; and Nadia Yarish, senior operating-room nurse of the medical company of the 1st Corps of the National Guard Azov.
“I am very pleased that every National Legend of Ukraine ceremony features many of our warriors, defenders and women defenders, because it gives us an opportunity to learn more about them,” Alla Mazur told Ukrinform.
Asked whether she considers herself a “legend,” Mazur replied: “No, I feel like a student, because life constantly forces us to learn.” At the same time, she said she liked the idea behind the National Legend of Ukraine award.
“And I believe it is very right, especially now, during the war,” she said.
Nadia Yarish, while accepting the award, drew attention to the Ukrainian soldiers of Azov who remain in captivity, saying that around 700 are still being held. “They suffer and are abused every day; with each passing day they lose their health and even their lives. At present, we know of 375 Ukrainian citizens who have been tortured to death in Russia. Bring them all home,” Yarish said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky established the National Legend of Ukraine award on August 16, 2021, by Decree No. 362/2021.
The award is presented to Ukrainian citizens, as well as foreign nationals and stateless persons, for outstanding personal contributions to Ukraine’s independence and statehood, the defense of the country and service to the Ukrainian people, as well as significant contributions to the national economy, science, education, culture, the arts, sports and healthcare, and for active charitable and civic engagement.
The award is made of gold and takes the form of a stylized flower with blue and yellow enamel-covered petals. At its center is a relief image of the Sign of the Princely State of Volodymyr the Great.

PARIS, August 25. /TASS/. France intends to formally restrict Ukraine’s purchases of weapons from countries outside the EU using money given to it by European countries, according to the Euronews television channel.
The European 2026-2027 program for the Kiev regime amounts to 90 billion euros to be disbursed for various needs, including military. The European Commission is supposed to approve all arms supply contracts it intends to pay for.
Under the prorgam, Ukraine cannot allocate more than 35% of the aid package to defense products manufactured outside the EU and the European Economic Area; however, it can request exemptions if certain goods are not produced in the EU or if production in the EU is more expensive or takes longer than required. According to the TV channel, Ukraine has secured exemptions that allow it to purchase weapons and equipment outside the EU using funds allocated by Europe, like Chinese components for drone production and US Patriot interceptors.
France’s military industry is one of the largest among EU countries. Together with Italy it produces the SAMP/T air defense system, which is Europe's version of the US Patriot.
"France, however, is pushing for these exemptions to be temporary, in an effort to ensure a greater share of the EU-backed funding ultimately supports European -- and potentially French -- production," Euronews said.
The TV channel also reminds that in July, the defense ministers of Germany, Denmark, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Finland, Sweden, and Estonia sent letters to chief of European diplomacy Kaja Kallas, and European Commissioner for Defense Andrius Kubilius urging them to grant Ukraine maximum flexibility in purchasing the equipment it needs.
On Tuesday, European Commission Spokesman Balazs Ujvari said that the EC has not yet allowed Kiev to purchase Patriot air defense systems from the US with the EU funds. He noted that, in total, Ukraine has already submitted weapons contracts worth 22 billion euros to the European Commission. In total, this year the EC wants to provide Kiev with 28 billion euros for weapons purchases alone. Thus, Kiev still has a "financial cushion" of six billion euros, within which it can request permission from the European Commission to purchase any non·European weapons, including Patriot, and the EC will consider it, but this has not been done yet.

Revealed: How undercover agents spied on anti-ICE protesters in Minnesota
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:56:15 UTC
01:56:15 KST

Newly disclosed records reveal how undercover federal agents posed as concerned community members to spy on residents and activists who opposed Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) crackdown in Minnesota.
Internal Department of Homeland Security (DHS) files, disclosed in federal court and reviewed by the Guardian, document the actions of several undercover agents, including one who went by the username “peanutbutterjelly” in Signal chats with activists. The documents show that the officer kept records of Signal conversations, screenshotting chats about protest plans and volunteer recruitment, and offering to help with fundraising efforts.
Another undercover agent took photos at demonstrations and protest planning meetings, including of demonstrators in frog costumes, a poster that mocked JD Vance with heavy eye makeup, and a protester writing an anti-ICE message in chalk. Other DHS agents trailed a protester as he left his home, got coffee and went to a church.
The records were released as part of the Department of Justice’s ongoing prosecution of 15 Minneapolis protesters, accused of being part of a “conspiracy” to “impede” ICE.
A tranche of internal DHS files disclosed in the case earlier this month revealed DHS extensively spied on prominent leftwing groups and protesters as part of its investigation into anti-ICE activity. DHS called the investigation “Operation Puppet Master”, the files showed, sending undercover agents to community meetings, infiltrating Signal chats and obtaining financial records of left-leaning non-profit organizations and unions.
The surveillance escalated during widespread anti-ICE protests in Minneapolis after the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in January. Civil rights groups and the protesters’ attorneys have argued the government was surveilling people without justification and is criminalizing lawful protest activity.
A DHS spokesperson declined to answer questions about the records, saying in a statement that Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), its branch that carried out the investigations, “does not comment on the existence or status of specific ongoing investigations, nor on investigative methods”. The spokesperson referred questions to the justice department in Minnesota, which declined to comment.
Undercover agent 9843, who went by the name “peanutbutterjelly” in the Signal chats of organizers, worked for HSI, the investigative arm of ICE, records show. In December 2025, the agent was deployed to “participate” in virtual and in-person meetings, records show. The agent’s objective was to “gather intelligence regarding any organized networks of conspirators – operating online and in person – who may be providing material support to violent opportunists and individuals engaged in impeding federal law enforcement”, DHS summarized in a February report.
The undercover agent attended a virtual “ICE watch” training on 3 December during which community members discussed how to monitor ICE officers’ activities. Organizers at the meeting “urged participants to observe nonviolently and obey law enforcement commands”, DHS said. The agent attended another “legal observer” training in person four days later, reporting there were no signs of “threats to public safety”.
The undercover agent was not just a passive observer in activist groups. In December, the agent got involved with advocates organizing protests at hotels where ICE agents were believed to be staying, with the agent offering to “assist with verifying the locations”, records show. In one Signal chat, the agent wrote: “also v interested in the financial organizing piece (I like numbers and data) & marrying that together with propaganda so would love to work on both sides of these groups!!” It was unclear what the agent was referencing. In other messages, the agent also offered to help with fundraising, hanging posters and designing flyers.
A DHS report labeled “Images from UCA [undercover agent] 9843’s phone” described photos and screenshots taken by the agent. The agent screenshotted a message about finding housing for members with Veterans for Peace, an advocacy group. The agent also kept records of messages about a march planned by a rightwing influencer and discussions of a counter demonstration. The agent further screenshotted a selfie one protester sent in a Signal group and recorded chats about signing up for an “ICE Out of MN” event.
The files released Tuesday also included summaries of DHS interviews with two other undercover agents who attended a January community meeting at a library hosted by Sunrise Movement, a national non-profit focused on the climate crisis and involved in protesting ICE. One agent recounted organizers giving a “historical breakdown of the Sunrise Movement” and then breaking into smaller groups discussing protest strategies.
“They were pretty big on peaceful protest,” the undercover agent summarized, according to a transcript of their interview with another DHS agent. A report disclaimer noted the transcript was produced by AI.
The undercover officer described having a one-on-one conversation with an activist, with the agent offering to provide supplies for demonstrations: “I told him that I work construction and I could do things with building whatever they need.” The activist took the agent’s phone number, the agent said. “I was like, look, I know you guys are peaceful and it’s cool,” the agent recounted, saying he told the protester he could “help” with “stuff that’s more direct”.
This agent also described the appearances of various people at the event, including a “chick dressed like Zelda”, a “full Asian girl” and a male “school teacher” with “longer hair”.
The other undercover agent at the library meeting said conversations were focused on actions “that wouldn’t be something that … people would get arrested for”. The agent described one “young white male” who “just in my opinion seems like somebody who wanted to to be more involved in illegal activity”. This agent had private conversations with activists in attendance and asked them “if they knew of any other groups that you know, I can participate in, especially for action”.
The records released Tuesday included extensive “miscellaneous photos” taken by this undercover agent on their government phone. That included photos from inside a community meeting where organizers had a presentation slide encouraging people to attend a city council meeting. There was also a photo of a table of books, including a coloring book about socialism and books about climate change and mass incarceration.
The agent further took photos of: a march where a demonstrator wore a “peaceful observer don’t shoot” vest; graffiti on a building that said “KILL ICE”; the agent’s handwritten notes about a calisthenics workout class hosted by a socialist group; a group of brass musicians performing in protest of ICE; pizza and snacks at a table; and a “Defend our democracy” flag.
This agent also attended a meeting in February of the Party for Socialism and Liberation, an anti-capitalist group, reporting the discussion was “political in nature” and “there was no indication that members of the group wanted to use violence towards ICE”.
The records also described the surveillance operation of nine agents deployed one day in February to trail four protesters to “determine a pattern of life and other potential intelligence”. A report shows those agents monitored one person at his home and followed him as he drove his truck and got coffee. Agents watched this individual go to a church and noted him holding “ICE OUT” signs and “shields”.
The files were submitted by an attorney for one of the Minnesota protesters charged with “conspiracy” against ICE. Some parts of the records are redacted and the context of the specific operations wasn’t always clear from the records.
The agents’ work was part of a vast surveillance operation following the directive of Donald Trump’s executive order issued last year designating “antifa” a “domestic terrorist” group responsible for “riots” targeting ICE. The indictment of 15 protesters focused on Direct Action Minnesota, a loose coalition of organizers accused of a “conspiracy” against ICE.
The indictment described a wide range of actions by protesters, but there are no charges of serious violence nor any allegations that the defendants injured specific ICE officers.

Joint Iran-Oman statement on Strait of Hormuz: Proposal for temporary corridor and mine clearance
TEHRAN- Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met with his Omani counterpart Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamood Al-Busaidi in Tehran on Tuesday.
During a working visit to Tehran, Al-Busaidi held constructive talks with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Islamic Republic of Iran.
The two sides discussed key bilateral and regional issues.
The discussions focused on the importance both countries attach to the resumption of safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, while upholding their sovereignty and sovereign rights. In view of the current situation in the strait – resulting from the recent war and its devastating consequences – the two ministers examined a phased framework that could provide a practical and workable basis for moving forward.
The proposed framework includes the establishment of a temporary joint maritime corridor through the Strait of Hormuz and an agreement to carry out a joint project for mine clearance in the strait. Technical negotiations between the two sides will continue with the aim of reaching an agreement on a permanent maritime corridor, the future administration of the strait, as well as mechanisms for information exchange, traffic management, and the provision of maritime and security services.
In this context, both sides emphasized the importance of holding joint consultations with the regional countries bordering the waters of the Persian Gulf. They also stressed the need to observe applicable international law and to respect the sovereign rights of the littoral states.
The Omani diplomat’s visit to Tehran comes as Iran has repeatedly emphasized its cooperation with Muscat to ensure the security of maritime traffic.
Tehran believes that, given the two countries shared maritime boundary in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran and Oman should have priority in shaping policies concerning one of the world’s most important waterways and its largest energy transit route.

UK citizens will be told to stock up on tinned food and take steps to ensure they are prepared for national emergencies as part of a new government campaign to improve the nation’s resilience.
The new campaign from the Cabinet Office will set out ways people can prepare for extreme weather events and potential attacks from hostile states, including stocking up on bottled water, sources told the Guardian.
The aim will be to ensure most households have basic supplies and knowledge about how to cope in a crisis, in order to free up immediate government resources for the most vulnerable.
Planning for a number of disasters, from cyber-attacks to extreme heat and flooding, has increased over the past few months after a number of incidents both in the UK and across the world. The plans, first reported by the FT, also include an internal reassessment of government preparations for a military attack by a hostile state affecting Britain.
The Cabinet Office minister Louise Haigh, who is Andy Burnham’s de-facto deputy, is also understood to be coordinating crisis planning across departments in Whitehall to allow swifter assistance to affected communities.
During his campaign to become Makerfield MP, Burnham spoke repeatedly about the threat of flooding to communities and the inadequacy of government planning and response.
Burnham convened a Cobra meeting earlier this month to coordinate the government’s response to the heatwave, amid a threat of spreading wildfires and drought warnings.
The government was criticised, however, for its decision to send an emergency phone alert warning of wildfires last week, which charities and domestic abuse survivors said risked the safety of people who might be hiding secret phones.
Haigh’s predecessor, Darren Jones, had said that work was under way on the so-called “war book” on how international conflict might affect the UK.
The Cabinet Office said: “Safeguarding national security is the first priority of any government.
“We’re committed to raising awareness of simple steps households can take to make themselves more resilient, as well as driving forward the home defence programme to build our country’s preparedness for various threats.”

More than 20 Marvel universe actors join campaign for release of Palestinian politician Marwan Barghouti
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

More than 20 Marvel universe actors join campaign for release of Palestinian politician Marwan Barghouti
- Mark Ruffalo, Benedict Cumberbatch, Ian McKellen and other featured Marvel actors sign international appeal calling for Barghouti's release from Israeli prison
Yasin Yorgancı
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
ANKARA
More than 20 actors who have appeared in Marvel universe films and TV series have joined an international campaign calling for the release of Palestinian politician Marwan Barghouti, who has been held by Israel and, according to the campaign, kept in solitary confinement since 2023.
"We express our grave concern at the continuing imprisonment of Marwan Barghouti, his violent mistreatment and denial of legal rights whilst imprisoned," the campaign, known as "Free Marwan Now," said on Instagram last week.
The campaign was launched by Barghouti's family and supporters and has attracted the backing of more than 200 figures from film, music, literature, and other cultural fields.
"We call upon the United Nations and the Governments of the World to actively seek the release of Marwan Barghouti from Israeli prison," the statement added.
Among the signatories are actors with prominent Marvel contributions, including Ian McKellen, who played Magneto in the X-Men series, plus Rebecca Hall, Riz Ahmed, Jason Flemyng, Elliot Page, Hugo Weaving (famed from the Matrix films), Zawe Ashton, Emma Corrin, May Calamawy, Brian Cox, Dan Stevens, Rob Delaney, and Kingsley Ben-Adir.
The campaign also includes Marvel Cinematic Universe stars Mark Ruffalo, who played Bruce Banner/the Hulk; Benedict Cumberbatch, who played Doctor Strange; and Don Cheadle, who played James Rhodes/War Machine. Cate Blanchett, who portrayed Hela in Thor: Ragnarok; Tilda Swinton, who played the Ancient One, Tatiana Maslany, who starred in She-Hulk, and Daniel Bruhl, known for his role as Zemo, are also among the signatories.
Who is Marwan Barghouti?
Barghouti was born on June 6, 1958, in the village of Kobar, northwest of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank. He joined the Fatah movement at the age of 15.
He was arrested by Israel in 1976, when he was 18, and spent a period in prison, where he learned Hebrew. During his university years, he was detained several times. In 1985, he was again placed in administrative detention and was later confined to house arrest.
Barghouti became one of the prominent figures of the First Intifada, which began in the Palestinian territories in 1987. Israel subsequently deported him to Jordan, where he remained for seven years.
He returned to the West Bank in 1994 under the Oslo Accords signed between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization.
In 1996, Barghouti was elected to the Palestinian Legislative Council representing Fatah in the Ramallah and Al-Bireh area. He subsequently rose rapidly within Fatah and became the movement's secretary-general.
In 2002, Israeli forces arrested Barghouti at his home in Ramallah. An Israeli court later convicted him on charges including murder and attempted murder and sentenced him to five life terms plus 40 years in prison.
Contemporary reporting says the sentence followed his conviction in connection with attacks during the Second Intifada that killed five people.
Barghouti studied political science at Birzeit University, earning a bachelor's degree in history and political science and a master's degree in international relations. He completed a doctorate while in prison.
He has also written books including The Promise, Resistance to Arrest, and One Thousand Days in a Solitary Confinement Cell.
In February 2024, Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir ordered Barghouti transferred from Ofer Military Prison to Ramon Prison, where he was placed in solitary confinement.
Israeli authorities said the move followed the alleged acquisition of intelligence concerning plans for an uprising in the West Bank. The decision prompted increased concern among Palestinians about Barghouti's safety.
The current campaign says its appeal is aimed at securing his release and urging international institutions and governments to intervene on his behalf.

Close attention was paid to preparations for forthcoming bilateral events at the top and high levels, including the next session of the intergovernmental commission, and to the expansion of the legal base the cooperation relies on.
As a result of the session Belarusian ministries and commercial entities were assigned concrete tasks with regard to the diversification of commodity flows between the two countries and with regard to the advancement of interbank, investment, technological, and interregional ties.

Brazil fines TikTok owner $29.8M for processing data of minors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:51:09 UTC
01:51:09 KST

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Brazil’s National Data Protection Authority (ANPD) fined ByteDance, the owner of TikTok, 153.7 million Brazilian reais ($29.8 million) on Tuesday for irregularities in the processing of children’s and adolescents’ personal data, according to the Official Gazette.
The fine was imposed following an administrative proceeding that identified violations of Brazil’s General Data Protection Law (LGPD).
The decision also orders the company to delete data collected irregularly and implement a compliance plan to improve the protection of children and adolescents on the platform.
The ANPD said the investigation identified irregularities in two forms of access to TikTok: the “feed without registration,” which can be accessed without creating an account, and the “feed with registration,” linked to a registered profile.
In both cases, the ANPD found that the platform processed personal data belonging to children and adolescents without an adequate legal basis under the LGPD, and failed to adopt effective measures to prevent such processing.
Under the compliance plan, TikTok will automatically apply its most restrictive privacy settings to accounts belonging to users under 16. The settings can only be changed with authorization from parents or guardians.
The company will also strengthen parental supervision systems and implement stricter content filters, according to the ANPD.
For users accessing TikTok without an account, the company will suspend advertising in Brazil, limit access to content appropriate for all ages and reduce the collection and processing of personal data.
The authority said the measures will also include limiting access to 12 hours and disabling features such as content creation, commenting, direct messaging, following other users and livestreaming for users without registered accounts.
The ANPD said its action resulted in commitments aimed at reducing risks to the rights of children and adolescents, including the full suspension of advertisements and the disabling of livestreams and direct messaging for users accessing TikTok without registering.
The findings were detailed in Technical Note No. 50/2024/CGF/ANPD, prepared by the ANPD’s Supervision Department (SFI-ANPD), which identified practices deemed inconsistent with Brazil's General Data Protection Law in both forms of access to the platform.
ByteDance has the right to appeal the fine to the ANPD’s Board of Directors within 10 business days of notification, according to the agency.

Russia unable to export oil as refineries can no longer process it after Ukrainian strikes
Average seaborne shipments of Russian crude oil fell to 3.46 million barrels a day in the four weeks leading up to 23 August amid Ukrainian attacks on refineries, Black Sea ports and tankers.
Source: Bloomberg
Details: Previously, shutdowns at Russian refineries had left more crude available for export. That effect has now been offset by a decline in shipments from the Black Sea following attacks on oil tankers.
Moscow was forced to redirect Kazakh oil to Novorossiysk. This freed up capacity for Russian crude at the Baltic port of Ust-Luga, which is considered less vulnerable to Ukrainian attacks.
Meanwhile, strikes on oil and gas processing facilities have reduced fuel production and exacerbated shortages on the domestic market. Kremlin bans on exports of petrol, diesel and aviation fuel are further restricting oil revenues for the Russian budget.
According to OPEC secondary-source estimates, Russia produced 8.887 million barrels of crude oil per day in July. Bloomberg says this was the lowest level in six years and almost 1 million barrels a day below Russia's permitted level under the OPEC+ agreement.
Meanwhile, Russia's seaborne crude exports remain relatively high: since the beginning of 2026, they have been about 9% above the highest annual average recorded since the start of the full-scale invasion.
Background:
- In July, Ukrainian strikes knocked out more than 30% of Russia's oil refining capacity, with daily processing volumes falling to their lowest level since 2005.
- In August, the first seaborne shipment of petrol from India arrived in Russia amid fuel shortages caused by attacks on refineries.

Mystery Chinese ‘stealth fighter’ was just a fire trainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:47:35 UTC
01:47:35 KST

- Chinese aerospace analyst Andreas Rupprecht confirmed a stealth fighter-shaped object at Jining Qufu Airport is a fire-fighting trainer mock-up.
- Photos from China's Eastern Theater Command show military firefighters using the mock-up in a live training exercise involving smoke and fire.
Satellite images showing a stealth fighter-shaped object at a former Chinese airport turn out to depict a fire-fighting trainer mock-up, according to Chinese aerospace analyst Andreas Rupprecht.
Rupprecht made the assessment in an August 25 post on X, sharing images that show Chinese military firefighters conducting a live training exercise around the mock-up, including one photo showing it engulfed in smoke and flame while crews hosed it down.
“You surely remember these strange J-20-look alike models, some claimed them to be a new single engined stealth fighter, at Jining Qufu AP, which I already back then rated as fire-fighting trainer mock-ups. Here finally two clearer images!” Rupprecht wrote.
The training photos, credited to China’s Eastern Theater Command on Weibo, show firefighters in protective gear spraying water on the mock-up’s fuselage and dousing a fire set at its base, with a black plume of smoke rising from the exercise. The mock-up’s canopy, twin tails and general silhouette closely track the J-20, though the aircraft’s actual radar-absorbent skin and internal systems would not be replicated in a ground training prop.
The object first drew wide attention in April 2025, when satellite imagery showed a stealth fighter-like shape with a modified diamond-delta wing platform, canards and twin vertical tails parked on the apron in front of the passenger terminal at Jining Qufu Airport in Shandong Province, The War Zone reported at the time. Planet Labs imagery reviewed by the outlet showed the object had been present since at least September 2024. The War Zone’s report was syndicated by Yahoo News, extending its reach well beyond the specialist defense press.
Jining Qufu Airport was officially closed in December 2023, according to The War Zone. The facility had previously been collocated with a People’s Liberation Army Air Force base, a detail that fed speculation the object was tied to a classified aircraft program rather than routine ground training.
At the time of the initial sighting, The War Zone noted the object bore some resemblance to the Baidi Type-B, a fictional “space fighter” concept China’s Aviation Industry Corporation displayed at the 2024 Zhuhai airshow, though with significant differences. Analysts also compared it to vaguely J-20-like shapes that had appeared at Lintao Air Base in 2022, which Rupprecht assessed at the time as likely decoys, potentially tied to film or television production rather than any operational aircraft program.
The Jining Qufu sighting emerged amid a broader wave of speculation about Chinese next-generation fighter programs. China’s tailless J-36 and J-XDS, also referred to as the J-50, had both surfaced in satellite and social media imagery in late 2024 and early 2025, drawing extensive coverage from outlets including Army Recognition, Interesting Engineering, National Security Journal and 19FortyFive, much of it built on unconfirmed claims about engine counts, stealth features and operational status. Some of that broader coverage folded the Jining Qufu object into the same narrative of an emerging single-engine stealth design, despite the object never being confirmed as an aircraft in flight or under active test.
The Eastern Theater Command imagery now confirms the mock-up’s actual role: a full-scale prop used to train ground crews and firefighters on responding to a burning stealth-shaped aircraft, a standard part of military airfield emergency preparedness.

Turkish Red Crescent continues aid efforts in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:45:27 UTC
01:45:27 KST

Ali Semerci, Ahmed Sayed, Gizem Nisa Demir
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
The Turkish Red Crescent is continuing humanitarian aid operations for the Gaza Strip, working to ensure assistance sent from Türkiye reaches the territory, its president said Tuesday.
Speaking at Egyptian Red Crescent warehouses in Egypt’s El-Arish, Fatma Meric Yilmaz said the Turkish organization has carried out various humanitarian aid operations for Gaza since 2023.
Yilmaz said the organization is closely monitoring the delivery of aid sent from Türkiye.
She said the latest vessel, dispatched during the first week of Ramadan, carried enough supplies to fill about 400 trucks for delivery to Gaza.
The aid was turned back at border crossings for various reasons and subsequently unloaded at warehouses in El-Arish, she said.
Currently, about 15 trucks carrying aid from Türkiye are able to enter Gaza each day, Yilmaz said.
“Quickly, the aid sent by Türkiye here is being directed inside,” she said.
Yilmaz emphasized the importance of the Egyptian Red Crescent’s coordination in delivering aid to Gaza. She said individual items sometimes must be removed from packages before they can be resealed.
She also praised Egyptian Red Crescent volunteers for their efforts throughout the process. 
Operations continue in Gaza
Yilmaz said the entry of aid into Gaza is not the organization’s only channel of assistance, with the Turkish Red Crescent continuing operations in the territory through its personnel and delegation.
The organization operates three soup kitchens in Gaza, she said.
“Every day, we prepare and distribute 30,000 hot meals. This amounts to an operation of approximately 100 million liras per month,” Yilmaz said.
She stressed that hot meals are particularly important for people unable to prepare food themselves and said aid is being diversified according to needs on the ground.
When the flow of aid into Gaza slows, the organization obtains food parcels from within the territory and distributes them, Yilmaz said.
It also distributes 100 tons of drinking water every day, she said.
The Turkish Red Crescent is also continuing psychosocial support programs, particularly for children, Yilmaz said.
The organization has launched a new prosthetics project for people who have lost limbs and is providing health assistance, she added. 
- ‘We are following through on what Turkish people entrusted to us’
Yilmaz said the Turkish public remains highly sensitive to the humanitarian situation in Gaza and that the organization will continue working to ensure aid entrusted to it reaches those in need.
“We are following through on what the Turkish people entrusted to us,” Yilmaz said.
She said the organization monitors the entire process, from delivering supplies sent aboard aid ships to Gaza to converting cash donations into hot meals, drinking water, toys and hygiene supplies.
Yilmaz said the Turkish Red Crescent would continue its efforts to ensure Gaza is neither forgotten nor allowed to fade from public attention.
“We are doing everything we can, and we will continue to do so,” she said.

Will the U.S. sanctions against Iran work if they don't include China?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:45:25 UTC
01:45:25 KST

If the U.S. wants to end the war with Iran by way of economic sanctions, China is key
The language used Monday by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent as he announced a new raft of sanctions against Iran was apocalyptic. The measures are part of the Trump administration's plan to use economic pressure to force Iran to capitulate, to bring an end to the nearly six-month war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
The U.S. is "no longer managing the Iranian threat, we are ending it," Bessent declared, with sanctions that he vowed would "sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone."
Operation Economic Outcast will expand the categories for secondary sanctions against countries and entities that do business with Tehran and introduce new sanctions in sectors including technology, shipping and digital assets.
But Iran experts have not been convinced the new measures will have the kind of impact that would force the theocracy to accept defeat in a war President Trump predicted would last no more than six weeks, not months.
For decades, various U.S. administrations have attempted to pressure Iran with sanctions. The regime has survived through a series of financial schemes and smuggling operations, according to the U.S. Treasury.
"They know how to cope," Kate Dourian, a nonresident fellow at the Arab Gulf States Institute, told CBS News' partner network BBC News on Tuesday. "They have the workarounds. So, I think most of what Mr. Bessent said was targeted at other countries, not Iran."
In his announcement, Bessent said countries that maintain business relations with Iran should "expect to share in the isolation of a withering regime."
Sixty entities deemed to be helping or trading with Iran were listed under the new sanctions on Tuesday, including in the United Arab Emirates, Singapore, Malaysia, Hong Kong, France, the U.K. and — crucially according to analysts — China.
But the sanctions only target some private Chinese businesses, stopping short of the more consequential step of hitting the country's major financial institutions. Without that, analysts say Bessent's doomsday predictions for Iran will flop.
"This was not economic D-Day," Brett Erickson, a Washington-based sanctions expert who runs Obsidian Risk Advisors, told CBS News, using Mr. Trump's own language to describe the measures. "If the United States is unwilling to meaningfully target China, can Washington reasonably justify damaging our international relations and global standing, for a strategy with only a far-fetched likelihood of achieving victory?"
Iran's life support system
Last week, the UAE, a U.S. ally, cut off all trade with Iran. That, experts say, could have a meaningful impact on the regime.
The Gulf country was the world's biggest importer of Iranian goods in 2024, according to the World Trade Organization, and around 80% of Iran's foreign currency exchange is done in Dubai, according to Miad Maliki, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies who is also a former senior U.S. Treasury official.
The "UAE is going to be very instrumental in cutting off the regime's access to procuring foreign currencies, but also getting access to its reserves — funds that it has generated from oil sales to China and are sitting in different banks," he told CBS News last week.
But China is considered Iran's real lifeline.
Last year, Chinese purchases of Iranian crude oil amounted to nearly 45% of the Iranian government's budget, according to a U.S. government report from March.
"Iran's economy today runs based on this kind of scheme of selling oil to China, and then either using the funds that are generated from sale of oil to China to pay for imports from China, but also moving some of those funds outside China," said Maliki.
He said sometimes the money Iran earns by selling its oil to China goes to support Iranian proxy groups in the Middle East, such as Hezbollah in Lebanon or the Houthi rebels in Yemen.
China's major, state-backed banks have been accused of giving loans to small "teapot" refineries in the country, which then process sanctioned oil from Iran.
The U.S. Treasury has also accused China of faking the origins of Iranian oil; of falsely changing the legal ownership of Iranian ships to make them look Chinese-owned; and of building airports and electric grids in Iran instead of paying Iran money, which means they can avoid the SWIFT global banking system, where sanctions are applied.
Asked Monday whether Chinese banks would be among those hit by the new measures, Bessent said "no one is above the reach of U.S. sanctions."
He also said there would be a "major announcement of a financial institution being sanctioned by the end of this week," but offered no hints.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian said Tuesday that China was firmly opposed to "illicit unilateral sanctions" and would "do everything necessary to firmly safeguard its rights and interests."
Iran "is and was ready"
Iranians have suffered under decades of U.S. sanctions. The Iranian currency has plunged in value against the dollar and the head of the Iran-China Chamber of Commerce told Khabar Online last month that Iran could not afford to lose its maritime trade.
"The siege is worse than the war," Hariri said, referring to the U.S. naval blockade of Iran's ports and ships, adding that maritime costs had skyrocketed.
But Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said Monday that the country was "fully prepared" for the new U.S. sanctions, which he predicted would be "another defeat" for the Trump administration.
"Our defense is no longer so defensive; the enemies should wait for an attack," he told Iranian state television, adding that neither China nor Russia had "accepted" the U.S. measures and that other countries would likely resist them, too.
"The government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," he said. "We also have our own tools and know how to play the game."

There’s no place like a revered writer’s home | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:44:35 UTC
01:44:35 KST

Your editorial (The Guardian view on writers’ houses: a museum of one’s own, 18 August) rightly laments that George Eliot has no publicly open home despite efforts to secure one. The same is true, remarkably, of William Blake, and he is at least as worthy a cause, and arguably even more influential.
Poet, painter, printmaker and author of the words behind Jerusalem, Blake has no open home anywhere. Of his nine addresses, only two survive. In London, the apartment he rented is disappearing behind new development. The other, his cottage in Felpham, West Sussex, where he and his wife, Catherine, lived from 1800 to 1803 and experienced an outburst of creativity, is the only one that could ever open to the public.
I am a trustee of the Blake Cottage Trust, which has spent two years saving it. In 2024 the roof was near collapse and the cottage was on Historic England’s at-risk register. Thanks to The National Lottery Heritage Fund and other foundations, artisans have rebuilt the roof and removed a Victorian extension, returning the cottage to its original form. But much of the fabric still needs full conservation before the cottage is truly saved and can be opened to all, and that work costs a great deal of money.
Raising it has not been easy. Even with the backing of the Heritage Fund and other trusts, we will need private philanthropy to fill a significant gap – and, as your article notes of Rydal Mount, heritage sites live or die on relevance and sustainability as much as repair.
That’s why our ambition goes beyond bricks and thatch to include opening an arts and education centre near the cottage, conceived not just as somewhere to visit but as a living place of creativity and inspiration in its own right – one with year-round appeal for the local community as much as for returning visitors, and one that properly honours Catherine Blake too, who learned to read under William’s guidance and helped hand-print and colour the plates of his illuminated books.
With the 2027 bicentenary of Blake’s death approaching, this is a moment when Guardian readers could make a real difference – to find out more, visit blakecottage.org
Richard Clemmow
Trustee, The Blake Cottage Trust
Your editorial gave a commendable overview of the important work that writers’ houses and museums have been doing to reconnect us with our literary heritage. Of course, turning a writer’s house into a museum is difficult, and not always viable. But this needn’t mean that the house cannot be saved for the nation and enjoyed by the public.
The late poet laureate Ted Hughes was born in a tiny end-terrace house in Mytholmroyd, West Yorkshire. He claimed his first years there “shaped everything”. But the house is too small to accommodate tour groups (who would inevitably inconvenience the neighbours), and parking is limited to just a space or two on a residential street. So, when the house was saved 20 years ago by The Elmet Trust, a local charity, it was opened to paying guests as a holiday cottage or writer’s retreat.
This fully immersive experience goes beyond a visit to any museum. It places you in the poet’s shoes. Sleeping in the cosy attic room that Hughes shared with his older brother, or in the bedroom where he was born, inspires because it impresses upon us how humble his start in life was. Leaflets guide you to his favourite walks through the glorious Yorkshire woods and hillsides where he played as a child. His writings often described these places, or the views from his windows, and indeed the rooms in the house itself. There are no display cases, no text panels in sight. This is about lived experience.
A George Eliot museum is indeed a worthy aspiration; a Ted Hughes museum scarcely less so. Yet while a museum is a fitting tribute to any great author, literary tourism at its best is about the readers and the fans as much as the writers. Interactive visitor centres such as Seamus Heaney HomePlace are as vital a part of the future as traditional museums. Engaging with literary landscapes and walks is no less important – for health, for wellbeing, for our environment, for our imaginations. But surely nothing can beat stepping inside the world of a writer by staying in their home, for which, as Genevieve Fox reported in a Guardian travel article in 2021, the range of options is surprisingly large.
Dr David Rudrum
Secretary, The Elmet Trust
Along with Rydal Mount and Dove Cottage, William Wordsworth also lived in two other Cumbrian houses which are open to the public. His childhood home, Wordsworth House in Cockermouth, owned by the National Trust, is currently only open for organised tours. The National Trust blames financial losses and low visitor numbers since the pandemic. Allan Bank in Grasmere, where Wordsworth lived briefly, is also owned by the National Trust, and open five days a week.
But Rydal Mount was considered by Wordsworth to be his favourite home, and it’s where he lived for most of his life, until his death in 1850. I spent several years working for the Wordsworth family and curators, and the house has a fascinating history as well as a glorious location and exciting future. Wordsworth himself was only a tenant; the house was eventually bought by the family – his great-great-granddaughter Mary Henderson acquired it in 1969.
Since then it’s seen the development of the five-acre gardens to plans drawn up by the poet. It has staged drama, music and poetry, co-hosted a film festival with the local cinema, and hosted weddings – including that of the poet’s great-great-great-great grandson Christopher Andrew. There was even, in the 1970s, a performance by the dance troupe Pan’s People when Miss UK contestants were filmed there.
It will be exciting to see how the Wordsworth Trust, which acquired Rydal Mount in March, takes the life of the house forward. The challenge is to re-engage visitors with the life and work of the greatest of the Romantic poets, and poetry generally. The Wordsworth family initiated a successful poetry competition for Cumbrian school pupils and planned to roll this out nationwide. Perhaps that will bring a new generation to appreciate more than just Daffodils.
Eileen Jones
Author of Rydal Mount: The Story of Wordsworth’s Home

Why the threat from the rampaging AI machine went ignored | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:44:28 UTC
01:44:28 KST

Jill Lepore asks why nobody listened to warnings about the threats posed from the AI revolution (Democracy v the machine, 18 August). As she is a Harvard professor, her piece is understandably US-centric. But in 1972 there was an international gathering of AI researchers and others in Italy to tackle the ethical and social implications of AI.
This “Serbelloni group” of global experts (they met at Villa Serbelloni on Lake Como) was led by my father, Donald Michie, the director of the University of Edinburgh’s department of machine intelligence. The group mapped out early concerns regarding potential political tyranny, the erosion of human autonomy and widespread social coercion driven by automation.
Why did nobody listen? In part because the next year the UK cut research funding for machine learning, robotics and AI, following the Lighthill report, which had been established – it has since been documented – for this purpose. Researchers had instead to focus on more immediately industrial-relevant work. My father’s attempts to reconvene the Serbelloni group to include experts from the humanities thus proved unsuccessful.
Jonathan Michie
Professor of innovation & knowledge exchange, University of Oxford
Jill Lepore rightly traces those welcoming the rampaging AI machine in a free market while modern humanists fear the unchecked machine. She mentions the underestimated American intellectual Lewis Mumford, who devoted most of his life to restraining the uninhibited city as a form of machine damaging people by the million. He hooked up with the British humanist Frederic J Osborn in a letter exchange that lasted over three decades, developing a sane town-planning system.
Mumford was wise enough to see that the automatic machine had the capacity to make man passive and purposeless in the same manner as did living in the city, and humans must resist induced passivity of all kinds. So the myth still prevails. Beware – AI is really not that smart, and a few well-chosen puzzles for it to solve expose its crippling obsession with data, not with the humans’ forte, knowledge.
Callum Brown
Professor emeritus in history, University of Glasgow

Reading Katriona O’Sullivan’s article (Can anyone be too poor to buy a toothbrush? Yes – I know, because that was me, 19 August) reminded me of when I was a community worker at the Park Hill estate in Sheffield in the 1970s.
When I (young and naive) asked the mums why they bought chips for their toddlers for lunch rather than spending the money on fresh fruit (I cringe now in embarrassment), they pointed out that a bag of chips was the price of a couple of apples and one of them filled the kids up. I began to understand, and to also see why they spent money on cigarettes. As O’Sullivan says, “a few bottles [of alcohol] can feel like an escape”.
My work there gave me a lifetime of experience in a few months, which I’ve never forgotten. 
Carol Taylor
Matlock, Derbyshire
What an excellent piece by Katriona O’Sullivan – a very timely riposte to those who pass judgment from the comfort of their broadcasting pods. George Orwell made similar points in The Road to Wigan Pier – desperately poor people still tried (occasionally) to go to the cinema or buy ice-cream rather than spend their subsistence national assistance on tripe.
It was – and is – a matter of human dignity and feeling that you are still living as a person, not as an automaton, as more fortunate people might expect you to be. Perhaps cheap toothbrushes should be free to our poorest citizens as a sensible public-health intervention.
Howard Williamson
Treforest, Rhondda Cynon Taf

Unknown

In light of the astonishing results achieved in lowering air pollution by the introduction of the ultra-low emission zone (Ulez) in London by Sadiq Khan (Ulez led to better lung size and function among London children, study finds, 18 August), should we now not extend this philosophy into every city in the UK to save lives?
Surely it is a human right to breathe clean air? Why does Ofsted or the Department for Education not insist on air-quality monitors and give data for each school so parents are aware of the risks?

Hijri's statement comes amid conflicting reports about the Syrian government's efforts to resolve the crisis that broke out after the fall of Bashar al-Assad, which included bloody clashes between forces allied to the new government and a pro-Hijri militia, as well as Israeli airstrikes on the presidential palace in Damascus.
"We are an integral part of the State of Israel... we even share the same ideology with it," Hijri said at a gathering in Syria's Suweida.

The Druze leader's latest remarks came days after talks in Jordan between Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and Israeli Mossad chief Roman Gofman, mediated by the United States. The talks touched on Israel's attacks on Syria, and attempts to reach a security agreement between the two sides.
Hijri has previously described Israel as the "protector" of Syria's Druze, and has advocated for Tel Aviv overseeing a transitional process for Druze self-rule.
Israel, which has framed some of its attacks on Syria as being in defence of the religious minority, has expanded its occupation of Syrian land and carried out numerous airstrikes and raids into the country since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.

Canada retaliates against US tariffs as trade tensions escalate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:41:59 UTC
01:41:59 KST

ALBAWABA- Canada is imposing retaliatory tariffs of up to 50% on roughly $20 billion worth of U.S. imports after trade talks between Ottawa and Washington collapsed, escalating an increasingly bitter dispute between the two countries.
The measures, covering about 700 products, including certain steel and aluminum goods, furniture, clothing, electronics, appliances and other consumer products, are scheduled to take effect on September 8, according to a senior Canadian government official cited by ABC News.
The move follows President Donald Trump’s decision to raise tariffs on some Canadian goods to as high as 50%, prompting Ottawa to respond dollar-for-dollar. The latest escalation comes after negotiations between the two governments failed to produce an agreement, with both sides increasingly adopting tougher positions.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has sought to project a firm but measured response, saying Ottawa will not accept an agreement simply for the sake of reaching a deal. “Our goal has always been to get the best deal for Canadians, never a deal at any price or on any time frame,” Carney said, emphasizing the protection of Canadian workers and strengthening Canada’s domestic economy.
The trade dispute has unfolded alongside increasingly provocative rhetoric from Washington. Trump has repeatedly referred to Canada as a potential “51st state,” comments Ottawa has rejected as an affront to Canadian sovereignty. The U.S. president has also threatened further economic measures against Canada as relations deteriorate.
The latest controversy came when Trump suggested that the United States was seriously considering renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America.” The proposal was immediately rejected in Canada, where officials stressed that the lake’s name was not up for negotiation.
Canadian Industry Minister Mélanie Joly responded defiantly, saying Canada would continue to call it Lake Ontario. She emphasized the lake’s importance to Canadian history and identity and said Ottawa would remain “smart” and “strategic” while defending the country’s interests.
The tensions have also extended to questions of Canadian national identity. Trump recently indicated that he had no intention of interfering with the French language in Canada, following Prime Minister Mark Carney’s criticism of any U.S. interference in Canadian domestic affairs, including suggestions that the status of French could become part of trade negotiations.
U.S. Vice President JD Vance has meanwhile criticized Canada and China over their retaliatory tariffs, describing them as among the countries taking the strongest measures against U.S. trade policy.
Provincially, Ontario Premier Doug Ford has urged Ottawa to respond forcefully, including by targeting politically influential “deep red states” with retaliatory measures. Ford has backed Carney’s call for a dollar-for-dollar response to Trump’s tariffs.
With negotiations stalled and tariffs escalating, the dispute is becoming more than a conventional trade confrontation. It is increasingly testing the political relationship between the two neighbors and Canada’s ability to defend its economic interests and sovereignty while managing its dependence on the United States, its largest trading partner.

Chinese border control rules likely to affect Taiwanese
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:41:18 UTC
01:41:18 KST

Beijing’s new cybersecurity and border control rules launching in October pose a significant risk to Taiwanese, Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) Deputy Minister Shen Yu-chung (沈有忠) said yesterday.
He made the comment in a conference on Chinese cyberspace surveillance hosted by the Association for Asian Political Economy and Peace at National Taiwan University in Taipei.
The Chinese government followed the implementation of its Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law with new rules governing Internet services, border control and cybersecurity.
Photo: Wang Yi-sung, Taipei Times
The most likely explanation for Beijing’s series of regulatory changes is a desire to strengthen the Chinese Communist Party’s grip on civil society ahead of next year’s 21st National Congress, Shen said.
They give regulators a broad remit in interpreting and enforcing the law, increasing the arbitrariness of China’s legal system, Shen said.
The cybersecurity regulations, which explicitly define broad applicability and give low-ranking public security officers a mandate to enforce their rules, heightened the legal threat to Taiwanese in China, he said.
Low-ranking Chinese officials are incentivized to apply the harshest interpretation of laws and regulations to avoid deviation from the party line, Shen said.
These laws and regulations include legal mechanisms that authorize the Chinese government to claim extraterritorial authority on foreign soil, raising fears of transnational repression worldwide, he said.
Taiwan’s response to these laws and regulations is to denounce Beijing’s long-arm enforcement and transnational repression as illegal and illegitimate, Shen said.
The government intends to severely punish any collaborators who aid China’s attempt to export its political repression in Taiwan, and countermeasures would be continuously reviewed and improved, he said.
The government is considering a law to make facilitating transnational repression a criminal offense, Shen said.
A poll by the council showed that 76.4 percent of Taiwanese would approve such legislation, he added.
The MAC is working with other ministries and agencies to organize defenses against Chinese efforts to target Taiwanese and Taiwan’s foreign residents, he said.
The government is providing people at risk of Chinese retaliation with defensive measures and other forms of assistance, Shen said.
Taiwan is deepening its cooperation with an international coalition of democracies to share intelligence, conduct joint security countermeasures, monitor legal or regulatory changes in Beijing and educate the public on transnational repression, he said.
The government’s longtime stance on cross-strait relations is that exchanges must take place under conditions of peace, mutual respect and maintenance of the “status quo,” he said.
There is no chance of healthy dialogue across the Taiwan Strait without derisking and depoliticizing such exchanges, Shen said.
The public is urged to carefully assess their level of risk before visiting China and use the MAC registry for people traveling in China, Hong Kong and Macau if they are detained incommunicado by Chinese authorities, he said.

====================================================================================================

The clock is ticking for Burnham’s plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:41:15 UTC
01:41:15 KST

Andy Burnham, the UK’s personable new prime minister, has been buoyed by his bounce in the opinion polls. However, the day of economic reckoning is fast approaching, with the budget just two months away.
Burnham displayed no Macbeth-like “infirmity of purpose” in seizing the crown from Keir Starmer in his ruthless coup, but he has wobbled on the economy. At the outset, he was forced to reassure the bond markets that he would stick to his predecessor’s fiscal rules — strictures he once dismissed as financial fetishism. With long-term borrowing costs hitting new highs over ballooning government deficits across the G7, it is just as well Burnham expressed contrition when he did.
Three wise men played their part in smoothing ruffled market feathers when it became known they were shaping Burnham’s financial thinking. Jim O’Neill is respected as the former chief economist at Goldman Sachs Group Inc and as an adviser to the last durable Tory chancellor, George Osborne. As deputy governor of the Bank of England, British Chambers of Commerce president Andy Haldane, was a lone voice in predicting an inflationary surge in 2022. Richard Hughes, as ex-chair of the Office for Budget Responsibility, promised to bring fiscal credibility.
O’Neill and Haldane share Burnham’s passion for reviving the fortunes of the rustbelt in their native North of England; O’Neill’s ideas motivated Osborne’s Northern Powerhouse initiative, while Haldane has long advocated boosting transport links and infrastructure spending to bridge Britain’s regional divides. So, natural allies, but also hardheaded realists.
However, none of the trio is taking an official position. O’Neill told the Financial Times on Friday that he has “decided to not take a formal role,” citing the constraints of having to put his financial assets into a blind trust.
“It’s not because of any policy disagreements,” he said, adding that he hopes to maintain an informal relationship with Burnham and his team.
Haldane not joining the government does seem to be policy based. In a blistering Financial Times article published last week, he condemned its former budgets as ”outright harmful” to the private sector. Haldane called for the government to announce “a moratorium on tax increases and regulatory burden on consumers and businesses for the remainder of this parliament. This would be the equivalent of a fiscal Hippocratic Oath to ‘do no harm’ to private-sector sentiment.”
Hughes, the third member of this trio, is ideally equipped to score the new government’s spending plans. In January he testified to the House of Lords that the Labour Party’s 2024 election manifesto looked “nothing like” its actual tax-and-spend trajectory once in government; but he too has failed to find a desk at No. 10.
Burnham commands the political stage after only one month in office, and has a limited time window to refine his pitch on prosperity. He is the first prime minister since Boris Johnson to cheer up uncommitted voters, his can-do optimism infinitely preferable to doomy Starmer. His “hopey-changey” message receives plaudits for echoing former US presidents Bill Clinton and Barack Obama at their most winning; Burnham’s mastery of social media has already made him better known than the pop star whose song has been at No. 1 for 20 weeks — he has 57 percent name recognition, Olivia Dean has only 55 percent.
Burnham beats the populist parties of the left and right at their own game. By saying he would get rough sleepers indoors by Christmas, to help cut the bills of pubs, clubs and musical venues at the expense of garish vape shops on the high street and in valuing “the hard hat as much as the graduation cap” in education, he reaches the parts other politicians do not and resonates with ordinary voters in ways neither Starmer nor his Tory predecessor Rishi Sunak could.
The Oct. 28 budget should force some sharper choices than the present loosey-goosey Burnham comments on how to put Britain back on the path to sustained growth. On Friday, the UK announced a surprise budget deficit of ￡1.8 billion (US$2.45 billion) — a dismal figure, because there is usually an income boost from scheduled payments of self-assessed income tax. The PM has stopped talking about alleviating cost of living pressures — over which he has little control, given the many international factors at play — and speaks empathetically instead about giving household budgets “breathing space” where he can, and talks about a major 10-year overhaul of utilities and energy dependency.
It does not demand an excess of cynicism to realize this change of emphasis kicks the can down the road and is intended to deflate expectations of how different life would feel for many in the short term. Having campaigned in earnestly stirring poetry, the Burnham government is getting ready to govern in prose.
Martin Ivens is the editor of the Times Literary Supplement. Previously, he was editor of the Sunday Times of London and its chief political commentator. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.
