Free flu, COVID-19 vaccination to start on Oct. 1
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:41:15 UTC
01:41:15 KST

The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) yesterday announced that government-funded seasonal influenza (flu) and COVID-19 vaccinations are to begin on Oct. 1.
While the number of flu and COVID-19 cases dropped slightly last week, prevention is important, especially as school starts next week, it added.
People aged 18 years or older who receive a dose of flu, COVID-19 or pneumococcal vaccine, whether government funded or paid out of pocket, would receive a “health coin,” CDC Director-General Philip Lo (羅一鈞) said.
Photo: Hou Chia-yu, Taipei Times
The health coin program is to be launched in October, and details of the program, including the amount of coins offered for each vaccine, would be announced tomorrow, Lo said.
The CDC has procured a record 7,050,150 doses of flu vaccines, and 2.4 million doses of COVID-19 vaccines, he said.
The vaccines include 200,790 doses of an enhanced influenza vaccine, which offer 20 to 30 percent better protection, for the first time, and they will be prioritized for elderly residents of long-term care facilities, he said.
Trivalent flu vaccines targeting an A(H1N1) strain, an A(H3N2) strain and a B strain have been selected for the upcoming flu season, Lo said, adding that they cover the dominant virus strain that is spreading locally and should provide good protection.
The COVID-19 vaccines include 2.2 million doses by Moderna — 1.9 million next-generation single-dose vaccines targeting the XFG variant and 300,000 doses of the current multidose vial vaccine targeting the JN.1 variant — and 200,000 doses by Novavax targeting the XFG variant, he said.
The next-generation single-dose COVID-19 vaccine has a less active mRNA ingredient per dose and offers robust immunity, but is only eligible for people aged 12 or older, while the multidose vial vaccine would be offered to children under 12, he added.
Eligibility for the first phase of flu and COVID-19 vaccination are the high-risk groups listed in previous years, Lo said.
However, the list has been expanded to include new categories: public health specialists, actual caregivers of infants under six months old, and non-temporary kitchen and administrative workers at childcare centers, he said.
For the COVID-19 vaccine, the category of “young children aged six months to before entering elementary” has been revised to “children under six who have never received a COVID-19 vaccine,” he said.
The second phase is to begin on Nov. 2, with people aged 50 to 64 years old eligible for both vaccines, Lo said.
Medical visits for flu last week totaled 94,340, 2.5 percent lower than the previous week, CDC Epidemic Intelligence Center Director Guo Hung-wei (郭宏偉) said, adding that 64 severe cases and 15 deaths were confirmed.
For COVID-19, 24,995 cases were reported last week, about 6 percent fewer than the week before, but 59 severe cases and 19 deaths were confirmed, he said.
As some schools are opening next week, and flu and COVID-19 activity remains high, people should still take preventive measures, Lo said.
The COVID-19 epidemic period is expected to continue into next month, while flu and enterovirus cases might increase after school starts, and the risk of dengue fever is increasing due to heavy rainfall, CDC Deputy Director-General Lin Min-cheng (林明誠) said.
There are still about 109,000 doses of free COVID-19 vaccines available for people aged six or older before Sept. 9, he said.
Aside from vaccination, washing hands thoroughly with soap, wearing a mask in crowded or poorly ventilated venues, resting at home when sick, and eliminating mosquito breeding grounds are encouraged to reduce risks of spreading diseases, Lin said.

The fire broke out at about 8:48pm on Monday at the well-known temple’s Lingxiao Hall in Taipei’s Wenshan District (文山) and was extinguished at 12:09am yesterday after burning for more than three hours.
The cause of the fire remains under investigation.
The Taipei Fire Department said the blaze damaged about 1,500m2 of the structure, destroying the first floor and damaging about one-third of the second floor.
Officials said the hall’s wooden structure and combustible materials, such as incense and joss paper, contributed to the rapid spread of flames.
The temple’s mountainous location, narrow roads and limited water supply also created difficulties, they said.
The fire was brought under control at 10:07pm on Monday, followed by several hours of mopping-up operations and cooling work.
The Taipei Department of Civil Affairs would lead a one-stop coordination mechanism involving the fire, cultural affairs, urban development and building management authorities, Chiang said.
After the fire investigation, experts would determine which parts of the damaged hall should be preserved and which can be removed, the mayor said.
Zhinan Temple Management Committee chairman Kao Chao-wen (高超文) said the Sanqing Hall (三清殿) and Tai Sui Hall (太歲寶殿) sections were the worst-affected areas, statues including the Three Pure Ones (Sanqing Daozu, 三清道祖) and the Queen Mother of the West (Yaochi Jinmu, 瑤池金母) were damaged.
Statues of the 60 Tai Sui deities on the rear of the first floor and the Jade Emperor on the second floor remained intact, Kao said.
He said temple officials were to discuss restoration plans later yesterday.
While Lingxiao Hall has been closed off, the rest of the temple remains open, he added.
The temple is one of Taipei’s most well-known religious sites, with a history dating to about 1890.
It primarily worships Lu Dongbin (呂洞賓), also known as Fuyou Dijun (孚佑帝君), one of the Eight Immortals in Taoism.
The damaged Lingxiao Hall was constructed from 1963 to 1966, and was among Taiwan’s early large-scale modern Taoist structures, featuring six stories and a reinforced concrete design.

Vondrousova appeals doping ruling at CAS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:41:07 UTC
01:41:07 KST

Former Wimbledon champion Marketa Vondrousova has appealed against her four-year doping suspension to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), the international body said on Monday.
“CAS can confirm an appeal,” a spokeswoman told reporters when asked about the Czech 2023 Wimbledon champion, who was sanctioned by the International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) for refusing to take an out-of-competition doping test in December last year.
A hearing date has not yet been set, but proceedings typically take place in the months following the appeal.
Photo: Reuters
It would be held behind closed doors unless Vondrousova requests a public hearing, with the final ruling issued several months later.
The ITIA said that Vondrousova had failed to open the door to an anti-doping officer.
Her suspension is due to run until June 21, 2030, and she has not played on the WTA Tour since January.
Vondrousova initially responded to the ban by saying she had “never doped.”
The 27-year-old in April said that she was scared when the officer rang the bell “without properly identifying themselves or following protocol.”
Players are required to log their whereabouts for an allotted hour each day so that authorities can conduct anti-doping tests outside of competition.
She has said that her fear was partly due to the knife attack on her compatriot and fellow former Wimbledon winner Petra Kvitova at her home in 2016.
“In that moment, fear clouded my judgement and I just couldn’t process the situation rationally,” Vondrousova said. “After what happened to Petra, we don’t take strangers at our door lightly.”
Last month, an independent tribunal ruled she had provided “no compelling justification” for refusing a test, adding that she had taken her dog for a walk 10 minutes later.
“This is a very unfortunate manner in which the player made a decision in the heat of the moment to refuse doping control, in a state of stress and anxiety, with significant consequences,” the tribunal said.
American world No. 3 Jessica Pegula called the suspension “harsh,” comparing it with the far lighter punishments handed out to Jannik Sinner and Iga Swiatek.
“I just don’t think that’s fair. I think the sentencing is so harsh,” Pegula said at Wimbledon in June.
Sinner accepted a three-month ban last year after reaching an agreement with the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) in 2024.
The Italian men’s world No.1 had tested positive for the anabolic steroid clostebol, before being cleared by an independent tribunal, which determined that he was not to blame.
Six-time Grand Slam champion Swiatek took a one-month ban in 2024 after testing positive for a banned substance.
“So I don’t quite understand the difference between that and then obviously what happened with Sinner and Iga. They justified what the rules were and why it was the way it was,” Pegula said.

EVA Air, partners sign sustainable fuel deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:41:06 UTC
01:41:06 KST

EVA Airways and AIT Worldwide Logistics yesterday signed an agreement to promote the airline’s Green Transportation Program, which is expected to help Microsoft reduce its carbon emissions by 15,000 tonnes in the first year.
The four-way partnership — comprising EVA Air, AIT Worldwide Logistics, Formosa Petrochemical Corp (FPC) and Microsoft — aims to accelerate the adoption of sustainable aviation fuel and decrease carbon emissions across the supply chains in the aviation, technology, transportation and energy sectors.
EVA Air president Clay Sun (孫嘉明) said at a ceremony in Taipei that the airline is committed to increasing the use of sustainable fuel, produced by FPC from used cooking oil, as part of its goal of achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050.
Photo: Huang Yi-ching, Taipei Times
“The civil aviation industry’s transition to the zero-carbon model requires collective efforts of airlines, aviation fuel suppliers as well as logistics service providers and their corporate customers,” Sun said.
The partnership can enable Microsoft, an important corporate customer of AIT Worldwide, to reduce its carbon footprint generated by cloud equipment transportation by approximately 15,000 tonnes of Scope 3 emissions.
No company can solve aviation’s decarbonization challenge alone, AIT Worldwide chief strategy officer Greg Weigel said, adding that sustainable fuel adoption requires both supply and demand.
Aside from airlines, corporate customers such as Microsoft can help create demand, he said.
“The more important thing is that it [the partnership] sets a foundation for the future,” Weigel said, adding that AIT Worldwide hopes that the initiative would encourage more airlines, fuel suppliers, freight forwarders and corporate customers across Asia-Pacific to participate.
FPC president Lin Ke-yen (林克彥) said that sustainable aviation fuel serves as an important means for the aviation industry to reduce carbon emissions.
However, the supply is limited, and the cost is relatively high, he said.
The partnership helps transform the need for corporations to reduce carbon emissions to a market demand for sustainable fuel, Lin said.
Increased use of sustainable fuel would help expand FPC’s production and lower operational costs, he added.
Vincent Shih (施立成), general manager of corporate, external and legal affairs at Microsoft Taiwan, said that Microsoft has set the goal of achieving carbon negative, water positive and zero waste by 2030.
The partnership helps the technology giant resolve the problems with Scope 3 emissions, which refers to carbon emitted at the logistics’ end, Shih said.
Civil Aviation Administration Director-General Ho Shu-ping (何淑萍) said that Taiwan last year launched the sustainable fuel demonstration project in the civil aviation industry.
Taiwan is capable of producing 6,500 tonnes of sustainable aviation fuel in a year, Ho said.
Microsoft’s goal for zero carbon emissions can serve as an important force to propel the further development of the market for sustainable aviation fuel, she added.
American Institute in Taiwan commercial deputy chief Eric Crowley said that Taiwan is the US’ fourth-largest trading partner, and the US has become Taiwan’s largest export market.
During the first five months of this year, Taiwan was the 18th-largest source of international visitors to the US, up 15 percent year on year, Crowley said.
About 170 passenger flights are dispatched between Taiwan and the US each week, while air-cargo demand between the two countries continues to grow rapidly, he added.
“This agreement represents a critical step forward in decarbonizing modern supply chains. The cross-industry partnership shows that economic growth and environmental protection can coexist, and serves as an example of how the US and Taiwan can promote green and sustainable trade together,” Crowley said.
The airline said that sustainable aviation fuel accounts for only 0.5 percent of its total aviation fuel consumption due to limited supply, and about two-thirds of sustainable fuel it uses is procured from other countries.
Sustainable aviation fuel costs about three to five times higher than regular aviation fuel, it added.

Families of detained Chinese Christians cling to faith in legal limbo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:41:05 UTC
01:41:05 KST

Clasping her hands together in prayer, four-year-old Huanle tells God she misses her mum, whom she hasn’t seen since Chinese authorities raided their home last year in a crackdown on their unregistered church.
Huanle’s mother Wang Cong is a pastor at Zion Church, one of China’s largest “underground” churches where some Christians choose to worship instead of government-regulated ones.
Chinese authorities detained more than 20 of Zion’s members last October, including 43-year-old Wang — one of a series of similar recent clampdowns across the country.
Photo: AFP
“My child saw everything, she cried,” said Ren Zhong, Huanle’s father, as he described how seven unidentified officers had entered their home in Beijing that night before he was held down. “She was in her mother’s arms, and they ripped her away.”
Wang was taken along with many of her books, and her family have not spoken to her directly since.
China’s constitution guarantees citizens religious freedom. However, the ruling Communist Party, which requires its members to be atheist, has historically regarded organized religion with suspicion. It recognizes Protestantism and Catholicism as official religions, but practicing organizations must register with the government — something many Christians feel yields an unacceptable amount of control over church affairs and teachings.
Scrutiny of the country’s many unofficial groups has tightened since President Xi Jinping (習近平) came to power, though enforcement can vary. Zion was forced to close in 2018, but flourished online during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Authorities detained its founding pastor Ezra Jin during the October crackdown but he was released in July, weeks after US President Donald Trump raised his case with Xi.
Wang and seven others are set to be tried in the southern Chinese coastal city of Beihai — where Jin lived — for fraud and illegally operating a business, criminal charges their families dispute.
“After I heard the news (of Jin’s release), I was shocked and afraid to believe it,” said 36-year-old Ren, also a preacher.
“But after joy came worry, worry for my wife, because she was still inside, suffering.”
Asked about the detentions, China’s foreign ministry said Beijing “manages religious affairs in accordance with the law.”
The Beihai public security bureau and local detention facilities said they said they would not accept interviews.
HARD TO JUSTIFY’
A single suitcase lay open on the floor at Ren’s temporary residence in Beihai.
Ren had initially hoped Jin’s release might mean his wife’s would soon follow.
Instead, legal proceedings quickened. Authorities indicted Wang and the others two weeks after Jin was reunited with his family in the US.
A trial was set for the middle of this month, but later postponed.
Relatives of the detainees argue they should no longer be held now that Jin is free.
“It shouldn’t be that the head pastor is fine, but people below him... are in trouble,” said Gao Guangjun, the father of detained pastor Gao Yingjia.
“It’s a little hard to justify,” the elder Gao, 76, said.
According to legal documents described by Ren, the basis for Wang’s detention is that her collection of church offerings was fraudulent because Zion is not registered.
Authorities say she gathered around 660,000 yuan (US$98,000) between 2019 and last year.
Ren insisted that financial giving — used partly to pay pastors — is part of Biblical teaching practiced by Christian churches.
“If it’s because of this that my wife has been charged with fraud, then I think this is actually not an accusation against my wife,” he said.
“It is a denial of the Christian faith as a whole.”
COSTLY CONVICTION
Jin has been recuperating in the US and spending time with his family, who relocated there as Zion came under pressure from authorities in 2018.
He said he feels “deep pain” knowing that colleagues were left behind.
“I am deeply conflicted, truly torn. I am free, yet in reality, I am not,” the pastor said.
The 57-year-old was visibly emotional as he described urging the eight detainees to have courage, in a text he had drafted for their lawyers the previous day.
“I hope that one day (their) children will understand that their parents’ separation from them — and their current detention — is a source of honor,” he said. “For the sake of a higher conviction, they are paying a price.”
At Ren’s Beihai flat, Huanle danced around to imaginary music, seemingly carefree.
But Ren said there are nights when his daughter refuses to sleep and tells him she’s scared.
‘NOT FORGOTTEN’
Having stopped full-time work in May, Ren spends his days caring for Huanle and advocating for his wife — posting case updates to an X account with a few hundred followers.
He said worry for his wife has faded, even though people convicted of fraud can face 10 years in jail.
“I believe God is just,” he said. “I know God has not forgotten about these eight people.”
Gao, also a Christian, hopes authorities will release his son, but acknowledged the outcome is beyond the families’ control.
“It’s for leaders to decide,” he said. “It’s not something ordinary citizens can influence.”

Father-son spy duo resentenced
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:41:04 UTC
01:41:04 KST

In a retrial by the High Court, former major Lee Hai-peng (李海鵬) and his son Sergeant Lee Chu-hsiang (李楚庠) yesterday were sentenced to 11 years and six months and 16 years in prison respectively for passing confidential information to China
The two were sentenced under the Anti-Corruption Act (貪污治罪條例) and the Criminal Code of the Armed Forces (陸海空軍刑法). The ruling may be appealed.
According to the ruling, Lee Hai-peng started working in tourism decades ago after retiring from the military and was recruited by Chinese intelligence officers during one of his trips to China.
Photo: Taipei Times
He enlisted the aid of his two sons, Captain Lee Yu-sheng (李輿聖) and Lee Chu-hsiang, as well as former acquaintance Lee Wen-sheng (李文生) to obtain military secrets for about six years before discovery, the court said.
The Investigation Bureau verified that the intelligence the defendants gave to China was genuine with the Ministry of National Defense, the court said.
In the first High Court trial, Lee Wen-sheng was given three years and two months, while Lee Yu-sheng and Lee Chu-hsiang received two years and two months and two years and four months respectively.
During a retrial, Lee Wen-sheng’s sentence was increased from three years and two months to 15 years, while Lee Yu-sheng was sentenced to two years and one month, a month shorter than the initial sentence.
Lee Chu-hsiang was sentenced to 10 years and six months, a large increase from the initial sentence of two years and four months.
The first retrial ruling stated that the defendants’ crimes were severe, and that they became Chinese spies despite the nation’s support and training, the court said.
The 15-year sentence for Lee Wen-sheng and two year, one month sentence for Lee Yu-sheng were finalized by the Supreme Court in December last year after their appeals were rejected.

Taiwan is in talks with Saint Vincent and the Grenadines about funding a national development bank and several social projects in the Caribbean nation, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said yesterday.

Kiribati detains Chinese ship over banned shark fin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:41:02 UTC
01:41:02 KST

Kiribati, a tiny Pacific neighbor to Hawaii that has grown ties with Beijing, detained a Chinese vessel this month for illegally harvesting shark fins, its maritime police said.
The practice of cutting fins off live sharks and throwing the carcasses back into the sea is banned in much of the Pacific Ocean, but persists due to demand in East and Southeast Asia.
The Chinese ship was among four vessels detained in a surveillance crackdown by 11 Pacific island nations from Aug. 3 to 14, assisted by the US Coast Guard in some areas and an Australian military aircraft. Kiribati, however, operates its own patrol boat.
Photo: Reuters
The vessel was licensed to ply Kiribati’s waters, but was detained by the maritime police after inspectors found shark fins on board, commander Tom Redfern said.
“It was escorted back to Christmas Island for further investigation,” he said, referring to a large atoll belonging to Kiribati and located south of Hawaii.
Kiribati has an exclusive economic zone spanning 3.5 million square kilometers of ocean, and has drawn interest from Chinese state companies since switching diplomatic ties from Taiwan in 2019.
It also hosts Chinese police, a decision the US has said risks fueling regional tensions.
“A Kiribati Police maritime boarding officer, not under a shiprider agreement, boarded and inspected it, finding that the vessel was breaching its condition of licence by keeping and retaining shark fins onboard,” Redfern said.
Kiribati has recently strengthened cooperation with France, with French military personnel due to arrive next month on Christmas Island to rebuild local police stations.
The practice of removing shark fins is banned across the region.
Andrew Chin, a fisheries researcher at Australia’s James Cook University, said finning had led to “massive declines” in shark numbers, prompting stringent controls in the Pacific.
“Because it is now illegal, if people are doing it, it is going to be hidden and really hard to detect,” he said.
Research on the DNA of thousands of shark fins sold in Hong Kong markets pointed to its origins in the region.
“We have seen evidence of illegal trade from the western and eastern sides of the Pacific,” said Demian Chapman, who conducted the research as director of the Sharks and Rays Conservation Research Program at Mote Marine Laboratory in Florida.
There have been other cases of Chinese vessels breaking the finning ban, he said.
Reduced demand in China for shark fin soup, including a ban on serving it at government functions, had contributed to a fall in the amount of fins being traded in Hong Kong, he added.

ENGLISH DIGEST 實用美語(空中美語)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:41:02 UTC
01:41:02 KST

When summer temperatures soar, humans reach for fans and air conditioning. But wild animals lack these luxuries, so they have evolved remarkable strategies to prevent overheating. From desert foxes to African giraffes, nature has engineered some surprisingly clever cooling systems.
One of the most iconic examples involves unusually large ears. Fennec foxes and jackrabbits, both inhabitants of hot desert environments, possess ears that function as natural cooling devices. Blood vessels close to the surface of the ears release heat into the air, helping lower these animals’ body temperature. When the weather becomes extremely hot, more blood flows through their ears, allowing heat to escape efficiently. This process works much like a radiator in an engine.
Some animals rely on their outer covering rather than their body shape to stay cool. Saharan silver ants, for example, are coated in tiny hairs that reflect sunlight away from their bodies. These hairs also help release built-up heat rapidly, allowing the ants to survive in temperatures that would be fatal to most other creatures. Without this protective coat, they would overheat within seconds of stepping onto the burning sand.
Photo: Freepik / 照片：Freepik
Perhaps the most visually striking mechanism belongs to the giraffe. Scientists believe that the giraffe’s distinctive spots help regulate temperature. Beneath each dark patch lies a network of blood vessels. Warm blood flows into these areas, where heat can dissipate through the skin. In this way, the pattern on a giraffe’s body may serve as a natural cooling system.
Not all cooling solutions rely on radiation, though. The Cape ground squirrel of southern Africa takes a more hands-on approach: it flips its bushy tail over its head like a portable shade. By raising its tail over its body like an umbrella, the squirrel reduces direct exposure to sunlight and keeps its body cooler while searching for food.
These creative solutions show that animals have developed diverse ways to cope with heat. By studying such natural designs, scientists may even discover new ideas for cooling technologies for everyday human use.
當夏季氣溫飆升時，人類會使用電風扇和空調。然而，野生動物沒有這些奢侈品，因此牠們演化出各種非凡的策略來避免過熱。從沙漠狐狸到非洲長頸鹿，大自然設計出一些出乎意料的巧妙降溫系統。
其中一個最具代表性的例子與異常巨大的耳朵有關。同為沙漠環境居民的耳廓狐和傑克兔都有能作為天然散熱裝置的耳朵。靠近耳朵表面的血管能將熱量釋放到空氣中，幫助降低這些動物的體溫。當天氣變得極端炎熱時，流經耳朵的血液會增加，使熱量能更有效地散逸。這個過程的運作原理就如同引擎中的散熱器。
有些動物則依靠外層覆蓋物而非體型來保持涼爽。例如，撒哈拉銀蟻的身體覆蓋著細小的毛，能將陽光從身上反射出去。這些細毛也有助於迅速釋放積聚的熱量，使牠們能在對其他大多數生物而言致命的高溫中存活。如果沒有這層保護外衣，牠們一踏上灼熱的沙地，幾秒內就會過熱。
或許最引人注目的降溫機制屬於長頸鹿。科學家認為，長頸鹿身上獨特的斑紋有助於調節體溫。每一塊深色斑紋下方都有一個血管網絡。溫熱的血液流入這些區域後，熱量可透過皮膚散發出去。如此一來，長頸鹿身上的斑紋可能可以充當一種天然的降溫系統。
不過，並非所有降溫方式都依賴散熱。生活在非洲南部的南非地松鼠採取更手動的方法：牠會把蓬鬆的尾巴翻到頭上，像一把可攜式的遮陽傘。透過將尾巴像傘一樣舉在身體上方，牠在覓食時能減少陽光直射並讓身體保持涼爽。
這些充滿創意的解決方案顯示，動物已發展出多樣的策略來應付高溫。藉由研究這些自然的設計，科學家甚至可能發現新的靈感來應用在人類日常使用的降溫技術上。
KEY VOCABULARY
1. luxury n. 奢侈（品）
Jeff only has an average salary, so he can’t afford luxuries such as a sports car.
傑夫的薪資不過一般，所以他買不起跑車之類的奢侈品。
2. remarkable adj. 非凡的；引人注目的
The latest space mission to Mars is considered a remarkable achievement.
前往火星的最新一起太空任務被視為非凡成就。
3. involve v. 包含；涉及
International diplomacy involves conducting negotiations between nations.
國際外交包含進行國家間的協商。
4. fatal adj. 致命的
The factory worker sustained a fatal injury while using dangerous machinery.
那名工廠工人在使用危險機械時受到致命傷。
5. regulate v. 調節；規範
Air conditioners can regulate humidity as well as temperature during hot summer days.
空調在炎熱夏天不僅可以調節溫度，也能調節濕度。
6. patch n. 一小塊；斑塊
The dog had a white patch on its fur, making it look very cute.
那隻狗的毛上有一塊白色斑點，看起來非常可愛。
7. radiation n. 散熱；輻射（能）
Proper ventilation helps improve radiation in rooms during hot summer days.
適當的通風能改善房間在炎熱夏天的散熱效果。
8. flip v. 翻轉；擲
Jay can flip a pancake perfectly without spilling any batter on the stove.
杰可以完美地翻煎餅，爐子上完全不會灑到麵糊。
9. cope with 應付；處理
Maria does yoga to cope with the stress stemming from her job.
瑪麗亞做瑜珈來應付工作造成的壓力。

China upgrades Antelope Reef
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:41:02 UTC
01:41:02 KST

Located in the southwestern Paracel Islands (Xisha Islands, 西沙群島), Antelope Reef (Lingyang Reef, 羚羊礁) holds a significant advantage over China’s outposts in the Spratly Islands (Nansha Islands, 南沙群島) due to its proximity to Hainan and the Chinese mainland. That position makes resupply, reinforcement and force protection easier.
China had dredged and filled about 6.03km2 at Antelope Reef as of March, according to the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative, making it one of Beijing’s largest land reclamation projects in the South China Sea. Satellite imagery reveals a 680m pier, a deep-water harbor, a helipad and more than 50 structures under construction. The northwestern shoreline, which runs more than 3km, could also provide enough space for a runway. Initial signs of excavation for a potential runway were also detected this month.
Given these developments, Antelope Reef is expected to become a multipurpose military outpost supporting surveillance and the deployment of aircraft and warships. Some assessments suggest that Beijing could eventually station anti-ship missile systems there, such as the YJ-12B and YJ-18. With an estimated 400km to 500km range, these systems can threaten naval operations and targets moving from the South China Sea to Taiwan.
Outposts such as Antelope Reef can also serve as forward sensing and attrition nodes in a potential conflict over the Taiwan Strait. They can play a role in detecting, tracking, weakening and slowing intervention forces before they reach the battlefield.
This development presents a troubling prospect for Taiwan and its allies. US forces approaching Taiwan from the South China Sea would have to deal with anti-ship missiles, air defenses, electronic warfare and anti-submarine capabilities from Chinese outposts. They might also be forced to take alternative routes. A dense network of these outposts could produce a 48-to-72-hour delay, which would favor Beijing during an amphibious assault or maritime blockade of Taiwan.
Antelope Reef could additionally figure into the Chinese People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) effort to build bastions in the South China Sea, which are tightly controlled zones meant to shield its strategic submarine fleet from US surveillance and anti-submarine operations. Only about 300km from the PLA South Sea Fleet submarine base in Sanya, Antelope Reef serves as a transit point.
Beijing is gradually transforming its scattered outposts into a network capable of creating strategic depth for the PLA. This network could help China better control southern access routes, force the US and its allies to disperse their resources and extend the time needed for adversaries to enter the operational area.
While countering China’s expansion in the South China Sea is challenging, Taiwan has viable options. First, it should develop multiple contingency scenarios, with response levels corresponding to different threat levels.
The base layer should be equipped with radar, surveillance systems, and radio communications for early detection, identification and warning. Then, uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) can track lower-risk targets, and fighter jets should only be deployed once a genuine threat emerges. Even when jets need to launch, Taiwan should choose the appropriate aircraft for each situation and avoid using high-end fighters for routine missions.
For this to work well, Taiwan must carefully manage its combat endurance. Rotating units, tightening maintenance cycles and expanding the use of high-fidelity flight simulation would sustain pilot and ground crew readiness.
Second, publicizing China’s coercive actions carries diplomatic value, although transparency alone cannot deter “gray zone” tactics. Exposing Chinese behavior must be paired with robust defense capabilities to impose costs and complicate Beijing’s operational objectives.
Taiwan needs to push harder on asymmetric, mobile and survivable defense capabilities. Priority should be given to mobile air defenses, anti-ship missiles, tactical UAVs, dispersed radar networks and command centers that can keep functioning under strike conditions. Taiwan’s ultimate objective should be a dispersed, resilient defense network that can raise the cost of any coercive action or kinetic attack.
Additionally, Taiwan needs a systematic mechanism to document and publicize Chinese “gray zone” incursions. Data gathered from radar, UAVs and other assets should be combined with analysis from research institutions to build an objective record of the frequency, scale and operational patterns of PLA operations. Sharing this data with international partners, think tanks and foreign media could help Taiwan push back against China’s efforts to normalize coercion.
Third, strengthening collaboration with other Indo-Pacific countries and the US can be achieved through military training exchanges, officer education, intelligence sharing and combat-experience sharing. Compared with large-scale military exercises, such low-profile programs are less provocative, yet they still provide Taiwan with vital expertise, enhance interoperability and foster shared operational approaches.
Finally, Taiwan must advance a whole-of-society approach to defense, which raises public awareness, encourages business and local government participation, and strengthens non-partisan institutions. Empowering the Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience Committee is necessary.
The economic dimension is equally important. Taiwan must continue reducing its excessive dependence on China by diversifying trade, investment and supply chains, while using the New Southbound Policy+ to expand ties with Southeast Asian countries, India and Australia. Upgrading high-tech industries, increasing research-and-development investment and building alternative supply chains would all help limit China’s capacity to use economic dependence as a tool of coercion.
Truong Tuan Kiet is a master’s student at the Taipei School of Economics and Political Science at National Tsing Hua University, and a columnist at the Vietnam Strategic Forum. Huynh Tam Sang is founder and editor-in-chief of the Vietnam Strategic Forum and a doctoral student at the Taipei School of Economics and Political Science at National Tsing Hua University.
The Iran and Ukraine wars are rewriting modern military strategy. These conflicts are demonstrating that a less conventionally powerful state, by leveraging asymmetric capabilities, can impose major costs on an aggressor and fundamentally reshape the outcome of conflict. Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. Taiwan cannot become a bigger wolf than China, but it can ensure that

Taiwan’s manufacturing confidence rose to a more than four-year high last month as the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom continued to drive orders for chips and related hardware, providing momentum for the export-reliant economy, the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research (TIER, 台灣經濟研究院) said yesterday.
The manufacturing climate index rose 2.48 points to 101.09 from the previous month, hitting the highest level in more than four years, the institute said in its monthly survey.
“Demand for AI, high-performance computing and new smartphone models boosted semiconductor shipments,” TIER Economic Forecasting Center director Gordon Sun (孫明德) told a news conference in Taipei.
Photo courtesy of the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research
Exports and overseas orders also improved from the previous month, prompting more manufacturers to expect business conditions to improve, while the share anticipating deterioration declined, Sun said.
Electronics and machinery companies continued to benefit from global demand for AI chips and infrastructure, as well as preparations for new smartphone launches, he said.
Capacity utilization was high at advanced-process fabs, advanced-packaging facilities and high-end testing operations, Sun said.
Demand was also improving for power-management chips, high-speed transmission components, memory and silicon photonics, supporting mature-node manufacturing as well as testing and packaging businesses, he said.
The survey showed that more than 40 percent of electronics and machinery firms were optimistic about their outlook, he said.
Chemical producers also expect conditions to improve, helped by higher oil prices, inventory restocking by downstream customers and the resumption of some production lines, Sun said.
The improvement in the manufacturing sector contrasted with weaker sentiment in the services sector, with the services climate index falling 1.29 points to 98.2, ending a four-month run of gains.
Financial market volatility was a major drag on the sector, Sun said.
Securities firms were hurt by corrections in stock markets and trading volumes, while banks remained relatively steady as lending, wealth-management and credit-card businesses held up, he said.
Retailers provided some offset, benefiting from travel, hot weather and demand for daily necessities ahead of typhoons, he added.
The climate index for the construction sector rose 2.96 points to 110.55, extending its advance to a fourth consecutive month despite higher costs for construction waste disposal and building materials, the survey showed.
Demand from AI and information and communications technology companies continued to bolster the sector, TIER Taiwan Industry Economics Database director Arisa Liu (劉佩真) said.
“The overall momentum is strong,” Liu said, adding that construction activity is expected to continue growing over the next six months.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs yesterday said the Taiwan Global Pathfinders Initiative had put forward 51 projects this year, providing 107 overseas internship opportunities for young Taiwanese, and a program for funding young people from Taiwan’s diplomatic allies that allowed 66 people to visit last year would be expanded to a target of 85 this year.
“‘Youth diplomacy’ is an integral part of ‘integrated diplomacy,’” Department of Policy Planning deputy head Eric Lin (林世欣) said. “The aim is to broaden young people’s global perspectives and practical experience, convey Taiwan’s core values to the international community and build networks connecting Taiwanese youth with their global peers.”
The Taiwan Global Pathfinders Initiative, announced by President William Lai (賴清德) in January last year, allocated NT$10 billion (US$313.8 million) over four years for people aged 15 to 30 to gain international experience, including volunteer work, training, internships or other exchanges.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs via CNA
Lin said the initiative approved 51 submissions this year, funding 107 Taiwanese to venture abroad, which would hopefully encourage more young people to go out into the world and share Taiwan’s story.
The ministry collaborates with the Ministry of Education on the Annual Flagship Project, with this year’s theme of “Diplomatic Allies Prosperity Project: International Youth Science and Technology Exchange” encouraging young Taiwanese to facilitate Taiwan’s technological advantages with its diplomatic resources to engage in overseas exchanges, he said.
The four main focuses for exchanges this year are: Semiconductor supply chain resilience, trusted networks and digital governance, sovereign artificial intelligence (AI), and cooperation in new energy and carbon credits, Lin said.
The ministry put forward 27 projects this year, providing 48 overseas exchange spaces for young Taiwanese to gain firsthand experience about local development needs, and bring Taiwan’s technological, innovative and industrial experience to the international community, he said.
The ministry encourages young people from Taiwan’s allies to visit on exchanges, either through programs set up by the ministry or on agendas proposed by the youths themselves, Lin said, adding that 66 people traveled to Taiwan last year.
The foreign ministry commissioned the International Cooperation and Development Fund to run the program this year and is offering 85 young people the chance to travel to Taiwan on exchanges, he said.
The four main focuses for the exchange programs set for this year include smart agriculture, sustainable tourism, smart healthcare and new energy and carbon credit cooperation, he added.
Separately, Lin was asked to explain a “2P1R” — prevention, protection and response — strategy for countering transnational repression, which the ministry mentioned a few months ago.
The foreign ministry last year instructed all of its overseas missions to update their emergency response plans in the event of transnational repression, he said.
Their planning is complete, but conditions vary by country, so plans are tailored to the ground they are on, rather than a standard ministry-wide procedure, he added.
“So far, we have not received any actual case of Taiwanese asking our overseas mission for protection due to transnational repression,” he said.
Lin said the ministry is working with like-minded countries to build a collective security network through multiple tracks simultaneously, including bilateral and multilateral, as well as governmental and non-governmental efforts.
Regarding bilateral efforts, Taiwan has been engaging in strategic communications with the US, Japan, European countries and other like-minded nations, he said, adding that several of them have voiced concerns and introduced countermeasures after China enacted an ethnic unity law this year.
Taiwan is using international conferences and platforms such as the Global Cooperation and Training Framework to call on the international community to seriously view and address the issue of transnational repression, he said.
Lin said Taiwan has been seeking cooperation through international mechanisms, such as the International Criminal Police Organization and international nongovernmental organizations.

China’s hackers are using AI tech to escalate cyberattacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:40:58 UTC
01:40:58 KST

Chinese hackers are ramping up attacks after integrating DeepSeek and other open-source artificial intelligence (AI) models into their operations, demonstrating attackers’ ability to leverage basic AI tools to hit targets abroad.
State-affiliated cyberwarfare groups more than doubled the amount of attacks they carried out since they began delegating mundane tasks to AI and using it to develop advanced malicious software, according to TeamT5, a Taiwanese research firm. Researchers said it was not always possible to identify the AI model they used, but in general DeepSeek’s offerings are popular among hackers in China because of its high performance and ability to be customized.
Concerns among US national security officials are mounting over the autonomous capabilities of advanced models from Anthropic PBC and OpenAI after a series of high-profile incidents in which they managed to break out of testing environments.
Researchers say experienced Chinese hackers are using far less capable AI to scale up their activities and achieve breakthroughs. While other models produced in the country are more powerful — including Moonshot’s breakout Kimi K3 model — hackers are drawn to DeepSeek’s relatively lax cybersecurity barriers and low operating costs, researchers said. They added that they had yet to record an incident involving Kimi K3, which they believe is prohibitively expensive for hackers to run.
“DeepSeek is the AI of choice for Chinese hackers because it is relatively powerful with very low cyber guardrails,” said Charles Li (李庭閣), chief analyst at Team T5. “Western models are highly sought-after, but their guardrails are much more strict and require a lot more effort to bypass.”
DeepSeek did not respond to a request for comment. Neither China’s embassy in Washington nor its Ministry of Foreign Affairs responded to messages seeking comment.
Along with a mix of other open-source models, DeepSeek has been adopted throughout multiple stages of an attack, conducting reconnaissance and generating means of attacking vulnerabilities, Team T5 said. They said in the past few months they have obtained scripts and logs showing the model being used by hackers affiliated with the Chinese government throughout their operations.
A group known as Grimfengxi used DeepSeek to create exploit codes. Another group, called Huapi, used a Chinese AI model, which researchers said was likely DeepSeek, to attack an e-mail system of a Taiwanese company. A third, known as Teleboyi, used the platform to collect 1,000 IP addresses from the Internet and map a company’s domains.
In some cases, Chinese hackers turned to American AI for help. The cybersecurity firm CyCraft said a company that sells hacking software used ChatGPT during an attack on a Western think tank. After obtaining a copy of an employee’s local Signal database from a compromised computer, the hackers used the chatbot to help build a software module designed to decrypt it, according to screenshots reviewed by Bloomberg News.
An OpenAI spokesperson said the company is committed to identifying, preventing and disrupting attempts to abuse its models.
Researchers made the discovery after finding a public shared drive with thousands of Chinese-language screenshots taken as recently as February. The images show the workflow of a small startup with about 10 employees developing hacking tools for sale. They 300,000 to 500,000 yuan (US$44,628 to US$74,380) for their software. Its customers were at least four separate hacking groups, each running their own campaigns. Activity linked to one of the groups overlaps with operations publicly attributed to Mustang Panda, which the US Department of Justice says is backed by the Chinese government.
Anthropic’s tools have also been used. A group known as Slime22 managed to use Claude Code to breach the systems of a Taiwanese technology company, Team T5 said. After gaining access to the company’s systems the group set up its own system using Kali, a famous penetration testing platform, and asked Claude to use it to conduct lateral movements. Hackers managed to bypass cybersecurity guardrails by posing as an engineer carrying out those cybersecurity tests, they added.
Anthropic did not answer questions seeking comment.
Anthropic has blocked its services from Chinese-controlled companies. Last year, it said Chinese state-backed hackers had used Claude Code in September to autonomously carry out attacks on 30 entities including large tech companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturers and government agencies. They tricked the tool into attempting to infiltrate the entities, the company said, adding it was the first documented case of a large-scale cyberattack executed without substantial human intervention.

Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. Industrial production index increases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:40:58 UTC
01:40:58 KST

The industrial production index rose 25.61 percent year-on-year to 145.24 last month, as demand for artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing applications continued to boost output in the information technology and electronics sectors, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said yesterday.
The manufacturing production index, which accounts for 93.72 percent of overall industrial output, rose 26.89 percent year-on-year to 147.65, the 29th straight month of growth, exceeding the ministry’s forecast growth range of 22 to 25.5 percent.
The better-than-expected performance was driven mainly by electronic components, computers, electronics and optical products, which showed greater momentum than anticipated, Department of Statistics Deputy Director-General Chen Yu-fang (陳玉芳) told a news conference in Taipei.
Photo: Ritchie B. Tongo, EPA
Output of computers, electronics and optical products surged 95.62 percent, driven by server demand as major designers of graphics processing units and application-specific integrated circuits launched new platforms this quarter, Chen said.
The increased output was also supported by switches, semiconductor inspection equipment and solid-state drives used in cloud and data center applications, she said.
That was followed by a 22.72 percent increase in electronic component output amid robust demand for 12-inch wafers, DRAM chips, and IC packaging and testing services, she said.
Production of flat-panel displays fell 18.43 percent, marking the third consecutive monthly decline, as recovering demand for small panels used in medical and automotive applications was offset by sluggish purchases of large panels, Chen said.
In traditional industries, machinery output rose 19.75 percent, marking a fifth consecutive month of growth, driven by investment in chipmaking, automation and power transmission equipment, as well as recovering machine tool orders, she said.
Base metal output rose 13.24 percent, supported by increased demand for metals used in semiconductors, electronic components and power batteries, she said.
Chemical materials output fell 5.88 percent amid weak demand, continued oversupply from China and maintenance shutdowns, while auto and auto parts output dropped 5.03 percent as some automakers cut production to reduce inventories, Chen said.
Traditional industries, particularly machinery, have shown steady growth since March and could maintain year-on-year gains throughout the year, supported by demand for equipment from fab expansions, she said.
Base metal production could also maintain positive growth, supported by demand for semiconductor materials, although a slower recovery in traditional steel demand could continue to weigh on the sector, she said.
This month, the manufacturing production index is projected to rise 25.5 to 28.9 percent year-on-year, Chen said.
As the second half is traditionally the peak season for the information and communications industry, production of consumer electronics such as AI PCs is expected to pick up and boost manufacturing output, she said.
Manufacturing output for the complete year is forecast to maintain double-digit growth, supported by demand for high-performance computing and AI-related products, she added.

Gwangju Biennale restores ‘Taiwan’ name: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:40:58 UTC
01:40:58 KST

The Gwangju Biennale Foundation has agreed to allow Taiwan’s exhibitors to use the name “Taiwan” in the exhibition venue and in official documents and promotional materials, South Korea’s Munhwa Broadcasting Corp reported yesterday.
The foundation made the decision after considering Taiwan’s stance that it would withdraw from the exhibition, opening on Sept. 5, if the name could not be used, the broadcaster said.
Earlier yesterday, the Ministry of Culture urged the foundation to respond by today to its request to restore the name of Taiwan’s participating exhibition from “NTMoFA,” the acronym for the National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts, to “Taiwan Pavilion.”
Photo: CNA
In a statement, the ministry “sternly protested” the foundation’s and the Asia Culture Center’s (ACC) refusal to restore the name and what it described as efforts to prevent Taiwan Pavilion personnel from entering the venue to set up the exhibition, originally scheduled to begin on Tuesday last week.
The statement did not specify what action would be taken if the organizers failed to respond.
The ministry said it issued statements on Monday and Wednesday last week explaining that the name “Taiwan Pavilion” was changed to “NTMoFA” without discussion or prior notice.
It also pointed to a statement issued yesterday by the Taiwan Pavilion’s curator and artists, titled “You Must Change Your Name,” which accused the foundation of repeatedly ignoring the museum’s objections to the name change and said an artistic institution should not become a tool for suppressing self-identification.
Over the past week, the ACC has refused to allow Taiwanese exhibitors to enter the venue to set up the exhibition, citing the lack of an official document from the foundation, the ministry said.
Although the museum received a copy of a foundation letter permitting them to enter the venue on Wednesday, the ACC continued to say it had not received the document and refused to allow NTMoFA representatives to enter, the ministry said.
After a museum representative took photographs to document the incident, ACC venue staff demanded to inspect the person’s phone and asked them to delete the photographs, it said.
Furthermore, the foundation proposed relocating Taiwan’s exhibition to an alternative storage space that was much smaller than the original site, the ministry said.
Members of the international artist community and art workers have also spoken out, urging the foundation not to use its authority to determine the name under which participants are identified and to restore the name “Taiwan Pavilion” as soon as possible, it said.
Earlier, the foundation said it would neither intervene in nor censor the content or expression of exhibitions, and would continue negotiations to ensure that the NTMoFA’s exhibition proceeds as planned.
The foundation said the exhibition is purely an artistic partnership and that it has never intervened, nor would intervene, in the NTMoFA pavilion’s curation, selection of works, installation methods or the expressions of its curator and artists.
It said it was concerned that the controversy had developed into a political and diplomatic issue, adding that the dispute stemmed from differing interpretations of administrative procedures and the agreement concerning the pavilion’s participating institution and how it should be labeled in official materials.
The foundation said that the agreement signed on Jan. 12 clearly identified the Gwangju Biennale Foundation and the National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts as the parties involved and that its implementation was based on that agreement.
In contrast, the ministry has insisted that the original agreement was that the name “Taiwan Pavilion” would be used and was only changed by the foundation in June.
The foundation argued that the labeling used in official documents and promotional materials should be distinguished from the exhibitor’s own self-identification.
Regarding the difficulties encountered by Taiwan’s exhibitors, the foundation said it had signed a contract with the venue for use of the exhibition space, but the contract did not specify the countries or institutions that would hold exhibitions there.
It said it would ask the ACC to open the space and cooperate with the installation and exhibition operations so that the NTMoFA’s exhibition can proceed as planned.
If further delays or difficulties arise, the NTMoFA could consider using an alternative space inside the biennale venue, it added.
The foundation concluded that both the autonomy of exhibitors and the official operations stipulated in the agreement should be respected, saying the priority was not for the two sides to “more loudly propagate their own stance,” but to quickly find a workable solution that would allow the exhibition to be held as scheduled.
Founded in 1995, the Gwangju Biennale in South Korea is Asia’s oldest and most prestigious biennial of contemporary art.
In an August titled “Who is Afraid of the Name ‘Taiwan Pavilion,” the coalition of South Korean artists has criticized the biennale for disregarding artists’ right to identify their own nationality and failing to engage in discussion and consultation, and said it is deeply troubling that such “political censorship” occurred in Gwangju, a city known as South Korea’s “sacred ground of democracy.”
“The Taiwan Pavilion case reflects a broader problem in the international art world, where discrimination based on nationality, race, gender, religion or political views has led to artworks being altered or removed, exhibitions and public statements being canceled, and artists and cultural workers being silenced,” the group said.

Illegal filming of patients punishable with jail time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:40:57 UTC
01:40:57 KST

The Legislative Yuan yesterday passed a series of amendments to the Medical Care Act (醫療法) that introduce a prison sentence of up to three years for medical personnel who photograph or film patients’ intimate areas without their consent, in response to a string of incidents involving beauty clinics secretly filming patients.
The amendments mandate that medical institutions and their staff must not use any tools or equipment to view clients’ intimate areas, or view or listen to their medical records, “without a valid reason.”
Those who arbitrarily record, photograph, film or make electromagnetic recordings of patients’ medical records or intimate areas would face up to three years in prison and could be fined up to NT$300,000, with the equipment used subject to confiscation.
Photo: Tien Yu-hua, Taipei Times
Those who intend to profit by supplying space or equipment for such recordings and those who intend to distribute the illicit content could be sentenced to between six months and five years in prison, with fines of up to NT$500,000.
The amendments were proposed after a series of franchised and independent beauty clinics across Taiwan filmed clients’ intimate parts without consent, resulting in fines or suspensions for at least 21 clinics.
Other revisions to the act were adopted yesterday to strengthen protections for medical personnel.
The fine for those who subject medical personnel to violence, coercion or threats was raised from between NT$30,000 and NT$50,000 to between NT$50,000 and NT$250,000.
Protections were expanded beyond doctors and nurses to include emergency response personnel and related staff.
“Public insults” directed at medical staff as a form of violence were added to the act, with a prison sentence of up to two years and fines of up to NT$200,000.
Medical institutions that fail to implement safety measures mandated by the central government to protect their staff may be fined NT$30,000 to NT$150,000.
The amendment mandates that whenever a medical corporation distributes surplus profits, it must allocate 10 percent toward improving employee welfare, enhancing patient rights and upgrading the quality of its medical environment.
Finally, the amendments update the nation’s medical advertising regulations to align with a 2023 Constitutional Court judgement, which found that banning individual physicians from advertising violated their constitutional right to free speech.
While the law used to say that only medical institutions could run medical advertisements, the revised act says that physicians are permitted to advertise, although they are limited to the specific medical institution where they are officially registered to practice.

Europe records at least 35,000 more deaths from heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:40:55 UTC
01:40:55 KST

At least 35,000 more people died during Europe’s four record-breaking, back-to-back heat waves this summer than would normally be expected, according to incomplete figures from barely half the continent.
Excess mortality in three of the EU’s larger countries — Germany, France and Spain — alone has already exceeded 25,000, according to the provisional national figures, and experts say the toll would rise significantly once this month’s totals are consolidated.
The consecutive heat waves across western Europe since May shattered all-time historical temperature records across hundreds of weather stations, and France recorded its hottest national average day on record.
Photo: AFP
Records fell for three straight days in Germany in late June, when 46 stations topped 40°C, while Spain endured persistent highs above 42°C. Scientists say human-made global heating is making such extreme events more frequent and intense.
The death toll is highest in Germany, which late last week reported an estimated 14,000 heat-related deaths from April 6 to Aug. 9. The Robert Koch Institute public health agency said 9,600 people had died in the week of June 22 to 28 alone.
Systematically compiled EU-wide excess mortality figures, available since 2008, show the only other summer week in which a higher rate of additional deaths has been recorded was in July 2022, when COVID-19 was still active.
Figures from the Carlos III health institute’s mortality monitoring system suggest 4,947 deaths in Spain from May to this week can be attributed to heat, making this year Spain’s worst year on record for heat-related deaths, exceeding the 4,520 recorded in 2022.
Different countries calculate and present their data in different ways. Spain and Germany model estimated heat-related deaths in real time, comparing daily temperatures and mortality rates to calculate deaths attributable to heat. Such estimations are necessary because heat is rarely stated as a direct cause of death. In most cases, heat aggravates a pre-existing health condition.
France, where more than 500 weather stations recorded temperatures higher than 40°C and at one stage 98 percent of the country was under heat alerts, reported an initial “all causes” excess death figure and definitive attribution later.
Its national health agency last week said that “all cause” excess deaths from late May to July 22 stood at 7,300. Figures for this month were not yet available and initial data were based on electronic death certificates, which account for only 80 percent of total mortality, it said.
Italy, whose national heat surveillance system uses local municipal data, meaning it is often subject to significant delays, has so far only reported incomplete real-time indicators rather than a consolidated national death toll.
Modeling suggests 2,700 more people died than usual from June 22 to 28 alone and epidemiologists have said the country’s total heat-attributable death toll would probably be between 5,000 and 8,000 by the time it is formally recorded.
Other European countries to have already reported excess death tolls include the UK, where the health security agency last month said that its modeling suggested the May and June heat waves had resulted in 2,877 heat-associated fatalities in England.
Belgium has said its preliminary data showed it recorded a 39 percent increase in mortality from June 18 to 29, equating to 1,222 additional deaths, and the Netherlands has said at least 900 more people than usual died from June 22 to July 5.
A rapid modeling study cited by the European Commission estimates that 1,070 more people than usual died in Poland during the late-June heat wave, and Swiss public health authority data suggests excess heat-related deaths of 220 in the same week.
Early figures from Luxembourg, Greece, Romania, Bulgaria and Denmark indicate about 40 excess deaths in each of those countries. Agence France-Presse has calculated that areas inhabited by more than 80 million Europeans experienced temperatures above 40<<0>>C this summer.
The WHO said in May that heat-related mortality in its European region had increased by more than 30 percent over the past 20 years and was on course to climb significantly as a result of the climate crisis and population aging.

Amendement waiving tuition for some passes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:40:55 UTC

The Legislative Yuan yesterday passed amendments to waive tuition for college students from economically disadvantaged backgrounds.
Under the amendments, economically disadvantaged students who attend university or college, are in the final two years of a five-year junior college program or are enrolled in a two-year junior college program would be exempt from tuition fees following an assessment of their financial circumstances.
The government would assess whether the student’s household income falls in the bottom 20 percent of the nation’s five income quintiles and other financial information to grant the exemption, the amendments state.
Photo: Tien Yu-hua, Taipei Times
The amendments would allow students to claim computer and Internet fees as a student loan expense and require the government to provide “repayment assistance.”
The amendments concern Article 58 of the Senior High School Education Act (高級中等教育法), Article 35 of the University Act (大學法) and Article 44 of the Junior College Act (專科學校法).
The Legislative Yuan’s Education and Culture Committee reviewed the draft amendments on June 11.
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) legislators pushed to fully waive interest on student loans using budget allocations from the Ministry of Education and extend repayment grace periods, while Democratic Progressive Party legislators supported a more flexible system rather than legal amendments.
The amendments would not apply to those who do not hold Taiwanese nationality and household registration.
The financial assistance would be funded through subsidies allocated by the agencies overseeing higher education institutions, while universities would submit lists of eligible students to request funding, the amendments state.
The ministry would be required to formulate regulations for the amendments that govern eligibility, subsidy amounts, rights and obligations, they state.
The legislature passed two accompanying resolutions, calling on the ministry to continue reviewing whether the next academic year’s budget could fully subsidize student loan interest and for the government to provide financial assistance to economically disadvantaged students and those who suddenly face economic difficulties.

Environmental Impact Assessment: Taiwan’s freshwater invaders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:40:54 UTC
01:40:54 KST

Taiwan’s rivers are significantly cleaner today than they were a few decades ago. The country’s rapid industrialization left many waterways polluted by untreated factory discharge, domestic sewage and runoff from livestock operations. Since the 1990s, expansion of municipal sewerage infrastructure and stricter enforcement of environmental standards have turned the situation around. However, freshwater ecosystems now face a very different threat — one that’s far less obvious to people living nearby.
“Southern Taiwan — Tainan, Kaohsiung and Pingtung — is facing a particularly critical crisis regarding freshwater biological invasions,” says Lin Yen-ting (林晏廷), an assistant professor in the Master’s Program in Biodiversity at National Taiwan University.
Lin says his recent surveys in that region have revealed “an alarming variety of invasive species originating from around the globe.”
Photo: Huang Ming-tang, Taipei Times
Among them are the giant snakehead (Channa micropeltes) and the Indian glassy fish (Parambassis ranga) from South Asia, African species such as the blackchin tilapia (Sarotherodon melanotheron) and the largemouth bass (Micropterus salmoides) from North America. These invasive creatures have “severely impacted southern Taiwan’s native and endemic fish populations,” Lin says.
He regards tilapia of the Oreochromis genus as posing the greatest threat to local freshwater ecosystems, saying: “Due to their rapid reproduction cycle, omnivorous diet and exceptional ecological adaptability, tilapia can now be found throughout almost all Taiwan’s rivers, lakes and reservoirs.”
What’s more, he explains, unlike the majority of fish species, tilapia are mouthbrooders, meaning females scoop fertilized eggs into their mouths and incubate them there for several days. This behavior boosts offspring survival rates by physically shielding eggs and fry from predators during their most defenseless stage.
Photo: Steven Crook
These fish harm local ecosystems “not only by preying on native aquatic animals, but also by outcompeting them due to their sheer numbers and high reproduction rates.”
Asked if there’s a single species that hasn’t been studied much, but which he thinks may become a serious problem in Taiwan in the future, he points to the blackchin tilapia. A native of coastal west Africa that’s been introduced to Asia and North America, he predicts this fish will become “a major threat.”
It’s already recognized as one of the most destructive aquatic invaders across Southeast Asia, where management and control have proven exceptionally difficult. Due to its rapid growth rate, broad environmental tolerance, and high ecological plasticity [capacity to adjust its expressed traits within a single lifespan to adapt to local conditions], the blackchin tilapia poses a severe threat to local aquatic ecosystems,” Lin says.
Photo: Hsu Chuo-hsun , Taipei Times
A July 5, 2026 report in The Guardian details the impact of the fish in Thailand, where some aquaculturists have given up shrimp farming after blackchin tilapia ate vast numbers of baby shrimp. Because female blackchin tilapia initiate courtship by digging pits and churning up sediment, they likely disrupt bottom-dwelling invertebrates and cloud the water enough to hinder photosynthesis in aquatic plants.
AQUACULTURE THREATENED
The species has already caused significant economic loss in Taiwan. Lin says there have been several cases of blackchin tilapia or striped snakehead (Channa striata, a native of South and Southeast Asia) infiltrating aquaculture facilities through intake water and preying on stock species. “Additionally, invasions by large predators like the giant snakehead and the jaguar cichlid (Parachromis managuensis) have led to sharp population declines in commercially valuable target species across lakes and reservoirs, as seen in Sun Moon Lake,” he adds.
Photo: CNA
Native species can also be invasive if specimens are transferred to other watersheds. “A prime example is in Miaoli County, where the translocated Holland’s carp (Spinibarbus hollandi) is heavily preying upon the critically-endangered native Iijima’s gudgeon (Squalidus iijimae),” Lin says.
A short paper co-authored by Lin and published late last year in Aquatic Conservation: Marine and Freshwater Ecosystems confirms the jaguar cichlid is now well established in New Taipei City’s Feitsui Reservoir (翡翠水庫), Taiwan’s second-largest reservoir by both surface area and storage capacity. This marks the northernmost recorded presence of this Central American species in East Asia.
Noting that previous research has underscored the reservoir’s “significance as a key habitat for various native and endangered aquatic species, including fish, amphibians and reptiles,” Lin and his co-authors state that the impact on native fish communities of the jaguar cichlid — first observed in Feitsui Reservoir in 2014 — has yet to be fully assessed.
Photo: Tung Chen-kuo, Taipei Times
The researchers captured 384 Parachromis managuensis specimens in Feitsui Reservoir between 2022 and 2024, and stomach-contents analysis of a subset revealed they “primarily consume native shrimp (genus Caridina, Macrobrachium) and small native fish, especially Sinibrama macrops.”
This matches previous findings, and is likely the reason why the growth of the jaguar cichlid population appears to have come at the expense of two other invasive species. In 2008–2009, Culter alburnus accounted for more than a quarter of the upper reach catch, but since 2014 it has almost disappeared. After 2016, Chanodichthys erythropterus declined from around 20 percent of the catch to less than 5 percent. Both declines, Lin and his co-authors suggest, “may reflect the aggressive, dominant feeding behavior of the jaguar cichlid.”
Between 2006 and 2020, the proportion of Sinibrama macrops in the catch averaged 12.6 percent. In 2024, it was barely 3 percent, and the authors warn that, given the jaguar cichlid’s reputation for triggering top-down trophic cascades, “the ongoing predation may lead to similar ecological disruptions in Feitsui Reservoir.”
FIGHTING BACK
Lin says Taiwan hasn’t had any notable successes when it comes to removing invasive freshwater fish species.
“There are no documented cases of complete eradication. Once an invasive aquatic species becomes established in open waters, total removal is extremely difficult. However, one of my ongoing research projects focuses on population control and localized eradication targeting a newly established invasive fish species currently restricted to a single small river system.”
Lin urges the government to provide more support for specialists studying freshwater invasive species. In the past three years, his research has documented four newly established non-native species in local freshwater systems, with several other species currently under investigation.
“We need more funding for foundational biodiversity surveys so we can formulate effective control and management strategies before invasions spiral out of control,” he says.
He also hopes for stronger public education and stricter enforcement. The proliferation of the jaguar cichlid and the tilapia genus is, in part, a consequence of Buddhist mercy-release rites (see the Aug. 9, 2023 edition of this column, “A bad thing done by well-intentioned people: the cruel practice of ‘mercy release’”). A non-religious equivalent is the introduction of fish to enhance recreational fisheries for anglers; in Taiwan, this is one reason for the encroachment of the largemouth bass and Holland’s carp.
“We need stricter oversight of the ornamental pet trade, as a majority of recently established invasive populations originated as escaped or released aquarium fish,” Lin says.
Steven Crook, the author or co-author of four books about Taiwan, has been following environmental issues since he arrived in the country in 1991. He drives a hybrid and carries his own chopsticks. The views expressed here are his own.
An interesting essay in the spring issue this year of International Security by Kerby Davis and Eugene Gholz explores the possibilities and outcomes of simulated missile attacks by the People’s Republic of China (PRC) on Taiwan’s ports to carry out a blockade. “Substantively,” they conclude in Blockade by Fire: China’s Potential to Blockade Taiwan Using Missile Attacks on Ports, “our article raises serious concern about Taiwan’s vulnerability to Chinese military coercion. Even if Taiwan and the United States take steps to better prepare for a Chinese blockade, they face a greater threat from China than analysts previously believed.” The authors

Aside from the exhibition at Nangang Exhibition Center, many participants are to visit suppliers in science parks in Hsinchu, Taichung, Tainan and Kaohsiung.
Photo: CNA

Parties spar over drone bill, timeline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:40:50 UTC
01:40:50 KST

As the legislature reviews a special drone budget this week, opposition lawmakers yesterday vowed to work out a drone development bill funded from the annual budget, amid concerns over funding delays and the constitutionality of the proposal.
The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) made the announcement a day after Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) opened interparty negotiations over funding the initiative to develop indigenous drones.
The Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) NT$210 billion (US$6.6 billion) drone bill is a special budget act, overseen by the Ministry of National Defense (MND), funding the acquisition of coastal surveillance drones, coastal attack drones, uncrewed one-way strike boats and more.
Photo: Huang Hsu-lei, Taipei Times
The government intended to implement its drone programs this year.
In contrast, the KMT and TPP proposals say that any funding for drones must draw from the annual government budget and that the Ministry of Economic Affairs must be the main agency in charge.
The KMT listed an NT$240 billion allocation for drones, to be doled out in increments of NT$40 billion a year from the annual budget over six years.
The TPP proposal included no funding sources and explicitly refused to fund uncrewed ground and surface vehicles.
Although the KMT’s version says that it should go into effect within six months of the legislation’s passage, the timetable is problematic, as the opposition could pass the budget no sooner than Friday.
This would delay the implementation of drone development by 17 months compared with the government’s version.
Moreover, it is unclear how the opposition’s drone bill could fit into the regular budget for this year or next year, as the budgets have already been proposed, meaning the government would not be able to spend money on drones until 2028.
Taiwan could seek to fund drones using supplementary budgets, but according to Article 79 of the Budget Act (預算法), only the Executive Yuan is authorized to make such proposals, casting the opposition bills’ legality into doubt.
Cabinet officials have maintained that the KMT and TPP had no authority to write a draft act for drones to begin with, as Article 70 of the Constitution forbids the legislature from adding items to the annual budget.
The opposition’s drone bills would not fund the three uncrewed systems the Taiwanese armed forces had planned to buy, MND Comptroller Bureau head Hsieh Chi-hsien (謝其賢) said on Thursday last week.
Although the opposition cited the passage on Aug. 14 of a NT$19.2 billion drone budget as evidence of their support for national defense, these funds were earmarked for government purchases of unarmed drones and industry subsidies, not uncrewed weapon systems.
A defense official commented on condition of anonymity that the acquisition of 210,000 surveillance drones, one-way strike drones and uncrewed kamikaze boats is critical to Taiwan’s defense.
The uncrewed platforms are the lynchpin of the armed forces’ asymmetric warfare concept, which envisions using drone swarms, rocket artillery and long-range precision strikes to counter the Chinese Liberation Army Navy’s (PLAN) vessels, they said.
Saturation strikes, with drones acting both as spotters and strike platforms, would be key to the defenders’ ability to overwhelm the PLAN’s air defense and hit amphibious assault ships, troop transports and supply vessels, they said.
The defense concept conforms to the “hellscape” strategy first coined by the US Indo-Pacific Command’s then-commander Admiral Samuel Paparo in 2024, the official said.
Uncrewed aerial vehicles are expected to play an important forward observer role, guiding strikes from direct and indirect fire weapons, and the Marine Corps is already trading armor and artillery battalions for drones, they added.
