Unusual dragonfly swarms sweep across California
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:40:46 UTC
01:40:46 KST

Californians are spotting swarms of dragonflies flitting around parks, chasing mosquitoes in ponds and hunting flies on farms, a phenomenon experts say was likely fueled by unusually warm spring rains.
Peter Veilleux, who owns a nursery in Oakland, said he started noticing the dragonflies — at one point spotting about 100 flying together — while walking his dog at a park near his house and around the city’s Lake Merritt.
“It’s been amazing to see them,” Veilleux said, adding that he started seeing big groups of dragonflies last month.
Photo: AP
He was so awed by the sight that he posted about it on Facebook, asking if anyone else was seeing the formidable predators in such large numbers. Dozens of people commented about their own sightings in the San Francisco Bay Area and elsewhere in California.
It is common to see dragonflies during the summer months, when they emerge from freshwater as flying insects. However, this year’s large numbers are probably due to the warm monsoon storms that came through the state in late spring and early summer, said Kathy Biggs, a dragonfly expert and co-author of the book Dragonflies of California.
She said most are likely wandering gliders, a highly migratory dragonfly that can appear in large numbers when conditions line up. Dragonflies, which can fly at speeds of up to 56kph, use air pressure changes to help them fly great distances, Biggs said.
“We could say that they’re surfing the pressure system, the monsoon,” she added.
Joe Del Bosque said he noticed swarms of them earlier this month at his farm in Fresno County, flying 3m to 6m above him.
“We do have them every year, but we had more than normal,” he said.
Del Bosque said he was happy to see the flying hunters because they eat aphids, whiteflies and fruit flies that feed on his crops. The insects, along with ladybugs working on the plants, are excellent pest control, because they eat tiny insects on the plants and larger winged ones, like adult aphids and moths, he said.
“They are like little fighter jets,” he said. “They zoom in for other insects and capture them in the air.”
Dragonflies spend most of their lives wingless and underwater. Their life cycle begins after female and male dragonflies mate and the female dragonfly lays tiny eggs in freshwater. After the eggs hatch, the young dragonflies, called nymphs, live underwater for at least six months and for up to five years for some species. They start hunting then and feed on mosquito larvae, tadpoles and even other nymphs.
Once they emerge from the water, they shed their skin and transform into four-winged insects that can move their forewings and hindwings independently. This allows them to fly forward, backward, up and down, and hover perfectly in place.
However, their life as flying animals is short, lasting a few weeks or months. They spend it looking for new lakes, rivers and ponds, preying on tiny insects and attempting to repeat the cycle of life.
“They’re super agile, super strong flying insects with really good vision, really good eyes, and really strong flight muscles, and they are voracious predators that are out there feeding on mosquitoes nonstop,” said Chris Grinter, senior collection manager of entomology at the California Academy of Science in San Francisco.
Dragonflies are among the most effective predators in nature, with more than 90 percent of their hunts ending successfully, Grinter said.
“They can eat hundreds of mosquitoes a single day,” he said.
Dragonflies have awed humans for thousands of years. To Native Americans, they are a symbol of purity and happiness. In Japan, they symbolize power, agility and victory. In some European folklore, they are considered to represent evil or bad luck.
To attract them to your garden, Biggs recommends avoiding pesticides and building fishless ponds and sunny areas with perches.
There are about 70 dragonfly species in California, but most are not migratory and remain near where they emerged, Biggs said.
Some of them might be out the very first thing in the spring, even as the snow is melting, and some of them are out in the Mojave Desert in the driest, hottest places in California, Grinter said.
Biggs said the migratory species keep moving on, “surfing” high-pressure systems in the air.
“They could be somewhere a few days and then leave,” she said.

16:40:46 UTC
01:40:46 KST

Typhoon Saudel is continuing to weaken and shift its path northward, with a sea warning expected to be issued this evening, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said yesterday.
The agency did not rule out issuing a land warning for outlying Lienchiang County (Matsu) tomorrow morning, although all storm warnings could be lifted by Friday night.
Saudel is expected to be closest to Taiwan from tomorrow night to Friday, bringing localized heavy rain to northern and southern Taiwan, as well as central mountainous areas, the agency said.
Photo: Lo Hsin-chen, Taipei Times
As of 2pm yesterday, the center of moderate Typhoon Saudel was about 890km east-northeast of Taipei, CWA forecaster Huang En-hung (黃恩鴻) said.
As atmospheric conditions are unfavorable for its development, the storm is continuing to weaken and its radius is shrinking, Huang said.
When it is closest to Taiwan between tomorrow night and Friday, it could weaken to the lower limit of a moderate typhoon or the upper limit of a light typhoon, he added.
Photo courtesy of the Central Weather Administration
Forecast models show that Saudel’s path is continuously shifting northward, meaning its impact in terms of wind and rain on Taiwan would be lessened, and the chances of its storm circle touching land have significantly decreased, he said.
Several airlines have announced flight cancelations to Okinawa for today, Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport said.
As of 6pm yesterday, a total of 16 flights had been canceled, including China Airlines flights CI121/120 between Taoyuan and Naha; EVA Air flights BR112/113/185/186 between Taoyuan and Naha; and Peach Aviation flights MM921/922/924/927/929/930 between Taoyuan and Naha.
Also canceled are Starlux Airlines flights JX890/891 between Taoyuan and Miyakojima, Okinawa, and Thai Lion Air flights SL380/381 between Taoyuan and Naha.
Moisture levels are expected to decrease today, although southern areas could still experience localized, brief heavy downpours in the early morning, with occasional showers expected throughout the rest of the day, Huang said.
He urged people nationwide to be aware of afternoon thunderstorms.
From tomorrow night through Friday, when Saudel would exert its strongest influence, localized, brief showers or thunderstorms could occur across the nation, Huang said.
Northern and southern Taiwan, as well as central mountainous areas, could experience localized heavy rain, while it would be cloudy elsewhere, he added.
After the typhoon moves away, Taiwan is still forecast to remain under the influence of a large low-pressure system through next week, bringing localized, brief showers or thunderstorms to central and southern areas, and brief afternoon thunderstorms to other regions, he said.
Huang said that high waves are likely to occur along the north coast of Keelung, the eastern coastline, the Hengchun Peninsula (恆春半島) and Lienchiang County until Saturday.
Furthermore, a large low-pressure zone remains over the waters east of the Philippines, and a new tropical system is expected to develop next week, Huang said.
It cannot be ruled out that it might strengthen into a tropical depression or a typhoon by next weekend, although its path requires further observation, he added.

NRL change rules to help Arrow reach 100
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:40:44 UTC
01:40:44 KST

Motor neurone disease is not likely to stop Jai Arrow trying to bring up a career milestone in Australia’s National Rugby League (NRL).
The NRL is planning an exception to its rules to allow the veteran forward a chance to be on the field for the South Sydney Rabbitohs in his 99th and 100th rugby league games for the club, if only for a few moments.
Arrow, 31, in May was diagnosed with motor neurone disease (MND), which MND Australia describes as an umbrella term for a group of progressive neurological conditions where the motor neurones degenerate. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is the most common form, and ALS is often called Lou Gehrig’s disease.
Photo: AP
As part of an agreement with the Rabbitohs, the NRL granted South Sydney — who are seventh on the NRL table on 30 points — special dispensation to include Arrow as an extra player on yesterday’s official team list and an extra substitution in their rotation for the game against the Gold Coast Titans (16th, 18 points) on Saturday. A similar dispensation has been allowed for South Sydney’s last regular-season game against the Sydney Roosters (third, 38 points).
According to the NRL, Arrow is to get dressed in South Sydney’s playing kit for the two NRL game days, lead the Rabbitohs team onto the field of play, be the team’s first interchange of the match within the first few seconds after the opening whistle without taking part in any play during the game and be able to sit on the interchange bench for the remainder of the game in his playing kit.
It would bring Arrow’s tally to 180 career games in the NRL and 100 for the Rabbitohs, on top of his representative games for Queensland in the annual State of Origin series.
Australian Rugby League Commission chairman Peter V’landys said it was a chance for the sport to be a “conduit to bring out the best of humanity.”
“This thoughtful gesture by the South Sydney Rabbitohs shows the true heart of our game,” V’landys said. “Jai has inspired millions of people around the world with the courage and strength he has shown in his fight with MND. He is not only a great player, but an extraordinary person.”
“Reaching 100 games for the Rabbitohs is a special achievement, one that Jai, his family and everyone who has supported him should be incredibly proud of,” he said. ”The entire rugby league community stands with Jai and is honored to celebrate this remarkable milestone with him.”
The other teams in the race for the post-season are: the Auckland Warriors (first, 38 points), the Penrith Panthers (second, 38 points), the Dolphins (fourth, 36 points), the Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks (fifth, 34 points), the Newcastle Knights (sixth, 32 points), the North Queensland Cowboys (eighth, 30 points), the Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs (ninth, 28 points) and the Manly Warringah Sea Eagles (10th, 26 points).

Tehran vows to retaliate after US widens sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:40:43 UTC
01:40:43 KST

Iran yesterday pledged to fight back against expanded US sanctions aimed at isolating its economy, expressing confidence that major trading partners would resist Washington’s pressure campaign.
Almost six months into a conflict the US has struggled to resolve, US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent on Monday unveiled a package targeting dozens of individuals and entities as part of what he described as “Operation Economic Outcast,” but stopped short of the most punishing sanctions.
While he said countries that continued trading with Iran risked being forced out of the US dollar-based financial system, he declined to give a timeline or identify which might be targeted, saying he would give them time to comply with the new directive.
Photo: West Asia News Agency via Reuters
“Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” he said, when asked why the measures had not gone further.
While the US Department of the Treasury announced new sanctions on 60 individuals, entities and vessels, the list did not feature any of the Chinese financial institutions suspected of facilitating Iran’s oil trade.
“We want to make clear here today that no one is above the reach of US sanctions,” Bessent said in response to a question about Chinese banks.
China has been the biggest buyer of Iranian oil for several years, although the US blockade of Iran’s ports has cut Iranian oil flows to China since Washington renewed it in the middle of last month.
Experts say Washington is wary of Chinese retaliation for any sanctions on its banks ahead of expected talks next month between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平), with any curbs on China’s exports of critical minerals especially sensitive.
In Beijing, Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Lin Jian (林劍) told a regular press briefing that China opposes unilateral sanctions and warned they risk worsening conflicts.
The most urgent task is to de-escalate tensions and return to negotiations, he said.
“China’s cooperation with Iran has always been conducted within the international framework and should not be interfered with or undermined,” he said. “China is closely monitoring relevant developments and will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own interests.”
Oil prices fell for a second day as traders brushed off the impact of the sanctions, although market participants remained wary of Iran’s continued ability to disrupt shipping.
Before news of the latest sanctions, Iran threatened both a possible military response and further reduction in oil exports from the Gulf in retaliation for any US economic measures.
After they were unveiled, Iranian Minister of Economic Affairs Ali Madanizadeh said that Tehran was prepared.
“Our defense is no longer so defensive; the enemies should wait for an attack,” he told state television.
Neither China nor Russia had “accepted” the US measures, he added, predicting that other countries would resist them.

Retail, food and beverage sales hit record for July
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:40:42 UTC
01:40:42 KST

Retail and food and beverage sales last month hit record levels for July as they rose annually for the sixth consecutive month amid moderate expansion of consumer spending, Ministry of Economic Affairs data released yesterday showed.
Retail sales increased 7.7 percent from a year earlier to NT$418.3 billion (US$13.13 billion), benefiting from a gradual recovery in the auto market, entertainment and shopping during the summer break, and diverse marketing activities by businesses, the ministry said in a report.
The ministry had forecast that retail sales would grow 8.4 to 11.4 percent from a year earlier.
Photo: CNA
Last month’s growth was led by a 12.6 percent rise in purchases of cars, motorcycles, auto parts and accessories, while sales at department stores rose 9.6 percent, and receipts at computer and home appliance stores grew 12.5 percent, the report said.
Big-box stores, convenience stores, and e-commerce and mail-order operators also contributed to sales growth, rising 10.3 percent, 4.2 percent and 5.9 percent respectively, it said.
Sales at fuel service stations increased 12.2 percent, reflecting higher oil prices, it added.
Food and beverage sales rose 2.5 percent to NT$88.7 billion last month, below the ministry’s projection of 4.7 to 7.7 percent annual growth due to Typhoon Bavi, the report said.
Restaurants and beverage shops posted sales growth of 0.8 percent and 9.7 percent respectively, benefiting from more dining-out and gathering opportunities during the summer vacation, the report said.
Catering and group meal services providers’ sales increased 7.7 percent amid a travel boom, it said.
In the first seven months of this year, retail sales climbed 4.6 percent to NT$2.88 trillion, a record for the period, while food and beverage sales rose 3.9 percent to NT$642.2 billion, also a record for the period, the ministry said.
Retail sales this month are expected to grow 5 to 8 percent year-on-year to NT$411.1 billion to NT$422.9 billion, benefiting from celebrations associated with Father’s Day, Lovers’ Day and Ghost Festival, alongside the launch of Garden City, a shopping mall at the Taipei Dome, the ministry said.
Food and beverage sales this month are projected to increase 1 to 4 percent to between NT$94.2 billion and NT$97 billion, boosted by dining out and festive gatherings, as well as demand for cold beverages, it said.

UN committee rebukes India over discrimination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:40:41 UTC
01:40:41 KST

India must better protect tribal peoples and disadvantaged castes subjected to extrajudicial killings, torture and violence by law enforcement, a UN watchdog said yesterday.
The UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) said the world’s most populous country also urgently needed to address hate crimes against Bengali-speaking Muslims.
“The committee was gravely concerned about reports of large-scale violations perpetrated by law enforcement officials against ethnic and ethno-religious groups, Indigenous and Tribal Peoples, including Scheduled Tribes, Scheduled Castes, particularly Dalits, and non-citizens,” it said in a statement on its findings.
Photo: Bloomberg
“These included racially motivated violence, excessive use of force, extrajudicial killings, arbitrary and prolonged detention without due process, torture, ill-treatment and sexual violence,” it said.
The committee urged India to investigate all such allegations and bring those responsible to justice.
Caste remains a powerful determinant of social status in India, shaping access to resources, education and opportunity. The millennia-old social hierarchy divides Hindus by function and social standing.
CERD, a committee of 18 independent rights experts, monitors adherence to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination by its 182 member countries.
Under the convention, which came into force in 1969, countries must eliminate racial discrimination, eradicate practices of segregation and guarantee equality before the law.
India appeared for review before CERD earlier this month, for the first time since 2007, with Solicitor General Tushar Mehta leading its delegation.
The committee highlighted an increase in law enforcement operations targeting Rohingya, Bengali-speaking Muslims, migrants and asylum seekers.
It said police stops and identity checks involving racial profiling had reportedly resulted in arbitrary arrest and detention without due process, as well as torture and mistreatment.
The committee also voiced concerns about deportations and forced returns of people needing international protection.
It urged India to “urgently address discrimination, hate speech and hate crimes” against such groups, protect their rights, and refrain from collective expulsions.
CERD’s opinions and recommendations are non-binding, but carry reputational weight.
In a statement, India’s mission said that during the review, its delegation “highlighted our pluralism; diversity; scale and complexity; constitutional and legal framework and safeguards ... as we continue our journey towards ensuring equality, dignity and opportunity for all Indians.”

Colombia cracks down on immigration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:40:36 UTC
01:40:36 KST

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has promised to deport thousands of migrants who are in the country without residence permits, mainly Venezuelans, as he attempts to make significant changes to the nation’s immigration policies that he says will reduce crime.
De la Espriella, who was sworn into office three weeks ago, said that he would order the national immigration service to conduct raids with Colombian police as early as this week.
He announced the new policy in a video released on Sunday night in his X account where he spoke of multiple measures to reduce crime and confront criminal groups.
Photo: Bloomberg
The ultraconservative leader, who is closely aligned with US President Donald Trump, said that law enforcement would first target migrants who are “committing crimes” and then, those who are living in the country without regular status.
“I will not accept any illegal immigrants, wherever they come from,” De la Espriella said in the video. “They will have to leave and be deported. It is a political decision I am taking responsibility for.”
Most migrants living in Colombia come from Venezuela, a nation that lost about one-fifth of its population over the past decade as Venezuelans fled a repressive regime that oversaw years of economic turmoil, and a 75 percent contraction in the nation’s GDP.
As of this month, about 2.8 million Venezuelans were living in Colombia, UN data showed, making it the largest Venezuelan diaspora. Last month, the national immigration service said it had granted temporary residence permits to about 2.3 million Venezuelans under a scheme rolled out in 2021 by then-Colombian president Ivan Duque during the peak of Venezuela’s immigration crisis.
De la Espriella’s effort to deport migrants who have no regular status marks a major shift for Colombia, which had long worked to protect incoming Venezuelans and grant them a pathway toward permanent residency.
Ana Karina Garcia, director of Juntos Se Puede, an organization that helps Venezuelan migrants in Colombia, said that the Colombian government stopped handing out new temporary residency permits three years ago. She said that De la Espriella’s administration should expand pathways to legal residency, instead of punishing people who cannot obtain residency permits.
“We understand that the president wants to protect Colombians,” she said. “But there is no need to protect them from migrants. It has been proven that foreigners do not commit crimes at greater rates” than the local population.
Arles Pereda, the president of an association that represents Venezuelans in Bogota, said the announcement worried him, because new groups of Venezuelans displaced by the twin earthquakes that rocked the country in June have been arriving in Colombia to seek opportunities.
“The doors seem to be closing,” Pereda said. “Not just in Colombia, but also in Chile, Peru and Ecuador,” where conservative leaders have also made it harder for Venezuelan migrants to get residency permits.
In a text message, Colombia’s national immigration department, Migracion Colombia, said it is currently without a director. The agency said it would only implement the new policies once a new director is appointed and installed.

Teens return to TikTok after world’s first usage ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:40:35 UTC
01:40:35 KST

Eight months after implementing a ban on under-16s accessing social media services like TikTok, Australia finds its younger users are returning in droves, new data from Qustodio showed.
As of last month, 26 percent of children aged 13 to 15 were on TikTo, just 1 percentage point below the rate prior to Australia’s groundbreaking rules coming into effect, the parental control software maker said.
The rate for children aged 10 to 12 is higher now than before the ban, the data showed.
Photo: AFP
The Australian government has been at the forefront of legislating to prevent underage users from accessing services such as Instagram and Facebook from Meta Platforms Inc and TikTok, owned by China’s ByteDance Ltd. Many argue the services are harmful to young users’ mental health and other countries are following Australia’s example, including New Zealand announcing plans this week.
“What we’ve seen is an immediate drop to a degree, but slowly but surely the numbers have started to increase again to almost equivalent levels” for some services, said Yasmin London, a global online safety expert at Qustodio.
Usage rates for Instagram and Snap Inc’s Snapchat are lower than TikTok, but have also begun to creep up after falling initially when the ban came into effect in December last year, the data showed.
Children could be obfuscating their ages, using virtual private networks that disguise their locations, or simply not encountering effective age checks on platforms, London said.
“In the end, kids want access because they want to be connected just like the rest of us,” she said.
The new data underscore concerns about the effectiveness of Australia’s age controls and Big Tech’s compliance with them. Regulators, tech firms and parents around the world are studying Australia’s experience as more than two dozen governments have implemented or are seeking to implement similar measures.
Australia is being “closely watched,” and has come to symbolize the issue of social media restrictions, said Minda Smiley, a senior analyst at Emarketer focused on social media.
“Even as other countries follow suit, I think a lot of people are paying particular attention to Australia and hoping it can provide some sort of blueprint,” she said.
The new data, which Qustodio said may understate the issue as it is collected only from devices that have its parental oversight software installed, also emerges as social media giants face numerous lawsuits in the US alleging they are harming their young users by making their platforms hard to resist.
Barcelona-based Qustodio’s research was based on anonymized information from 19,000 Australian families. It measured the percentage of children who had unblocked access to the apps and used them at least once per month for more than five consecutive minutes.
One service seeing an increase in usage is Meta’s WhatsApp, which is not subject to the government’s restrictions. About 27 percent of children aged 13 to 15 were on the messaging platform prior to the ban compared with 36 percent now.
TikTok, Snap and Meta did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The Australian government in June said the social media companies were not doing enough to comply with the age restriction, which mandates that the firms take reasonable steps to keep under-16s off or face fines. It pledged to double the maximum penalty for violations to A$99 million (US$71 million) and to give the country’s online safety watchdog extra enforcement powers. No social media platform has been fined for breaching the ban.
Australia’s online safety regulator, known as eSafety, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the new data.
Governments looking for clues as to whether or not Australia’s rules are working will likely take the long view, Smiley said.
“It’s still early enough in the game that I think Australia will keep pressing,” she said. “The ban has come at a time when social media is under more scrutiny than ever, so I’d say they have public sentiment on their side.”

Teachers’ safety and inclusion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:40:35 UTC
01:40:35 KST

A disturbing incident in Taichung this month has raised difficult questions about safety, inclusion and responsibility in schools. A junior high-school teacher was seriously injured after a student reportedly broke a broom and attacked her with the handle. The severity of her injuries generated concern among teachers and the wider public.
However, incidents such as this require careful interpretation. They should not be used to suggest that students with disabilities, autism or other forms of neurodivergence are inherently dangerous. They are not. Nor should a single act of violence become an argument for retreating from inclusive education.
The more important question is whether schools are being given the resources necessary to make inclusion work well for everyone.
Inclusive education rests on an important principle: Students should not be excluded simply because they learn, communicate, behave or regulate emotions differently.
However, inclusion cannot mean merely placing students with diverse needs in a standard classroom and expecting one teacher to manage every challenge that arises.
True inclusion requires support, which might include special-education professionals, classroom aides, behavioral specialists, counselors, careful transition planning between schools, collaboration with families and clear procedures for responding when a situation begins to escalate. Some students might require more intensive assistance. Recognizing such needs does not diminish their dignity. On the contrary, providing appropriate support allows them to participate more successfully in school life.
Teacher safety is part of this equation. Discussions of teacher well-being often focus on stress management, resilience or work-life balance. Teachers also need to know that they are safe, that administrators will support them and that help will arrive when a difficult situation exceeds what one classroom teacher can manage.
No amount of mindfulness training can compensate for an environment in which teachers feel they are facing serious behavioral crises alone.
Thousands of Japanese public-school teachers take mental-health leave each year, and government reports identify student guidance, workplace relationships and administrative responsibilities among the pressures. These figures should not be interpreted as evidence that students are responsible for teachers’ mental-health difficulties. When multiple responsibilities accumulate in schools for long periods, teachers can become the point where those pressures converge.
This is a challenge across East Asia. Schools are expected to respond not only to academic needs, but also to social isolation, family stress, mental-health problems, bullying, behavioral difficulties, disability, poverty and other concerns. When governments expand what schools are expected to do without expanding the professional support, teachers can become society’s shock absorber. That is not fair to teachers or good for students.
Taiwan should resist framing the debate as a choice between students’ rights and teachers’ rights. Students have a right to dignity, education and protection from exclusion. Teachers and classmates also have a right to learn and work in a safe environment.
Respect for neurological difference does not mean assuming that every student should receive identical support. Neurodiversity asks us to recognize variation in how people think, communicate and experience. An inclusive response takes those differences seriously enough to provide environments in which all students can succeed.
Sometimes that requires additional personnel. Sometimes it requires behavioral expertise, smaller instructional settings for part of the day, structured transition plans or cooperation among educators, families and mental-health professionals. Such measures make meaningful inclusion possible.
The Taichung incident should not be used in an argument against neurodivergent students or special education. It should prompt an institutional question: Are schools providing enough support before a crisis occurs?
A sound policy principle would be simple: No student or teacher should be left alone with risks that the system can anticipate.
Inclusion without adequate support is not genuine inclusion. It shifts institutional responsibility onto individuals — and eventually everyone in the classroom bears the consequences.
Toshiaki Sasao is a professor emeritus of psychology at International Christian University in Tokyo whose work focuses on community psychology, teacher well-being, inclusion and peace psychology.
The Iran and Ukraine wars are rewriting modern military strategy. These conflicts are demonstrating that a less conventionally powerful state, by leveraging asymmetric capabilities, can impose major costs on an aggressor and fundamentally reshape the outcome of conflict. Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. Taiwan cannot become a bigger wolf than China, but it can ensure that

US set for largest visa revocation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:40:33 UTC
01:40:33 KST

US President Donald Trump’s administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the US.
If it happens, the move would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history and would likely face legal challenges.
Unless challenged or revised, the US Department of State is expected to announce in the coming weeks the revocation of so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and this year whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, according to State Department documents obtained by The Associated Press and two US officials.
Photo: AP
The action will be taken in coordination with the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
“We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said.
He declined to comment on the number of visas that might be revoked, saying “as the process will be ongoing, the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis.”
The revocations would not necessarily result in their immediate deportation, the officials said.
Most of those with asylum cases currently pending would be recategorized, but would lose their status as business or tourism travelers, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the revocations are not final yet.
Since Trump took office for his second term last year, his administration has steadily ramped up restrictions on visa applicants — demanding more information about their social media histories, requiring the posting of expensive bonds for the processing of visas, and outright banning the issuance of visas to citizens of certain countries.
In a social media post on Monday, US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau called out people who he said try to use tourist and business visas to get into the US and then apply for asylum.
“People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims,” Landau wrote on X. “Asylum isn’t supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law,” he said.
Landau cited the case of a Colombian citizen who came to the US in 2015 on a tourist visa and then applied for asylum.
B1 visas are generally issued for business trips and B2 visas are generally issued for tourism, family visits or medical care. It was not immediately clear from the documents or the officials how many of these visa holders are seeking or have sought asylum in the US and would be affected by the revocations.
Current applicants for B1 and B2 visas are asked to affirm that they will not apply for asylum in the US and prove that they intend to return to their home countries.
In the past 18 months, the State Department has revoked about 175,000 visas for people who have been convicted or accused of crimes ranging from drunken driving to rape and robbery, as well as for people who have spoken out publicly against US policies, particularly in the Middle East.
The administration has also moved to crack down on so-called birth tourism, a practice the administration claims is used by foreign pregnant women to come to the US to give birth so that their child will benefit from birthright citizenship.
Trump has tried several times to end birthright citizenship, but those challenges have been rejected by courts, including the Supreme Court.
The State Department documents obtained by the AP suggest screening of current B1 and B2 visa holders began after the State Department received information about asylum requests from the US Citizenship and Immigration Services.

AM Intelligence, part of the group that owns renewable energy producer Greenko Group PLC, has placed a binding order under an US$8 billion project, part of a broader plan to set up 1GW of computing capacity. Its Hyderabad facility is meant to run trillion-parameter AI models and next-generation agentic AI applications.
The group would offer computing capacity at competitive prices to customers in India, the US, Finland and Malaysia, Mahesh Kolli, founder and president of Greenko Group, said in a video interview.
The initial capacity has already been purchased by a US customer, Kolli said, declining to identify the buyer because of a non-disclosure agreement.
Customers are “hunting desperately” for capacity, he said, adding that India faces few operational constraints because undersea cables allow US companies to use AI compute with latency of about 300 milliseconds.
AM Intelligence’s advantage lies in the group’s access to low-cost renewable power, Kolli said.
“In global token economics, energy prices play a huge part,” he said. “We’re one of the lowest-cost AI computation infrastructure players globally.”
The group plans to fund its proposed buildout with a mix of debt and equity.
“Capex to cash flow in this business is very short,” Kolli said. “We can partly support it via our balance sheet, plus we have experience tapping the bond market.”
The company aims to reach 5GW of data center capacity by 2030 across India, Europe and elsewhere.
“The electron-to-token opportunity allows us to take this capability further, converting power infrastructure into frontier AI compute at scale,” AM Group chairman Anil Chalamalasetty said.

The Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) yesterday called on China to stop using culture to wage political warfare, after Taipei City Councilor Lin Liang-chun (林亮君) called out the group Small Yi Hanfu (小義子漢服) for using Taipei’s Confucius Temple to film a video with strong “united front” rhetoric.
The group in June last year won a bid to rent part of the temple’s Minglun Hall for NT$15,000 per month to promote Confucianism and traditional Han clothing styles, Lin said.
The group shot a video featuring the temple during last year’s Dragon Boat Festival promoting this year’s cross-strait Han traditional clothing event, which contained significant “united front” language, Lin said.
Photo courtesy of Taipei City Councilor Lin Liang-chun
The group traveled to Xiamen on a journey “seeking their roots” and was interviewed by state-affiliated television network Xiamen Star (廈門衛視), , Lin said, adding that it planned to hold a “Taiwan Hanfu Festival” near the Red House in Taipei’s Ximending (西門町) area in November.
MAC Deputy Minister Shen Yu-chung (沈有忠) yesterday said that as elections draw near, China is stepping up its efforts to interfere with similar events.
Taiwan’s government has not changed its stance, and maintains that such events should be depoliticized and conducted in a healthy and orderly manner, Shen said.
Commenting on the Confucius Temple incident, Shen said that culture and artifacts should be neutral, adding that Taiwan is a culturally diverse nation, and such activities should not become a tool for political ideology.
Beijing uses institutions such as the Confucius Institute or traditional Han clothing to spread its political message, which is antithetical to the inclusiveness of Chinese culture, Shen said.
Taiwan would refute any act by the Chinese Communist Party to use culture as the basis of political interference, Shen said.
The greatest difference between China and Taiwan is their political systems, not their culture and language, Shen said, adding that as long as China attempts to maintain its authoritarian rule, it would be difficult to promote cross-strait dialogue.

Taichung ad budget should be scrutinized
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:40:27 UTC
01:40:27 KST

The Taichung City Government had a marketing and promotional budget of NT$14 million (US$439,312) for the Taichung Hot Pot and Grill Festival this year. The contract was awarded to China Television Company (CTV), headed by Mayor Lu Shiow-yen’s (盧秀燕) younger sister, Lu Hsiu-fang (盧秀芳).
Upon entering Taichung City Hall, one is met not with the culinary specialties of the city’s local establishments, but with a giant portrait of the mayor in an apron with her arms spread wide.
This has raised concerns over conflicts of interest and highlighted how public funds can be commandeered for publicity purposes.
The billboard hanging in the city government lobby reflects the dual decline of public aesthetics and political self-restraint during the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) eight years in power in Taichung. During last year’s Taichung Jazz Festival, promotional materials were similarly filled with her own image, and the mayor even took to the stage to play conga drums on opening night, drawing criticism that she was stealing the spotlight from the event itself.
The Hot Pot and Grill Festival appears to have followed the same pattern. Millions of dollars have been spent on the campaign, producing not real images of local businesses and authentic culture, but close-ups of the mayor reminiscent of the personality cults of a bygone era. This not only undercuts civic pride and treats public funds as capital for political showmanship, but also shows contempt for taxpayers and local industries.
The Act on Recusal of Public Servants Due to Conflicts of Interest (公職人員利益衝突迴避法) was designed to prevent situations that could invite suspicion of impropriety or dubious transfers of benefits.
Although the city government has attempted to clear its name by citing the “open selection procedure” under the Government Procurement Act (政府採購法), that tens of millions in public funds went to a media company run by a first-degree relative of the mayor should itself warrant rigorous scrutiny.
There should be transparency around how the selection committee was formed, whether the mayor’s relationship with CTV’s chair was fully disclosed, and whether assessments were substantively influenced — these concerns cannot be dismissed with vague claims that the process was compliant.
Most perplexing is the double standard in some sectors of public opinion. In the past, when central government agencies or state-owned enterprises spent large sums on brand identity projects or image makeovers, they were subjected to intense scrutiny by opposition parties and accused of wasting public funds. Yet now, when a local government splashes out on a multimillion-dollar contract awarded to a company headed by the mayor’s younger sister — and the resulting promotional materials pay no heed to urban aesthetics with their enormous portrait of the mayor — those who once led the charge in chastising such practices have fallen silent.
The true protagonists of a city food festival are local restaurants and grassroots culture. Using vast sums of public money to promote a politician inverts priorities and erodes public trust in clean and competent governance. If local governments cannot draw a clear line between public-sector promotion and personal political branding in the awarding of marketing budgets, it is taxpayer money that is ultimately serving a person’s political ends.
Yang Chih-chiang is a teacher.

====================================================================================================

Three ways AI could change the course of humanity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:40:25 UTC
01:40:25 KST

Over the long sweep of history, three forces have driven humanity’s greatest transformations, for good and ill: disease, war and economic growth. By reducing costs and increasing the availability and productivity of a vast array of goods and services, artificial intelligence (AI) could have a profound impact on all three.
History is strewn with plagues and pandemics that altered the trajectory of human population growth. The Black Death, for example, killed 75 million to 200 million people across Europe, Asia, the Middle East and North Africa between 1346 and 1353.
Thanks to technological advances and medical innovations that helped prolong life expectancy and reduce infant mortality, the global population has grown from one billion in 1804 to two billion in 1927 to more than eight billion today. At the same time, the advent of effective contraceptives has helped contain population growth.
Illustration: mountain people
AI could accelerate this progress, improving the quality and quantity of human life through preventive diagnostics, faster drug discovery and more personalized medical care. It could reduce the human and economic costs of noncommunicable diseases such as cancer and neurodegenerative brain disorders, including Alzheimer’s. It could enable faster responses to outbreaks of communicable diseases by predicting where viruses are likely to spread and how mutations might unfold. AI is already being used to combat antimicrobial resistance.
AI could drastically reduce healthcare costs, which have been largely resistant to technological advances. As a 2022 American Enterprise Institute chart showed, US hospital-service costs rose more than those of all other goods and services over the past quarter-century.
War is the second force that has repeatedly changed the course of human history. An estimated 70 million to 85 million people died during World War II, almost 30 million of them in the Soviet Union. These losses had far-reaching demographic and economic consequences for the USSR, especially since so many of those killed were working-age men. Armed conflicts destroy productive capacity, disrupt everyday life and deter the investments needed to stimulate economic growth.
Technological advances have made war far more destructive. World War I was the first large-scale mechanized conflict involving mass-produced guns, tanks and aircraft. WWII, in turn, catalyzed a massive military-industrial buildout, pulling the US economy out of the Great Depression and fueling decades of postwar growth.
AI is ushering in a new era of technology-driven conflict as countries increasingly rely on drones and autonomous weapons. In Ukraine, drones account for 70 to 80 percent of battlefield casualties. AI-powered systems are playing a growing role in the Iran war, from accelerating minesweeping in the Strait of Hormuz to tracking submarines and gathering intelligence.
The third major driver of historical change is economic upheaval. In the aftermath of WWI, hyperinflation devastated the German economy, setting the stage for the rise of Nazism. Similarly, the 1929 stock-market crash — together with 1930s banking panics and the Dust Bowl — plunged millions of Americans into poverty, with hardscrabble encampments of displaced people springing up across the US.
Economic transformations can bring enormous gains, even as they create disruption and despair. The Industrial Revolution unleashed rapid productivity growth, raised living standards, reconfigured societies and propelled human development to new heights.
Much of this was the result of rapid industrialization and mechanization, which continued to redefine the relationship between capital and labor well into the 20th century as workers moved from agriculture to manufacturing and then into the services sector. In the US, agriculture’s share of employment fell from more than 40 percent at the turn of the 20th century to less than 2 percent today.
Early studies say that AI could supercharge productivity, particularly in knowledge-based industries, although evidence of its direct contribution to economic growth remains inconclusive. A 2018 McKinsey Global Institute report estimated that AI could add roughly US$13 trillion to global GDP by 2030, while a 2023 McKinsey report projected that generative AI could deliver US$2.6 to US$4.4 trillion in economic value annually.
AI’s destructive potential is just as great. Warnings of an AI-driven “jobocalypse” have become increasingly common in the past few years, with Silicon Valley venture capitalist Vinod Khosla predicting that AI would be capable of performing 80 percent of jobs by the early 2030s, rendering traditional employment obsolete.
Whether or not these grim predictions prove accurate, widespread job displacement could upend the structure of economies and societies. It could greatly expand the role of the state, as governments face growing pressure to provide income support.
To be sure, the AI super cycle is in its early stages. Even now, it seems inevitable that technology could radically change how we combat disease, fight wars, foster economic growth and change how we understand what sets humanity apart.
Dambisa Moyo, an international economist, is the author of Edge of Chaos: Why Democracy Is Failing to Deliver Economic Growth - and How to Fix It.

Taiwan’s semiconductor material suppliers are ushering in a new phase and seeking greater self-sufficiency in the age of artificial intelligence (AI), as key materials play a critical role in advancing chip manufacturing technology.
Amid persistent geopolitical risks and trade-policy uncertainty, boosting local supply chain resilience has become a necessity. Taiwan was the world’s biggest semiconductor materials market for 16 consecutive years, with sales of US$21.7 billion last year, SEMI statistics show.
SEMI Taiwan on Friday last week launched the SEMI Taiwan Materials Alliance. Local semiconductor companies have relied heavily on imported raw materials due to the time and financial resources needed to develop critical materials such as specialty chemicals, gases and photoresists.
There is a “golden opportunity” for Taiwanese companies to secure a foothold in the semiconductor materials market, given that the AI boom is increasing semiconductor demand, Taiwan Chemical Industry Association chairman and Everlight Chemical Industrial president Chen Wei-wang (陳偉望) said at the launch.
More than 30 domestic and foreign companies have joined the alliance, including ASE Technology, GlobalWafers and its affiliate Taiwan Speciality Chemicals, LCY Chemical, Sunlit Fluo and Chemical, and others.
The alliance aims to enhance supply chain resilience, SEMI Taiwan said.
Most alliance members are relatively small companies, but are rising to prominence. For example, LCY and Sunlit, two privately owned companies that are smaller than their global rivals, have become key suppliers of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC), taking advantage of their geographic proximity, technology upgrades and operational agility. The companies say they can quickly respond to customer requests, sometimes just in a few hours, through on-site support. It can take two to three days for foreign competitors to respond to customer issues, they say.
Local companies face disadvantages such as scale disadvantage, limited intellectual property patents and steep market entry thresholds. The alliance can help them create strategic collaborations to increase their technical capabilities and overcome resource constraints. The short-term goal for such companies should not be to replace their global rivals, but to play a supplementary role or be an alternative to first-tier suppliers.
Leading semiconductor material suppliers such as Japan’s JSR and Shin-Etsu Chemical, and Germany’s Merck, are long-standing partners of TSMC and other major players in the business. Those material suppliers have immense revenue scales and strong patent portfolios. They cannot be displaced in the short term.
A good starting point for them could be supplying semiconductor material consumables or investing in selective materials, an industry expert said.
Taiwanese companies in the supply chain have already started making money from the AI boom, and they should allocate more resources to developing key next-generation materials, in other words, spend more on research and development, equipment and talent, ASE vice president Hiro Huang (黃義從) said.
Building close partnerships with international suppliers and assisting them in producing semiconductor materials in Taiwan is another option, Huang said.
In addition, some companies might consider focusing on something less mainstream such as niche material development. As leading-edge logic enters the Angstrom era and unconventional silicon sealing approaches physical limits, chipmakers are exploring new transistor architectures and materials. Separately, wide-bandgap materials are replacing silicon in some power-electronics applications.
Another area Taiwanese companies should eye is key materials used in advanced packaging, where emerging technologies are creating new opportunities for suppliers. With diminishing economic returns from geometric IC shrinking, advanced packaging is becoming critical in semiconductor evolution and one of the most sought-after technologies. Taiwanese companies are in an advantageous position to gain market share. They could benefit from local chipmakers’ aggressive expansions.
The AI boom is expected to last for at least a few more years, and the nation’s semiconductor material suppliers should capitalize on this opportunity to build core technological strengths and prepare for next-wave growth.
The Iran and Ukraine wars are rewriting modern military strategy. These conflicts are demonstrating that a less conventionally powerful state, by leveraging asymmetric capabilities, can impose major costs on an aggressor and fundamentally reshape the outcome of conflict. Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. EU approvals, easier sterilisation rules to speed device access
Unknown

Faster access to some newer medical devices. (Representative image)
NEW DELHI: Patients in India could get faster access to some newer medical devices already approved in the European Union, with the government expanding its list of trusted foreign regulatory jurisdictions while also easing licensing requirements for manufacturers outsourcing sterilisation.The Health Ministry has amended the Medical Devices Rules, 2017 to include the European Union among jurisdictions recognised for waiver of clinical investigation requirements for eligible medical devices that do not have a predicate device in India. The list earlier included the US, UK, Australia, Canada and Japan.The change means eligible devices that have already received regulatory approval in the EU can potentially avoid a fresh clinical investigation in India, reducing the time and regulatory steps required before they can be made available to patients. The waiver remains subject to the conditions prescribed under the rules.The government said the move would reduce regulatory timelines for manufacturers and importers and facilitate faster availability of advanced medical technologies in India. The addition of the EU also brings India’s medical-device regulatory framework closer to international regulatory practices.Separately, manufacturers outsourcing sterilisation to a facility with a valid licence will no longer need a separate loan licence, reducing paperwork, compliance costs and delays.
However, they will still have to print the sterilisation facility’s licence number on the device label, with six months to comply. The labelling requirement had drawn industry concerns over added compliance burden and possible export delays.
The government has also introduced a standard fee schedule for testing and evaluation of medical devices. The new charges include Rs 5,000 for implantation tests, Rs 2,000 for sterility testing, Rs 1,000 for syringes and needles and Rs 3,000 for surgical sutures. Testing fees for condoms and intrauterine devices have been fixed at Rs 2,500 each.For tests not specified in the schedule, the charges will be decided by the concerned laboratory or medical device testing officer. The prescribed fees will automatically rise by 5% annually.The three changes are aimed at cutting regulatory duplication, making compliance costs more predictable and speeding up access to medical devices while retaining requirements for quality, safety and traceability. The sterilisation and testing-fee amendments were notified as the Medical Devices (Second Amendment) Rules, 2026.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Wafer testing equipment supplier Hermes Testing Solutions Inc (漢民測試) yesterday said revenue from thermal management modules would double next year as heat dissipation becomes increasingly critical for advanced and artificial intelligence (AI) chips.
The company expects wider adoption of thermal management modules for the production of AI graphics processing units (GPUs) this year, which would extend to AI accelerators such as tensor processing units (TPUs) and central processing units (CPUs) next year.
“We are preparing materials [for the production of thermal management modules] through the first half of next year,” Hermes president Steven Wang (王子建) told a news conference in Taipei.
Photo: Lisa Wang, Taipei Times
“This year, it is already used in GPU [production]. Next year, the usage may be extended to TPU, or CPU. This is a trend,” Wang said.
Thermal management is critical for high-end wafer testing primarily because advanced silicon nodes and 3D stacking cause extreme power density that alters electrical characteristics and can destroy the wafer during probing.
Hermes’ thermal management modules use air cooling to lower temperatures of probes during testing and maintain test stability.
The equipment contributed more than 30 percent to Hermes’ total revenue in the first half of this year and is expected to be 30 percent next year, Wang said.
In addition to thermal management modules, Hermes is also pushing for adoption of its new testing equipment and services used in advanced chip-on-wafer-on-substrate packaging, wafer bumping and even for upcoming panel-level packaging on 310x310mm panels, he said.
The company also aims to tap into high-speed DRAM testing sockets, Wang said.
Hermes is collaborating with FiconTEC Service GmbH to supply testing equipment used in the manufacturing process of copackaged optics, Wang added.
The new products are to contribute meaningful revenue from 2028 or 2029, Wang said.
Hermes’ revenue skyrocketed 128.18 percent to NT$2.67 billion (US$83.78 million) in the first seven months of this year from the same period last year, surpassing the NT$2.42 billion it made in the whole of last year.
Semiconductor equipment and customized products contributed more than 50 percent of the company’s revenue, it said.
Hermes attributed the growth to increased demand for wafer testing services for AI and high-performance computing applications.
In the first half of this year, net profit soared 390.76 percent to NT$584 million from NT$119 million in the same period last year.
Earnings per share advanced to NT$21.5 from NT$5.02, while gross margin improved to 54.88 percent from 46.05 percent.
SinoPac Securities Investment Service Corp (永豐投顧), an underwriter of Hermes’ initial public offering on the Taipei Exchange next month, forecast the company's revenue to surge about 82 percent to NT$9.04 billion next year from NT$4.96 billion this year.

Sanctions or missiles? Why Gulf may not relish Trump’s new Iran approach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:39:24 UTC
01:39:24 KST

Sanctions or missiles? How Gulf will view Trump’s new Iran approach
As Washington pressures Tehran, Gulf states weigh sanctions against the risk of escalation.
Nearly six months since the United States and Israel launched the first missiles in their war on Iran, Washington is pivoting to a strategy of tougher sanctions and economic isolation in a bid to force Tehran to accept its terms for a peace deal.
On Monday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced “Operation Economic Outcast”, targeting Tehran’s remaining sources of revenue while also threatening penalties against those who continue doing business with Iran.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4What to expect in elections in South Carolina, Georgia and Oklahoma
- list 2 of 4Israeli forces raid UNRWA training centre in occupied East Jerusalem
- list 3 of 4‘We can’t breathe’: Indonesians battle wildfire haze
- list 4 of 4Two killed, refinery on fire in Russia’s Krasnodar after drone attack
Bessent described the latest wave of sanctions as “the single greatest financial offensive ever” against Iran, and warned that banks and businesses would share in Iran’s isolation if they refuse to cooperate.
“No one is above the reach of US sanctions,” he told reporters.
Gulf states have repeatedly found themselves caught in the crosshairs during the US-Iran war as Iran has targeted US military assets and infrastructure in neighbouring countries.
Economic pressure may appear preferable to another round of US and Israeli missile strikes. But analysts warn the strategy carries its own risks, with Iran potentially responding to mounting economic pressure by targeting more US assets and energy infrastructure across the region.
Iran’s Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei said last week that if “any countries surrounding Iran join the Americans in their economic war, not a drop of oil will leave the Persian Gulf and the strait of Hormuz”.
In peacetime, one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas is shipped by Gulf producers through the critical waterway, which has become the main bone of contention in the war since Iran effectively closed it to shipping at the start of the war.
Iran’s stance leaves Washington’s Gulf allies facing an uncomfortable paradox: the US military presence helps protect them from Iranian missiles and drones, but also makes their territories potential targets.
Now, because of their security relationship with the United States, they are under increasing pressure to cut economic ties with Iran, which could provoke further Iranian retaliation and risk drawing them deeper into the conflict, experts say.
While the United Arab Emirates (UAE) moved last week to decisively cut economic ties with Iran, other Gulf countries such as Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Oman may have different strategic calculations to make. Analysts say they have strong incentives to preserve diplomatic channels with Tehran and to push for a deal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
From military offensive to ‘economic D-Day’
Bessent described the US measures aimed at isolating Iran as “economic D-Day”.
While the US and other countries have sanctioned Iran’s oil and financial sectors for decades, the latest wave will target five of Iran’s most important remaining economic lifelines: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping.
Bessent also said Tehran’s trading partners are at risk of secondary sanctions if they continue helping turn Iranian oil into revenue. The Treasury imposed specific sanctions on 60 entities, vessels and individuals across the UAE, Hong Kong, China, Singapore and Switzerland, accusing them of facilitating Iranian trade.
But Iranian political analyst Mostafa Khoshcheschm dismissed the announcement as a “political show” intended to intimidate Iran’s neighbours.
He compared the campaign with Trump’s “maximum pressure” policy during his first term as US president, which was aimed at forcing Iran to renegotiate the US President Barack Obama-era Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) on its nuclear programme. That, Khoshcheschm noted, failed – ending with Trump withdrawing the US from the agreement instead in 2018.
The latest measures, the analyst argued, are “even weaker than that”.
The ramped-up emphasis on economic pressure comes as months of war have failed to produce a decisive outcome for the US, contrary to Trump’s indications at the start of the war that it would last for a matter of weeks. Meanwhile, US media reports that supplies of missiles and air defence interceptors in the Middle East may be running low – vehemently denied by the Trump administration – have incentivised Washington to pursue other means of pressuring Tehran, observers say.
The disruption to energy exports in the Strait of Hormuz has sent gas prices soaring in the US, making the war even more unpopular at home, even though efforts to establish alternative shipping routes have helped mitigate some of the economic fallout, experts say.
Despite this, Washington appears to believe the economic balance is in its favour. Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the US-based Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, said Washington calculates that rerouting maritime traffic through Oman – combined with a wider shift away from Gulf oil – has reduced the effectiveness of Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz, while the US blockade has sharply constrained Tehran’s ability to sell its oil.
“The result, in Washington’s view, is a status quo that imposes greater costs on Iran than on the United States,” Parsi told Al Jazeera.
That calculation, he said, has led Trump to believe Washington can afford to wait Tehran out and that, for the first time since the war began, “time is working in America’s favour”.
But the effectiveness of this strategy may ultimately depend on whether major economies such as China, India and Russia believe Washington is prepared to impose meaningful penalties on them for continuing to trade with Iran.
Washington’s calculation may also be less comfortable for its Gulf allies. If the US believes it can withstand a prolonged economic war with Iran, it may be more willing to tolerate continued disruption in the Strait of Hormuz – a far more damaging prospect for Gulf economies heavily dependent on energy exports through the waterway.
That leaves Gulf states to calculate just how far they are willing to follow Washington’s economic campaign, particularly if doing so risks prolonging the confrontation with Tehran.
UAE moves first
The UAE has already moved further than its Gulf neighbours, with Abu Dhabi saying last week it was ending trade with Iran.
Miad Maleki, an Iran analyst at the pro-Israel think tank the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said a comprehensive UAE financial and trade cutoff, if enforced, “may be the most consequential economic action of this war for Iran”, potentially exceeding the impact of the US embargo.
That’s because Dubai has long played an important role in Iran’s access to foreign currency, while the UAE has been Iran’s greatest source of imports even during the war.
Ultimately, though, the UAE has been hardest hit by Iran during the war with the US. It is also one of the few signatories to the US-led Abraham Accords, which seek to normalise relations between Israel and Arab states.
Simon Mabon, professor of international relations at Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera the UAE’s position therefore reflects both its experience of Iranian attacks during the conflict and its increasingly close security relationship with Washington and Israel.
“The Emiratis are furious with Iran and they have taken a beating from Iran over the last few months,” Mabon told Al Jazeera. But he described the UAE as an “outlier” in the Gulf, adding he does not expect Saudi Arabia, Qatar or Oman to follow its lead.
‘Formidable escalatory options’
Then there is the likely response from Iran.
Additional economic pressure may not produce the outcome Washington wants, analysts say.
“The pattern that we have seen so far is that when faced with either surrender or escalation, the Iranians escalate,” Parsi said.
With Bessent’s campaign aimed at forcing Tehran to capitulate or risk economic collapse, Parsi said escalation is “the most likely response” if the sanctions begin seriously hurting Iran, which retains “formidable escalatory options”.
That prospect is concerning for neighbours such as Qatar, where continued disruption to the Strait of Hormuz as well as strikes on its LNG operations have already inflicted economic pain. While alternative routes have allowed some oil exports to bypass the waterway, liquefied natural gas and many petrochemical products are harder to reroute.
Qatar has also supported mediation efforts and shares a vast gas field with Iran, giving Doha further incentive to preserve a functioning relationship with its neighbour.
Oman has its own reasons for resisting pressure to isolate Iran. Its longstanding role as an intermediary between Tehran and Washington depends on maintaining diplomatic channels with both sides. For one, it is locked in direct talks with Iran over the future management of the Strait of Hormuz.
Rashid al-Mohannad, vice president of the Doha-based Center for International Policy Research, said recent diplomatic activity, including a visit to Tehran by Oman’s foreign minister, “shows that there is a willingness from the mediating parties to try to pull both the US and Iran back to a diplomatic track”.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia has taken a different approach, staying out of the recent mediation efforts while also showing little appetite for ramping up economic pressure on Tehran.
Mabon said that a decade ago, Riyadh might have been expected to follow Washington and Abu Dhabi in imposing tougher measures against Iran. Indeed, at one point the US seemed hopeful it could be persuaded to sign the Abraham Accords.
These days, Saudi has made a credible path towards the formalisation of a Palestinian state a condition for signing, which Israel refuses to accept. Furthermore, the kingdom has indicated an appetite for diversifying its security away from reliance on the US. To this end, it signed the Mecca Pact on mutual defence with Pakistan and Turkiye earlier this month.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has also adopted a more pragmatic approach towards Tehran in recent years, culminating in the restoration of diplomatic relations under a China-brokered agreement in 2023.
Furthermore, while Riyadh may desire a weakened Iran, Mabon said, it is wary of the instability that could accompany the collapse of its government.
Joining Washington’s economic campaign could also further expose Saudi Arabia to attacks from Iran or the Iran-backed Houthis, which it has been fighting in Yemen and which are currently targeting Saudi-linked ships in the Red Sea.
On the horns of a dilemma
Restoring diplomacy between Tehran and Washington – something neither side seems able to do – has become increasingly essential for regional security.
That leaves Gulf capitals with a dilemma they cannot easily escape.
Going along with the US plan for economic pressure may appear preferable to another barrage of missiles. But joining Washington’s campaign could well provoke an Iranian response, raising the prospect of renewed attacks across the Gulf.
Gulf countries will likely continue to push hard for “dialogue and diplomacy” over renewed hostilities or tougher sanctions, which may ultimately be little more than yet another “gateway to further instability from Iran”.

Cash is no longer king in home sales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:38:40 UTC
01:38:40 KST

As the residential real estate market continues to lose steam, competition is weakening, and cash is no longer necessary to win a deal.
The share of cash sales during the first four months of this year was 31.4%, down from 32.3% during the same period a year ago, according to Realtor.com that looks at both new and existing homes. Buyers using mortgages are getting a boost from cooler prices, higher inventory and less confidence among sellers.
Cash buyers are actually dropping out faster than the overall market decline. Total home sales during that same period were down 8.5% year over year, but the number of cash sales fell 11.2%. That coincided with slower price growth. The national median price was up just 0.2% annually, far less than the 1.8% growth in 2025 and well below the 15.4% peak seen in 2021.
"Cash buyers aren't disappearing; they're simply becoming less dominant as the housing market finds its footing," said Hannah Jones, senior economist at Realtor.com, in a release. "More inventory and moderating prices are giving financed buyers more opportunities to compete. Cash still matters, but today its biggest advantage isn't just winning bidding wars. It's also giving sellers confidence that a deal will close quickly and with fewer surprises."
Cash had been seen as necessary in some of the most competitive markets during the height of the pandemic housing boom, and that continued for several years due to historically lean supply and especially after interest rates rose. The share of all-cash sales in July of this year was 26%, down from 31% in July 2025, according to a survey from the National Association of Realtors, looking only at existing homes.
While cash sales are declining nationally, some markets are still seeing gains. Pittsburgh, Austin, Texas, and San Francisco all saw a rise in the share of cash transactions compared with a year ago. This wasn't just because of fewer total sales. It was because the actual number of cash purchases increased.
Dana Bull is a real estate agent in the Boston area and said she is seeing fewer cash buyers in her market, even though Boston is still quite competitive.
"There was certainly a period of time when cash was king, which was right after interest rates climbed and aggressive bidding wars were commonplace. It's been tapering off," said Bull.
She said she is still seeing waived financing terms, and in hotter neighborhoods she recommends that buyers get pre-underwritten versus just preapproved in order to compete against cash.
"I had a client win a bidding war against about 15 offers this spring (financed with pre-underwriting), and my team member just beat out 27 other offers on a house in Arlington (also financed). I don't think this would have happened in 2022-2025 during the cash craze," said Bull.

The Military Committee meets at the level of chiefs of defense twice a year, in January and May, at NATO Headquarters in Brussels. In addition, once a year, one of the Allies hosts the Military Committee Conference, bringing together all 32 chiefs of defense. Other extraordinary meetings may also be convened during the year when deemed necessary.
The Military Committee meets to discuss NATO operations, missions, exercises, capabilities and other issues. Its main role is to provide the North Atlantic Council with unrestricted consensus-based military advice on how best to respond to global security challenges. Its day-to-day work is carried out by the military representatives of Allied countries at NATO Headquarters in Brussels.
As reported, former NATO Military Committee Chair Rob Bauer said Europe should prepare for a prolonged period of instability and that Ukraine should become an integral part of the future European security architecture.

"I find the removal of this photograph deeply troubling because the image documents something that should not be hidden," Abu Srour told The New Arab.

"For me, this photograph represents both the brutality of the destruction and the resilience of Palestinians who continue to play football and live their lives amid the devastation," Abu Srour said.

Former pets. Expert explains how animals end up in the catch system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:34:00 UTC
01:34:00 KST

MINSK, 25 August (BelTA) - Nadezhda Sevruk, Deputy Head of the Housing Department at the Belarusian Housing and Utilities Ministry, spoke about how animals end up in the catch system in a new episode of BelTA’s The Nation Speaks project.
“The majority of animals that end up in the catch system are those that were once abandoned by their owners. Unfortunately, that is the reality. Only a small portion of those caught were born and raised on the streets,” she said.
The law defines both the concept of cruelty to animals and the concept of abandoning them. There are penalties for both. For example, cruelty to an animal that does not result in its death carries a fine of up to 15 base units. Abandoning an animal carries a fine of 10 to 30 base units.
The deputy department head stressed that the provisions of the law are aimed not at punishment, but at fostering a sense of responsibility among citizens. The law is intended to help people recognize their duty as citizens of Belarus or as individuals present in the country to comply with the law.
According to her, microchipping could play a significant role in identifying cases of animal abandonment, but it remains a right of the citizen, not an obligation. Sometimes an animal that is allowed to roam freely ends up in the catch system. In smaller settlements, catchers often know who the animal belongs to. However, sometimes the animal is returned to an owner who does not always realize the consequences of their actions.
“If a request is submitted to 115.bel about an abandoned animal, for example in a yard, and the maintenance worker responsible for that area knows who it belongs to, they contact the owner directly. Our goal is not to punish anyone. If a situation arises where a dog has migrated for some reason, it is caught. Measures are then taken to find the owner. If the owner does not look for their pet and does not contact anyone, this is considered abandonment,” Nadezhda Sevruk said.
“There are cases when housing and utilities workers, in response to citizen complaints or during housing inspections, identify violations related to animal cruelty. Such situations are usually associated with unsanitary conditions. In such cases, housing and utilities workers inform law enforcement agencies, which handle their own investigations, while the housing organization addresses its own responsibilities. If information about cruelty comes from citizens to the housing organization or through 115.bel, it is also forwarded to the internal affairs bodies,” the deputy department head said.

Ukraine's National Bank 3-month deposit certificate yield drops 0.12 pp at second tender
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
19:33:51 EEST
01:33:51 KST

At its second tender for the placement of three-month certificates of deposit (CDs) under the new operational framework, the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) placed the offered UAH 40 billion at a weighted average annual rate of 18.59%, compared with 18.71% at the inaugural tender.
According to NBU data, demand for three-month CDs amounted to about UAH 52.1 billion. Seventeen banks submitted 76 bids at rates ranging from 18.00% to 18.91%, of which the regulator accepted 39, with a maximum annual rate of 18.68%.
"The placement volume is UAH 10 billion higher than at the previous auction, but unmet demand increased to UAH 12.1 billion from UAH 7.1 billion, while the shortfall rose to 23% from 19% previously," Kyiv School of Economics (KSE) Senior Macroeconomist Mykhailo Rebryk wrote on Facebook.
The NBU's effective rate following the second tender fell by another 6 basis points, to 16.39%, Rebryk said.
As reported, starting August 7, 2026, the NBU changed the mechanism for placing three-month certificates of deposit: instead of fully satisfying banks' bids, the regulator conducts interest-rate tenders with an announced volume once every two weeks. This was the first stage in modernizing the operational framework of monetary policy.
As before, banks' ability to place funds in three-month CDs depends on their activity in the retail market for hryvnia term deposits, but the actual placement volume is determined by the outcome of the tender.
